name: Buying to sell on
card: Tomatoes are KSh 2,000 a crate in Limuru and KSh 3,200 in Nairobi this week. Buy a load to sell on?
note: You buy food to sell it somewhere else: traders, wholesalers and market women moving food from where there is plenty to where there is little. You look at the prices in both places, ask or take an offer, agree the price, pay, take the goods and sell them on. It can be one load or a regular run. A price gap is not a profit: you note what you expect to sell for and when, and the card shows what the trip would cost you (transport, fees, food that spoils) and what else the money could do. Money a seller lends you, and any promise to buy only from them, shows as a loan beside their price, with what leaving costs. What you pay on the way (porters, tolls, market fees) goes on the load, so you see what it really cost. Kept apart from Subscribing (food for your own regular use); Waiting to sell for a better price (the gap is in time, not place); Importing food (it crosses a border and takes weeks); Ordering stock (a business orders from a supplier and pays later); and Buying and selling food to use (you buy to use, not to resell). It usually starts when the price in one place is well under the price in another, a farm or market has more food than anyone can sell, or a buyer asks for more than you hold.

examples.card: Buy fish at the landing place to sell inland.
examples.filled: Sardines are GH₵ 300 a box at the Tema quay and GH₵ 420 in Kumasi. Buy a load to sell on?

examples.card: Buy cheap fruit at a wholesale market to sell in another town.
examples.filled: Oranges are cheap at the Valencia wholesale market this week, and dear in Lyon. Buy pallets for your Lyon stall?

examples.card: Buy a truckload where the farm price has fallen.
examples.filled: Onions at Lasalgaon, India, are ₹6 a kilo under the Delhi price. Buy a truckload to sell on?

examples.card: A dawn round bought by voice
examples.filled: You bought at Kaneshie this morning, from four sellers. Do you put it all out now or hold part back?

examples.card: Buy eggs from a woman who walks in.
examples.filled: A woman from Kiambu brought 8 trays of eggs to your Nairobi duka. Take them?

examples.card: Buy rations at a camp gate to sell in town.
examples.filled: Maize meal is cheap at the Kalobeyei gate on distribution day. Buy ten sacks to sell in Lodwar?

examples.card: A dawn round bought by voice
examples.filled: You took 12 crates of cabbage off a farmer's lorry at the road for 900 each. Do you sell the lot at your stall or split it with the stall next to you?

you do this when: You buy food to sell it somewhere else, where it is dear: a trader's load from where it is cheap. Not for your own use, not on account from a supplier.

name: Buying at auction
card: Young cows sold for R$12 a kilo at last Thursday's market, and the market adds 8% to the winning bid. Set your top bid for this Thursday?
note: You bid at a market or exchange for food or animals: traders, butchers and roasters buying fish, livestock, tea, coffee and produce. You ask to take part, bid, the highest bid wins, you pay, and the goods are handed over. The auction records the winning price. The card shows the fees the market adds, when you must pay and collect, and any deposit, because a winning bid binds you. FoodOS can bid for you only within the most you set for each lot, how many lots, and until when. In a sealed auction nobody sees the bids until it closes. You can pull out before the sale. Kept apart from Ordering stock (you order from a supplier at their price); Buying and selling food to use (at the seller's price, not by bidding); Running or answering a tender (an institution asks sellers for sealed quotes); Buying animals (young or breeding animals from a breeder or dealer); and Buying together (others join and share the cost). It usually starts when it is sale day, a list of lots is published, your stock is running low, or last week's prices make a bid look worth it.

examples.card: Bid at a livestock market within a top price you set.
examples.filled: FoodOS can bid for young lambs at Thursday's market in Pelotas, within the most you set. Set your top price?

examples.card: Buy tea, coffee or fish at an auction or exchange.
examples.filled: The Mombasa tea auction has bags for your blend. Bid for them?

examples.card: Bid for fresh fish at the morning auction.
examples.filled: Peterhead fish market sells haddock at 7am, and last week's boxes went for £44 to £52. Bid for boxes for your chip shop?

examples.card: Bid for a high-value catch at a wholesale auction.
examples.filled: Toyosu market opens at 5am and has tuna in. Last week it went for ¥700,000 to ¥900,000. Set your top bid?

examples.card: Writing down what you expect it to give
examples.filled: You have picked a bullock at the Thursday market. What will it give you, in your own words?

examples.card: Writing down what you expect it to give
examples.filled: Four lambs from one dealer. Do you write what you think of them before you buy?

examples.card: Writing down what you expect it to give
examples.filled: You are bidding on a pen of pigs. How will they kill out?

you do this when: You bid at a market or exchange, so the price is found by bidding.

name: Checking one food
card: That looks like kohlrabi. Eat it raw in a slaw, or roast it?
note: You ask what something is: an unknown vegetable, a label, a word on a pack, a menu in another language, how to cook or store a food, or where it came from. You point the camera or ask, FoodOS reads what is in front of you and tells you what matched and what it cannot tell from here, you can ask more, and it is done. What a word on a label means in law comes from your place's rules. When only an expert can say, it says so and what that costs. Checking food is right for you: You ask whether a food suits you or the person you are feeding: allergies, diet, nutrition, values (animal welfare, how far it travelled), an institution's rules, drinks against your limits, or what a dish probably contains. You look at the food or label, FoodOS checks it against what you have told it and says yes, no or why, and you decide. Nothing is sent to anyone. A rule that came from your doctor's signed record counts the same as one you set, and shows its source. Checking food is still good: You ask whether food is still all right to eat, at the fridge or on the shelf. You show or tell FoodOS what you have and how it was kept, and it shows what decides it: how long, how warm, opened or sealed, whether the date is a use-by (safety) or a best-before (quality), and for which foods the risk is real and for whom in your household. It suggests keep, use today or bin, and you decide, with what binning it wastes beside it. When you decide to bin it, that is written down as food lost: what it was and about how much. Kept apart from Choosing between products (picking one of several); Finding a recipe (something to cook); and Planning what to eat (it checks one food, not a week). It usually starts when you meet a food you do not know, a label you cannot read, or a first-time buy; as Checking food is right for you, when you pick up a product, are handed a menu, pack a lunch under school rules, cook for a guest with an allergy, or the maker's new label for something you buy again adds something your diet rules out; as Checking food is still good, when you open the fridge and are unsure, a date has passed, a power cut has happened, or food has been left out.

examples.card: Look up how to cook or store something you do not know.
examples.filled: You have half a cut avocado in your Mexico City kitchen. Ask how to store it so it stays green?

examples.card: Understand what a label really means.
examples.filled: 'Natural' on this pack has no legal meaning; the real ingredients are listed at the back. Read them before you buy?

examples.card: Identify an unknown food from a photo.
examples.filled: A mushroom you found near Tromsø looks like a deadly one, and a photo cannot show the difference. Send it to a local expert?

examples.card: Find out where your food comes from.
examples.filled: Trace the eggs you bought in Cork to the farm that laid them?

examples.card: Understand a menu or sign in another language.
examples.filled: A photo of a Thai street menu: each dish in English, and which have peanuts or fish sauce. Pick a dish without them?

examples.filled: Soil on your lower field is short on nitrogen. Send a sample from the upper field too?

examples.filled: The 'house sauce' at a Jakarta warung is likely to contain egg and peanut; ask to be sure. Ask the cook before you order?

examples.card: Checking food is right for you
examples.filled: This granola has hazelnuts; Noah's nut-free rule says no. Pick the oat one?

examples.card: Check food after a power cut.
examples.filled: You had no power for a day after the storm in Houston. Check what in the freezer is safe to eat?

examples.card: Check an open tin or jar.
examples.filled: Your open tin of tomatoes has been two days in the fridge in Nairobi. Use it, or throw it out?

examples.card: Check a harvest in store.
examples.filled: Your stored potatoes in Nepal are sprouting. Check how far they have gone?

examples.card: Check someone's fridge for out-of-date food.
examples.filled: Gran's fridge in Oslo may hold expired dairy. Check it on Sunday?

examples.card: Tell FoodOS the day you opened it.
examples.filled: You opened the ham on Thursday in your Dublin flat. It is within its 3 days today. Eat it tonight, or freeze it?

examples.filled: Your fridge in Nairobi felt warm this morning and your thermometer reads 9 degrees. Check what in it is safe?

known as: Checking food is right for you
you do this when: You ask one question of one food in front of you: what is it, is it still good, does it suit me; the question is the fact. Not choosing among several, not finding a recipe.

name: Choosing between products
card: Yeo Valley has half the sugar at the same price, and your son ate it last time. Swap it on your list?
note: You have several things in front of you and want to see the differences and pick one: products on a shelf, dishes on a menu, a multipack against a single, or two ways of getting something done (cook or order in, grow or buy, rent a machine or own it, do your own books or hire someone). FoodOS looks at the options and suggests one by the rules you set, and shows the rule ('half the sugar, because you asked for less') and what each option uses. In a shop you act with your own hands, so it shows the suggestion and its reason with no decision to tap; a decision card comes only where FoodOS can carry it out ('Swap it on your list?'). It speaks only about differences it can point to: your own limits, the price per portion, and the allergens the law names. A rule from your doctor's signed record counts among your limits, and shows where it came from. Kept apart from Running a trial (trying one on purpose to learn); Comparing offers (offers with terms and dates); Checking one food (one food against your needs); Finding a place to eat (where to go); and Switching to a better deal (leaving what you pay for now). It usually starts when you stand at a shelf or a menu, sit down to order for a group, a job comes round again, or you are about to buy a machine or hire help.

examples.card: Compare similar products and pick the best one for what you need.
examples.filled: In a Sydney supermarket the avocados on the left will be ripe for Thursday and the firm ones for the weekend. Add the left ones to your list for Thursday?

examples.card: Pick the dish on a menu that fits your diet or goal.
examples.filled: From the menu in front of you in Lisbon: the fish with greens fits low salt; skip the sauce. Order it?

examples.card: Choose dishes for a group so everyone is fed within a total.
examples.filled: Six of you in Singapore with S$120: two sharing platters, one vegan main, a dessert each. Order that?

examples.card: Work out what each unit costs in a multipack or case.
examples.filled: The 12-pack is 40p a can; the 6-pack is 52p. Swap to the 12-pack?

examples.card: Order the right amount for your group.
examples.filled: Four of you at a table in Istanbul: order three mains and two meze to share, not eight dishes?

examples.card: Cook tonight or order in?
examples.filled: Stir-fry: 25 minutes, R$15. Takeaway: R$62, here in 30, in São Paulo. Cook it?

examples.card: Own the machine or rent it?
examples.filled: A combine for 3 weeks a year in Nakuru: rent it for KSh 180,000, or buy it for KSh 9,000,000?

you do this when: Several things are in front of you and you want the differences to pick one.

name: Complaining and putting it right
card: A regular in Leeds says Tuesday's loaf was underbaked. Replace it free or refund £3.50?
note: You put right what went wrong for a customer, a resident or a pupil: a refund, a replacement, a credit towards next time, or a money-back promise you made and now honour. They tell you what went wrong, you offer what you will do, they accept or answer, and you pay or hand it over. A refund is money back. A credit is a promise to take off a future bill, with an end date, and they choose which they want. Complaining about an order: You bought something and the order is wrong: missing, late, damaged, overcharged, a disputed weight, spoiled on the way, refused at the door. What you are owed is read from the order you both agreed and the law where you live, and shown before you ask. You ask, they offer a fix (refund, credit, delivery again, part refund), and you accept or push back. It ends when it is put right. Photos and records go to the seller only if you allow it. If you cannot agree, it goes to Asking for a ruling on a dispute. A public review is its own act. Kept apart from Giving a gift (a present); Paying a fine or levy (money owed to an authority); Recalling food (a whole batch pulled back from everyone); Returning something (you send it back by choice); Claiming on a warranty (a fault months later, often against the maker); and Acting on a recall (a whole batch pulled back). It usually starts when a customer complains, a fault is found, a money-back promise is claimed, or a batch is found bad; as Complaining about an order, when an order arrives short, late or wrong, or a bill is wrong.

examples.card: Refund or credit a customer for what went wrong.
examples.filled: Ben in Manchester says his order arrived cold. Refund €8 or send a credit?

examples.card: Replace something that arrived wrong.
examples.filled: A customer in Delhi got the wrong curry. Send the right one?

examples.card: Honour a money-back promise.
examples.filled: A box from your farm in Sicily arrived crushed. Refund it?

examples.card: Ask for a refund or credit for what was wrong, missing or late.
examples.filled: Your delivery arrived 90 minutes late with one item missing. Ask for a refund?

examples.card: Ask an inspector to re-check a weight, grade or amount you dispute.
examples.filled: You were billed for 50 kg of potatoes but weighed 46 kg. Ask for the difference back?

examples.card: Check you were charged the right amount for what you ordered or bought.
examples.filled: The bill charges for two desserts, you ordered one. Ask them to correct it?

examples.card: Say what was damaged on arrival and ask for a fix.
examples.filled: Half the eggs in your Saturday box arrived broken. Ask for a refund or new eggs?

examples.card: Ask for a refund when goods are refused at the door.
examples.filled: The supermarket in Nairobi turned back 20 crates of your tomatoes at the door. Ask the buyer to pay for the ones they took?

examples.card: The supplier's driver collects the rejects
examples.filled: Your fruit supplier will send a van for 8 crates of mouldy strawberries. Do you ask the driver to sign for the 8?

examples.card: Weigh what you bought and say what it came to.
examples.filled: The 1 kg of tomatoes from the stall weighs 860 g on your kitchen scale. Raise it with the stallholder on Saturday?

examples.card: The supplier's driver collects the rejects
examples.filled: The milk lorry took back 20 cartons that were warm on arrival. Do you ask for a credit note on the spot?

examples.card: Complaining about an order
examples.filled: Your delivery is missing the milk. Ask for a refund?

you do this when: Something you bought arrived wrong and the seller puts it right, or you are that seller: a wrong order, a missing item. Not a fault months later under a warranty, not a return by choice, not a pulled batch.

name: Asking for a ruling on a dispute
card: The farm says the potatoes were 50 kg; your scale says 46. Ask the grader you both named to decide? Fee KSh 300, ruling in 3 days, KSh 4,000 held meanwhile.
note: You and the other side ask someone you both named in advance to decide a disagreement: a grader, a market committee, an elder, a checker. You pay their fee as agreed. You can also agree new terms between yourselves without any of this. Someone you did not both name can only suggest; a court acts under the law. Money in question can sit with a named third person who may not use it until the ruling comes. The card shows the fee, the days to a ruling, what is held and any deadline to ask for the money. It serves trades and groups (the flatmate who never pays, a co-op row), including when a machine or an agent got it wrong. It ends when you both accept or the ruling is given. Ruling on a dispute: You are the neutral both sides named to decide a disagreement: a grader, a market committee, an elder, an arbitrator (someone both sides trust to decide), a co-op's panel. They agree up front to your ruling and to what you may decide. You hear both, read what each signed, decide, and give your ruling with reasons; it holds them as far as they agreed. Your fee, if any, and who pays it is agreed before you start. Whether your rulings are public is one typed term of your own signed offer, `rulings: public`; left out means private. That a ruling went unhonoured, and your record as a judge (rulings given, how many honoured), are always public. Kept apart from Complaining and putting it right (you ask the seller to put it right); Bargaining for your members (terms for many); Naming a judge for a deal (writing the judge into a deal before any quarrel); Grading produce (checking quality with no dispute); and Deciding as a group (members decide together). It usually starts when a delivery does not match, a payment is late, a machine or agent got it wrong, or a group row grows; as Ruling on a dispute, when two sides name you in a deal or after a disagreement, when a ruling is due, or when one side asks you to look again.

examples.card: Ask someone neutral to decide a disagreement, with money held until then.
examples.filled: A grader settles 50kg vs 46kg; KSh 4,000 held until they rule. Accept the grader's ruling?

examples.card: Settle a row inside a group.
examples.filled: The flat's elder will decide who owes for the gas. Ask for a ruling?

examples.card: Settle what an agent got wrong.
examples.filled: Your agent ordered 20 crates instead of 2. Ask the supplier and a checker named in advance to settle it?

examples.card: Confirm that you owe something before it counts as a debt.
examples.filled: Dan says you owe $40; confirm or dispute it. Confirm it?

examples.card: Take a big buyer to the body the law sets up.
examples.filled: A chain has paid you more than 60 days late on 6 invoices this year, against 30-day terms. Take it to the body that rules on how grocers treat suppliers?

examples.card: Agree to rule on a disagreement.
examples.filled: A trader and a fisher in Mombasa ask you to decide the weight of a disputed catch. Agree, for KSh 1,000 from each?

examples.card: Hear both sides before you rule.
examples.filled: The landlord and the café in Lisbon have each sent their side. Read both before you set a hearing?

examples.card: Give your ruling with reasons.
examples.filled: You find the maize was graded wrongly in Kitale. Rule that the buyer pays the grade 1 price?

examples.card: Ruling on a dispute
examples.filled: A buyer and a farmer named you to rule on 30 bags graded 'poor'. Hear both and rule by Friday?

you do this when: A quarrel has begun and the judge you both chose is asked to rule, or you are that judge. Not naming a judge before any quarrel, not sealed bids with no judge.
no mirror: a named third: the judge you both named acts in Ruling on a dispute, pointing at this deal

name: Buying together
card: A 25 kg sack of rice is ₦45,000, so ₦15,000 each between three. Last month you paid ₦19,000 for the same in small bags. Ask the two neighbours who also buy rice?
note: You team up with others to buy for less: split a bulk sack, share a regular box, gather neighbours to ask a seller for a group price, or ask a maker to make a batch only if enough others want it. You ask others to join; when enough say yes, you order together, each pays a share and collects theirs. If too few join, it does not go ahead. Whoever pays the seller first is out of pocket until the others pay, so each person puts in a deposit and you agree up front what leaving costs once the order is placed. At collection you pay and the organiser signs for it, so everyone's share shows as paid. Kept apart from Buying and selling food to use (your usual household shop); Subscribing (you join a seller's fixed regular offer); Ordering stock (a business orders from a supplier and pays later); and Leading a group buy (one person runs it for many neighbours, for pay). It usually starts when there is a bulk offer in the shop (25kg for the price of two 10s), when neighbours or housemates buy the same thing each week, or when a seller's price drops at a larger amount.

examples.card: Buy in bulk with others and split it.
examples.filled: 25kg of rice is ₦38,000 in Kano, and two neighbours also buy rice. Ask them to split it three ways?

examples.card: Split a regular box or subscription with someone nearby.
examples.filled: Share a weekly veg box with the flat upstairs in Bristol and split the cost?

examples.card: Gather people nearby to ask a seller for a group price.
examples.filled: Ask neighbours in Medellín to ask a farm for a lower price on a big weekly order?

examples.card: Ask a maker to make a batch for you if enough others want it.
examples.filled: Ask the baker in Lyon to make a rye loaf if five of you want one?

examples.card: Ask neighbours to share one vet visit.
examples.filled: Your sheep are due their jabs in the next 3 weeks, and so are two neighbours'. Ask the vet for one visit to all three farms?

you do this when: You team up with neighbours to buy for less: a bulk sack, a shared box, a group price. Not shopping for one person, not leading a group buy for a cut.

name: Doing a favour
card: You pass the market at 5 and Anna asked for lemons. Pick some up for her?
note: You do an unpaid job for someone: pick up their lemons, carry a neighbour's shopping upstairs, mind their food, water their plants while they are away, or give a hand at their work when it is busy. You offer or they ask, you say yes, you do it and hand it over, and that is the end of it. What you mind for them stays theirs. Whether you keep count is your own business, never their debt. Asking someone for a favour: You ask someone for a small job, for nothing: pick up your eggs, take in a delivery, water the tomatoes while you are away, feed the starter, start the slow step of a recipe. You ask, they say yes or no, they do it and hand it over, and it ends when it is done or you withdraw. If they spend their own money for you, paying them back and when is part of it. They may say no, and owe no reason. Kept apart from Doing or getting a job for pay (the same job done for a price); Volunteering with food (free work for a place that feeds people); Asking for volunteers (you want unpaid time from many people); and Lending and borrowing something (you want a thing back, not a job done). It usually starts when you are passing a shop and a neighbour needs something, someone goes away, or a friend's job gets busy; as Asking someone for a favour, when you need something done and know someone who is near, going there, or free, or when you will be away and something living needs care.

examples.card: Carry someone's delivery on a trip you are already making.
examples.filled: Ana in Seville has a parcel of eggs for a friend on your route to work. Drop it off?

examples.card: Offer to help someone carry or mind their food.
examples.filled: A neighbour in a Hong Kong tower block has heavy bags and a broken lift. Offer to carry them up?

examples.filled: Jo is away in Lisbon for a week. Feed her sourdough starter?

examples.filled: Your brother's matatu leaves for Eldoret at 6. Ask him to bring back a sack of maize flour?

examples.filled: Ana is away for three weeks and asked you to water her plot. She said take a share. Do you pick on Friday?

examples.filled: You are in hospital and your plot needs watering. Who do you ask?

examples.card: Covering a plot
examples.filled: Your neighbour picked your beans while you were away. Do you leave her a jar?

examples.filled: Sam is at the shop now. Ask him to grab your eggs?

you do this when: A small job is done for nothing between people: you ask, or you do it. Not paid, not a volunteer place.

name: Swapping with someone
card: Your neighbour has spare eggs and wants your courgettes. Swap?
note: You swap with someone and nobody pays: each of you gives something and gets something. It can be food, seeds and plants, a skill for a lesson, the use of a tool or space for food or help, or a share of a catch or a field. One of you asks or offers, the other says yes, you both hand over, and it can repeat as a standing swap. If one of you gives now and the other later (seed now, a cockerel in spring), you agree the later date. FoodOS puts no price on either side; you decide if it is fair. An idea is not property (Kinsella), so a recipe or a method swapped is told, not handed over (see Passing on a recipe); only things and work change owner here. Kept apart from Buying and selling food to use (you pay money for it); Giving a gift (nothing comes back); Lending and borrowing something (you hand the thing back); and Renting out land (your garden for a share of the harvest). A shift swapped with a colleague is in Working for someone, and cooking in turn between households is Hosting a meal. It usually starts when you have a spare and want something, when a harvest or batch is bigger than you need, when sowing time comes, or when a neighbour has what you lack.
no mirror: self: both sides do the same thing

examples.card: Swap what you have spare for someone's food or help.

move words.card: Your hall on Saturday 14 March: do you open the swap table for seeds and seedlings, or keep it to the people on your path?
move words.note: Many swaps at one table: a seed or plant swap day, with each swap noted between the two who made it. Nobody puts a price on either side.

name: Changing money
card: The bureau gives 1,640 naira a dollar and the app gives 1,672 after its fee. Change $300 with the app?
note: You change one kind of money for another, for a fee or at a rate: cash into mobile money or a bank balance and back, or one currency into another (dollars from a sale into shillings, rand to buy stock in Johannesburg). Mobile money is a promise from its provider, cash is in your hand, and the rate or fee on the day is the changer's price. You compare what each changer gives after fees, agree, hand over one money and take the other. The law may limit how much you can move or ask who you are, and the card shows that. Changing money for others: You change money for customers: a mobile-money agent point (cash in, cash out, airtime and bills, with a commission from the provider) or a currency changer's stall or counter. A customer asks, you agree the amount and the fee, the money moves, and you note it. The float is the cash and mobile money you keep ready for customers. The mobile money on your phone is a promise from the provider, and the money you hold for a customer's pending move is not yours to use. The law may ask you to check who customers are and report large moves. You keep enough cash and mobile money on hand and top up at the bank or from a bigger agent. At the end of the day you count the cash and the mobile money you hold, beside the day's changes. Kept apart from Sending money home (money to family far away); Keeping money with a bank or wallet (keeping it there); Importing food (the change is one part of a larger deal); Agreeing a price for later (a rate fixed for a later day); and Counting the till (the day's cash count). It usually starts when you run out of cash, your mobile money builds up, the till is full at closing, you are paid in a money you cannot spend, or you must pay a supplier in another money; as Changing money for others, when the float runs low, a payday or market day brings crowds, a customer asks for airtime or a bill, or the day's cash is ready to bank.

name: Lending and borrowing something
card: Your neighbour needs a big pot for Sunday. Lend yours?
note: You lend something you own and get the same thing back: a big pot, a mixer, a ladder, a ram, space in your freezer, a field for a season. You lend it when asked, or post what you can lend to people near you. You agree when it comes back, who bears damage, and a small deposit if it is valuable. For a field you also say what may be planted and the day it comes back, so a season's use stays a loan. Then you hand it over and they return it. You can ask for it back any time; keeping it past the day you asked costs the sum you both signed. Borrowing something: You borrow a tool, a dish, kit or an animal and give back the same thing: a mixer, a ladder, a big pot, a ram for the season. You ask, they accept, they hand it over, you use it and give it back when agreed. Who bears damage, and whose the young of a borrowed animal are, is agreed up front. Kept apart from Lending and borrowing food or seed (the same kind comes back, not the same thing); Renting something (money is paid); Storing food with someone (a fee for holding goods); and Renting land or a place to trade (ground). It usually starts when a neighbour needs a thing you are not using, it has been out too long, a field lies empty in the season, or you notice you have idle kit; as Borrowing something, when you need something for a day or a recipe, or when what you borrowed has been out too long.

name: Renting something
card: Your mixer sat idle 3 weeks of the last 4 and 3 neighbours have asked for one. Rent it out, at a daily price you set?
note: You rent out what sits idle, for money: a mixer, an oven by the hour, a van, a room, a charging spot, a ram for the season. You offer it at your price, they accept, you hand it over, they pay before or on return, and it comes back. A deposit, who pays for damage, and the sum it costs to end a long rental early are agreed first. If you come too and do the work yourself, that is selling a service instead. A lease is a share: what you rent out (bench 3, Tuesdays, until 30 June) is a part of the place that the tenant owns until the date, by the day or by the hour. If you sell the place you sell only what you still held, so the tenant keeps her Tuesdays, because you had already sold that use; she may sell hers on and the new holder keeps it. A share limits one place or one thing, and never reaches copies, offspring or what the thing makes (the eggs of a hired hen are the owner's) unless the lease says so. Renting something: You rent what you need and pay for it: a kitchen for the morning, a machine, press time, a room for the night, a ram or bull for the season. You ask, they offer, you say yes, you pay before or after as agreed, you check the condition together when you take it and when you hand it back, and you give it back. Any deposit is yours and comes back by what the two checks show. Who pays for damage, or for the death of a hired animal, and what cancelling late costs, are agreed up front. Kept apart from Running a shared kitchen (stations rented to many makers on a schedule); Lending and borrowing something (free); Renting out land (fields or quota by the season); Storing food with someone (you hold their goods); Renting land or a place to trade (a shop, stall or kitchen for years); Making products for others (you make the food for them); and Doing or getting a job for pay (they do the work). It usually starts when kit stands idle, neighbours ask for it, or a quiet week leaves capacity free; as Renting something, when you need a kitchen or kit you do not own, when a booking nears its end, or when a season for a breeding animal comes.

name: Letting someone use your recipe or brand
card: A factory wants to make your chilli jam under your name, 5% of sales. License it for 2 years?
note: You let others use what you know, for money and for a while: a recipe, a way of working, a plant variety, a name or brand, photos. You offer terms, they accept, they pay as agreed (a fee, or a share of their sales), and it ends or renews. You can check their work against the standard you set. One baker per town, or a fee each time a machine runs your recipe, are terms you can ask for. What ending costs, and how their stock is sold off, are agreed first. Each payment arrives with the count of takings it was worked out from. Paying to use someone's recipe or brand: You use someone else's recipe, method or name, and pay for it, for a while: you open a franchise, make their recipe under licence, or run a creator's dish in your kitchen. You ask for terms, they offer, you say yes, you pay as agreed (a fee per plate, a flat fee or a share of takings, on stated dates), and it ends or renews. You agree up front what you may still use afterwards and whether you promise not to sell a rival's. Kept apart from Selling your know-how (you sell it for good); Renting something (a thing, not know-how); Sharing a recipe (no terms, no fee); Buying someone's know-how (bought outright); and Developing a recipe (you make it yourself). It usually starts when someone asks to use your name or recipe, an agreement nears its end, or an outlet is due a check; as Paying to use someone's recipe or brand, when you see a recipe or brand you want in your kitchen, or when a licence nears its end.

name: Cleaning
card: The chopping board had raw chicken on it. Scrub it with hot soapy water before the salad?
note: You clean a space or equipment to your own standard, within what the law asks: a kitchen, milking parlour, van or stall, on a schedule. Washing up at home counts; so does clearing the kitchen before a festival such as Passover. You start the clean, change the list, note what was done, hand a job to someone, and mark it done; it repeats daily or weekly. Proof of cleaning is Logging food safety checks. Kept apart from Making water safe to drink (treating water); Keeping equipment and places in order (servicing and repair, not cleaning); and Controlling pests (it keeps rodents and insects out). It usually starts when a service ends, after raw meat, at a set time on the rota, or before an inspection or festival.

name: Keeping equipment and places in order
card: Code E4 on the dishwasher means a blocked drain pump. Clear it yourself in 5 minutes, or book the engineer?
note: You keep your machines and tools working: service them before they break, check that scales and thermometers are accurate, find out what a fault light means and fix what you can, decide whether to repair or replace, and stop a machine when something is wrong until a named person says it is safe again. You start the job, change the plan, note what you found, hand it on, and mark it done; it repeats on a service cycle. Maintaining a place: You keep the places where food is made, kept or grown in working order: fences, drains, roofs, wells, roads, terraces, ponds. This is upkeep, so what you built does not wear away. You plan the rounds, write down what you fixed, bring in help, and it repeats each season. Kept apart from Cleaning (hygiene); Repairing and treating for pay (you pay someone); Keeping people safe at work (the people using it); Keeping the power on (its energy); and Building or improving a place (making something new). It usually starts when a service or check is due, a fault code appears, an alarm trips, or a new machine arrives; as Maintaining a place, when a season changes, after a storm or flood, or when something starts to give way.

name: Building or improving a place
card: Paddock 4 floods every March. Lay a drain in August before the ewes go out?
note: You build or improve the places where food is made, kept or grown: a building, a drain, a borehole, a road, a kitchen fit-out, a polytunnel, solar panels, a biogas digester. It adds something that lasts, once. You plan the work, do it, invite helpers, and finish it. The card shows the other ways to get there (a builder, renting the capacity). On rented land, the lease says who owns the improvement. Work that touches a neighbour or a shared source needs their yes. Kept apart from Keeping equipment and places in order (upkeep); Doing or getting a job for pay (paying a builder); and Making a batch (food, not the place). It usually starts when a place floods or breaks, a season is about to start, an order needs more room, or energy costs rise.

name: Keeping people safe at work
card: The man-overboard drill is due and two crew are new. Run it Thursday?
note: You keep the people who work with you from getting hurt: drills, protective gear, risk checks, training on machinery and chemicals, life jackets, a liferaft, a first-aid kit. You start the check, change what is needed, note what was done, invite the crew, pass it on, and mark it done; it repeats on a calendar and pauses off season. Accidents go to Logging. Kept apart from Keeping equipment and places in order (it is the machine itself, not the person using it); and Keeping the power on (it is the energy, not the people). It usually starts when a drill or inspection falls due, when a new worker joins, when a new machine or chemical arrives, or when the weather turns dangerous.

examples.card: Run drills and checks so no one gets hurt.
examples.filled: Your trawler out of Peterhead has two new crew. Run the man-overboard drill today?

examples.card: Check protective gear before a task.
examples.filled: Your spray team in Punjab goes out at dawn. Check their masks and gloves first?

examples.card: Run a fire drill in a kitchen.
examples.filled: Your restaurant in Lagos has new staff before Friday service. Run the fire drill now?

examples.card: Show new staff the knives and the fire exit.
examples.filled: Your two new line cooks in Manchester start Monday. Show them the knives and the fire exit before service?

examples.card: Spray re-entry and heat breaks for pickers
examples.filled: Rows 5 to 8 were sprayed this morning and pickers can go back at 4 p.m. Note the time rows reopened, and the foreman's word?

move words.card: The fire drill is over. Note who took part?
move words.note: How many people you actually fed or who came, and how many you turned away: the number a scheme, a client or next week's cooking is planned and paid on.

examples.card: Count everyone out after an alarm.
examples.filled: The fire drill is over. Count who came out against today's list?

move words.trigger: A meal, service or event she runs has ended.

you do this when: You keep the people who work with you from getting hurt: drills, gear, risk checks.

name: Guarding against theft
card: The honesty box was emptied twice this month, both after 9pm. Take the cash in at 8?
note: You protect stock, cash, kit, crops and animals from being taken: an honesty box, shoplifting, stolen machinery, stolen cattle, and marking or tagging what you own so it can be traced. You start the guard, change it as a pattern shows, note what you saw, hand over a watch, and mark it done; it repeats and can pause. A theft that happened is Logging; a gap in the count is found in Checking stock against your records. Losses to foxes, hawks or dogs at night count too. Kept apart from Guarding against scams (tricks, not taking); Controlling pests (animals eating stores); and Keeping money with a bank or wallet (where the money sits). It usually starts when a loss shows in your records, a pattern appears such as empties after dark, new kit is bought, or the season for harvest theft comes.

examples.card: Protect stock, cash, kit or animals from theft.
examples.filled: The honesty box at your farm stall in Somerset is full by evening. Take the cash in at 8pm?

examples.card: Mark and track machines and animals.
examples.filled: The new quad bike and the heifers on your ranch in Montana can be marked so they are tracked. Tag and brand them?

examples.card: Guard a crop before harvest.
examples.filled: Your maize in Zambia is two weeks from picking and thieves are about at night. Set watchmen on it?

examples.card: Watch the ponds at night.
examples.filled: Two nets were cut at pond 4 and lines were left on the bank last night. Pay a neighbour to watch the dyke at night?

examples.card: Walking the floor: empty packs and a pattern
examples.filled: Empty tag cases keep turning up in the coffee aisle after six. Do you change who is on the floor?

examples.card: Examples for harvest and animal theft
examples.filled: Two goats were gone from the pen this morning. Do you want to log it and tag the rest?

examples.card: Walking the floor: empty packs and a pattern
examples.filled: A stack of meat packs is half empty by the door but the till sold few. Do you move them nearer the counter?

you do this when: You protect stock, cash, kit, crops and animals from being taken.

name: Buying equipment
card: A new combi oven is $9,000, or $260 a month to rent. Buy it?
note: You buy kit that lasts: an oven, mixer, tractor, cold room, a cooking robot or a home farm, new or second-hand, for a business or a home. You say what you expect it to bring, ask a seller, agree a price, pay and take delivery. You pay at once or over time (a pay-as-you-go solar pump, hire purchase on a van); over time, the seller stays the owner until the last payment, and you agree what happens if you miss one and what you get back if you stop. The card shows the price, each way to pay, the warranty, and what else the money could do (renting, repairing the old one, waiting). Later you can set what you expected beside what happened. Second-hand kit comes with proof it is the seller's to sell, and its service log becomes yours. Kept apart from Renting something (it never becomes yours); Borrowing money (you owe a lender, and own the kit from the start); Buying together (kit others share); Running or answering a tender (an institution asks for sealed quotes); and Ordering stock (what a business uses up). It usually starts when kit is failing or old, when demand outgrows what you can make, when a rental bill keeps growing, when a good used machine appears nearby, or when a payment falls due.

examples.card: Say what you expect a new machine to bring before you buy it.
examples.filled: A second oven costs £900 in Leeds. You expect it to let you bake 40 more loaves a week. Buy it?

examples.card: Buy second-hand kitchen equipment from someone nearby.
examples.filled: A used stand mixer 2 miles away in Austin is $50. Buy it?

examples.card: Buy a machine that grows or cooks for your household.
examples.filled: A hydroponic kit is KSh 80,000 in Nairobi. You expect it to grow your family's greens all year. Buy it?

examples.card: Buy a used machine with its papers.
examples.filled: A used tractor in Eldoret is KSh 1.4m with its service log and proof of ownership. Buy it?

move words.card: The new oven was installed today. Record it as in use from today, for your books?
move words.note: The day kit you bought starts working for you: your books count its use and wear from then.

examples.card: Record when new kit starts working.
examples.filled: The cold room in Nakuru ran its first full day. Record it as in use from today?

move words.trigger: Kit she bought has been handed over or installed, and her record has no day it went into use.

you do this when: You buy kit that lasts and becomes yours: an oven, a tractor, a cold room.

name: Selling equipment
card: Your old chest freezer in Kumasi still works and a caterer asks for it. Sell it to the caterer?
note: You sell kit you no longer use: an old mixer, a second oven, or all your kit when you close. You offer it, a buyer accepts, you hand it over and they pay, at once or over time; over time, you agree the payments, what happens if one is missed, and when it becomes theirs. Kit you still owe money on is not yours to sell until the lender says so. Renting it out, or keeping it as a spare, are the other choices. Kept apart from Selling spare food (food); Selling and buying in bulk (what your work leaves over); Lending money (you lend money, not kit); and Selling your business (the whole business). It usually starts when kit has sat unused for months, when you upgrade, when a business closes, when someone asks to buy it, or when a payment is due or missed.

examples.card: Sell kit you no longer use.
examples.filled: Your second mixer in Pune hasn't been used in 6 months. Sell it?

examples.card: Sell up your kit when you close.
examples.filled: Sell the van, fridges and ovens when the stall in Manchester closes?

examples.card: Sell a machine you have replaced.
examples.filled: You replaced your tractor in Eldoret. List the old one for sale?

examples.card: Sell equipment on monthly payments.
examples.filled: A juice bar in Nairobi wants your blender for KSh 36,000 over 6 months. Agree?

examples.card: Hand it over at the last payment.
examples.filled: The last payment for your van in Leeds came in. Hand the papers over to the buyer?

you do this when: You sell kit you no longer use, or all your kit when you close.

name: Handing something down
card: You are stepping back from the stall in Kisumu. Hand your pitch and regulars to your niece?
note: You pass your farm, business or herd to the next person while you are alive, often in stages over years. You agree the steps, what they give in return (work already done, care, a share of the harvest, or nothing), and who carries the debts. You offer, they accept, you hand over in stages, and either side can pause on the terms agreed. Your records are copied for them, and each customer still chooses where to buy. An idea is not property (Kinsella), so a recipe goes with a business as your signed word and a copy of the notes, and the people, the kit and the record are what change hands. Kept apart from Leaving something in a will (after you die); Settling an estate (finishing a dead person's affairs); Selling your business (for a price); and Giving a gift (one present). It usually starts when someone nears retirement, a child is old enough or has earned a share, or a stage of a handover is due.

examples.card: Pass a farm or business to the next generation, often over years.
examples.filled: Ella has run the dairy most days for 3 years. Hand her a quarter share this year?

examples.card: Pass a herd or a boat to a younger partner.
examples.filled: Your nephew has run the goats near Arusha for two seasons. Hand him half the herd this year?

examples.card: Pass a boat or a small shop to a child.
examples.filled: Your son has crewed your boat in Kerala for five years. Hand him the boat in stages?

you do this when: You pass your farm, business or herd to the next person while you live, often in stages.
mirror: Taking over a family farm or business

name: Inheriting something
card: Gran left you her plot with its water rights and a KSh 40,000 loan. Take it on, or decline?
note: You receive what someone left you when they died: land and its rights, a café and its recipes, a herd and its grazing, money, a record, with whatever debts come with it. The will decides the shares, or the law or custom where there is no will, and you may share it with others. Until the estate is settled someone else holds it, and debts and tax are paid first. You accept, question the terms, or decline, and it is handed over when the estate is settled. An idea is not property (Kinsella), so a café's recipes come to you as a copy of the notes and the signed word of the executor, not as something owned. Kept apart from Taking over a family farm or business (from someone alive, in steps); Buying a food business (you pay for it); and Receiving a gift (a single present). It usually starts when a will is read, an estate is settled, or a share is ready to hand over.

examples.card: Receive land or a business left to you.
examples.filled: Your father left you his orchard near Shiraz with the pressing shed. Take it on?

examples.card: Inherit a café's record.
examples.filled: Your aunt left you her café with its recipes and suppliers. Take it on?

examples.card: Take on a herd or flock with the grazing rights that go with it.
examples.filled: Your uncle's goats in Mongolia, with his summer pasture. Take on the herd this spring?

you do this when: You receive what someone left you when they died, with whatever debts come with it. Not a gift while alive, not writing the will.

name: Checking how things are going
card: Your brownies sold out before 11 on 9 of the last 10 days. Bake more tomorrow?
note: You read your own results: what sells and what is left (a café), what each crop brought in and cost (a farm), what the kids finish (a home), the month's spending, waste, time, health and footprint against your goals. FoodOS shows your own takings, costs, waste and time side by side, and marks what crosses a line you set or repeats in your record ('sold out by 11 on 9 of the last 10 days'). You choose the yardstick: last week, last year, your goal, or others who chose to share openly. It often starts other acts, and the card says what the change would take from something else. A bet you made is read in Looking back at what you expected. Each figure says how it is known: counted by a payment system, counted by you, or your word. Kept apart from Checking market prices (what things are worth outside); Running a trial (a change made on purpose); and Choosing between products (picking now). It usually starts when a day, week or month ends, a stock keeps running out or going to waste, or a goal needs checking.

examples.card: Work out which items sell well and which do not.
examples.filled: The soup sells out at your Dublin café, while the quiche is half binned. Make less quiche tomorrow?

examples.card: Work out what you earn per hour on each thing you sell.
examples.filled: Your jam earns more an hour than your cakes at your Brno stall, and it is gone by noon. Bake more jam next week?

examples.card: Work out what a crop earns against what it costs to grow.
examples.filled: The tomatoes on your plot in Naples brought in 380 and cost 140 to grow. Plant the same again?

examples.card: Work out feed costs against what the animals earn.
examples.filled: Each hen on your Devon smallholding eats 14 pence of feed a day and lays eggs worth 18 pence. Keep the flock as it is?

examples.card: See how your household's month went.
examples.filled: Takeaways up 30%, waste halved, cooked with the kids twice. Savings on track, veg behind. Plan more veg this week?

examples.card: See how old the money owed to you is.
examples.filled: Shops owe you 118,000: 71,000 under 30 days, 29,000 from 30 to 60 days and 18,000 over 60, of which 11,000 is one shop. Which do you look at first?

examples.card: Read each supplier's record from your own goods-in checks.
examples.filled: From your goods-in checks over six months: one supplier came on time 30 times in 44 and complete 38 times; another came on time 41 times in 50. Take this to the renewal talks?

you do this when: You read your own results against your goals: sales, costs, waste, spending, time.

name: Running a trial
card: Half the flock on the new feed for 4 weeks, weighed every Friday. Start Monday?
note: You change one thing on purpose and compare: two prices, a new feed for half a flock, a trial service, a storage test, a new seed. You decide what to change, for how long and the most you will lose, and you write down what you expect before you start. You run it, measure, then see what you expected beside what you measured, and keep the change or drop it. The card shows what the trial uses. Kept apart from Checking how things are going (results you already have); Looking back at what you expected (after a bet has run); and Switching to a better deal (moving to something already found). It usually starts when you wonder whether a change would pay, a new feed or seed arrives, a season begins, or a trial is offered.

examples.card: Try two prices and keep the one that earns more.
examples.filled: Your stall in Bristol could sell at one price this week and a higher one next, then compare. Run the test?

examples.card: Try a new service for a trial period and see if it pays.
examples.filled: Your café in Taipei could try weekend brunch for 6 weeks and compare takings. Start the trial?

examples.card: Try a new feed on half your animals.
examples.filled: Half your flock on your New Zealand farm could go on the new feed for 4 weeks, weighed every Friday. Start Monday?

examples.card: Try a new seed beside the old one.
examples.filled: You have seed of a new wheat on your farm in Punjab. Plant two rows of it beside the old one?

examples.card: Test how long a food keeps a new way.
examples.filled: You could store your tomatoes two ways at your Accra stall and check them after a week. Try it?

examples.card: Try a different net, with a stop you set.
examples.filled: On 9 of your last 11 trips with the 40 mm mesh you threw back undersized fish. Try a larger mesh on the next four trips, and stop if landings fall below a level you set?

examples.card: Try a tighter fill against the declared weight.
examples.filled: Your 500 g tubs averaged 509 to 516 g over the last 12 runs. Try a tighter filler setting for 5 runs, with a loss limit you set?

move words.card: You want to try a Sunday brunch for 6 weeks. Set the most it may lose before you start?
move words.note: Before a trial starts, set the most you are willing to lose (money, stock or time). FoodOS cannot go past it, and the trial stops when it is reached.

examples.card: Set the most a trial may lose.
examples.filled: You will test a new pie at the Accra market for a month. Set the most it may lose before you start?

move words.trigger: A trial of hers is about to start, or is running, with no loss limit set.

you do this when: You change one thing on purpose and compare: two prices, a new feed, a new seed.

name: Setting prices
card: Your chapati and beans sell at KSh 120; two stalls nearby post KSh 150 this week. Change your price?
note: You decide what you charge: a price, a rate or a fee, for food or for your own work. You set it, change it when your costs or other people's prices move, and pause or end it. Everyone can read your prices, with the date they hold until; the reasons behind them stay on your device. Different prices for different people, prices that follow stock, time or demand, and a premium for your own work are yours to set. Taxes the law adds show in the price. FoodOS shows the prices others post and your own record, and you decide. An agent pricing for you stays between the lowest and highest price you give it. When the recipe and your invoices are in your record, each ingredient shows its last price and date beside the dish's price. Nothing works out a margin or picks a price for you. Kept apart from Setting a budget or how you need to be served (what you spend); and Setting what, how much and where you sell (which products). It usually starts when a cost changes, someone else's price moves, a platform changes its commission, or a new dish or service needs a price.

examples.card: Cost a dish from what goes into it and set its price.
examples.filled: A burger takes about KSh 250 of food to make. What do you want to charge for it?

examples.card: Set your prices to cover what a platform takes.
examples.filled: The delivery app now takes 30% of each order. Change your menu prices there?

examples.card: Match a lower price a customer finds elsewhere.
examples.filled: A rival shop shows a price for the same loaf. Match it, or keep yours?

examples.card: Set the rate you charge for your own work.
examples.filled: You're thinking of €45 an hour for private dinners in Lisbon; nearby cooks post €38 to €55. Set €45?

examples.card: Set a fee for a regular client.
examples.filled: Your usual client in Melbourne has come monthly for a year. Keep his rate or change it?

move words.card: Most orders are £18 and each delivery costs you £4. Set a spend above which delivery is free?
move words.note: Free delivery once an order reaches an amount, shown plainly.

examples.card: Offer free delivery above an order size.
examples.filled: Your Bangalore kitchen's orders average ₹420. Make delivery free over ₹600?

move words.trigger: Her delivery costs and order sizes are in her record, and no free-delivery amount is set.

you do this when: You decide what you charge: a price, a rate or a fee, for food or for your own work. Not what you take in payment, not your hours.

name: Setting what, how much and where you sell
card: Your soup sold 4 a day this week and squash is in season. Swap it in?
note: You choose what is on offer: the menu (café), your range (shop), this week's box (farm), what is on the stall, the services you offer as a firm of one, tonight's licensed dishes in your kitchen. You start it, change it as things sell or come into season, and end or pause it. It goes out as a standing offer when you publish it, with when each thing is offered from. Where things go on the shelf is Stocking shelves, and new products are Developing a product. Setting how much you take on: You set a limit on how much you will take: orders, bookings, tables, boxes, places on a class, minimum orders, notice needed, collection slots. You start it, change it as the day goes, pause it when you are full, and end it. 'Sold out' and 'only 3 left' show your own count, never a scarcity that is not true. Taking more bookings than seats is your own call on no-shows, and the card says what you offer if everyone comes. Setting where you serve: You set where you sell, deliver or work: a delivery radius, the markets you go to, the towns you cover, the countries you ship to, the farms you will drive to. Every offer and order reads it, and you change it when you like. Kept apart from Setting a diet (what you eat); Setting prices (how dear); Setting your terms of trade (when); and Opening another site (a new place of your own). It usually starts when a dish sells badly, a crop comes into season, stock needs using up, or the week's box has to be chosen; as Setting how much you take on, when orders near your limit, the kitchen is swamped, a busy day is coming, or you want to be away; as Setting where you serve, when you start delivering, when a route costs too much, when orders come from further away, or when a market adds or drops a day.

examples.card: Change the menu from what sells and what is in season.
examples.filled: Drop the slow lamb dish, add the squash soup. Change the menu?

examples.card: Make a menu from what you can make and what it costs.
examples.filled: A one-page menu of six dishes you cook well, priced to a margin, ready to print. Print it?

examples.card: Make a special from what you need to use up.
examples.filled: A soup special from tomatoes and stale bread, priced and written for the board. Put it on the board?

examples.card: Choose what goes in this week's farm box.
examples.filled: Your Lancashire farm box has too many leeks and no kale. Swap in beetroot for next week?

examples.card: Choose which creators' dishes your kitchen runs tonight.
examples.filled: Tonight your Seoul ghost kitchen can run any of five licensed recipes. Pick the two that sell best?

examples.card: Set how many orders you can take, how much notice and a minimum for a day or week.
examples.filled: You can't bake more than 20 cakes a week. Set a weekly limit and the notice you need?

examples.card: Pause online orders when the kitchen is too busy, and turn them back on after.
examples.filled: Pause delivery orders for 30 minutes until the queue clears. Pause them now?

examples.card: Take more bookings than seats, by your own no-show record.
examples.filled: One in ten tables doesn't show on Fridays. Take more bookings than seats?

examples.card: Setting how much you take on
examples.filled: You have 30 orders for Saturday, your limit. Close orders?

examples.card: Set how far you deliver.
examples.filled: Most orders come from near your Accra kitchen, but some ask from further. Change how far you deliver?

examples.card: Add a market to where you sell.
examples.filled: The Sunday market in Bath has a free pitch. Add it to where you sell?

examples.card: Stop shipping where it doesn't pay.
examples.filled: Shipping to the islands has cost you more than customers there pay, six orders running. Stop shipping there, or keep going?

examples.card: Setting where you serve
examples.filled: Customers 8 km out keep asking, and you deliver within 5. Change how far you deliver?

known as: Setting how much you take on
you do this when: You fix the range of your own offer: what you sell, how much you take on or where you serve; which one is the fact. Not the price, not your hours.

name: Developing a product
card: Your test batch of chilli jam sold out at the feira at R$22. Add it to the range?
note: You add something new to sell: name it, say what is in it, and try it on people first. It could be a new plant variety or a jam you first made in small batches. You say what you expect (how many, by when) and the card shows what it takes from what you sell now: stall space, cooking hours, ingredients. You start it, change it, invite people to taste it, and stop it for good if you drop it. A new version that keeps the original is a new product. What you create is yours unless a contract you signed at work says otherwise. Kept apart from Developing a recipe (the way to make it); Setting what, how much and where you sell (what is on your list); and Setting prices (what it costs). It usually starts when a test batch sells out, an ingredient gets dearer, a customer asks for something, or a season brings a new crop.

examples.card: Create a new dish and try it on people before it goes on the menu.
examples.filled: You have a new pie ready. Test it on 10 regulars before listing it?

examples.card: Develop a product together with a producer.
examples.filled: A nearby grower offers to co-make a smoked chilli sauce with you. Say yes?

examples.card: Launch a product from trial batches.
examples.filled: Your small batches of chilli jam sold out at the Porto feira. Add it to the range?

examples.card: Make a variation of a product that keeps the original.
examples.filled: You could add a mild kimchi for children at your shop in Seoul; the original stays on the list. Add it?

move words.card: Your flapjack's oats went up 20%. Change it to the cheaper oats, same taste test?
move words.note: Change what is in it, how it looks, or how it is packed, or stop making it. Its price is Setting prices; which products you sell is Setting what you sell.

examples.card: Reformulate, relabel or repackage a product.
examples.filled: Cheaper oats in the flapjack after a taste test.

examples.card: Retire a product.
examples.filled: Drop the winter soup in spring.

move words.trigger: A cost, supplier or rule behind a product of hers has moved, or its sales or tests show it no longer works as it is.

you do this when: You add something new to sell: name it, say what is in it, try it on people.

name: Posting an offer or a want
card: Your new pies are out Friday. Tell your 40 regulars?
note: You get the word out about what you offer: the menu, today's bakes, a listing with a photo and your price, a flyer for a stall, a price board, a menu in another language, the days you are free to cook or work for pay, or a message to the regulars who asked to hear. It is for anyone who sells, including a one-person business. You write it, say how many and until when, put it out, change it, and take it down when it is done. Posting what you want: You say what you want and what you would pay, so sellers can come to you: a café buying 100 kg of tomatoes a week at its price, neighbours asking a shop to stock oat milk, a job ad for a night baker, an offer to buy eggs whenever they are under a price you set. A post says how much, at what price and until when. You write it, put it out, change it, and take it down when you have enough. Kept apart from Paying to be shown (paying to be shown); Labelling food (facts on the pack); Giving your word on something (answering customers); Finding someone to deal with (you go looking); Running or answering a tender (sealed quotes and an award); and Employing someone (the job itself once someone applies). It usually starts when something new is ready, something runs out, a market day is coming, prices change, or a customer asks to be told; as Posting what you want, when you keep buying the same thing, something is hard to find, a season of need is coming, or a job is open.

examples.card: Tell your regulars and people nearby what you offer and what is new.
examples.filled: A suya spot in Lagos adds a new peppered gizzard stick on Friday. Tell the 40 regulars on your list?

examples.card: Make a flyer or post for your stall, event or special.
examples.filled: Your flyer for Saturday's cake stall in Cork is ready, with the time, place and three headline items. Put it out?

examples.card: Write a listing for something you want to sell.
examples.filled: Here is a short listing with a photo for six jars of jam at a Tbilisi market. Post it?

examples.card: Update your menu or prices everywhere at once.
examples.filled: The fish is sold out at your Lisbon tasca. Take it off every menu?

examples.card: Translate your menu or sign for customers who speak another language.
examples.filled: You could put your Dubai café's menu in Arabic and Tagalog beside the English, with allergens kept exact. Post it?

examples.card: Tell people which days you are free to cook or deliver for pay.
examples.filled: You can cater events on weekends in Bogotá. Tell your regulars?

examples.card: Tell people nearby what you have spare to sell.
examples.filled: Post that you have spare tomatoes in Kisumu, ready today?

examples.card: Show a rating where customers can see it.
examples.filled: A takeaway in Cardiff has a 5-star hygiene rating. Show it on your listing?

examples.card: Post what you want and the price you will pay.
examples.filled: A café in Nairobi posts that it will pay KSh 80 a kilo for 100 kg of tomatoes a week. Let growers come to you?

examples.card: Ask a shop to stock an item you want.
examples.filled: Three neighbours in Leeds ask the corner shop to stock oat milk. Add your name to the ask?

examples.card: Put out a job ad for work you need done.
examples.filled: Your bakery in Tbilisi needs a night baker from March. Post it?

examples.card: Leave an offer to buy under a price, for your agent to fill.
examples.filled: You buy eggs every week in Porto Alegre. Post that you want them, at a price you name?

examples.card: Posting what you want
examples.filled: You buy 100 kg of tomatoes a week. Post what you'll pay and let growers come to you?

you do this when: You tell everyone what you offer or what you want to buy, hire or find; which it is is read from the words. Not paying to be shown.

name: Finding someone to deal with
card: Opening in March and need 30kg of fish a week. 3 boats within 20 miles land daily, two with hygiene certificates. Ask them for quotes?
note: You look for anything you need from others, as a business or a person: goods, services (a vet, a contractor, an agronomist), a kitchen or land to rent. You say what you need, FoodOS reads open listings and your own record, and shows who can give it, with minimum orders, delivery days, payment terms and what each one costs over time, papers they chose to show, and paid places labelled. You choose whom to ask, often for quotes. How many suppliers you use is your choice; FoodOS can show how much rests on one. Finding buyers: You look for anyone who wants what you have: customers, cafés, buyers for a glut, clients for your work. FoodOS reads posted bids and wants from open indexes, and shows who nearby wants what you have, with their price, when they want it, and how and when they pay. You choose whom to offer to. Work you offer is a service sold, so a client's rate, scope, pay date and terms show. Your own invoices show how much of your sales goes to each buyer. Nothing says how much is too much. Looking for work: You look for work in food for yourself: a job, a season, a trial shift, or day work where workers wait to be picked. You say what you want, FoodOS reads open job posts and shows those that fit, with the pay (per hour, day or piece), when it is paid, how it can end, and any agent's fee; nothing about you is sent until you apply. You apply, and a trial shift may follow. It leads on to Working for someone or Working a day for pay. Finding staff: You look for people to work for you: the search, interviews, references, a trial shift. You say who you need and when, FoodOS shows people nearby who have said they are free and what they chose to show (a certificate, past work), sorted by your rules, and you ask them. Your offer shows the wage, when it is paid, whether the trial is paid, and the terms for ending. An agency's cut is shown. It leads on to Employing someone or Hiring help for a day. Finding funders: You look for people who might put money into what you do: a lender, an investor, a grant fund, a crowd of customers, a buyer who advances money, a supplier who gives credit. You say what you need it for, how much and when, and see who offers what, at what cost, and what each asks back. What you choose leads on to Borrowing money, Putting money into a business, Applying for a grant or Raising money from your community. Kept apart from Switching to a better deal (leaving a supplier you have); Checking market prices (what things are worth today); Checking how things are going (your own results); Posting an offer or a want (the job ad itself); Supplying workers from an agency (an agency supplies them); Comparing offers (offers you already have); and Applying for a grant (one application). It usually starts when you are opening, running out, growing, or a supplier lets you down; as Finding buyers, when a glut is coming, a harvest is picked, a new product is ready, or sales slow; as Looking for work, when you lose a job, finish a season, move to a new place, or want better pay or hours; as Finding staff, when someone leaves, a busy day or season is coming, or a business is opening; as Finding funders, when you plan to grow, when kit or stock costs more than you have, or when a funder opens a round.

name: Running a loyalty scheme

note: You run a standing scheme that rewards customers for coming back, with rules anyone in it can read: a stamp card, points, levels, a reward for bringing a friend, first pick of a new batch for members, or a card you share with a nearby seller. You set the rules, customers join and earn, you give each reward when it is earned, and you can change or end the scheme. A change applies from now on, never to rewards already earned. A reward earned is your promise, so you can see what you owe, and the end date is said when it is earned. A shared card says who pays whom. Kept apart from Giving a customer a treat (a one-off treat you choose for one person); Offering customers a deal (a price for everyone, with no earning); and Selling subscriptions (a plan the customer pays for). It usually starts when the same customers keep coming back, a nearby seller suggests a joint card, or a customer reaches a reward.

note: You make an offer that ends: a flash deal, a trial price for something new, a bundle for the season, a quiet-hours offer, a joint deal with a nearby business, a pay-what-you-can day. You decide who it is for and when it ends. Customers take it while it lasts, you keep to the price you said, and it ends at its time or when you stop it. A joint deal says who bears what. A price with no end date is a price, not a deal. Kept apart from Taking orders in advance (made once orders are in); Setting prices (a standing price); Agreeing a price for later (a price promised ahead); Running a loyalty scheme (rewards earned by coming back); Selling spare food (leftovers and surplus); and Running a food event (an event people come to on a date). It usually starts when business is quiet, when stock needs to move, when a new product launches, or when a nearby business suggests a joint offer.

mirror: Buying and selling food to use

name: Buying and selling food to use
card: 4 people are queueing and the second till is closed. Open it?
note: You sell across the counter: someone walks up, orders, pays and gets it. You offer, they accept, they pay, and you hand it over. Where nothing rings the sale up (a drawer, a tin, a notebook), the sales are not written one by one: your takings are what you count at close, and what left the shelves is worked out from what came in and what you count. FoodOS never asks you to key in each sale. Most of it is done for you (the order goes to the kitchen, the sale is rung up, stock is updated), and a card appears only when you have a real choice. Credit is Selling on credit, orders ahead are Taking orders in advance, and cooking the dish to order is Making to order. At close you count the takings and what is left, so the average you actually got for each thing shows beside the price you posted. Going out to eat: You eat at a place: a restaurant, café, canteen, supper club or festival, alone or with others, from booking a table to paying. You ask for a table, the place says yes on its own terms (a deposit, a no-show fee, how late you may cancel), you turn up and eat, and you pay. A service charge the house sets is part of the price and shows before you book; a tip is your own gift at the end. A waitlist is the place's promise to call you. Doing the shopping: You do the household shop: the list, the trip or the online order, the delivery slot, substitutes and the receipt. Gas and charcoal for cooking are bought here too. You make the list, ask the shop, they offer what they have, you pay, and it is handed over or delivered. It is paid for there and then. Food a seller wants gone (end-of-day bags, reduced food near its date, seconds that look wrong but are fine) is bought the same way, at the seller's price, collected by the time they say. Delivery fees, bag charges and any change in price for a substitute show before you pay. Paying later is Selling on credit, and metered power and water are Selling power and water by the meter. Ordering a takeaway: You order food for now, collected or delivered: from an app, a phone call or the counter. You ask, they accept, you pay, they make it and hand it over or deliver it. The card shows the whole price: the kitchen's price, any app fee, the delivery fee and tax, and an app price above the kitchen's own is shown as such. A tip for the rider is your own gift. Serving tables: You look after guests at your tables: seating, pacing courses, turning tables, taking orders to the kitchen, the bill and tips. A party arrives, you seat them, take the order and pass it on, serve, bring the bill and take payment. A service charge is part of the price and shows on the bill as its own line; a tip is the guest's own gift, and who gets it is your signed rule. A tip is a line of the same payment as the bill, signed by whoever takes it, and it goes onto that worker's own record. Selling takeaway and delivery: You sell food that is made for now and goes out the door: collected by the customer or taken by a rider. An order arrives, you accept or turn it down, make it, hand it to the rider or customer with the receipt, and are paid. You can say how long it will take and mark items sold out. The customer can change or cancel before you start. Every order is one small sale. Your standing relationship with a delivery app is Selling through an app. Kept apart from Selling at a stall, a gate or a screen (a stall on market day); Catering for an occasion (a cake or catering made for a date); Ordering stock (a business orders from a supplier on account); Buying together (it needs others to join); and Taking table bookings (holding a table ahead). It usually starts when someone walks up or messages to order, when a regular arrives, when a customer asks a question, or when something goes wrong and needs putting right; as Going out to eat, when you have a free evening, a plan with friends, a birthday, a regular night out, a waitlist table freeing up, or hunger at lunchtime; as Doing the shopping, when the week's shop is due, when the cupboard runs short, when a plan for meals needs ingredients, when a big event is coming, or when a price drops under what you set; as Ordering a takeaway, when it is mealtime and you do not want to cook, it is your usual night, a group is together and hungry, or a favourite place is open; as Serving tables, when a party is waiting for a table, when a table has sat too long, or when a bill is asked for; as Selling takeaway and delivery, when an order arrives, an order is ready, a rider is nearly there, or an item runs out.

mirror: Selling at a stall, a gate or a screen

name: Taking orders in advance
card: Christmas cakes take 6 weeks. Open orders in Leeds now at £25, £10 down?
note: You take orders before the food is made: bakes, sauces, festival sweets, a special batch. This is for anyone who sells, a firm of one included. You open orders, customers order and pay a deposit, you make the batch if enough people order, then you hand it over and are paid. An order agreed by voice or in a chat is written down from your own words. What a customer says about their allergies is their word, kept with that order and cooked around first. Money paid for a batch you never made is owed back to the customer, unless the order said you keep it (a booking fee, or a forfeit if they do not collect); a promise nobody paid for that goes unkept is a broken word, shown and never a debt. Kept apart from Buying together (the buyers' side of a group order); Selling at auction (the price is found by bidding); Offering customers a deal (an offer that ends); and Selling subscriptions (the same thing again every week or month). It usually starts when a festival or holiday is coming, when requests from several people pile up, when a batch is only worth making above a number, or when a new product is ready to test.
