name: Eating and drinking
card: The first strawberries are perfect today. Eat them after lunch, outside?
note: You eat or drink: a meal, a glass of water, a vitamin, a blessing, the first strawberries of the season. You say what you had, change the plan, and mark it done; it happens in one go. Eating together at a set time, when nobody is hosting, is here too. FoodOS brings it up only when you asked (water, vitamins, fasting times), when it matters for your health, when you have eaten alone for a while, or when something is at its best. Kept apart from Logging (your body's records); Giving and receiving food (someone hosts, while here nobody does); Observing a fast (the fast itself); and Feeding your children (you feed them). It usually starts when it is a meal time, when a rule you set applies, when a sensor shows a need, or when something is at its best.

name: Logging
card: You felt sick after lunch again. Log what you ate and how you feel?
note: You write down your body's records, or the body of someone who asked you to write it, where FoodOS could not see them or could be wrong: blood tests (a photo of the lab report, or results from your doctor), weight, a glucose monitor, symptoms after eating, how a baby takes a new food, a child's reaction, a clinic's growth card, a mother's arm-band reading. It is written in one go. Machines log by themselves; you log to correct them or to add what they cannot see. What you ate is Eating and drinking; a harvest weight is Growing crops. A log can lead to Setting a diet, Planning what to eat or Sharing a record. It is some of the most private data you have: only you choose who sees it, not even your household by default; a child's or an elder's log is theirs, held by whoever answers for them. You may log a reading, such as a weight, and choose not to see it; only whoever you share it with sees it. Logging an incident: You write down something that went wrong, or nearly did: a cold dish, a cut finger, a guard left open, a diner who felt unwell, hail on the beans, a cow in the neighbour's maize, a night raid on the store. You note what, when and where, with a photo if you have one, and it is done. What someone else said (a diner's account, a worker's injury) is theirs and kept only with their yes. Several of one kind close together are counted and shown together. An injury or an illness the law makes you report is Reporting to an authority, putting a customer right is Complaining and putting it right, and a loss you insured goes to Taking out insurance. Logging stock: You keep count of what you hold: a home's cupboard, fridge and freezer, a stall, a café, a farm store, a food bank's donations in and parcels out. It covers the count, food that came in without a receipt (a cash market, a gate stall, a gift, a harvest), the date on the pack and the day it was opened, what is running out (a gas cylinder or a sack of charcoal too) and what is about to go off. It also covers what leaves without a sale, and why, in your own words: thrown away, broken, made wrong, came back on a plate. You can say how much in your own measure: a tin, a scoop, a handful. Each line says whether it is yours or held for someone else (goods on sale-or-return, donated food you may not resell). Pointing the camera at a shelf, a receipt or a date on a pack to count it is the act; what the camera only happens to see is never logged. A use-by date is about safety and a best-before about quality, and a line says which it carries. Seed, sprays and medicines carry their batch and expiry. Keeping accounts: You keep the business's money record: what came in and what went out, and the receipts you keep for tax. Most of it is already in your record as payments and receipts; you add only what has none (cash, a cost with no receipt). The week or the year is done when it adds up. FoodOS shows money in and money out and names what is not in the figures (your own pay, your premises); it does not print a profit. The tax rules come from your place, and any records the law says to keep, you keep. Rating what you've had: You remember and rank what you loved, for yourself: meals, places, wines, cheeses, your best of the year. You put things in order and in words (better than, best of the trip, top five), not points out of ten. What you order again is already in your record without asking; ranking is for your memory or for sharing, never a chore. Making it public is Giving your word on something. Logging hours you worked: You write down the hours or pieces you worked, as you go: shift times, crates picked, deliveries made, meals served. It is your own record and stays yours, beside whatever your employer records. When you are paid you can lay one beside the other and see if they match. Moving things between your home and your business: You record money or goods moving between your household and your business: pay you draw, money you put in, stock you take home, the van used for the family. It is never income or a cost of the business; it is you moving your own things between your home and your business, and your books read it that way. Working out what your things are worth: You put your own value on what you hold on a date: kit, stock, a herd, a building. It is your signed word, with what it rests on: an offer someone made, a recent sale, what replacing it costs from a signed quote, or your own estimate marked as yours. Your books show these values beside money in and out; the value is always yours. Kept apart from Logging food safety checks (a fridge temperature, about food, not you); Checking stock against your records (what you should hold against what you counted); Counting the till (cash); Keeping food fresh (use-by reminders); Looking back at what you expected (a bet against its result); Keeping a want-to-try list (what you have not tried); Putting money aside (saving); and Checking market prices (others' prices). It usually starts when a test result arrives, after a meal that upset you or a child, when a doctor asks you to track something, or when a baby tries a new food; as Logging an incident, when a customer complains, a worker is hurt, a dish comes back, something nearly goes wrong, or a storm, a flood or a raid leaves damage; as Logging stock, when the weekly count comes round, a delivery, gift or harvest arrives, something runs low, or it is closing time and goods are left; as Keeping accounts, when the week ends, a receipt is handed over, a tax date nears, or someone asks to see the figures; as Rating what you've had, when you finish a meal you loved, a place has been visited several times, or the year ends; as Logging hours you worked, when you start or end a shift, when you finish a piece of work, or when your pay comes; as Moving things between your home and your business, when you take money or goods from the business, put your own money in, or use business kit for home; as Working out what your things are worth, when a year ends, before a sale or a loan, or after a loss.

name: Logging food safety checks
card: Monday and Tuesday's sheets are blank; the fridge sensor logged both days. Attach its readings, marked as sensor readings, for the inspector?
note: You keep the records the law, or the buyer's standard, makes a kitchen, field or packing shed keep: fridge temperatures, allergen contact, proof of cleaning, handwash stations and toilets on a picking day, checks against your food-safety plan. You note each check as it happens and sign the sheet for the day or shift; you answer for what it says. A sensor's readings fill gaps marked as sensor readings, and a blank sheet is never filled in to look hand-done. Kept apart from Writing a food-safety plan (the plan); and Logging (something went wrong). It usually starts when a shift opens or closes, a timer comes round, a delivery arrives, a picking day begins, or an inspection is booked.

name: Giving and receiving food
card: Sunday works for all 6, and Jo is vegan. Invite them for 1pm?
note: You gather and feed people yourself: hospitality given, nothing asked back. You plan the menu around what guests can eat, work out how much food you need, invite them, keep a back-up plan, cook and serve, and send leftovers home. A funeral or mourning meal is one too. What guests cannot eat comes from what they chose to share with you. If you expect to be invited back, that is your own expectation, never their debt. Going to someone's meal: You are invited to eat with someone and it is free. Answering is the first step: yes or no, and what you can eat. Then you ask what to bring, take a slot on the sign-up, turn up, and say thanks. What you cannot eat goes to the host only for that meal. If you mean to invite them back, that is your own note, not a debt. Giving food away: You give spare food away for free to people near you or people you choose: an extra portion for a neighbour, apples you will not use, a bit of starter, plants or animals, or a pot shared among the people it is for. You offer it, someone accepts, you hand it over, and that is it. They can decline. Food near or past its date is said to be so. Who you offer it to is your choice. Letting someone pick your field's leftovers is the other side of Giving and receiving food. Getting free food: You take food given for free: a neighbour's spare apples, a bit of starter, food from a shared fridge, what is left after a party, a food bank parcel, a referral voucher, a free community meal, emergency food after a loss or a disaster. You find out where, ask or are referred, accept, collect, say thanks if you like, and come back when you need to. What you share about yourself to get it is your choice, and only what the giver asks for. What you do with it afterwards is yours: eat it, swap it, sell it or share it. It is recorded as it happened, never marked against you, and the giver sees it only if you share it. Spending a voucher you were given is Buying and selling food to use, paying with it. Giving alms: You give food to monks, nuns or holy people who go out for it: dana to monks on their morning round, bhiksha to a sadhu, food to a temple's community. They receive in their own way, often in silence. You prepare it, give it, and it repeats on the days you choose. Gleaning: You pick what is left in a field after harvest, with the grower's yes: potatoes the machine missed, fruit too small to sell, the last of the beans. The grower says when, where and how much, and you pick, take it, and give or share it on. Giving and receiving food groups often take it to food banks. The pick ends with a count that the grower signs. Kept apart from Giving a customer a treat (a treat in your shop); Bringing meals to someone (taking food to them); Cooking together (everyone cooks and nobody hosts); Running a community kitchen (feeding a community); Getting meals from a canteen (meals you are owed); Donating surplus (a business gives surplus to a charity); Giving a gift (a present to one person); Running a community fridge (a shared fridge for a street); Handing out food parcels (parcels for a registered list); Receiving a gift (a present to you in particular); Claiming benefits (money or stamps from an authority); Making an offering (to gods or ancestors, nobody receives); Giving to a cause (money to a group); Foraging (wild food); and Working a day for pay (picking for wages). It usually starts when an occasion comes, a rotating circle's turn comes, or you want to see friends; as Going to someone's meal, when an invitation arrives, when the date of the meal nears and you have not answered, or when the host's list is still missing something you could bring; as Giving food away, when something is going spare, a harvest is too big, or a neighbour could use food; as Getting free food, when money runs short before the next pay, when a neighbour, shop or food bank offers food, when a place nearby opens or changes its hours, when a referral is ready, or when children on free school meals near a holiday; as Giving alms, when a holy day comes, before a monks' round passes, or when a family day or a death is remembered; as Gleaning, when a harvest is done, when a grower says the field is open, or when a gleaning group calls a day.

name: Checking on someone
card: Mum has left her lunch untouched two days running. Call her, or drop round for tea?
note: You notice how a person you care for is eating and reach out: families with an older or ill member, care-home key workers. FoodOS reads the part of their record they shared with you, for as long as they said ('Mum shares meals with you until 31 December'), and shows what breaks their usual pattern or crosses a line they set; you decide how to respond: call, visit, or tell the family. Their record is theirs, and they can stop sharing it. It repeats for as long as they share. You see only what is recorded (by a kitchen robot, a till, a log they keep), and it says so. A meal at a neighbour's or a day centre is not seen, and nothing is read into it. Kept apart from Following someone (it keeps a person's posts coming, while this watches how a person is doing); Screening for malnutrition (it measures people against a programme's line); Checking one food (it asks about one food, not a person); Finding company to eat with (it looks for company at meals); and Checking who you are dealing with (someone new you might trade with). It usually starts when a pattern in their record breaks, such as meals left untouched, no cooking logged for days, or an overdue fridge check.

card: Tomorrow's ward menu closes at 10. The fish pie fits your low-salt diet. Pick it?
note: You choose from a menu that comes with a place you are in, or pre-order a child's meals: a pupil, a patient, a resident or a prisoner picks what they will eat, within their diet. Someone pays: a parent, the state, an insurer, the place itself, and the card says who. A canteen card balance is money paid ahead to the caterer, so it says whether it comes back if you leave. name: Growing crops
card: Frost at 3am, −2°C, and your seedlings are outside. Cover the seedlings tonight?
note: You grow plants for food, in a pot, a garden, a field, a shared plot, a tunnel or a lit indoor room: sowing, tending, protecting and harvesting, season after season. Seed and work go in now for food later, so when you sow you note what you expect (yield, price, date) and set the harvest beside it. Each sowing notes the seed lot, so a poor lot can be traced to the dealer; each picking notes its weight in your own measure; what you find walking the field (pests, disease, hail, flood, frost, ripeness) is noted with the date and a photo, your proof of when you knew. Whoever does a job in the field, a hired hand, a neighbour on a swap day or your own family, has it on their own record too. A spray's record and harvest wait may be required by law. A shared plot shares its harvest by the group's rule. When the harvest is in you say where it went: sold, eaten at home, given away, spoiled or left in the field. A neighbour or someone in the family who worked a day can ask you to sign it, and it stays on their record. Kept apart from Growing trees and vines (years before the first crop); Raising animals (animals); and Planning what to grow or feed (the plan, before any seed goes in). It usually starts when sowing time or the last frost comes, a weather warning arrives, a pest is found, or a bed is left empty.

name: Raising animals
card: This hen is hunched and not eating; two others look fine. Call the vet if she is worse by tomorrow?
note: You look after animals day to day: feeding, watering, checking, treating and protecting them, from hens and sheep to a hive, a fish pond or a shellfish lease, with milking, collecting eggs, shearing, taking honey and harvesting fish as steps noted with their yield. You start the care on the day the animals arrive, with how many and from where, count them at the evening round, change the care as the animals change, note each job, invite a vet or helper, and end it when the animals go. Fish and shellfish cannot be counted alive, so their number is what you stocked less what you counted dead, checked by your samples and your harvest. Milk, eggs, honey or fish from a treated animal are held until their date. Selling them is Selling animals, sending them away is Moving animals, and an order in an outbreak is Following an official order. At the round you say where each missing animal went: sold, eaten, given, died or strayed. Kept apart from Looking after someone's animals (animals that are not yours); Breeding animals (parents and births); Looking after a pet (not for food or sale); Moving animals (to another place); Slaughtering an animal; and Breeding plants and saving seed (plants, not animals). It usually starts when there is a daily round, a sick animal, a change in yield, a season such as shearing, a pond or lease to stock, or a hot spell, a cold night or a power cut puts the animals at risk.

name: Breeding animals
card: Scanning shows 12 ewes empty. Put them to the ram again, or mark them to sell?
note: You choose which animals to breed from and see the year through: choosing the father animals, artificial insemination, scanning, lambing and births, and culling. You start the season, change the pairings, note each result, bring in a vet or breeder, pass a task on, and finish when the births are in; it repeats each year and pauses between seasons. It is a bet made months ahead, so you note what you expect (lambing rate, price) at the start; hiring a ram or bull for the season is the other way. Births are reported through the records the law asks for. Kept apart from Raising animals (daily care and health); Selling animals (animals you sell, culled or not); and Moving animals (taking them somewhere to breed). It usually starts when the breeding season opens, a scan shows animals are empty, your records show your best animals, or births are due.

name: Moving animals
card: Paddock 4 has two days of grass left. Move the virtual fence to paddock 5 at dawn?
note: You move animals from one place to another: paddock to paddock, housing and turnout, between farms, up to summer pasture, to market or the abattoir (paying a haulier is Carrying for pay). On grazing farms it is daily. You start the move, change the plan, note the count and place, bring in help, and mark it done; it repeats and can pause. The law may stop animals moving for a time or ask you to report a move; you follow it. Grazing on a shared pasture follows its group's rule. The card shows grass left against the work of moving. You count them at the new place, and the count sits beside the one you started with. Kept apart from Moving food to someone (food, not living animals); Carrying for pay (paying someone to haul them); and Raising animals (daily care). It usually starts when grass runs low, a season changes, animals reach market weight, or a sale is made.

name: Foraging
card: Wild garlic is up in the woods by you. Pick some this week?
note: You gather wild food that nobody planted: wild garlic, blackberries, mushrooms, shellfish on the shore, honey from a wild nest, caterpillars in season. Some places let anyone pick. Others belong to someone, or have a season, a limit or a licence, and the card says which. When you come back you say what you found and about how much, and it goes into your stock. FoodOS can say what something looks like, never that it is safe to eat; ask a local expert. Where you pick, and when it came up there, is your own knowledge, shared only if you choose. Selling what you gather is selling. Selling what you pick may need the landowner's yes and a food registration; a buyer may ask where and when it was picked, and you choose whether to say the place. Kept apart from Fishing (it takes food from nature with quotas and licences); Growing crops (you planted it); and Hunting (it takes food from nature with tags and animals). It usually starts when a season opens, when the weather suits, when a fruit ripens near you, or when something you know is wild and in season is nearby, such as a patch where it came up last year.
no mirror: none: nature

name: Keeping food fresh
card: The chicken's due tomorrow. Move Friday's stir-fry to tonight?
note: You keep food good for as long as it should be: use what is going off first, freeze or store it, move stock oldest to the front, and decide whether to finish, box up or share what is left. You start, change the plan, note what is used or moved, ask the people you share with, and mark it done. 'Is this still good?' is Checking one food, and the count is Logging. Food that went off and was thrown out is written down as lost, with how much. Kept apart from Ageing food or drink (it gets better as it waits); Guarding against theft (loss to people); Controlling pests (loss to pests); Storing a harvest (a crop held for months); and Cleaning (dirt). It usually starts when a use-by date nears, you bring home a haul, a freezer or power cut threatens, or something is at its peak.

name: Getting rid of waste
card: A neighbour has a compost bin with room. Share it?
note: You get your waste taken away or put to use: the bin on collection day, a food waste collection, a bin you share with neighbours, a compost heap in the street, scraps fed to animals, a compost or biogas scheme, empty chemical drums, a dead fridge or scrap machine. You ask or offer to share a bin or a run, accept or decline, put it out, and hand it over; it repeats on collection days. A collection fee, or what a scrap dealer pays you, is part of the deal. The rules for business waste where you are apply, and the collector's signed note stays in your record for as long as the law asks. Where the law forbids feeding kitchen waste or meat to farm animals, especially pigs, the card says so. Food an authority orders destroyed is Following an official order. Where the law forbids feeding catering waste or meat scraps to farm animals, that shows before scraps go to them. Kept apart from Collecting waste for others (the collector's side); Moving food to someone (food someone wants); Returning containers (for the deposit); and Dealing with a dead animal (a farm animal that died). It usually starts when the bin is full, it is a collection day, or equipment dies.
no mirror: none fixed: who pays whom varies (a collection fee, a scrap price paid to you), so a collector's side, Collecting waste for others, is matched by the deal's terms

name: Getting a permit or registration
card: Your hygiene certificate runs out in 30 days. Renew it?
note: You get, renew or give back the permission the state asks for before you trade or operate: a hygiene certificate, an alcohol or late-night licence, a fishing licence, a pitch at a fair, an export health certificate, a food-truck permit, a work permit. You fill in the form, pay the fee the law sets, and the authority decides. You keep the licence and renew it before it runs out; you can drop the application before it is granted. The card shows the fee, the wait, and what trading without it can cost under that country's rules. FoodOS fills in what it can from your record. Money asked outside the published fee is Paying someone who demands it. Registering your business: You make your food business official with the state: you choose a name, fill in the form, pay the fee, and get a registration number. You keep it up and close it if you stop. Kept apart from Registering your brand (a name or invention the state protects); Taking out insurance (cover against loss); Getting or giving a certificate (a private mark buyers pay for); Applying for a grant (money, not permission); and Paying tax on what you earned (the money you owe once you are registered). It usually starts when a certificate is about to run out, you cross a legal line such as a turnover or staff number, you plan to sell somewhere new, or you buy a machine that needs a permit; as Registering your business, when you begin to sell regularly, a customer or bank asks for it, you cross a legal line such as turnover or staff, or your sales over twelve months near a line the law sets for registering.

name: Setting a budget or how you need to be served
card: R$180 left for food this week and Friday's shop usually costs R$210. Raise the budget by R$30, or plan a cheaper shop?
note: You set how much you will spend, at home (food this week, eating out) or in a business (pay yourself, tax aside). A line for treats is a real part of a budget, not a leak. You start it, change it when the week runs differently, and end it. Each budget has a period. It stays on your device; giving an agent a budget is Letting someone act for you, with the amount, what for and until when. Tax put aside is compelled, not a choice. At the end of the period, what you spent beside what you planned is yours to read. Setting how you need to be served: You set a standing fact about how you need to be served, such as step-free access, a quiet table, knocking twice and waiting, help reaching shelves, or a call before 4. You say it once, usually the first time you tell someone, and choose who may see it. After that it goes out with every booking, order and delivery, and you are never asked again. It is shown only to whoever serves you, who may not pass it on, and you change it when your needs change. FoodOS never guesses a need you have not written. It is read by Buying and selling food to use, Buying and selling food to use, Moving food to someone, Buying and selling food to use and Giving and receiving food. Kept apart from Setting prices (it is what you charge, not what you spend); Setting a diet (it is a limit on what you eat, not what you spend); and Setting house rules (rules for your own place, not for those serving you). It usually starts when a week or month starts, pay arrives, a shop costs more than planned, or you give an agent a job to buy for you; as Setting how you need to be served, when you book a place, order food to be brought, or a driver or shop is about to serve you.

name: Putting money aside
card: You earned $620 from jobs this week. Put your tax share aside?
note: You set your own money aside for what is coming, the job an employer used to do for you: a tax pot, a rainy-day fund, a lean-month pot, your own pay drawn from the business. You keep it yourself, in a tin or a pot of your own. You start the pot, change the share by your own rule, note each amount, and end it when it closes. Setting tax aside is not paying it. Kept apart from Keeping money with a bank or wallet (someone else holds it); and Saving in a group (you save with others). It usually starts when money comes in, at the end of a week or month, or when a tax date nears.

name: Setting a diet
audience: whoever must know, by her grant
card: You had about 40 g of protein a day this week. Set a protein aim?
note: You set a standing rule about what or when you eat: more protein, vegetarian, no peanuts, lower sugar, a doctor's goal, an eating window, a few weeks without a food and then bringing it back. Every other act must fit it. It is a fact about you, shown only to whoever must know, if you allow it. For someone who cannot answer, whoever they named earlier may act on it, but the rule stays theirs. A rule about medicine comes from your doctor's record. Kept apart from Setting a budget or how you need to be served (how you are served, not what you eat); Observing a fast (a set period kept by a calendar or a vow); and Setting a goal (a target). It usually starts when a doctor gives advice, Logging health shows a low result, a new year begins, or you wish to feel different.

name: Borrowing money
card: A $6,000 loan at 6% over 14 months costs about $250 in interest. Borrow it for the combi oven?
note: You take money now and pay it back later: for a combi oven, seed and fertiliser, a delivery bike, or to bridge a slow month. The lender's offer shows everything you will repay in one total, with the dates; the interest is the price of having it now. You ask, the lender offers, you accept, the money arrives, and you repay on the dates agreed until it is done. What backs it (guarantors, goods pledged, your own record of sales) is agreed up front, and so is what paying early or late costs. It can come from a bank, a SACCO, a lender who knows your record, or a friend. Each figure the lender reads shows how it is known: signed by the other side, counted, or your word. Kept apart from Borrowing against stored stock (stock in a warehouse backs it); Saving with a collector (you hold others' money); and Applying for a grant (nothing is paid back). It usually starts when something you need costs more than you hold, a repayment date is near, or an advance on your crop is offered.

name: Lending money
card: The bakery on your street needs KSh 200,000 for a second oven, repaid in 6 months. Lend some?
note: You lend cash to someone you know or trade with: a bakery's new oven, a grower's fertiliser, your sister, a member of your chama. The money is theirs until repaid, and you are owed it. You agree what comes back and when, in one total with every fee ('20,000 now, 21,000 in June'); repaid in bread credit or in beans at harvest says what and when. A loan with no date says it has none. What backs it (a guarantor, pledged goods, who judges a default) is agreed up front, and pledged goods are taken only by those terms. Taking a share of profit instead of interest is a term too. Writing off what is left is a gift. Kept apart from Selling on credit (goods now, money later); Putting money into a business (a share, not a loan); and Guaranteeing someone's loan (you pay only if they do not). It usually starts when someone asks for money, when a payment is due or missed, or when a security falls due.

name: Taking out insurance
card: Cover for the stock in your freezer (¥120,000 at what you paid) is ¥2,400 a year, paid if power fails for over 6 hours. Take it?
note: You pay an insurer to take on a risk for you: loss of stock, a freezer, a vehicle, a crop, an animal, a machine, harm to a customer, your own ability to work, or a machine's mistake. You ask for cover, the insurer quotes, you accept and pay, and it runs until it ends. The card shows what you pay, what it pays out and when, what is left out, who decides if it pays and how fast it pays. Cover that pays on a rain gauge or a satellite reading pays on that number, not on your own loss. When you make a claim, the card shows the policy's notice deadline and takes your own dated record of the loss (photos, count, date); the assessor's report is the insurer's word, kept beside yours. The other choice is to carry the risk yourself or share it with others. If you ask it to pay out, the money is only a promise until it arrives. Cover the law requires is shown as required. Cover can be for stock in ponds, cages or boats. Kept apart from Insuring each other (mutual cover between members); Getting a permit or registration (the state's permission); and Getting or giving a certificate (a private mark buyers pay for). It usually starts when a policy is about to end, when you add stock, a machine or an animal, or when a risky season is near.
no mirror: none: an insurer outside the food economy; mutual cover is Insuring each other

name: Sharing a record
card: Your dietitian asked for 2 weeks of meals. Share until the 30th?
note: You decide who sees your record, which part, and for how long: your dietitian until the 30th, a lender only the answer it needs, a researcher for a year for a fee. Any record of yours counts, including a worker's sales and tips. You can stop a share at any time. That ends further reading, but what was already read stays with the reader unless their signed terms say they delete it. Asking for someone's record: You ask to see what another person or business holds about themselves: a lender checking a grower's sales, a café checking a cook's tips and regulars before hiring, a buyer checking where food came from, a researcher paying to read meal logs. You ask, they decide whether to grant it, for which part, until when, and what you may keep afterwards; you may pay; you read it, and the access ends when they or the time say. A read cannot be unread, so the card says what you keep. What you read is their signed record, including what others vouched about them, and you decide what it is worth. It is always asked for, never taken. Kept apart from Getting your record back (records held outside FoodX); Letting someone act for you (the right to act, not to read); Reporting to an authority (records the law makes you give); Checking who you are dealing with (reading only what they already show everyone); and Sending proof (they send it without being asked). It usually starts when someone asks to see it, a share is about to run out, or you set up something that needs it; as Asking for someone's record, when a decision depends on facts only they hold: a loan, a hire, an order, a study.

name: Learning a food skill
card: Week 3 of your 10 basics: risotto. Cook it Thursday?
note: You get better at something with food on your own: a set of basic dishes, knife skills, bread, a cuisine you love. You choose what to learn and by when, practise step by step, and mark each part done; a plan like ten basics can run over weeks. What you can do is your own record, and it counts for more when others have eaten it. Learning from a teacher is Teaching a food skill. Kept apart from Teaching a food skill (a teacher, usually paid); Getting trained for work (the certificate a job needs); and Finding a recipe (one recipe to cook, not a skill). It usually starts when a new year or a free weekend comes, you wish to cook something you ate, or you want to stop buying something you could make.

examples.card: Learn to cook a set of basic dishes by a date, one at a time.
examples.filled: Learn five dishes by June, starting with omelette. Start with the omelette tonight?

examples.card: Practise one skill a week on your own.
examples.filled: Knife skills this week: dice two onions a night with the video. Start tonight?

examples.card: Mark a skill done on your own record.
examples.filled: You made sourdough that rose three weeks running. Record bread as something you can do?

you do this when: You get better at something with food on your own, with no teacher.

name: Teaching a food skill
card: Jo wants to learn your bread. Teach her Saturday?
note: You pass on how to do something with food: how to cook a dish, grow a vegetable, run a kitchen. It covers a parent with a child, a neighbour at a vegetable bed, a paid evening class or course. Someone asks or you offer, you agree a time (and for a class the price, the dates and what a refund costs), you teach, and it is done when the learner says they have it. Free teaching is a gift and promises nothing; a paid class is a service you sell. A paid class can name the fewest places it runs with, and below that it is called off with a full refund by a date you set. A learner's allergy or diet is their own word and shows beside the recipe for the class. Taking a class: You pay to learn a food skill from a teacher: a cooking class, a butchery course, a wine tasting course, a beekeeping day. You choose the class, book, pay, go, and what you learned goes on your own record, with the teacher's word if they give it. What a refund costs if you cannot go is said before you book. Kept apart from Doing an apprenticeship (years of work and teaching); Showing your machine how you do a task (a machine learns); Training your staff (training the law asks for, signed off); Learning a food skill (learning on your own); and Getting trained for work (a certificate your job needs). It usually starts when someone asks to learn your dish, a child is old enough to help, the season to sow comes round, or you decide to put a class on; as Taking a class, when you want to learn something new, when a class you like opens, or when someone gives you one as a present.

examples.card: Teach someone to cook a dish.
examples.filled: Your son wants to learn your soup. Teach him to make it?

examples.card: Teach someone to grow food.
examples.filled: A neighbour wants to start a vegetable bed. Show her how?

examples.card: Teach a food class or skill for pay.
examples.filled: People keep asking how you make pasta. Run a paid evening class?

examples.card: Help a teenager take over feeding themselves.
examples.filled: Tomás works the stove alone on Thursdays in Valencia. Hand him the lentil stew tonight?

examples.card: Lead a paid foraging walk or bee course.
examples.filled: Four people asked to learn mushroom foraging. Put on a Saturday walk for six, with the landowner's yes and cover for strangers?

examples.filled: A Thai cooking class in Chiang Mai is ฿1,200 tomorrow morning. Book it?

examples.filled: A beekeeping course near Nairobi runs 4 Saturdays for KSh 8,000. Book it?

examples.card: Taking a class

you do this when: A food skill is taught for money: a class you teach or take. Not training the law makes you give your staff, not a certificate course, not an apprenticeship's years of work.

name: Letting someone act for you
card: Leah closes the shop most evenings. Let her reorder stock, up to a weekly limit you set?
note: You let a person or a machine act for you or your group, within limits and until a date: your sister buys groceries up to $60 a week, a shift lead reorders stock, the chama treasurer pays out up to KSh 50,000, FoodOS reorders milk up to a sum. They can pass on only part of what you gave, and you can narrow or end it at any time. A machine never answers for itself; its owner does. Kept apart from Choosing who decides for you (if you can no longer decide); Guaranteeing someone's loan (staking your money); Selling through an agent (selling for a cut); and Deciding as a group (choosing together). It usually starts when someone new takes a role, a limit is hit, an end date nears, or you review what you have given.
no mirror: the one given the role answers by accepting it

examples.card: Let someone you trust spend for you up to a limit.
examples.filled: Let your sister buy groceries for you, up to $60 a week?

examples.card: Set what a machine may do on your behalf.
examples.filled: Your delivery drone in Rwanda flies up to 200 litres a day. Stop it when rain is forecast?

examples.card: Give a role in a group its power to spend.
examples.filled: The chama in Kampala elects a new treasurer. Let her pay out up to KSh 50,000 without a meeting?

examples.card: Let a supplier see your stock and top you up.
examples.filled: The bakery supplier can see your flour level and deliver when it is low. Allow it?

examples.card: Let a neighbour collect your ration when you cannot queue.
examples.filled: Your neighbour Fatuma will collect your ration at Dadaab on Monday while your leg heals. Let her collect for you this month?

examples.card: Let a neighbour's SIM receive your transfer.
examples.filled: You have no ID for a SIM. Your neighbour Joseph will receive your cash transfer and hand it over. Let him, until the end of the year?

examples.card: Let someone mind the stall and take cash, up to a limit.
examples.filled: You buy at the wholesale market from 4 to 8 five mornings a week. Let your helper sell and take cash at the stall then, up to a limit you set?

examples.card: Name someone to claim a benefit for you.
examples.filled: Your son filled in your last three forms. Name him as the person who claims for you, which you can end at any time?

move words.card: The year's catering budget is £180,000. Give the kitchen manager authority to spend it?
move words.note: Handing down a spending limit to a role.

examples.card: Give a role its spending limit.
examples.filled: Kitchen manager: £180,000 a year.

move words.trigger: A new budget year or term has begun and a role in her business has no limit set, or a department's limit has run out.

move words.card: Mia turns 16. Hand over her diet, allergies and food history to her?
move words.note: A parent handing a child the record they kept of them.

examples.card: Hand a child their own record.
examples.filled: Mia's allergies and food history.

move words.trigger: The date she set to hand a child the record she kept of them has come.

move words.card: Suppliers write to you on WhatsApp. Let FoodOS read and answer there, up to your limits?
move words.note: You let FoodOS read and send through a channel you choose, such as email, WhatsApp or SMS. It acts only inside the limits you set, and you can disconnect it at any time.

examples.card: Let FoodOS use your email for orders.
examples.filled: Your orders from 6 bakeries in Leeds arrive by email. Let FoodOS read them and reply within your limits?

examples.card: Let FoodOS use the messaging app your trade runs on.
examples.filled: Your fish buyers in Dakar order by WhatsApp voice note. Let FoodOS read and answer there, with orders capped at CFA 50,000 each?

move words.trigger: Her record shows orders, receipts or messages arriving through a channel that FoodOS cannot yet read or send on.

move words.card: You are about to let FoodOS reorder milk up to £60 a week. See what it would have done over the last 4 weeks, with nothing sent?
move words.note: Before you grant a standing rule, FoodOS shows what it would have done over recent weeks, using your own record. Nothing is sent and nothing is spent.

examples.card: See a standing rule run on past weeks before you grant it.
examples.filled: You are about to let FoodOS pay your flour supplier up to $200 a month. See the last 8 weeks as if the rule had run?

examples.card: Test a limit on your own records first.
examples.filled: A limit of 40 litres of diesel a week for the generator on your farm in Kenya. See what it would have bought in the last 6 weeks?

move words.trigger: She has drafted a standing rule or limit that is not yet granted, and her record holds past weeks of orders or events it can be run against.

move words.card: FoodOS has placed 9 orders since Monday under your £60 limit. Undo them all and stop the grant?
move words.note: You undo every move made under one grant since a time you choose. Each undo is a new signed move, and the grant stops. What cannot be undone, such as food already delivered, is listed for you to deal with.

examples.card: Undo what an agent did since a chosen time and stop it.
examples.filled: FoodOS booked 5 deliveries since Tuesday for your stall in Lagos. Cancel them all and stop its permission?

examples.card: Take back a helper's moves and end their authority.
examples.filled: Your nephew bought 3 sacks of rice for the shop in your name since Friday. Reverse them and end his authority?

move words.trigger: She has told FoodOS that a move made under a grant was wrong, and that grant is still live.

you do this when: You let a person or a machine act for you within limits and until a date: your sister buys groceries, a shift lead reorders. Not a choice for when you cannot decide.

name: Choosing who decides for you
card: Nobody is named to sign for you if you fall ill. Choose who it should be?
note: You choose who will decide for you if you can no longer: who looks after your money, food and health, who signs for you if you lose your memory, and who keeps your record and runs your FoodOS after you die. You choose while you can still decide, they say yes, and it is signed and kept. It starts only when its condition is met, judged by someone you named (a doctor, two friends, a death record). They can do only what you named. Some places make you register it and pay a fee. Your open deals pass to whoever answers for you. You can change or end it while you can still decide. Kept apart from Letting someone act for you (authority you give now, while you still decide); Answering for someone (you answer for another person); Handing something down (passing things on, not the right to decide); and Inheriting something (taking on what is handed down). It usually starts when a diagnosis comes, a child is born, a will is made, old age or a long trip is near, you set up your record for the first time, or people depend on you and you have named no one to decide for you.
no mirror: the person you name answers by accepting it

examples.card: Name who looks after your records if you die.
examples.filled: Name who holds your recipes and records after you. Choose your daughter?

examples.card: Name who decides for a parent who may lose capacity.
examples.filled: Your father in Dublin has early dementia. Help him name who will decide for him while he still can?

examples.card: Promise who will feed your children if you cannot.
examples.filled: Your twins are 2 and nobody has promised to feed them if you cannot, in Nairobi. Ask your sister to make her own promise to them?

examples.card: Name who runs your business record if you cannot.
examples.filled: Your stall in Lima has no one named if you are ill. Name your son to run your record, from the day a doctor says you cannot?

you do this when: You choose who will decide for you if you can no longer: money, health, your record. Not acting for you now.

name: Deciding as a group
card: The co-op needs a yes on the new supplier. Put it to a vote?
note: You and your group make a choice by the group's own rule: a vote, a meeting, or talking it through until everyone agrees. Someone puts a question, members answer, the rule counts the answers and the result is announced. A decision binds members only by the rule they signed when they joined, and anyone who disagrees can leave on the terms agreed then. The card shows what the decision would cost you. Kept apart from Enforcing your group's rule (acting on one member); Taking part in a group (your own joining, leaving, paying); Striking together (acting once decided); Boycotting together (refusing to buy once decided); and Asking for a ruling on a dispute (one clash). It usually starts when a co-op needs a yes, a new rule is wanted, or an annual meeting comes up.

examples.card: Vote on a change with the members.
examples.filled: Vote on a new rota. Cast your vote?

examples.card: Ask your group what they want to eat and settle by a vote.
examples.filled: Ask four housemates: curry or pizza, results at 5. Send the question?

examples.card: Agree what a shared label will mean.
examples.filled: Fifty egg farmers in Brittany vote on how many hens per square metre their label means. Cast your vote?

examples.card: Pick the day the group meets.
examples.filled: Your allotment society meets monthly. Ask the 30 members: first Sunday or second Saturday? Send the question?

examples.card: Ask members about the pool's price rule.
examples.filled: Deliveries to the pool are down for 5 weeks while buyers in town posted above the pool's price. Ask members: keep the rule, change the price, or let members sell outside?

move words.card: The co-op votes on the new buyer by Friday: 34 of 60 have voted. Cast yours?
move words.note: Your vote, counted by the group's rule.

examples.card: Vote on a group decision.
examples.filled: Yes to the new buyer.

move words.trigger: A group she belongs to has a question open and the date its rule closes the vote is near, and she has not yet answered.

you do this when: A group makes a choice by its own rule, by vote or talking it through. Not acting on the choice afterwards.

name: Running a group
card: You and 5 neighbours have bought rice together 4 times. Make it a buying group?
note: You start a group that lasts, or one for a single job: a household, a co-op, a lunch club, a chama, a machinery ring, a caterer's crew for one wedding. You set its rules: who holds the money and how many must sign, who does which job, what members pay, how people join, get fined and leave. Then you run it: collect dues, show members the accounts, share out what is left as the rule says, and merge it, split it or close it. Members can be people or other groups. A machine is shared by the group but is never a member. Closing a group pays what it owes first, then gives back what each put in, then shares the rest. The count of the box is signed by two members, the second named by the group's rule, so a shortfall never rests on one person's word. Kept apart from Taking part in a group (your side, as a member); Deciding as a group (the vote itself); and Having a business of your own (a firm of its own). It usually starts when neighbours keep buying the same thing, a job needs a crew, a shared kitchen or machine is wanted, or a year closes.

examples.card: Start a household, co-op, club or savings group.
examples.filled: 10 market traders want a chama. Start the group?

examples.card: Start a machinery ring with neighbours.
examples.filled: Five farms could share one weeding robot. Form the group?

examples.card: Start a buying group.
examples.filled: Six neighbours buy rice separately. Start a group to buy it in bulk?

examples.card: Ask members for a fee to belong.
examples.filled: The co-op needs money for running costs. Ask members for a monthly fee, and set how much?

examples.card: Start a shared food kitty for a household.
examples.filled: Four flatmates in Leeds buy food from one kitty. Set it up as a group, with the rules written down?

move words.card: Tom has moved out and owes £14 for the shared shop. Settle his share and take him off the list?
move words.note: The group's side. Your own joining or leaving is Taking part in a group. A machine is never a member: to connect a drone to your farm, add it and let it act for you, in one tap.

examples.card: Invite someone to join your group.
examples.filled: Invite Jo to join your household.

examples.card: Remove someone from your household, friends or team group.
examples.filled: Remove Sam from the food kitty.

examples.card: Set how much a member may owe the group.
examples.filled: Rosa: up to €300 below zero.

examples.card: Elect someone to a role for a term.
examples.filled: Ama as treasurer for 2 years.

examples.card: Hand over a role to the next holder.
examples.filled: Books, keys and bank mandate to Ama.

move words.trigger: A new holder of a role has been chosen by her group and the date for the handover has come.

examples.card: Collect members' dues.
examples.filled: Reminders to 12 members.

examples.card: Fine a member under the group's rule.
examples.filled: KSh 500 for 3 missed work days.

move words.note: Paying back what the group earned, by what each member supplied, bought or worked, as its rule says; never per head unless the rule says so.

examples.card: Share the year's surplus by what each did.
examples.filled: £18,000 by hours worked.

move words.trigger: The group's year has closed with a surplus and its rule says how it is shared.

move words.card: The yearly meeting is in 2 weeks. Send members the accounts, checked by someone outside the group?
move words.note: Showing members the accounts, checked by someone outside the group. It is done when members have read them.

examples.card: Show members the group's accounts.
examples.filled: Year's accounts at the AGM.

move words.trigger: The group's yearly meeting is close and its accounts have not yet been shown to members.

move words.card: The two chamas vote on joining into one. Merge, with both pots and all members?
move words.note: Two groups joining; each decides by its own rule, then members, things and open deals pass across.

examples.card: Merge two groups into one.
examples.filled: Two chamas join into one.

move words.trigger: Two groups' records show shared members, things or deals, and both have put the question to their members.

move words.card: The north village wants its own water group. Split off with its share of the fund?
move words.note: Part of a group forming its own, with its share of members and things.

examples.card: Split a group in two.
examples.filled: The north village forms its own water group.

move words.card: Hill St is ending: the fridge, the £240 kitty and the shared rice. Pay what's owed, then split the rest?
move words.note: Ending a group or a household: pay debts first, then share out the pot and shared things by the rule; copies of shared records go to everyone.

examples.card: Wind up a group and share what's left.
examples.filled: Pay debts, then split the kitty and the fridge.

move words.trigger: Her group has decided to end, or the date she set to close it has come, and debts and shared things are still on record.

you do this when: You start a group that lasts, or one for a single job: a household, a co-op, a chama, a machinery ring.

name: Taking part in a group
card: You've moved out of Hill St. Leave the house group and settle your share?
note: You take your side of belonging to a group: asking to join, buying in, paying dues, taking a role, stepping down, leaving and getting your share back. What you put in is said up front: a share (you share the group's risk), a deposit (kept whole and never lent or paid out, so yours back on demand) or a loan to the group (owed back to you on a date, or in the order members ask). Money the group lends or pays out, as a rotating pot does, is a loan or a share, never a deposit. What leaving costs, and what comes back, is signed when you join. A fine under rules you signed is yours to pay by your own consent; a fine from the state is not this act. Belonging by birth or place (a clan's grazing rights) is shown as that, and membership the law makes compulsory is shown as compulsory. Kept apart from Deciding as a group (the group choosing); Running a group (starting and running it); and Striking together (acting as one). It usually starts when a co-op opens for members, dues fall due, you move house or leave a trade, a role ends, or a fine arrives.

examples.card: Join a co-op to buy and sell together.
examples.filled: A local growers' co-op takes new members. Ask to join?

examples.card: Take a role in a group.
examples.filled: The allotment society needs a new treasurer from April. Put your name forward?

examples.card: Leave a group and settle your share.
examples.filled: You've moved out of the Hill St house. Leave the group and settle what you owe?

examples.card: Pay the regular dues to a group.
examples.filled: Your union dues of £14 are due this month. Pay them?

examples.filled: Your fishing co-op in Kerala is raising money for a cold store. Buy in at the co-op's price of 10,000 rupees?

examples.filled: The riders' co-op in Jakarta has a place for you. Join?

examples.filled: A women's savings group at your market has five open places. Ask to join?

move words.note: Paying for your share when you join.

examples.card: Buy your share when you join.
examples.filled: KSh 5,000 for the mill co-op.

move words.trigger: A group she has been accepted into asks a price for a share, and the date to pay it is near or has come.

move words.card: You're moving away. Sell your mill share to Kofi for KSh 5,500?
move words.note: Passing your share to someone else; the group may need to agree.

examples.card: Sell your share when you leave.
examples.filled: Your mill share to Kofi.

move words.trigger: She has said she is leaving a group or place where she holds a share, and a buyer or the group's buy-back rule is open to her.

move words.card: Your union dues of £14 are due this month. Pay them?
move words.note: Regular dues, fees or subs: a union, a co-op's yearly fee, a club's subs, water or grazing fees.

examples.card: Pay your regular dues.
examples.filled: £14 a month to the union.

move words.card: The dairy co-op takes new members in April. Ask to join?
move words.note: Applying to a group; it answers by its own rule, and a member may vouch.

examples.card: Apply to join a group.
examples.filled: The allotment society's waiting list.

move words.note: The group buys your share back when you leave, by its rule, less what you owe.

examples.card: Get your share back when you leave.
examples.filled: KSh 5,000 back over 2 years.

move words.trigger: She has set a date to leave a group whose rule gives back a share, and the group's terms for paying it are on record.

move words.card: You missed the meeting: the chama fine is KSh 200. Pay it?
move words.note: A fine under the group's own rule.

examples.card: Pay a fine to your group.
examples.filled: KSh 200 for a missed meeting.

move words.trigger: A group she belongs to has recorded a fine against her under its own rule, and it is unpaid.

move words.card: Your term as treasurer ends in March. Step down and hand over?
move words.note: Leaving a role in the group; the role goes on.

examples.card: Step down from a group role.
examples.filled: Treasurer, at the AGM.

move words.trigger: The term of a role she holds in a group is ending by its rule, or the date she set to hand it on has come.

move words.card: The co-op's second payment is 3 weeks late and lower than the buyer's signed price. Ask for the accounts, line by line?
move words.note: A member asks the group to show what it sold for (the buyer's signed note), its costs, and how the split reached her share. It is the member's side of Present the accounts.

you do this when: Your own side of belonging to a group: asking to join, paying dues, taking a role, leaving and getting your share back.

name: Setting a goal
card: You want a third of your veg home-grown by summer. You're at 1 in 10. Plant the beans this week?
note: You choose an end you aim for: money, growth, health, craft, family, safety. Budgets and diets are limits; a goal is what you are aiming for. Only you know your ends, so a goal orders the cards FoodOS shows you; with none set, FoodOS shows facts and never assumes what is good for you. What you then choose may differ from the goal, and FoodOS shows the gap as it is, never overriding your choice. The card says what a goal will take (time, land, money). Set together, it is a household's or a group's goal, seen by its members; otherwise it stays on your device. You start it, change or drop it, note progress, and end it. Kept apart from Setting a budget or how you need to be served (a limit); Setting a diet (a limit); and Planning how much to make (how much to make). It usually starts when a new year or season begins, a result comes in good or bad, money allows, or a household sits down together.

examples.card: Set a target for what you make or sell and track progress.
examples.filled: Sell 200 loaves this month; 120 done. Bake extra on Friday?

examples.card: Set a goal for what you grow yourself.
examples.filled: Cook one meal a week from your own garden. Set it as your goal?

examples.card: Set a goal for your business.
examples.filled: Open a second stall at Gikomba market by 2028. Set it as your goal?

examples.card: Set a goal for your family's food.
examples.filled: Cook with the kids every Sunday. Set it as your goal?

examples.card: Set a money goal.
examples.filled: Save 300,000 rupees for the farm deposit by March. Set it as your goal?

examples.card: Set a goal together.
examples.filled: Our flat wastes no food this month. Set it as the flat's goal?

examples.card: Take on a food challenge with friends and keep each other to it.
examples.filled: A dry-month challenge with Tom and Eli, with a weekly check-in. Join in?

examples.card: Find a swap for something you want to eat less of and stick to it.
examples.filled: Swap crisps for popcorn and track it. Make the swap?

examples.card: Set a goal for what you throw away.
examples.filled: Set a goal to halve what you throw away by March, with each week's kilos shown beside it?

you do this when: You choose an end you aim for: money, growth, health, craft, family, safety.

name: Slaughtering an animal
card: The 6 cockerels reach killing weight this week. Slaughter Saturday with the freezer cleared, or keep them another week?
note: You turn a living animal into a carcass: at home, on the farm, at the abattoir, or as a rite with others (qurbani on Eid al-Adha split in thirds, a family matanza, a hangi). You fix the day and place, bring in helpers, write down what was done (the count and tags, who cut and by which rite, what the inspector said, and anything held until a result comes), and it ends at the carcass. Cutting it up is Preparing food for sale, and keeping it is Preserving food. Giving a third away is Giving and receiving food; paying someone else to do it is Having food processed. Kept apart from Preparing food for sale (a carcass already food); and Preserving food (it starts with food). It usually starts when animals reach killing weight, a festival or family tradition is near, or the season turns cold enough to hang meat.

examples.card: Slaughter for a festival.
examples.filled: Eid al-Adha is in nine days. Slaughter the qurbani sheep at Hassan's farm outside Lahore and split it in thirds?

examples.card: Kill and pluck birds at home.
examples.filled: Six cockerels in a Devon garden are at killing weight and you have freezer space for six. Slaughter them this weekend?

examples.card: Butcher a pig together.
examples.filled: Your family's matanza near Salamanca is in November: one pig, chorizo and morcilla for the year. Book the day?

examples.card: Prepare an animal for a shared feast in the old way.
examples.filled: Your hangi pit in Rotorua is dug for Sunday; the pig goes in at dawn. Start the fire Saturday night?

move words.note: What the inspector decided about each carcass: passed, held, or part or all condemned and why. It goes on the kill record the owner sees.

examples.card: Note the inspector's call.
examples.filled: Carcass 4 has lungs with scars. What did the inspector say?

examples.card: Note the inspector's call.
examples.filled: An old cow was judged unfit before the kill. Sent home, or killed as a casualty?

examples.card: Note the inspector's call.
examples.filled: There is no inspector today. Do you write that, and what you saw yourself?

move words.trigger: A kill run is marked done at a place the law inspects, an inspection visit is booked, or the record shows animals were killed with no call written yet.

move words.card: A sample is at the lab for these four pigs. Hold the carcasses until the result is back?
move words.note: Hold and Release already exist for a batch. A carcass held for a result is the same move, and today the hold is a chalk X on a hook with no name and no time.

examples.card: Hold the carcass.
examples.filled: You sent trichinella samples on the boar. Hold it until the lab replies?

examples.card: Hold the carcass.
examples.filled: The vet marked two carcasses held for a check. Do you hold them?

examples.filled: The result is clean. Release the four?

move words.trigger: A test is open on the run in Getting something tested (a lab result, an older-cattle test, a residue or trichinella test) or the inspector marked the carcass held.

you do this when: You turn a living animal into a carcass: at home, the abattoir or as a rite.

name: Getting your record back
card: Your 3,200 Deliveroo deliveries are yours. The 4.9 rating stays your customers' word. Ask Deliveroo for the deliveries?
note: You ask whoever holds your history to give it back: a delivery app's record of your deliveries, a café till's record of your sales, tips and regulars, a marketplace's sales, a social app's posts, a supermarket's loyalty shops, a diet app's meal logs. In many places the law says they must, by a deadline. FoodOS asks, checks what arrives, and adds it to your record with where it came from. What you did is yours. What others said of you, like ratings and reviews, stays their word and is kept beside your record. When you join, FoodOS can ask every place at once, found in your inbox if you allow it. A record an aid agency holds about you (fingerprints, household, ration history) is yours to ask for, and to have deleted when you leave. What comes back is only what they held: the period and kinds it covers are kept beside it, and your own count for the same period is set beside theirs, so what is missing reads as not returned. Kept apart from Adding your own records (your own photos, books and chats); Getting back in after losing your phone (getting into your record again); and Sharing a record (who sees it once it is in). It usually starts when you join, when you leave a job or app, or when an export arrives.
no mirror: none: a platform or employer outside FoodX, which must hand it over by law

examples.card: Bring your delivery ratings with you.
examples.filled: Your 4,000 Deliveroo deliveries over 3 years are yours; the 4.9 rating stays your customers' word, kept as evidence. Bring them into your record?

examples.card: Take your sales record when you leave a job.
examples.filled: Your 2 years of tables, tips and 140 regulars sit in the café's till. Bring them into your record?

examples.card: Keep your audience when you leave an app.
examples.filled: Your 12,000 followers and 300 recipe posts are on Instagram. Bring them into your record?

examples.card: Bring your sales history from a marketplace.
examples.filled: Every Jumia order for your honey since 2023 can come into your record. Bring it in?

examples.card: Get your shopping history from a supermarket.
examples.filled: 2 years of loyalty-card shops can come in, so FoodOS knows your usual on day one. Bring them in?

examples.card: Bring your food diary from another app.
examples.filled: 18 months of meals from MyFitnessPal can come in, kept private. Bring them in?

examples.card: Bring in your food history from everywhere at once.
examples.filled: 7 places found in your email: Deliveroo, Tesco, OpenTable, Instagram and 3 more. 4 of 7 are back so far. Ask for the other 3?

examples.card: Take the parts that are yours when you leave.
examples.filled: You leave the Toronto bakery on Friday. Ask for your hours, ratings and regulars count to take with you?

examples.card: Ask the agency for your registration before a resettlement interview.
examples.filled: Your interview is in March. Ask the agency for what it holds on your family?

move words.card: Your 3 years of Deliveroo ratings are now in your record. Ask Deliveroo to delete your account and the data it still holds?
move words.note: Once your history is in and checked, you ask the platform to delete your account and the data it still holds. You ask by your legal right where the law gives you one, and the platform answers on its own time.

examples.card: Delete an account once its history is safely in your record.
examples.filled: The 2 years of orders from your Tesco account are in your record. Ask Tesco to delete the account and its data?

examples.card: Close a marketplace shop and have it erase what it holds.
examples.filled: Your Jumia seller history is in your record and you have closed the shop. Ask Jumia to erase what it holds?

move words.trigger: An export from a platform has landed in her record and been checked, she has left or closed her account there, and the law where she lives (a public fact) gives her a right to have it erased.

you do this when: You ask whoever holds your history (an app, a till, a platform) to give it back.

name: Vouching for someone
card: Ama worked your kitchen line for 6 months and applies at Lucca. Vouch for her, up to €200 until the end of the year?
note: You put your own money behind a person or business you worked or traded with: 'I stand behind Jide for up to £100 until June.' You say who, the most you will pay (the cap) and the day it ends, and what it rests on (shifts, orders, years you have known them), from your record or in your own words. It pays only if a judge named in a deal says the one you vouch for let someone down in that deal. Each payment is for one named deal, never goes past the cap, and the record shows how much is left; a claim made after the day counts for nothing. You write it, they accept it, and you can narrow it or let it lapse, but a claim already made stands. The one you vouch for may sign back, 'if you pay for me, I owe it back, plus £10': that is his own promise, and it is his to give. A vouch can also stand behind a title ('if a judge confirms another owner has a better claim to these goats, up to £200 of mine is the buyer's'), or behind a lot and so to whoever holds it, so the eater who bought through a shop can claim under the maker's own vouch. It binds only you. A word with nothing behind it is not a vouch: it is a recommendation, a review or a proof, and is shown as that. Your word sits beside theirs, and whoever reads it decides what it is worth. Kept apart from Guaranteeing someone's loan (you step into one lender's place for one loan); Giving your word on something (a private word with nothing behind it); and Sending proof (certificates and results). It usually starts when someone leaves a job, applies elsewhere, asks for a reference, takes on a big first deal, or a long run of shifts or deliveries makes your word worth backing.

examples.card: Vouch for someone who worked for you.
examples.filled: Ama worked on your line in Lyon for six months and did the plating on Saturdays. Vouch for her, up to €200 until the end of the year?

examples.card: Vouch for a picker.
examples.filled: Tomás picked on your fruit farm in Murcia for three harvests, fast and clean. Vouch for him, up to €150 until next season?

examples.card: Vouch for a supplier.
examples.filled: Hill Mill has delivered to your Leeds bakery on time for two years. Vouch for it, up to £500 until March?

examples.card: Vouch for a new member of your group.
examples.filled: A chama in Nairobi: you have known Wanjiru for ten years. Vouch for her, up to KSh 10,000 for her first year?

examples.card: Vouch for someone you hired for a job.
examples.filled: Leo catered a 40-person party in Cape Town: spotless and on budget. Vouch for him, up to R2,000 until June?

examples.filled: Sam is leaving a café in Dublin. Write a plain reference, or put €100 behind your word and vouch for him?

examples.card: Vouch that a family is who they say and how many they are.
examples.filled: Your neighbour Aisha fled the same village in Kasai. Tell the desk her family is five, as a plain word or with $50 behind it?

examples.card: Vouch for a new member, and take his pay-back.
examples.filled: Jide joins the bakers' co-op in Lagos and two members each stand behind him for ₦50,000. He signs back that he owes it if either pays. Sign your vouch?

examples.filled: A broker at the border market in Moyale sells 12 goats. Vouch that if a judge finds another owner has a better claim, up to KSh 30,000 of yours is the buyer's?

examples.card: Vouch for a lot, to whoever holds it.
examples.filled: Your dairy's cheese reaches eaters through shops. Vouch for each lot up to £500, so the last holder can claim under it?

move words.card: Ama's record from Lucca says she served you 40 times. Confirm it?
move words.note: Confirming the history someone brought from another platform; it puts your name behind it.

examples.card: Confirm someone's imported history.
examples.filled: 40 orders served by Ama at Lucca.
