move words.card: You worked 8 months under Chef Luca at Lucca. Ask him to put a signed word on your record?
move words.note: You ask someone you worked or traded with to put their money and signed word behind you. They can say yes, say no or not answer, and you cannot edit what they write.

examples.card: Ask a boss for a vouch when you leave a job.
examples.filled: You picked for 3 harvests at a fruit farm in Murcia. Ask the farmer to vouch for you?

examples.card: Ask a regular buyer to vouch for your goods.
examples.filled: A buyer in Kumasi has taken your shea butter every month for a year. Ask her to vouch for you?

move words.trigger: Her record shows a long run of shifts, orders or deliveries with one person, the job or deal has ended, and no signed word from them is on her record yet.

you do this when: You put your own money behind a person you worked or traded with, up to a cap and a day, on any deal they make. Not one named loan.

name: Following someone
card: Kofi's farm posts what's picked each morning, 2km away. Follow it?
note: You choose to keep hearing from a chef, a farm, a friend's cooking, a food truck's location, a restaurant's specials, a market stall or a supplier's prices. You say how often, which kinds and until when, and only they see that you follow; you can stop any time. What they post reaches you in the order you set. When someone you follow moves, they say where, and you choose whether to follow again. Kept apart from Finding someone to deal with (looking once); Checking market prices (prices at one moment); and Checking on someone (how a person you care for is doing). It usually starts when you like a chef or farm, find a supplier you trust, or want to know when a price moves.

examples.card: Follow a chef.
examples.filled: You loved the ramen at a chef's place in Fukuoka. Follow every new recipe from them?

examples.card: Follow a food truck.
examples.filled: The dumpling truck in Portland moves each day. Follow where it parks?

examples.card: Follow a farm's harvest.
examples.filled: Kofi's farm posts what is picked each morning, 2 km away in Kumasi. Follow it?

examples.card: Follow a supplier's prices.
examples.filled: Your café in Leeds buys flour from Hill Mill. Follow its price and be told when it moves?

examples.card: Follow a friend's cooking.
examples.filled: A friend in Lagos bakes on Sundays. Follow her bakes?

you do this when: You choose to keep hearing from a chef, a farm, a stall or a supplier's prices.

name: Putting money into a business
card: 40 regulars buy from you every week. Offer them a share of the bakery to pay for a second oven?
note: You raise money by selling part of your business, to regulars, a co-op, a neighbour or a partner. What each share earns and what it decides are terms you set. You ask or offer, they accept, they pay, and you hand over the share. How someone with a share can sell, who has first right, and how a share is valued when someone leaves are agreed first. Buyers see your own signed accounts, never a promise of what they will earn. The law on selling shares differs by place, and the card reads it from there. A loan is Borrowing money, because a loan is paid back and a share is not. Investing in a business: You put money into a food business for a share of what it earns: a regular backing the local bakery, a farmer buying into a co-op. You ask, the business offers a share, you accept and pay. Later you take what it pays out, sell your share on, or cash it out. What you can do and when (what cashing out early costs as a signed sum, how your share is valued, any vote) is in the terms you sign up front; the business signs the figures. If it fails, you are paid after everyone else. Tax on what it pays you is shown as required. Kept apart from Sharing ownership with your team (a share for the people who work there); Selling your business (you sell the whole business, so the owner changes); Selling land, water or quota (the thing sold is ground or rights); Buying a food business (you take the whole thing over); Paying ahead for a share of the harvest (you share one season's luck, not the business); Buying land, water or quota (you buy the thing itself for good); and Lending money (a loan, not a share). It usually starts when you need money for something, such as a second oven, when regulars or a co-op want to back you, or when a partner asks to buy in; as Investing in a business, when a business you use asks its regulars for money, when a co-op opens shares, when you have savings and a food business you trust, or when a share is offered for sale.

examples.card: Sell part of your business to raise money.
examples.filled: Your bakery in Cork needs a second oven. Offer some of your regulars a part of the business?

examples.card: Let neighbours buy into something you run together.
examples.filled: Your village mill in Pokhara, Nepal, needs a new press. Offer neighbours shares in its earnings at 2,000 rupees each?

examples.card: Bring in a partner who buys a part of the business.
examples.filled: A chef from Lyon asks to buy a fifth of your restaurant. Accept?

examples.card: Buy a share of a bakery or café that asks its regulars.
examples.filled: Hill St Bakery is selling 10% to its regulars for £5,000. You buy there every week. Put in?

examples.card: Buy into a co-op you sell through.
examples.filled: The dairy co-op in Anand is opening new shares at ₹2,000 each. Buy some?

examples.card: Buy a stake in a business a friend is starting.
examples.filled: Your friend's coffee roastery in Austin sells 5% stakes at $2,000, no vote, cash-out after 3 years. Put in?

examples.card: Investing in a business
examples.filled: Your cousin's juice bar in Accra needs GH₵ 20,000 for a second blender line and offers 10% of profits. Put in?

move words.card: The bakery signed a profit of £18,000 for the year; your 1% pays £180 or 60 loaves. Take it?
move words.note: Your share of profit, in money or in kind.

examples.card: Take your share of the profit.
examples.filled: £180 or 60 loaves.

move words.trigger: A business she holds a share in has reported what it earned, or the payout date in her terms has come.

move words.card: Ana will buy your 1% of the bakery for £550. Sell it?
move words.note: Passing your stake to someone else; the business may need to agree first.

examples.card: Sell your stake to another backer.
examples.filled: 1% of the bakery to Ana.

move words.trigger: Someone has offered to buy her stake, or its value in her record has moved well away from what she paid.

move words.card: You can cash out your £500 stake from June, at £470, the value the co-op signed. Ask?
move words.note: Getting your money back out, with its rules and the risk that it is worth less.

examples.card: Ask to cash out your stake.
examples.filled: £470 from a £500 stake.

move words.trigger: The date from which her terms let her take money out has come, or the sum she signed for cashing out early is about to apply.

known as: Selling a share of your business

sides.from: Selling a share of your business

you do this when: Money goes into a business for a share of what it earns: you invest or you sell part of yours. Not a loan, not the whole business.

name: Receiving a gift
card: Ama sent you a £20 voucher for the market café. Send her a thank-you?
note: You receive something given to you: food, money, equipment or a voucher. You can take it, say no, thank the giver, or pass it on to someone who can use it. A gift asks nothing back. If you want to give something back later, that is your own note, not a debt. An idea is not property (Kinsella), so a recipe told to you is not a gift received. Kept apart from Giving and receiving food (the food is shared with no giver you thank in particular); and Inheriting something (land, a business or a record is handed down). It usually starts when something arrives from someone, a thank-you is still unsaid, or a gift is one you cannot use.

examples.card: Write a thank-you to someone who fed or helped you.
examples.filled: A neighbour dropped soup when you were ill. Send a warm note?

examples.card: Pass on a gift you cannot use to someone who can.
examples.filled: The neighbour gave you a turkey; you are vegetarian. Pass it to Jo?

examples.card: Decline a gift you cannot take, kindly.
examples.filled: A cousin in Lagos offers you a goat for the festival, but you have nowhere to keep it. Thank him and say no?

examples.card: Accept a gift of food or money.
examples.filled: Your aunt in Pune sent a box of mangoes with the driver. Take them and call her tonight?

move words.card: Aunt Wanjiru gave you 2,000 shillings at your wedding. Her daughter marries on 3 May. Note to give the same then?
move words.note: Some gifts carry a duty to give back at the giver's own occasion, matching what they gave. You note the duty and the date.

examples.card: Note a gift to match at the giver's own celebration.
examples.filled: Your neighbour in Lagos gave a goat at your naming ceremony. His son's is on 12 June. Note to give a goat then?

examples.card: Note a wedding gift to return in kind.
examples.filled: Your cousin in Seoul gave an envelope of 100,000 won at your wedding. Her wedding is in October. Note to give the same then?

move words.trigger: A gift she received is in her record, and the giver's own occasion falls on a date that they or a public calendar have shared.

you do this when: You receive a present given to you in particular: food, money, equipment, a voucher.

name: Grading produce
card: This week's tomatoes sort at 60% grade A. Sort the rest for the sauce maker?
note: You sort, grade, clean and weigh what was harvested or caught, before it is sold: mangoes into export, local and juice, fish by size for the auction, teff threshed and winnowed. You start the sort, write down the weights and grades, bring in helpers, and pass the lots on. It repeats with each harvest or landing. A buyer's grade and yours can differ, so say which standard you graded by. Kept apart from Making a batch (a new product); Preserving food (keeping a glut); Preparing food for sale (small packs); and Storing a harvest (drying and holding). It usually starts when a harvest or catch arrives, or when a buyer names the grades they want.

examples.card: Sort and grade a harvest before you sell it.
examples.filled: Sort 300 kg of mangoes into export, local and juice at your packhouse in Multan?

examples.card: Size the catch before the auction.
examples.filled: Your boat in Galicia lands hake at dawn. Sort it by size for the 7am auction?

examples.card: Winnow and clean grain before it is weighed.
examples.filled: You've threshed your teff in the Ethiopian highlands. Winnow it before the trader's scale tomorrow?

examples.card: Say where the graded-out produce goes.
examples.filled: You graded 140 kg of mangoes out in Kitale. Offer them to the juice maker, feed the pigs next door, or compost them?

examples.card: Sort eggs by size and set cracked and dirty ones apart before you sell.
examples.filled: Your 360 eggs this week at the packing shed in Lancashire sort into small, medium, large and cracked. Sell the large to the shop and keep the rest for the stall?

examples.card: Machine rejects
examples.filled: The egg grader threw out two trays at day's end. Do you count the cracked eggs or sell them as seconds?

examples.card: Decide what the cosmetic rejects become.
examples.filled: Your farm in Kent graded out 600 kg of misshapen carrots. Offer them to the food charity, or sell them to the juicer?

you do this when: You sort, grade, clean and weigh what was harvested or caught before it is sold. Not repacking or cutting it.

name: Recalling food
card: Batch 14 of the soup may contain sesame; 38 jars went to 6 shops. Recall it and tell them now?
note: You pull back food, seed, sprays or farm inputs after they have gone out. You work out who has the batch, tell all of them, and watch each one confirm they have pulled it ('told 38, confirmed 31'). It stays open until you close it. Everyone who returns it gets back what your notice or the law says: money, a replacement or a fix. The people you told pass it on in Acting on a recall. If an authority orders the recall, the report to it is Reporting to an authority. Buyers you cannot name, such as cash customers at a stall, are reached by a notice at the stall or a public warning, and are shown as reached by notice, not confirmed. When a batch is destroyed, you add a photo and the word of whoever watched or collected it. Each return is counted as it comes in; whoever has not answered is shown as not heard from and is tried another way, and what has not come back is shown as still out. Kept apart from Reporting a problem to someone who can act (a buyer warning the public); Warning people nearby (a heads-up to neighbours, not a pull-back); and Labelling food (facts on the pack before it goes out). It usually starts when a test or a complaint finds a fault, an allergen is missing from the label, a seed lot or spray fails a test, or a supplier recalls something you used.

examples.card: Recall a batch and tell everyone who has it.
examples.filled: Batch 14 of your soup in Glasgow may contain sesame. 6 shops told, 31 of 38 jars back. Tell the last two shops now?

examples.card: Recall or correct a product and tell everyone who has it.
examples.filled: Your bakery in Perth found a wrong label, and 23 customers bought the loaf. Send them the notice?

examples.card: Recall a seed lot that failed its test.
examples.filled: Lot 22 of your maize seed failed germination in Kitale; 140 farmers bought it. Recall it and tell them now?

examples.card: Tell diners about a dish you served.
examples.filled: The chicken salad went to 41 diners on Saturday: 29 booked ahead and 12 paid cash. Message the 29 and put a sign on the door for the rest?

examples.card: Tell people when a bed you picked from is closed.
examples.filled: The council posted a closure on the cockle bed on Tuesday, and you sold 2 kilos from it on Saturday. Tell the stall and your sister?

you do this when: You pull back food, seed or inputs after they have gone out.

name: Controlling pests
card: The weekly trap check at your bakery found no catches. Sign the pest record?
note: You keep rodents, flies and insects out of kitchens, stores, markets and granaries: traps, checks, and blocking the gaps they get in by. You start the plan, change it when something turns up, note each check, and mark it done; it repeats weekly. A pest firm you pay is Doing or getting a job for pay. Where the law asks for a pest record, you keep one. Crop pests are part of Growing crops. Kept apart from Cleaning (dirt); Guarding against theft (people); Keeping food fresh (loss to age); and Storing a harvest (keeping a crop dry and sound). It usually starts when droppings or a sighting turn up, a check falls due, an inspection is coming, or a delivery or season brings pests.

examples.card: Check traps and keep a pest record.
examples.filled: The weekly trap check at your bakery in Cork found no catches. Sign the record?

examples.card: Call a pest firm when you see signs.
examples.filled: Two mouse droppings by the flour sacks this morning in a Sheffield kitchen. Call the pest firm today for about £90, or set traps yourself?

examples.card: Block a store against rodents.
examples.filled: Your grain store in Punjab is weeks from harvest. Fit metal sheeting to the door bottom and seal the gaps?

examples.card: Keep flies off food at a market stall.
examples.filled: Afternoon heat brings flies to your fish stall in Dakar. Cover the display and set fly strips?

examples.card: Check the henhouse for red mite and rats.
examples.filled: A white cloth under the perch in your henhouse in Kent shows red mite at dusk. Treat the house this weekend?

examples.card: A fumigation visit and when the store may open
examples.filled: The man came to fumigate the maize stack. When did he say it is safe?

examples.card: A fumigation visit and when the store may open
examples.filled: You found weevils in two bags near the door. What did you do about them?

examples.filled: You plan to treat the granary on Saturday, and two children sleep in the next room. Do it when they are away?

name: Checking market prices
card: Tomatoes are posted at KSh 40 a kilo at Wakulima today by 6 traders, and your 300 kg are ready. Take them in tomorrow?
note: You find out what food or work is going for, before you buy, sell or take a job: the market, the mandi, the fish wharf, the exchange, a price board, a phone group, and the day rates for work like yours. FoodOS shows each price with its source, place, date and hour ('told by phone, not posted' where so), and never 'the market price'. Prices for delivery later are shown apart from today's, and rates for work are shown per day, kilo or piece. You read them and decide where and when. Each price says whether it was asked, told or paid; the prices paid come from records people shared with Share only the answer. Kept apart from Checking how things are going (your own sales and costs); Finding someone to deal with (who will take your goods); Following someone (prices coming to you over time); and Switching to a better deal (leaving what you pay for now). It usually starts when it is the evening before market, a harvest is picked, before you place an order or accept a rate, or when a price you rely on has moved.

examples.card: Check the day's price before you buy or take produce to market.
examples.filled: Onions are KSh 60 at Marikiti and KSh 52 at Kangemi. Buy at Kangemi?

examples.card: See how your prices compare with others nearby.
examples.filled: A photo of the next stall's price board in Brixton: your tomatoes are 30p a kilo dearer, your eggs the cheapest. Change your tomato price, or keep it?

examples.card: Work out what a batch is worth and where to sell it.
examples.filled: Forty kilos of apples: about £60 a crate at the market in Bath, £45 to a shop nearby. Take them to Bath?

examples.card: Check the fish price at the landing wharf.
examples.filled: Kochi wharf this morning: the first boats are in and sardines are posted at 90 rupees a kilo. Place a bid for your fish shop?

examples.card: Check a mandi price before selling grain.
examples.filled: Wheat is posted at Rs 2,300 a quintal at the Indore mandi, Rs 2,240 at Ujjain and Rs 2,190 at Dewas. Take yours in tomorrow?

you do this when: You find out what food or work is going for outside, before you buy, sell or take a job.

name: Fetching water or fuel
card: The borehole queue is short before 7. Fetch two jerrycans now?
note: You fetch what you cook and drink with rather than buy it: water from a well, a river, a standpipe or a borehole, firewood from the field's edge. In many homes it takes hours a day, and the card shows the trip in time and carrying. You make the trip and bring it home. A shared standpipe's hours or rota are its group's rule. Kept apart from Selling water or fuel by the load (from a tanker or kiosk for a price); Foraging (wild food); and Moving food to someone (an order made for you). It usually starts when the queue is short at its time of day, the jerrycans run low, a source is rationed or dries up, or the wood store is down.
no mirror: none: nature, or a shared supply

examples.card: Fetch water for the day's cooking.
examples.filled: Two 20-litre jerrycans from the borehole. Go now while the queue is short?

examples.card: Collect firewood for cooking.
examples.filled: A bundle of dry wood from the edge of the field. Fetch it this evening?

examples.card: Draw water from a shared tap at the hour it runs.
examples.filled: The standpipe in the Dharavi lane opens at 5am for an hour. Fill the drums now?

examples.card: Gather fuel for a stove before the rains come.
examples.filled: The rains start in a week in Malawi. Collect and stack wood for the month?

you do this when: You collect water or firewood yourself, for nothing, rather than buy it.

name: Ordering stock
card: Flour is under 2 bags and Allied takes orders until 4pm. Put the order in?
note: You order from a supplier and pay later: a café, a home baker, a trader or a boat, in time for the supplier's last order time, with a delivery note and an invoice. What a business uses up but does not sell (a boat's fuel and ice, packaging, gas for the kitchen) is here too. You ask, they accept, the goods arrive and are checked in, and you pay the invoice later. The supplier's terms (2% off within 10 days, 30 days to pay) are part of the order. A standing reorder is a permission you give FoodOS, with a quantity, a level that triggers it and an end date. Kept apart from Buying to sell on (a trader buys to sell elsewhere); Supplying on contract (terms agreed with a supplier for a time); Buying and selling food to use (paid for there and then); and Subscribing (a seller's fixed regular offer). It usually starts when stock runs below a minimum, when a supplier's last order time is near, when next week's bake or trip needs supplies, when an invoice falls due, or when the same item keeps being noted as a missed sale or thrown away.
no mirror: none: each order falls under a supplier's standing terms, whose side is Supplying a business

examples.card: Pay an invoice on the day that suits your cash.
examples.filled: Pay the £800 invoice on the 28th after your takings, still within terms?

examples.card: Buy what you'll use or sell next week.
examples.filled: Buy 40 kilos of flour for next week's bake?

examples.card: Chase a late order or delivery with a polite message.
examples.filled: Veg due Tuesday has not come. Send the supplier a note asking for a new time today?

examples.card: Buy fuel and ice before a fishing trip.
examples.filled: Order 200 litres of diesel and 1 tonne of ice for Friday's trip from Walvis Bay?

examples.card: Buy on the spot at a cash-and-carry.
examples.filled: You bought rice, oil and sugar for Rs 18,400 at the wholesale yard in Pune. Photograph the bill and check the goods in?

examples.card: Delivery left on the step
examples.filled: The milk was on the step at 5.10, one carton short. Check it in with a photo?

examples.card: Order the week's flour and lentils for the kitchen.
examples.filled: The langar kitchen in Leicester has two days of flour left. Order 50 kg from the wholesaler, to be paid from the fund?

examples.card: Weigh a supplier's offer against how past ones sold.
examples.filled: The distributor gives 2 free cartons for every 20 until Sunday. The last three times, 14, 9 and 17 cartons were still unsold six weeks later. Take it, take part, or skip it?

examples.card: Pay inside an early-payment window.
examples.filled: The dairy's invoice says 2 percent off if paid by Friday, otherwise due on the 26th. Pay it now?

you do this when: A business orders what it will use or sell from a supplier and pays later, in time for the supplier's cut-off. Not a trader's load bought where it is cheap.

name: Buying growing supplies
card: The long rains start in 3 weeks. The Kitale dealer has certified maize seed at KSh 6,200 a bag, with its certificate. Buy some?
note: You buy what a farm needs to grow: seed, seedlings, fertiliser, animal feed, medicines, vaccines and sprays, in time for the season. Medicine or medicated feed bought without a vet goes on your record with its label, batch and expiry; a photo is enough. Miss the planting window and you wait a year. You ask the dealer, they offer, you accept, and it is handed over. You pay now, or from the harvest in grain or its price; from the harvest, you agree what you owe and when, often who you must sell the crop to, and who bears a failed harvest, and the card shows the cash price today beside it. A promise about seed or fertiliser (certified, how many seeds sprout) is shown only with the certificate for that lot, and the dealer's return terms. A government voucher for farm inputs is spent at the dealers on its list. Feed bought ahead is a bet on the price, so you note what you expect. Live inputs (predator mites, wasps, bumblebee hives, young plants) arrive on a set day and last a few weeks. Kept apart from Supplying on contract (standing terms with one supplier); Borrowing money (you are lent money, not given inputs); Ordering stock (other things a business uses up); and Buying animals (live animals). It usually starts when the planting window is weeks away, rains are forecast, feed runs low, a subsidy voucher arrives, or last season's repayment falls due.

examples.card: Use a subsidy voucher to buy inputs.
examples.filled: Your e-voucher at the agro-dealer in Kano covers half the fertiliser. Use it before the season?

examples.card: Buy feed before the dry season makes it dear.
examples.filled: Hay is ₹8 a kilo in Rajasthan now; last April it was ₹16. Buy some to store?

examples.card: Buy seedlings for the planting date.
examples.filled: The nursery near Wageningen has lettuce seedlings for the 15th. Order them?

examples.card: Buy spare plants or seed that someone has too many of.
examples.filled: A neighbour in Ibadan has spare tomato seedlings at ₦50 each. Take some?

you do this when: You buy what a farm needs to grow, in time for the season: seed, feed, fertiliser, medicines.

name: Buying animals
card: Day-old chicks at Kenchic are KSh 110 each. Book 300 for the 12th?
note: You buy young or breeding animals to raise: chicks, piglets, heifers, fingerlings, semen straws (frozen seed for breeding). You ask the seller, they offer, you accept and pay, and the animals are handed over with health papers and movement records, and often a quarantine period (kept apart before they join your herd). When you book ahead you pay for animals that come later: the card shows the deposit, what backs the seller's word (health papers signed by their vet, live arrival, a replacement for early deaths), and the steps the law requires (movement permits, tests, ear tags, reports) as costs. A butcher or an abattoir buying finished animals straight from a farm buys here too. Kept apart from Buying at auction (animals bought at a market by bidding); Buying growing supplies (feed and seed); Paying ahead for a share of the harvest (a herd share is a share of what the herd gives); and Supplying on contract (a supply agreed for a term). It usually starts when a house or pen is empty, when a breeding plan says it is time, when stock is lost or sold, or when a season suits raising a batch.

examples.card: Buy young animals to raise.
examples.filled: Eight-week-old piglets at a farm near Lublin are zł 300 each. Book them for March?

examples.filled: Straws from a proven bull for your herd in Punjab are ₹900 each. Order some?

you do this when: You buy young or breeding animals to raise. Not at a bidding market, not feed.

name: Getting your product made
card: Your chutney sells 400 jars a month. A co-packer (a maker who makes products for other brands) quotes 90p a jar for 2,000. Ask for a sample run?
note: You have a co-packer (a factory or kitchen that makes products for other brands) make your product to your recipe and label, so you can sell more than your own kitchen can make. You give the brief, they make a sample run, you order, they make it, quality checks follow, and you pay, often in stages. Your recipe stays with you; it goes to the maker only on terms you set (this maker, this product, until a date, never for anyone else). The smallest order, set-up costs, deposit and who answers for the label, allergens and a recall are agreed up front. You can pull out before the order. Kept apart from Having food processed (your own food goes in and comes back changed); Doing or getting a job for pay (a job that is not your product); and Ordering stock (goods you order and pay for later). It usually starts when orders outgrow your kitchen, when a shop wants volume you cannot meet, or when a co-packer sends a quote.

examples.card: Have a maker make your product.
examples.filled: A maker in Leicester quotes 90p a jar to make 2,000 of your chutney. Ask for a sample run?

examples.card: Have a factory make a product to your recipe and label.
examples.filled: A juice maker near Nairobi can bottle your mango juice at KSh 40 a bottle. Ask for a sample run?

examples.filled: A women's cooperative kitchen in Kigali can make your chilli oil in batches of 500 jars. Ask for a sample batch?

examples.filled: The co-packer in Leicester wants your chutney recipe. Share it for this product only, until 2027, and never for sale to others?

you do this when: A co-packer makes your product to your recipe and label, so you sell more than your own kitchen can make.

name: Buying a food business
card: The mill near Mbale is for sale with its two machines and its customers. Ask the price?
note: You take over a café, bakery, mill or farm business that is already running: its kit, stock, lease, contracts, name and the record of what it did. You ask to see the books, make an offer and agree terms. It is handed over in stages: a deposit, then the day you take the keys, sometimes with part of the price paid later from what it earns. The landlord, suppliers and staff each say yes to their part, licences are applied for again, transfer tax is due, and any debts you take on are part of the deal. Its customers come with the name, but each one still chooses whether to keep buying. Kept apart from Putting money into a business (a share); Selling a brand (a name only); and Buying land, water or quota (land or rights). It usually starts when an owner retires or moves on, when a business you use is listed for sale, or when you want to grow by taking over a neighbour.

examples.card: Take over a food business with its regulars.
examples.filled: The corner bakery in Lyon is for sale with its ovens, lease and sales history. Make an offer?

examples.card: Take over a café with its lease.
examples.filled: The café on Mill St is for sale with its lease, its kit and its sales history. Ask to see the books?

examples.card: Take over a working farm.
examples.filled: A 12-acre vegetable farm near Pune is for sale with its stock and its sales record. Ask to see the accounts?

you do this when: You take over a running business whole: kit, stock, lease, name and record. Not a share, not the ground alone.

name: Buying land, water or quota
card: An acre with a borehole near Thika is offered at KSh 1.4m. Check the title and the water rights?
note: You buy a field, a plot, water rights, grazing rights or fishing quota for good. You ask, check who holds it (a registry title, or the family or clan where tenure is customary), have it surveyed, agree a price, pay a deposit held by someone neither side controls, and the transfer is made. A water right or a quota is permission the state or a basin authority gave and may change. Stamp duty and transfer tax are due, and a loan to pay for it is Borrowing money. You can sell it later. Kept apart from Renting land or a place to trade (for a season or a lease); Putting money into a business (a share of a business); and Buying a food business (a whole business). It usually starts when land next to yours comes up, a quota is offered, your farm outgrows its water, or a lease is about to end.

examples.card: Buy land, quota or water rights for good.
examples.filled: Buy 2 tonnes of permanent hake quota in Galicia?

examples.card: Buy the field next to yours.
examples.filled: The 3-acre field next to yours is for sale at KSh 900,000. Check the title?

examples.card: Buy a water right for your farm.
examples.filled: A well-water right in Mendoza is offered at $4,000. Check the records?

you do this when: You buy a field, water or fishing rights for good. Not renting, not a share of a business.

name: Selling at a stall, a gate or a screen
card: A shopper offers £10 for 4 jars of your jam priced at £3 each. Take it?
note: You run a stall on market day: setting out, selling, haggling and packing up what is left. It covers growers, makers and traders, and repeats each market day or season. Haggling is offer and counter-offer, and different prices for different people are yours to set. A pitch is rented from the market, or paid as a fee the authority sets. At the end of the day you count what is left, and it sits beside what you sold. A sale someone will pay for tomorrow is marked as owed. Selling on the move: You sell by going to where the buyers are: on foot with a head tray, a cart, a bike, in the traffic queue, on a train. You walk to the crowd, the crowd does not walk to you. You go to the crowd, sell, hand over, take payment and move on. The day ends with a count of what you carried out and what you brought back. Selling at your gate: You sell from your own gate, farm shop or roadside stall, with no market day and often no one there. You set out what you have, put prices on it, take cash, mobile money or a card, and restock. Customers choose and pay at the stall, or leave money in a box. Each restock is a count, and emptying the box is the cash count set beside it. Selling online: You sell to people you already reach by message, a group chat or your own page, without an app taking a cut. You post what you have and the price, they reply and pay, and you hand it over or send it. An order or a quote agreed by voice note, a call or at the school gate is written down from your own words. If a courier collects the buyer's cash, that money is owed to you until the courier pays you, and you can chase it. An order that comes in a message, a voice note or a photo becomes the order, with its date, deposit, allergies and pickup, so the thread is not the record. Kept apart from Buying and selling food to use (a counter in your own place); Selling spare food (clearing leftovers); Selling as a group (growers pool produce); Taking orders in advance (orders for a batch made later); and Selling through an app (a platform in the middle). It usually starts when market day comes round, produce comes into season, or a shopper stops at the stall; as Selling on the move, when a crowd gathers at a place and time you know from your own days selling, such as a bus stage at lunch, when stock is ready, or when a public event brings people near; as Selling at your gate, when produce comes in, when passing trade is busy, or when the table is bare; as Selling online, when you have something to sell, when people in your group ask, or when an order comes in by message.

move words.note: A day she did not trade, with her own word for why. It keeps the days worked and the days lost in her record, which she carries and can share. It does not close anything and does not judge.

mirror: Buying and selling food to use

name: Selling through an app
card: Uber Eats took 30% on your 41 orders last month; your own link took 0% on 22. Change your app prices?
note: You keep a standing relationship with a platform that sells or books for you: a delivery app, a table-booking service, a listing site. You join on its terms, list your menu and prices, take payouts, see your ratings, pay for promotions, and leave or are removed. The platform's cut shows as a line on every payout. Promotions you pay for are labelled as paid to customers. Ratings and ranking are the platform's own. A promise not to charge less elsewhere may be in what you signed, and it shows before you change prices. Your orders and customers are your record too, and you take your copy when you leave. A travel agent or tour operator who books for a commission is the same shape as an app. Kept apart from Buying and selling food to use (each single order); Selling through an agent (a person who sells for a cut); and Supplying on contract (a direct deal with a business). It usually starts when a platform invites you, when a payout statement comes, when fees or ranking change, when a promotion is offered, or when a payout covers fewer orders than your own list.

name: Selling subscriptions
card: 8 people buy your bread every week. Offer them a monthly subscription?
note: You sell a veg box, a bread round, a milk delivery or a meal plan that comes regularly, paid ahead or monthly. You offer it, they accept and pay, you hand over each delivery, and they can skip, pause or cancel. For money paid ahead, the card shows what you owe in deliveries and what comes back if you stop. Kept apart from Paying ahead for a share of the harvest (subscribers share the season's luck); Selling vouchers (a pass used when they like); Taking orders in advance (orders for a date); Running a loyalty scheme (rewards earned, not paid for); and Supplying on contract (standing supply to a business). It usually starts when someone buys the same thing every week, a renewal date nears, or a subscriber skips or cancels.

examples.card: Ask a one-time buyer to become a regular.
examples.filled: Ana has bought the same loaf from you three Saturdays running. Ask if she wants it every week?

name: Supplying on contract
card: A school in Kampala wants 200 kg of beans a month at UGX 3,800 a kilo. Agree?
note: You supply a shop, café or processor on standing terms: the price, the days, quality bonuses and penalties, invoices and days to pay. You ask or offer, the buyer agrees, you hand over on each delivery day, they receive and pay, and quality is noted. On a regular run you note each handover as you go (the litres to the cooler, the kilos of leaf at the buying centre, the crates to the school), and when the statement comes your tally is laid beside it. Either side can change or end it on the terms agreed. Buying on contract: You agree terms with one supplier for a time: a standing order, a volume, a discount for buying only from them. You ask, they offer, you accept, and the terms run: orders arrive and are paid for until the term ends. The card shows any amount you must take or pay for, and what leaving early costs. A price fixed ahead on its own is Agreeing a price for later. Kept apart from Growing to a buyer's contract (a crop grown before there is anything to deliver); Selling through an agent (left on sale or return); Selling and buying in bulk (one big sale); Running or answering a tender (a public contract); Buying growing supplies (inputs for one season); Subscribing (a seller's fixed offer); Ordering stock (one order on account); and Buying to sell on (to resell). It usually starts when a buyer asks for steady supply, a delivery day comes, stock runs low, the price changes, a statement arrives, or an invoice is due; as Buying on contract, when you buy the same thing often, when a supplier will cut the price for a promise, when a term ends, or when prices are about to rise.

name: Running or answering a tender
card: The county schools' tender for a term's beans closes Friday. Prepare a bid?
note: You bid to supply a school, hospital, council or aid agency. You read the spec and ask about it, send your sealed quote, hear whether you won, and if you did, accept and supply against the contract. A deposit or guarantee, and papers you must have first (tax clearance, registration), are set by the buyer. Public buyers often pay in 60 days or more, so you wait for your money, and the card shows the days and what they cost you. The buyer's scoring is theirs. You can withdraw before the close. Running a tender: You buy the way schools, hospitals, councils and big kitchens do: you write down what you need, ask suppliers for sealed quotes, and choose one by the rules you published. Nobody reads the quotes until the closing time. You compare them with what you asked for and pick one; the act ends there, and the contract it makes runs as Supplying on contract, with each delivery ordered as Ordering stock. What backs a quote (a deposit, a guarantee the supplier will deliver), who judges quality disputes and how many days you take to pay are in the call for quotes. A rule that you must ask for competing quotes may bind you. Kept apart from Selling and buying in bulk (one sale to a trade buyer); Selling as a group (growers pool produce); Selling under a scheme (a shopper paying with a voucher or card from a scheme); Supplying on contract (a standing deal agreed directly); Buying at auction (the price is found by bidding); and Ordering stock (orders on an account). It usually starts when a tender is published for something you supply and its closing date is near, or when a contract you hold ends and is tendered again; as Running a tender, when a term is about to begin, a supply contract is ending, a budget is approved, or a rule says you must ask for competing quotes.

name: Catering for an occasion
card: Final numbers for Saturday are due: 112 confirmed, 9 vegan. Send the order to the supplier?
note: You do the whole job of feeding an event for a client: enquiry, tasting, quote and deposit, final numbers and diets, crew, hired kit, serving on site and clearing down. It covers an office lunch, a wedding, a funeral meal or a village feast. A quote, or a payment in instalments for a large order, belongs to it. A client asks, you quote and they accept with a deposit, you confirm numbers and diets, serve on the day, clear down and get paid. Whether the deposit comes back, who bears food already bought if the client cancels late, who keeps what is left over, and what a late addition on the night costs are agreed first. How many came, what was left and what was added on the night are noted on the day, each with the client's word beside yours. Diets and allergens are the client's signed word. Here the client buys a whole job with a date. The quote can set a number of guests below which the price does not fall, and the date until which numbers may change. Ordering food for an occasion: You order a cake, catering or a big order for a date: a birthday, wedding, funeral, festival or office lunch. You give the brief, they quote, you accept and pay a deposit, final numbers and diets are agreed by a date, and it is collected or delivered. The deposit, what you lose if you cancel late, and when the rest is due are agreed up front. Diets come from the people the food is for, with their yes; who pays may be a group. Kept apart from Running a food event (you sell tickets to guests); Giving and receiving food (the meal is free); Cooking for a household (you cook for a household for pay); Making products for others (you make a product under someone else's label); Buying and selling food to use (food for now); Subscribing (food that comes regularly, not for a date); and Ordering stock (a business orders on account). It usually starts when an enquiry arrives from a client, a tasting is booked, the date for final numbers and diets comes, hired kit must be reserved, or the day of the event arrives; as Ordering food for an occasion, when a date is set, when numbers are known, when a baker's diary is filling, or when the same occasion comes round again.

name: Cooking for a household
card: The Shahs want 4 dinners a week for ₹3,000. Take it?
note: You cook for one household for pay: a private cook in their kitchen with their food, or weekly meal prep or a tiffin round you cook at home and deliver. You agree what, how often, who buys the ingredients, and when you are paid: weekly ahead, or monthly after, so one side waits. Their diets are theirs to tell you, for as long as they say. Cooking at home to sell needs your home-kitchen rules, read from the place. Either side can stop at any time; stopping early or at short notice costs the sum signed. A live-in or fixed-hours cook is Working for someone. Kept apart from Catering for an occasion (one event for a client); and Making products for others (a product under someone else's label). It usually starts when a household asks for regular meals, a new week begins, a family's diets or numbers change, or the next day's tiffins need cooking.
no mirror: none yet: a household hiring a cook for one job is Getting a contractor in; a cook on hours is Employing someone

name: Making products for others
card: A café chain in Lisbon wants 300 pastéis de nata a day under its name. Quote?
note: You make someone else's product to their recipe, spec and label: co-packing, own-label, contract baking. You are asked, you quote, they accept, you make the batch, hand it over and they pay. Their packaging and ingredients in your care stay theirs, and you use them only for their product; the run's losses are agreed up front. Their recipe is theirs and you promise not to make it for anyone else; your record of the run is yours, and they sign off the batch. When your machine does the work, such as a robot kitchen overnight, you answer for what it makes. Kept apart from Catering for an occasion (one event for a client); and Cooking for a household (meals for one household). It usually starts when a brand or shop asks for a batch, a delivery date is near, their packaging or ingredients arrive, or your kitchen or machine has free time.

name: Having food processed
card: Three neighbours brought 600 kg of cassava to your grater in Ibadan. Grate it for ₦40 a kilo?
note: You mill, hull, press, juice or slaughter other people's food: the posho mill, the atta chakki, the oil expeller, the community press, the slab or abattoir. People bring their food or their animals, you weigh or count it in, agree the fee (per kilo of what came in, per head, or a share kept back such as the bran, the cake, the pomace or the hides), do the work, weigh it out and hand it back. For animals you write the count and the tags at the gate, any papers that came with them, the inspector's call on each lot, what was held back (a condemned liver, the hides you keep as your fee), and the weights out, as one kill sheet the owner keeps. While it waits it is theirs and you may not use it, and the weights in and out are written down, so nobody is short-changed. The queue order and any price for going first are yours to set. You can pass a load to another mill when busy. The fee may be money or a share of what is processed (the bran, the cake, the hides), which is then counted as what you kept. Getting your food processed: You send your own food in and it comes back changed: maize to the posho mill, wheat to the atta chakki, paddy to the huller, apples to the press, an animal to the slaughterhouse, a catch to the smokehouse. You ask, they quote per kilo or keep a share (the bran, the pressed pulp, the hides), you hand your food over, they process it, and you pay and collect. While they hold it, it is yours and they may not use it; the weight in and out are written down, so you can check the yield. Yields other customers posted are shown only with their source. The fee may be money or a share of what is processed (the bran, the cake, the hides), which is then counted as what the processor kept. Kept apart from Making products for others (you make their product to their recipe, not just mill or press what they bring); Looking after someone's animals (animals that stay with you, not animals killed for food); Doing or getting a job for pay (a job with no food handed back); Repairing and treating for pay (your kit fixed); and Getting your product made (their materials to your recipe). It usually starts when customers queue with grain, seed, fruit or animals, the harvest comes in and the queue grows, a festival is near, or the machine has spare time on a quiet day; as Getting your food processed, when a harvest is in, when flour or oil runs out at home, when a pressing season opens, or when an animal is ready.

name: Selling through an agent
card: A honey farmer in Oaxaca asks you to sell her jars at your stall for 10%. Agree?
note: You sell a grower's produce for them and keep a cut: the market agent, the broker, the mandi commission agent. The grower sends produce, which stays theirs until it sells; you sell it at the day's price, within any reserve they set, and pay them the takings less your cut, with a sales sheet showing the prices the buyers signed. Where buyers paid cash and signed nothing, the sheet is your own tally and says so. The grower can read it and answer beside it. Money you hold for them is theirs, and the card shows how long you hold it. Cash or inputs you advance against a load are a loan, with its interest shown apart from the cut. A promise to sell only through you is signed, with what leaving costs. Having someone sell your produce: You send produce to someone who sells it for you: a market agent who sells at the day's price and keeps a cut, or a shop that takes it on sale-or-return and pays you only for what sells. The produce stays yours until it sells. You choose who, send the load with what you expect it to fetch (and a lowest price, if you want one), and they sell, send you the sheet of what each buyer paid, and pay you what is left. Kept apart from Shopping for others (you buy for someone); Buying to sell on (a trader owns the goods and bears the price); Selling and buying in bulk (you sell your own); and Selling at a stall, a gate or a screen (you sell at your own stall). It usually starts when a grower sends a load, a market day opens, the load is sold and the grower waits for the sheet and payment, or a new grower asks you to take their produce; as Having someone sell your produce, when a harvest is ready to go, when a market day nears, when the last load's sheet and payment arrive, or when you must pick who gets the next load.

name: Carrying for pay
card: A co-op near Eldoret needs 200 bags of maize at the depot by Friday. Quote for the haul?
note: You move other people's goods for a fee: a lorry, a van, a boda or a boat. You find or are offered a load, agree a rate and when you are paid (on delivery, half up front, or later), pick it up with a receipt, carry it, and hand it over with proof of delivery. While you hold the goods you answer for them as agreed. Tolls, market fees and weighbridge charges show apart from your rate. A rate agreed on a call counts, and an advance for the road is shown apart from the rate. A photo at pickup and at handover shows the state of the goods. Days you wait at a border or a weighbridge are noted as they pass, and what a post demanded is Paying someone who demands it. If you pass the load to another truck, you stay answerable until the shipper releases you. One truck can carry several shippers' goods on one trip, each a haul of its own with its own pay date. Warnings others post about the road show on a haul in progress. Booking transport: You pay a lorry driver, a boda (motorbike taxi) or a courier to move your goods. You find a truck, they quote per trip or tonne, you accept, hand the goods over with a receipt, and pay against proof of delivery, often part on loading and the rest on arrival. While the carrier holds the goods they answer for loss and spoilage as agreed, and a cold chain is proved by its temperature readings (a probe reading by hand at loading and at handover, signed at each end, or the carrier's logger printout if he has one), and a missing reading stays missing. Tolls, local produce taxes and weighbridge fees the law charges show as required, not in the driver's price. A load can be people: seats in a van to a farm or a kitchen, posted by the driver and asked for one by one. A carrier you have not used is looked at through Checking who you are dealing with. Delivering orders for pay: You deliver orders for a fee: shifts or per-drop pay, many drops a day, through an app, a co-op or straight from a kitchen. A job is offered, you accept, collect, hand each order over and are paid. How your pay is worked out is shown exactly, beside what your own last shifts paid. A fee to be paid now rather than at the weekly payout is a price for time, shown. Your own side of the day stays yours: the cash you took at doors and handed in, tips handed to you, the time you were logged in and waiting, and what the day used (fuel, charging, a repair), beside the app's payout. The day ends with your own count of cash handed in, tips and what you spent, laid beside the app's payout. Kept apart from Moving food to someone (bulk moves over distance and borders); and Working for someone (a wage as an employee). It usually starts when a load is posted that fits your route, a pickup time is set, your vehicle is heading back empty, or proof of delivery is due for payment; as Booking transport, when a harvest or order is ready to move, when a market day is near, when a buyer asks you to deliver, or when a neighbour is sending a load the same way; as Delivering orders for pay, when a shift opens, a kitchen has orders ready, a regular round is due, or the rate on offer beats what you earn elsewhere.

move words.trigger: Shows after a breakdown or hub stop is noted, or when the driver says he is handing the load on.

move words.card: Your lorry leaves for Nakuru at 6 with a third of the space empty. Offer the space left?
move words.note: Offering the space left on a trip, in a store or in a kitchen that is already going, to anyone, at a price you set. It is tied to that trip or slot, and only you know there is room.

examples.card: Offer spare space on a trip already going.
examples.filled: A third of the lorry to Nakuru, leaving at 6, offered at 3,000 a pallet.

move words.trigger: A trip, a store or a booked slot of hers is going with space left.

move words.card: Two neighbours send maize to Wakulima on Thursday. Share the lorry and pay a third each?
move words.note: Sharing one truck with neighbours and splitting the cost.

examples.card: Share a truck with neighbours.
examples.filled: One lorry to Wakulima, a third each.

move words.trigger: Neighbours or sellers she knows are sending goods the same way on the same day, and a truck she has booked has room left.

move words.card: A customer put cash in your hand at the door. Keep it as yours, or put it in the pool your kitchen shares?
move words.note: A tip handed to you is yours: your own note of it, kept in your record. Pooling it happens only by an agreement you signed.

examples.card: Note a tip.
examples.filled: A customer on Park Lane handed you cash at the door. Keep it as yours or put it in the pool?

examples.card: Note a tip.
examples.filled: Your kitchen shares its drivers' tips at the end of the week. This one came in cash: put it in the pool?

examples.card: Note a tip.
examples.filled: A regular left a bag of mangoes with a note. Write it down as a gift to you?

move words.trigger: A drop is finished and the customer paid cash or in the app and the tip in cash is not noted in his record.

you do this when: Someone carries goods for a fee, a load or many small drops: you book the lorry or courier, or you do the carrying; which side is you is read from who signs. Not your own free delivery.

name: Selling your business
card: You are retiring from the bakery in Lyon and your two bakers want to buy it over 5 years. Offer them terms?
note: You sell your food business whole: its kit, stock, lease, name, recipes and the record of what it did. Its followers go with it, and each customer still chooses whether to keep buying. You choose which figures buyers see, a buyer makes an offer, you agree terms, and you hand over in steps. If the price is paid over time, you are lending the rest, so you agree what backs it (a deposit held by someone neither side controls, or a guarantor). If part of the price comes from later earnings, you share in how the business does. Licences that cannot pass need the authority's yes, and staff transfer by the law of the place. You can withdraw before the buyer accepts. The figures you show say how each is known: counted, signed by the other side, or your word. What you have counted is worth more to a buyer. Kept apart from Putting money into a business (part of it); Selling land, water or quota (the ground or rights alone); and Selling a brand (the name only). It usually starts when you decide to retire or move on, a buyer makes an offer, or a lease or licence is up for renewal.

examples.card: Sell your food business as a going concern.
examples.filled: A buyer offers KSh 4M for the shop with its stock and lease. Ask for proof of funds?

examples.card: Value your business before selling.
examples.filled: Your café in Cardiff has five years of takings in your record. Put it up for sale and choose which figures buyers see?

examples.card: Hand over regulars and followers.
examples.filled: The sale of your stall is agreed. Tell your regulars it has a new owner, so each can choose to stay?

you do this when: You sell your food business whole: kit, stock, lease, name, recipes, record.

name: Selling land, water or quota
card: The top field in Wales has been fallow for three years. Put it up for sale at your price?
note: You sell a field, a plot, water or grazing rights, or fishing quota for good. You set your price, a buyer accepts, a deposit is held by someone neither side controls, the transfer is made, and they pay. Who must agree can be your family, your clan or the register, and a neighbour or the state may have first right to buy. A water right or quota is a right the state issued, with its own register. Taxes on the sale are set by law and shown apart from your price. A right let for one season is Renting out land. Kept apart from Selling nature credits (credit for what the land does); Putting money into a business (part of a business); and Selling your business (the whole business). It usually starts when a field stops being farmed, when you leave fishing or farming, when a buyer asks, or when the family decides to sell.

examples.card: Sell a field you no longer farm.
examples.filled: Your lower meadow in Powys has been grazed by no one for two years. Put it up for sale?

examples.card: Sell quota you will no longer fish.
examples.filled: You are selling the boat in Galicia. Sell your 40 tonnes of permanent hake quota with it?

examples.card: Sell a plot with the family's yes.
examples.filled: Your brothers have agreed to sell the lower plot in Muranga. Offer it for sale?

examples.card: Sell a water right you no longer use.
examples.filled: Your farm in Murcia holds a water right you have not used in three years. Offer it to a neighbour who asked?

you do this when: You sell a field, water or fishing rights for good.

name: Saving in a group
card: The VSLA's year closes next week: your 40 shares and what the loans earned come to KSh 18,400. Take it all out, or leave some in for next year?
note: You and your group build a fund that grows: members save in shares, the fund lends to members at a rate the group sets, and savings plus what the loans earned are shared out at the end of the cycle. It covers VSLAs, table banking, SACCO and credit-union savings, and stokvels. What your savings are is said up front: lent to the fund until share-out, a deposit you can take out, or shares that can lose value. You pay in on the schedule, take out savings only where the rule allows, and share out at the end; leaving mid-cycle follows the terms agreed when you joined. Who holds the box or account, and how many must sign to move money, is the group's rule. Borrowing from the fund is Borrowing money. Kept apart from Saving in turns (each takes the whole pot in turn); and Pooling money (a pot one person spends for the group). It usually starts when a group forms, at each meeting date, when a member needs a loan, or when the cycle closes.

examples.card: Save in shares each week and borrow from the group fund.
examples.filled: 5 shares a week at KSh 100 in a VSLA in Kisumu; borrow up to three times your savings. Join the group?

examples.card: Save all year with a grocery stokvel for the December buy.
examples.filled: R300 a month in a Soweto stokvel; bulk buy in December. Join the stokvel?

examples.card: Share out savings and profit at the end of the year.
examples.filled: The VSLA's year closes next week in a village in Malawi: your 40 shares and what the loans earned come to MK 18,400. Take it all out, or leave some in for next year?

move words.card: The year closes: your share with what the loans earned is KSh 18,400. Share out?
move words.note: The end-of-cycle payout of savings and profit.

examples.card: Share out savings and profit at year end.
examples.filled: KSh 18,400 each in December.

move words.trigger: The group's cycle end date has come and the fund is ready to be divided by the rule on record.

move words.card: You need KSh 5,000 for school fees. Withdraw it from your savings?
move words.note: Taking your own savings out, where the group's rule allows.

examples.card: Withdraw savings from the group fund.
examples.filled: KSh 5,000 for school fees.

move words.trigger: A date she has recorded for a big cost, such as school fees, is near and her cash will not cover it, while her savings in the group can be taken out under its rule.

you do this when: A group builds a fund that grows: members save in shares, the fund lends, and the earnings are shared out.

name: Selling as a group
card: The coffee co-op near Moshi has a buyer for 20 tonnes. Add your 300 kg to the lot?
note: You and other growers pool your produce to sell as one lot through a co-op or group, and share what it earns. Each time you bring produce in it is weighed and graded in front of you, and you and whoever takes it in sign the slip; a neighbour who carried it for you is named on it. The pool holds the produce, the group's rule sets the price and the split, and you are often paid in two parts: an advance on delivery and the rest when the lot sells, which is you lending to the pool meanwhile. Members see the buyer's signed price, the costs, the weight in and out of the lot, and the split, and your own slips lie beside your pay statement. A rule to deliver everything to the pool binds only those who signed it, with what leaving costs agreed up front, and it never stops anyone else selling to the same buyer. Kept apart from Selling and buying in bulk (one grower's sale); Supplying on contract (standing supply); and Selling at a stall, a gate or a screen (a stall on market day). It usually starts when a buyer wants more than one grower has, when a co-op opens a pool for the season, when the harvest is in and members' stock is counted, when each delivery is weighed, when the lot is sold and the split is due, or when your pay statement arrives.
no mirror: none: the pool sells to a trade buyer, whose side is Buying to sell on

examples.card: Pool your produce with other growers for a bigger sale.
examples.filled: The co-op has 4 tonnes of members' tomatoes; the processor pays more for 5. Add your 600 kg?

examples.card: Arrange shared quotas for a group of growers.
examples.filled: The buyer wants 6 tonnes and 12 growers in the co-op have stock. Agree how much each grower fills?

examples.card: Share what the sale earns.
examples.filled: The pool has sold 5 tonnes. Split it by weight?

examples.card: Ask the society for the final payment.
examples.filled: Lot 14 sold 12 weeks ago and the final part has not come. Ask the society for the date?

move words.card: Wanjiru carried in 9 of last month's 11 days of milk and the whole payout came to you. Send part of the next payouts to her?
move words.note: Sending part of a payout to someone who did part of the work, by your choice; you set the part.

examples.card: Share your pay.
examples.filled: Wanjiru carried in 9 of last month's 11 days of milk and the whole payout came to you. Send part of the next payouts to her?

move words.trigger: Her last slips name someone other than the member as the carrier, again and again.

move words.card: The co-op's second payment is 3 weeks late and lower than the buyer's signed price. Ask for the accounts, line by line?
move words.note: A member asks the group to show what it sold for (the buyer's signed note), its costs, and how the split reached her share. It is the member's side of Present the accounts.

examples.card: Ask your group to show what it sold for and how your share was worked out.
examples.filled: The co-op shows the buyer's signed price, the costs and your 14 bags in the split.

move words.trigger: A pooled sale pays less than the signed price, a payment is late, or a share looks wrong.

you do this when: Growers pool their produce to sell as one lot through a co-op and share what it earns.

name: Claiming benefits
card: Your SNAP renewal is due on the 30th. Fill it in now?
note: You ask for money or food support that an authority owes you under its rules: food stamps, WIC, Universal Credit, free school meals, food on prescription, drought relief. You check you qualify, apply, answer questions, receive it, and renew when it falls due. You show only the answer to an eligibility question, and only if you allow it. A benefit balance can buy only what its rules allow and cannot be sold, so it is not the same as cash. The card shows what applying costs in time and what extra earnings would do to the payment, by the rule. Reports the rules require are their own act. Asking an authority to assess what help you need at home, and to pay for it, is claiming too. Spending a loaded balance is Buying and selling food to use, paying with it. Kept apart from Giving and receiving food (charity); Applying for a grant (a competed award); and Asking for donations (an appeal). It usually starts when your situation changes, a renewal date comes, a payment is late, a new school term begins, a scheme's published rule fits facts already in your record and you have not claimed, or a balance you were given nears its end date.

examples.card: Claim and renew a food benefit.
examples.filled: Renew SNAP before the 30th with last month's payslips. Start the renewal?

examples.card: Apply for free school meals when income drops.
examples.filled: Your hours were cut in Birmingham. Check if your children qualify for free school meals?

examples.card: Collect a cash transfer from a national food programme.
examples.filled: Your Bolsa Familia payment lands on the 18th in Recife. Your card was reissued in March. Collect it at the bank this week?

examples.card: Claim food support after a disaster or a lost harvest.
examples.filled: The drought in Turkana qualifies your household for relief. Register at the chief's office on Monday?

examples.card: Sharing only the answer about the hours you care
examples.filled: You have cared for your father about 40 hours this week by your notes and his two countersigns. The carer's allowance form asks if it is 35 or more. Do you send only the yes?

examples.card: Sharing only the answer about the hours you care
examples.filled: The council's paid family carer scheme wants a timesheet signed by the person you care for. Your mother signs on Fridays. Do you send the week's page?

examples.card: Sharing only the answer about the hours you care
examples.filled: Your brother also cares for Dad on weekends. The scheme pays one carer. Do you apply, or does he?

examples.card: Collect a ration before the month ends.
examples.filled: Your household's November ration from the ration shop has not been collected, and the shop posts 9 to 1 until the 30th. Collect it?

examples.card: Check support a diagnosis brings.
examples.filled: Your clinic record shows coeliac disease, and in your area gluten-free staples can come on prescription. Check if you qualify?

move words.card: The office turned your claim away at the desk without a letter. Note what happened and ask for it in writing?
move words.note: Short weight, spoiled or wrong food, a scoop that was not full, being turned away, or no distribution at all. Your word, with a photo or your own weighing if you have one, goes to the giver, who can answer beside it. If you cannot agree it can go to Asking for a ruling on a dispute.

examples.card: Say what went wrong.
examples.filled: The sack you collected on Sunday weighed less than the card says. Tell the agency?

move words.trigger: The giver's step for a distribution day shows less than the entitlement, a day passes with no distribution, or she says she was refused.

you do this when: You ask for money or food support an authority owes you under its rules: food stamps, school meals, drought relief. Not a payment tied to land.

name: Applying for a grant
card: The county's cold-room grant closes in 9 days and you qualify; it needs a 20% match and a report by June. Apply?
note: You apply for money or donated kit that many people apply for: a county cold-room grant, a small-farm fund, a donated polytunnel. You say what you will do and by when, wait to hear, and if you win you spend it as promised and report back beside what you said. Many grants pay after you spend, so you lend the funder the money until then. The card shows who goes first, any match you must find, the reporting, and what you must give back if you miss a condition. Donated kit may come with a condition, such as keeping it in use. Kept apart from Finding someone to deal with (looking for grants); Claiming benefits (an entitlement); Raising money from your community (from people you know); and Asking for donations (food or goods to give out). It usually starts when a grant you qualify for opens, a closing date nears, you win and a report is due, or a deadline for spending approaches.

examples.card: Apply for a grant for your food business.
examples.filled: A county cold room grant of KSh 400,000 is open. Apply?

examples.card: Fill in a grant application you have started.
examples.filled: Your small-farm fund form is half done and closes Friday. Finish it tonight?

examples.card: Report back on how a grant was spent.
examples.filled: The seed fund in Punjab wants your receipts by the 15th. Send the report?

examples.card: Apply for donated equipment from a charity or company.
examples.filled: A foundation in Kigali gives solar dryers to women's groups. Apply for your co-op?

move words.card: Your programme gave out 380 parcels last week to 412 booked households. Send the funder your numbers and the reason for the gap?
move words.note: Telling the funder what you did with what you won, beside what you said you would do, filled from what you already recorded: what was handed out, to whom, and any gap and why.

examples.card: Tell the funder what you did with what you won.
examples.filled: 380 parcels to 412 booked households, with the reason for the 32.

move words.trigger: A report date set by the funder is near.

you do this when: You apply for money or donated kit that many people apply for, say what you will do, and report on it. Not an entitlement.

name: Raising money from your community
may the holder use it: yes, only for what was agreed
card: 40 regulars said they'd back the second oven, and the quote is KSh 200,000. Open a harambee for it?
note: You raise money given freely by people near you for a venture or a need: a harambee, a crowdfund, a community appeal. Nothing is owed back. You open it with a goal and a date and ask. People pledge, some only if the goal is met. When it is met, the money goes to a named person or committee, such as a treasurer, who may use it only for the stated purpose. FoodX never holds it. Money given for goods later is Taking orders in advance, money to be repaid is Borrowing money, and money for a stake is Putting money into a business. Kept apart from Sending money home (family sends it); Applying for a grant (a funder judges); and Asking for donations (food or money you pass on to others). It usually starts when people say they would back you, when a need arises, or when the money for a plan is short.

examples.card: Raise money for a new venture from your community.
examples.filled: 80 regulars have said they would back a second shop. Open a fund for it?

examples.card: Open an appeal for a family emergency.
examples.filled: Your neighbour's roof fell in during the storm in Manila, and the repair quote is 150,000 pesos. Open a collection for it?

examples.card: Fund a community project by pledges, with a goal and a date.
examples.filled: Your village in Ghana needs a cassava mill, and the mill costs 20,000 cedis. Open a harambee closing at month end?

examples.card: Ask your regulars to back a new venture.
examples.filled: Your regulars in Brooklyn say they would back a bakery. Open a campaign for the cost of the oven?

you do this when: People near you give money freely for a venture or a need: a harambee, a crowdfund.

name: Splitting costs
card: Dinner was KSh 6,000 for 3. Ask Ali and Ben for KSh 2,000 each?
note: You and others divide what a group spent: a bill one person paid, a shared shop, a haulier shared to market, an order placed together. Whoever paid first has lent the others the money until they pay. Someone asks, the others accept or question, money is handed over, and it ends; nothing is held. Kept apart from Settling up with trading partners (traders cancelling what they owe each other); Pooling money (money put in before the buying); Splitting takings (dividing what a group earned); and Insuring each other (a pot for those who are hit). It usually starts when a bill arrives, after a shared shop, or when someone says you owe something.

examples.card: Split the bill or shared food costs with the people you share with.
examples.filled: Four people, £62, split by what each had, after dinner in Edinburgh. Send the split?

examples.card: Share a trailer or haulier run with a nearby farm.
examples.filled: Share the haulier to market with the farm down the lane, half each?

examples.card: Order food together with your group and split the bill.
examples.filled: Five of you, one order, split by what each had?

examples.card: Share the cost of a parent's food with your siblings.
examples.filled: You paid 212 for your mother's shopping, shared three ways, and your brother has paid nothing. Ask him for his share?

you do this when: You and others divide what a group spent: a bill one person paid, a shared shop. Not takings, not a whip-round.

name: Sharing a place
card: Ana has taken the top fridge shelf. Agree it's hers?
note: You share a place with the people you live or work alongside: fridge shelves, a store cupboard, a stall or pitch with someone else. You ask for a share or offer one, agree it by the household's or group's rule, and give it up when you leave. Sharing a garden: You and neighbours grow food in one garden or allotment, each with a bed or a row. You ask for a bed, plant and look after it, and share the jobs the garden needs, such as watering, composting and mending the fence. You give the bed back when you stop, and the rule says who takes it next. Kept apart from Sharing a commons (water, grazing or a fishing ground shared by many under one rule); Letting someone use your place (one owner says yes); Sharing a machine (hours on equipment); Taking turns to work for each other (labour); and Growing crops (what you grow). It usually starts when someone moves in or out, a shelf or share frees up, or a rule is broken; as Sharing a garden, when beds come free in spring, when you move into the block, or when the group sets jobs.

examples.card: Agree what is shared and what is your own in a shared fridge or store.
examples.filled: The shared flat in Utrecht needs the fridge cleared by Friday. Label your food and clear it?

examples.card: Share storage space with others.
examples.filled: In a hostel kitchen in Valparaíso, Ana has the top shelf. Take the bottom?

examples.card: Agree how much each person can use of something you share.
examples.filled: Your flatmates in Glasgow want the fridge split in three. Agree a shelf each?

examples.card: Share a stall or pitch and its fee with someone else.
examples.filled: The cheese stall asks to share the Saturday pitch at a Bath market. Split it half each?

examples.card: Ask for a bed in a community garden.
examples.filled: The community garden on your street in Leeds has a free bed this spring. Ask for it?

examples.card: Take your turn at a shared garden job.
examples.filled: It is your week to water the allotment beds in Nairobi. Take the Saturday morning slot?

examples.card: Give your bed back when you move.
examples.filled: You are moving out of the block in Berlin next month. Give your garden bed back to the waiting list?

examples.card: Sharing a garden
examples.filled: Your block's garden has four free beds this spring. Ask for one?

move words.words: Do your job in the garden
move words.card: It is your week to water the beds and open the gate at the Elm Street garden. Have you done it, and do you want to swap with someone?
move words.note: Saying your job in the shared garden is done, or swapping it with someone.

examples.card: Do your job in the garden.
examples.filled: It is your week to water the beds at the Elm Street garden. Have you done it, and do you swap with someone?

examples.card: Do your job in the garden.
examples.filled: The compost needs turning and it is your day. Did you turn it?

examples.card: Do your job in the garden.
examples.filled: The fence is still broken at the end bed. Will you mend it on the working day?
