move words.card: Your bed has had no work since August. Do you want to give it up or work it?
move words.note: Letting your share go back to the group.

examples.card: Give up your share.
examples.filled: Plot 14 back to the society.

move words.trigger: Her record shows she no longer has the thing the share is for, such as the animals or the plot, or she has said she is leaving.

move words.card: Your turn to water is when you are away. Do you want to ask someone to swap?
move words.note: Trading turns with another member.

examples.card: Swap turns with another member.
examples.filled: Your March for Njeri's June.

move words.trigger: A member has asked to trade turns, or her own plans show she needs the money in a different month.

you do this when: A few people share a shelf, a pitch, a bed or a garden in one place. Not a commons many use under one rule.

name: Counting the till
card: The drawer is ₹1,500 short of the till. Count again?
note: You count the day's takings at close against what the till says: the cash in the drawer, and card and mobile-money payments against the sales. Where there is no till, the count is set against what your stock says went out (what you started with, plus what came in, less what is left), or against the cups and cartons the day used. Cash paid out of the drawer or the apron during the day (the ice man, a porter, the milk van) is noted at the time, and the count expects it gone. When the drawer changes hands you count again, so a gap belongs to one person. You note any difference and sign the count, and it is done. A difference is the cashier's and your record; the law may stop you taking it from wages. Tomorrow's starting cash in the drawer is something you set. Banking the cash is Keeping money with a bank or wallet. Counting each time the drawer changes hands shows where a shortfall comes from. It is on the cashier's record and the owner's, and the law may forbid taking it from pay. Kept apart from Logging (the business's money over time); and Checking stock against your records (goods against the count). It usually starts when it is close of the day or the stall, when the drawer changes hands, when the till and the drawer disagree, or when the till is short on the same day or shift again and again.

examples.card: Count the cash at close and check it matches the day's sales.
examples.filled: The till says ₹41,200 cash but the drawer holds ₹39,700. Count again?

examples.card: Leave the starting cash for tomorrow.
examples.filled: Leave R$300 in small notes in the drawer for the first customers at your stall in Salvador?

examples.card: Match the day's mobile-money payments to the till.
examples.filled: The till shows KSh 18,400 by M-Pesa today; the M-Pesa statement shows 17,900. Check the 500?

examples.card: Count the cash from a landing before you share it out.
examples.filled: Your list of sales from Saturday's landing adds to GH 2,640 and the bag holds GH 2,540. Count again before the shares?

examples.card: Count a drawer when there is no till.
examples.filled: Your drawer in Nairobi holds KSh 9,400. You started with KSh 1,500 and paid out KSh 3,000. Save the count?

examples.card: Cash lifted from the till to the safe
examples.filled: You take a bundle to the safe at lunch. How much is in it?

examples.card: Own drivers' cash handed in
examples.filled: Three drivers handed in cash at close. Count it beside the orders marked paid in cash?

examples.card: Change some cash before you go home.
examples.filled: You counted 41,000 in cash at closing. The agent at the gate posts 55 for moving 5,000 into your wallet. Change part of it before you go?

move words.card: Your nephew Musa takes the apron at the Toi stall while you go to the wholesale. Do you count the cash together and both sign?
move words.note: Cash you collected for someone else, counted and handed in, with what you spent on the way. Both of you sign the count, so any later difference belongs to whoever held it.

examples.card: Hand in the cash.
examples.filled: Your nephew takes the apron while you buy at the wholesale. Count and sign together?

move words.trigger: A named helper is on the stall, or she says she is leaving the stall; the button shows when someone else is about to hold the cash.

move words.words: Take cash out of the till
move words.card: The ice man is at the back door. How much are you taking out of the drawer for him?
move words.note: Cash taken out of the drawer during the day, how much and what for, so the count at close still adds up.

examples.card: Take cash out of the till.
examples.filled: The ice man is at the back door. How much are you taking out of the drawer for him?

move words.trigger: A supplier is waiting for cash, the drawer holds more than she set as the float, or she says she paid someone from the till.

you do this when: You count the day's takings at close against what the till says.

name: Having a business of your own
card: You've sold mandazi 40 days running. Registering costs KSh 1,000 and a yearly return, and opens bigger buyers and a loan. Register, or keep trading as you are?
note: You make a food business of its own, apart from your household: its name, its own money, and who answers if it owes (you, or only the business). Registering, licences and tax numbers are steps the law requires, each its own act; the card shows what they cost and give, and where your place lets a small trader sell without them. Closing a business: You end a food business of its own: pay what it owes first, end open deals on their terms, file the last returns, and what is left is yours. Everyone who may be owed is invited to state their claim in their own signed word, so the list is built from claims, not from your memory. Kept apart from Opening another site (a new place for a business you run); Putting money into a business (putting money in); Running a group (a group); Selling your business (someone else takes it on); and Paying what you can to everyone you owe (when you cannot pay everyone). It usually starts when you have sold steadily for weeks, a bank or buyer asks for a business, or a partner wants to join; as Closing a business, when sales stop covering costs, you retire, or you decide to stop.

examples.card: Trade under a name of your own.
examples.filled: You've sold mandazi 40 days running in Mombasa. Give the stall its own name and keep its money apart from home?

examples.card: Choose who answers for the business's debts.
examples.filled: Registering the bakery in Leeds as a company limits what you owe if it fails, for £50 and a yearly return. Do it?

examples.card: Tell the tax office you now trade.
examples.filled: Your cakes now sell every week in Leeds, and the tax office needs to know you trade. Set up as a sole trader?

examples.card: Close a business and settle what it owes.
examples.filled: Your stall in Leeds market has not covered its rent since spring. Close it and settle with the market?

examples.card: Stop trading and file the last returns.
examples.filled: Your market stall in Leeds stops trading in December. File the last tax return and close the business?

examples.card: Sell the equipment to pay what is owed.
examples.filled: You are closing the bakery in Lima. Sell the ovens and the mixer to pay the bank first?

examples.card: Closing a business
examples.filled: You are closing the juice bar in Accra. Pay the suppliers, end the lease on its terms, and keep what is left?

you do this when: You make a food business of its own apart from your household, and later end it: starting is its first move and closing its last.

name: Creating for a client
card: A juice brand wants three new recipes for its summer range, £600 each. Quote and send a first draft by Friday?
note: You make something new for a client who then may use it as you agreed: recipes for a brand's range, a menu for a café, food photographs, a label design, a cookbook written for someone else. You get a brief, quote your price, make drafts, change them as agreed, hand over the final work, and are paid, in stages or with a share of sales. You go first, so a deposit, stage payments and a fee if they cancel are agreed up front; the right to use it is theirs, by your signed word, when they have paid in full, unless the terms say otherwise. An idea is not property (Kinsella), so a recipe, a design or a text is not owned by either of you: what is sold is your signed word about who may use it and whether you will too. Kept apart from Making products for others (making their product to their recipe); Doing or getting a job for pay (a job with nothing new to own); Developing a recipe (your own recipe); and Letting someone use your recipe or brand (you keep it). It usually starts when a brand or business asks, your own work brings an enquiry, or a season needs new dishes.

examples.card: Develop recipes for a brand that will use them.
examples.filled: A juice brand in Cape Town wants three summer recipes. Quote for the work?

examples.card: Design a menu for a café.
examples.filled: A new café in Hanoi asks for a 12-dish menu with costings. Quote for the work?

examples.card: Shoot food photographs for a client.
examples.filled: A bakery in Melbourne needs photos of 20 products for its website. Book a shoot day?

examples.card: Choose to give the right to use them or keep it.
examples.filled: Your recipes for a cereal brand go over on Friday. Give the brand the right to use them when you are paid, or keep it and let the brand use them for a year?

you do this when: You make something new for a client who then owns it: recipes for a range, a menu, photographs.

name: Opening another site
card: Your Jakarta delivery orders have doubled in 6 months. A small kitchen for delivery only is Rp 15 million a month on a 2-year lease. Open it?
note: You open another place for a business you already run: a branch, a kiosk in another town, a dark kitchen for deliveries. It brings together renting the place, the fit-out, the licences, the staff and what you will sell there. You say what you expect it to take and by when, and the card shows the rent, the fit-out, the loan, what leaving the lease early costs, and your other choices. Licences are their own acts, because the law requires them. Kept apart from Having a business of your own (a new business); Building or improving a place (work on a place you have); Selling at a stall, a gate or a screen (another pitch on market day); and Letting someone use your recipe or brand (someone else opens under your name). It usually starts when you sell out every day, customers come from far away, a good place comes free, or a second shift could use the same team.

examples.card: Open a branch where customers come from.
examples.filled: A third of your Lisbon café's customers come from Alfama. Look at the empty unit there?

examples.card: Open a delivery kitchen.
examples.filled: A delivery-only kitchen is free in Kemang, where most of your Jakarta orders go. Visit it?

examples.card: Open a branch in a second town.
examples.filled: The empty unit in Nakuru is KSh 45,000 a month for 3 years, plus fit-out. Open a second shop there?

you do this when: You open another place for a business you already run: a branch, a kiosk, a dark kitchen.

name: Cooking a meal
card: You've got eggs, spinach and rice going off Friday. Make egg fried rice tonight?
note: You cook a meal, from what you have or from a recipe: tonight's dinner, a dish you try again with changes, a lunch for a crowd. You start, change the plan as you go, write down what you did, pass a job on, and finish with the meal done. The card shows what each way uses (time, what is used up) next to a takeaway. Allergies are cooked around first. Kept apart from Cooking together (others cook with you); Making to order (a customer's order); Making a batch (a run made to sell); and Cooking ahead (food for later). It usually starts when food is nearing its date, it is evening and nothing is planned, guests are coming, or someone sets a theme night.

examples.card: Turn what is going off or left over into a meal.
examples.filled: Three ripe bananas and stale bread in your Manchester kitchen could be banana bread pudding. Make it?

examples.card: Cook a meal that fits the time and energy you have tonight.
examples.filled: You have 20 minutes and eggs, rice and spinach in your Lagos kitchen. Make egg fried rice in one pan?

examples.card: Cook one base meal and finish it differently for each person's needs or tastes.
examples.filled: One chilli in a Texas home: plain for the kids, spicy for you, vegan topping for a guest. Cook it that way?

examples.card: Plan a cooking timeline back from serving time for a big meal.
examples.filled: Thanksgiving in Ohio: turkey in at 11, serve at 3, potatoes in at 1:30. Follow that plan?

examples.card: Say what went into the pot.
examples.filled: Dal tonight with two handfuls of lentils and the last onion in your Mumbai kitchen. Take them off what you have?

move words.card: The dal was for six and four of you ate. Put the rest in the fridge, or freeze it?
move words.note: Cooking a meal done with more made than eaten: the leftover becomes a line in stock with the day it was cooked.

examples.card: Put the rest away.
examples.filled: Tonight's dal in your Pune kitchen made six bowls and four were eaten. Fridge for tomorrow, or freezer?

examples.card: Put the rest away.
examples.filled: Sunday's rice in your Kano kitchen was cooked at 1. Put it away by 3, or finish it today?

examples.card: Put the rest away.
examples.filled: Half the roast from Sunday in your Bristol flat. Keep it for Tuesday, or give it to Ana?

move words.trigger: A meal she cooked is marked done and her record shows more portions made than people at the table.

you do this when: You cook a meal now, from what you have or a recipe, for yourself and yours. Not food made now to eat later.

name: Cooking ahead
card: Sunday's chilli makes plenty. Freeze the extra for the week?
note: You cook now so that food is ready later: a big pot on Sunday, portions in the freezer, packed lunches, a slow step like soaking beans the night before, or a few easy meals for nights you cannot cook. It repeats weekly for many people. Kept apart from Making a batch (it is a run to sell); Cooking a meal (food made to eat tonight); and Preserving food (you turn a glut into jars or stores). It usually starts when it is a quiet time such as Sunday afternoon, you know a busy week is coming, or a recipe needs a slow step.

examples.card: Cook a big batch ahead and keep portions for later.
examples.filled: It is Sunday in your Leeds flat. Cook chilli and freeze the extra?

examples.card: Pack a lunch for yourself or someone.
examples.filled: Tomorrow's lunchbox in Osaka can use leftover rice and pickles. Pack it tonight?

examples.card: Start the slow step of a recipe ahead.
examples.filled: Tomorrow's pot in Mexico City needs soaked beans. Put them on to soak tonight?

examples.card: Keep a few easy meals ready for nights you cannot cook.
examples.filled: Your freezer in Pune is down to a few portions of dal. Cook more to top it up?

you do this when: You cook now so that food is ready later: a big pot on Sunday, portions in the freezer. Not tonight's dinner.

name: Preserving food
card: 12 kg of tomatoes are ripe at once. Bottle passata on Saturday?
note: You turn a glut into food that keeps, to eat or sell later: jam, pickles, kimchi, passata, cured ham, smoked or dried fish and fruit. You start, change the method, write down the date and batch, bring in helpers, and mark it done. It repeats each season and waits for the ferment or cure. The card shows the days, the racks and the jars it takes, next to eating or selling it fresh. Drying a crop in its own form is Storing a harvest, and years of ageing are Ageing food or drink. You say how much you started with and how many jars you ended with, and a batch that went bad is written as lost. Kept apart from Making a batch (a product made to sell now); Cooking ahead (food for the next few days); and Keeping food fresh (food kept as it is). It usually starts when many things ripen at once, a price is low at the market, or a ferment is ready to jar.

examples.card: Preserve food by pickling, drying, curing or fermenting.
examples.filled: The kimchi cabbage in your Busan kitchen is salted and rinsed. Pack it into jars tonight to ferment?

examples.card: Turn a glut into jars.
examples.filled: Twelve kilos of tomatoes ripened at once on your allotment in Bologna. Bottle passata on Saturday?

examples.card: Dry the catch or harvest for the lean months.
examples.filled: You have more dagaa than you can sell from your boat on Lake Victoria. Sun-dry it on the racks tomorrow?

examples.card: Cure and smoke meat for the winter.
examples.filled: Your hams in Vermont have had ten days in brine. Smoke them at the weekend?

examples.card: Feed or rest a starter.
examples.filled: Your starter has not been fed for 5 days in your Berlin kitchen. Feed it, or put it in the fridge?

you do this when: You turn a glut into food that keeps: jam, pickles, cured or dried fish.

name: Storing a harvest
card: The maize is at 13% moisture. Seal it in airtight bags today?
note: You ferment, dry, cure, bag and hold a crop so it stays sound: cocoa in heaps or boxes with the days and turns, coffee cherry on raised beds, moisture, pests, mould, heat. You start the store, change the plan, note the moisture and the count, bring in help, and mark it done when the crop is sold or used; it repeats each harvest. Weight in and weight out are your own two figures, so the loss from wet to dry shows. Sorting before the sale is Grading produce; holding it on for a later price is Waiting to sell for a better price, and borrowing against it is Borrowing against stored stock. Kept apart from Guarding against theft (people taking the crop); Keeping food fresh (everyday food); Controlling pests (the pest checks); and Preserving food (turning it into another food). It usually starts when the harvest comes in, the moisture reading is right, or rain or heat threatens the store.

examples.card: Dry and bag grain to a safe moisture.
examples.filled: Dry the maize to 13% and bag it in 90 kg sacks in the Rift Valley. Start drying today?

examples.card: Hold roots through the winter.
examples.filled: Your potatoes in Poland are ready to store. Clamp them in straw and earth, checked every fortnight?

examples.card: Cure a crop before storing it.
examples.filled: Your garlic from near Cuenca needs three weeks hanging, then nets in a cool loft. Hang it today?

examples.card: Dryness by feel, hermetic bags
examples.filled: The maize was on the tarpaulin four days, and the salt-jar test came out dry. It is in six bags in the roof store. Do you want a reminder to look for weevils after the first rains?

examples.card: Example: wet to dry
examples.filled: You pulped 180 kg of cherry on Saturday. After drying the parchment weighs 34 kg. Do you take it to the mill or hold it?

examples.card: Dried on the yard
examples.filled: Your paddy has dried three days on the yard. Do you note the bite test result?

examples.card: Cold store through the winter
examples.filled: You put 120 bins of Braeburn in cold room 3 on 12 October. Log the count and plan to open the room in January?

move words.card: Field 6 wheat came in at 17.5% and bin 3 holds 90 tonnes. Dry it tonight down to the moisture you set for storing, and record the weight when it is done?
move words.note: A drying run: the lot, the moisture before and after, the weight before and after. The weight lost is mostly water, and it shows beside the stock you hold, so a lower count is not a surprise.

examples.card: Dry it.
examples.filled: Two lorries of maize came in at 22% in Nakuru and the dryer is free from 6pm. Dry them tonight?

examples.card: Dry it.
examples.filled: The fan on the ventilated floor has run since Monday on Field 2 barley. Record 15.5% from your probe and keep it on?

move words.trigger: Grain is in the store above the moisture she set for keeping, or a load came in wet by her harvest note.

move words.card: You took a tin of maize from the store at Mama Njeri's. How much was it, and was it for the house, for the hens, or to sell?
move words.note: Stock that left because you used it yourself: grain for the house or the hens, seed kept back, feed for your own animals, diesel, flour taken home. Sales, waste and gifts are recorded by their own acts.

examples.card: Take some out.
examples.filled: You took out two tins of maize this morning. Is it for the house, for the animals or for sale?

examples.card: Take some out.
examples.filled: You scooped the bottom of the sack that had weevils. Where did it go?

examples.card: Take some out.
examples.filled: A neighbour took a tin of beans from your granary. Did she pay, borrow or is it a gift?

move words.trigger: Her record shows a count for this store and it has been more than a few days since she last said anything about it, or the end of the lean season is near.

you do this when: You ferment, dry, cure or hold a crop for months so it stays sound.

name: Feeding your children
card: Zane has eaten no veg for three days. Try the carrot sticks with hummus at tea tonight?
note: You feed your children, from the first milk to the teenager making their own dinner: breast, bottle or formula, weaning onto solids, a toddler who will only eat beige, school-age meals. You offer the food, note how it went and how much, hand the feeding to someone else for a day, and share the feeding with others; what they tell you back is their own word. It repeats every day. Nobody signs for a baby: you make your own promise to the child, and as they grow their own say grows. What a child ate is the child's record, which you keep beside your own notes until you hand it to them. Ideas for a fussy eater are offered as one way to try, never a rule. Advice on feeding names its source and date (a health service, the WHO, your clinic), beside other advice the family follows. When a child reaches the age you set, they can take over their own part of the record (Letting someone act for you). Kept apart from Feeding someone you care for (an adult who needs help); Teaching a food skill (a child learning to cook); Cooking ahead (a packed lunch made for later); and Treating malnutrition (a clinical programme). It usually starts when a meal time comes round, a night, a school day or a trip is coming, or a child reaches a new stage.
no mirror: none: the child receives, and your promise to them is your own

examples.card: Track feeds and have the next one ready.
examples.filled: Last feed was 2h40m ago, left side. Bottle ready for 3am?

examples.card: Prepare food for a baby ahead of the night or a trip.
examples.filled: Tonight's sleeper from Delhi to Jaipur is long. Prepare four bottles?

examples.card: Offer a fussy child a food they have refused before, in a new way.
examples.filled: Zane turned down peas again in Leeds. Serve them mashed into the potato tonight?

examples.card: Get a school-age child's meal ready for a long day.
examples.filled: Amara has football until 6 in Lagos. Send a second snack of groundnuts and banana?

examples.card: Move a child to a new stage of feeding.
examples.filled: Mia is 6 months and sitting up well. Start with a first food?

examples.card: Note what came back in the lunchbox.
examples.filled: Amara's rice came back untouched three days running in Lagos. Pack groundnuts and banana instead?

examples.card: Note how much of a bottle a baby took.
examples.filled: Mia took 90 ml of her 120 ml at 10 and left the rest. Note it, and make the next one smaller?

examples.card: Keep track of expressed milk in the fridge.
examples.filled: You expressed 150 ml in the Dublin office at 2. Note it for tonight's feed?

examples.card: Note the amount a baby takes at night.
examples.filled: Mia took 60 ml at 3am in Cork. Note it and warm the next bottle at 6?

move words.card: Mia is 6 months and sitting up well. Start with mashed sweet potato this week?
move words.note: Starting solids from about 6 months: first foods, textures moving on.

examples.card: Start a baby on solid food.
examples.filled: Mashed sweet potato at lunch, a teaspoon to start.

move words.trigger: The child's age in her record reaches about six months, or the date she set for starting solids for that child.

move words.card: Mia had egg twice with no reaction. Try peanut next, in the morning so you can watch her?
move words.note: Common allergens brought in early and one at a time, watching for reactions.

examples.card: Introduce new foods to a baby or child a little at a time, and note how they take them.
examples.filled: Introduce egg to Mia on Tuesday and note any reaction.

move words.trigger: A new food has been tried by the child with no reaction logged in her record, and the next food on her plan for that child is due.

move words.card: Gran has Zane until Sunday. Send her his nut-free rule, his last feed and tonight's tea?
move words.note: Passing someone's feeding to another carer for a while, with their food rule, what they last ate and any dose due.

examples.card: Hand over the feeding.
examples.filled: Gran has Mia in Cork from Friday. Send her Mia's feeds, the formula and the egg she is trying?

examples.card: Hand over the feeding.
examples.filled: Zane starts at the nursery in Leeds on Monday. Send them his allergy rule and ask for a note at pick-up?

examples.card: Hand over the feeding.
examples.filled: Amara goes to her aunt's in Lagos after school. Send the groundnut rule and ask her to say what she ate?

move words.trigger: A day or night is coming in her plan on which someone other than her is down to feed a child, or a nursery or childminder day starts.

move words.card: Zane's antibiotic is due with tea at 5. Note it given when he has had it?
move words.note: Noting medicine given with food, as the doctor or label says, so nobody gives it twice. The dose is the doctor's; you only note it given.

examples.card: Give a dose with food.
examples.filled: Zane's antibiotic in Leeds is with tea at 5. Note it given?

examples.card: Give a dose with food.
examples.filled: Mia's iron drops in Kisumu are with breakfast, and not with milk. Note them given?

examples.card: Give a dose with food.
examples.filled: Mia's vitamin D drops in Dublin go in her first feed. Note them given?

move words.trigger: A dose time or a with-food instruction from the doctor is in her record for a child, and a meal is planned near it.

you do this when: You feed your children from first milk to teenage dinners.

name: Feeding someone you care for
card: Gran ate half her lunch again, the third day this week. Ask her nurse about softer food?
note: You feed an adult who needs help to eat: a parent with dementia, someone after a stroke, a partner who is ill. Care plans, soft or thickened food, what is eaten and drunk (however little: half a bowl, two sips of tea), their weight each month, a medicine with food, and notes for the other carers are part of it. You start a plan, hand over meals, note what is eaten and drunk, share notes with other carers, hand the feeding to the next carer, and change it as needs change. A page of the care book at the house can be photographed and brought in. What you may decide for them follows what they set up earlier (a power of attorney, a wish written down), and their own yes or no counts whenever they can give it. Their health details go to a doctor or dietitian only with their permission. A paid care worker is also Working for someone. When you hand the feeding to the next carer, they sign that they have taken it, so each shift is written down on both sides. Kept apart from Feeding your children (a child); Bringing meals to someone (a rota for a short stretch); and Treating malnutrition (a clinical programme). It usually starts when a meal time comes round, when a shift of carers changes, when a care plan changes, when a note arrives from another carer, or when you have done every meal for a long stretch with no one else taking a day.
no mirror: none: the person cared for only receives

examples.card: Cut up, soften or thicken food for someone who finds it hard to chew or swallow.
examples.filled: Dad in Cork finds chewing hard. Mash the vegetables and thicken his tea to stage 2?

examples.card: Share what someone you care for has eaten with their other carers.
examples.filled: Gran in Leeds ate half her lunch and had her pills. Tell her other carers?

examples.card: Follow someone's care plan on what they may eat, and report any breach.
examples.filled: Check Mum's lunch in Dundee against her thickened-fluids plan and tell her nurse if it was not followed?

examples.card: Weigh the person you care for each month.
examples.filled: Dad is due to be weighed in Cork on the 1st. Weigh him and keep it in his record?

examples.card: Note what and how much they drank.
examples.filled: Mum in Cork drank two cups of tea and half a glass of water today. Tell her other carers?

examples.card: Three ways a note reaches the record
examples.filled: Ayo left at nine. The care book says Dad had porridge and half a cup of tea. Do you ask his doctor about the tea, or see what tomorrow brings?

examples.card: Count cups through the day.
examples.filled: Mum has had three cups today in Dundee, on a thickened-fluids plan. Note the fourth?

move words.card: Auntie Bola takes over Dad's lunches on Thursday. Send her his soft-food plan and today's notes?
move words.note: Passing someone's feeding to another carer for a while, with their food rule, what they last ate and any dose due.

examples.card: Hand over the feeding.
examples.filled: Your sister takes Mum's supper in Dundee. Send her the thickened-fluids plan and what Mum ate at lunch?

examples.card: Hand over the feeding.
examples.filled: The agency carer starts Monday at Gran's in Leeds. Send her soft food, no pork and today's notes?

examples.card: Hand over the feeding.
examples.filled: You are away from Dad in Cork until the 14th. Send his plan and the pills to your brother?

move words.trigger: A shift of carers is about to change in her plan, or someone else is down to feed the person.

move words.card: Dad's tablet is due with breakfast. Note it given when he has taken it?
move words.note: Noting medicine given with food, as the doctor or label says, so nobody gives it twice. The dose is the doctor's; you only note it given.

examples.card: Give a dose with food.
examples.filled: Dad's tablets in Cork are with breakfast. Note them given, and tell his daughter?

examples.card: Give a dose with food.
examples.filled: Gran's tablet in Osaka must be two hours apart from milk. Note it given and move her milk?

examples.card: Give a dose with food.
examples.filled: Mum would not take her morning tablet with her porridge. Note that, and tell her nurse?

move words.trigger: A dose time or a with-food instruction is in the person's record and a meal is planned near it.

you do this when: You feed an adult who needs help to eat: a parent with dementia, a partner who is ill.

name: Running a canteen
card: Three soft diets today, but the supply has none. Order from the central kitchen, or change the menu?
note: You run the meals of a school, hospital, care home or prison: the menu to the place's rules, each person's diet, the daily numbers, the meal round, and orders to the kitchen. You set the menu, take the numbers, serve the round, count who ate, and note what came back. A diet or a nil-by-mouth order comes only from a signed order and is applied as it arrives. If one is missing, that meal stops until a person decides. A card appears only when diets and supply clash. The place, a council or a contract pays; payments from a scheme are Claiming back from a scheme. Kept apart from Selling under a scheme (a shop selling to people a scheme entitles); Running a community kitchen (feeding a community for a cause); Giving and receiving food (guests at your table); and Giving a customer a treat (one free thing for one customer, once). It usually starts when numbers or diets change, a meal time nears, or a menu must be set.

examples.card: Run the day's meal round to each person's diet.
examples.filled: Lunch for 32 residents at your care home in Ghent: 6 soft, 2 diabetic. Run the round?

examples.card: Update diets for new admissions.
examples.filled: Two residents arrive at your care home in Ghent tomorrow, one on soft food. Add them to tomorrow's round?

examples.card: Plan a school menu to the rules.
examples.filled: Your school kitchen in Lyon must meet new menu rules. Plan the term's menu?

examples.card: Add a diet from a letter you were handed.
examples.filled: A mother at your school in Lyon hands you a doctor's letter for her son's egg allergy. Add it to the diet list?

examples.card: Add a texture level from the therapist.
examples.filled: The speech therapist at your care home in Cork wrote Dad's drinks as stage 2. Add it to the diet list?

examples.card: Change a dish and check it against the diets.
examples.filled: The fish did not come for lunch at your school in Oslo. Swap in pasta and check it against the 11 diets?

examples.card: Give a child lunch when the card is empty.
examples.filled: Mia's lunch card at your school in Manchester is empty. Give her lunch today and tell her mother?

move words.card: Ward 4 has 3 discharges and 2 admissions. Send today's numbers to the kitchen?
move words.note: A ward or class telling the kitchen how many and which diets.

examples.card: Send today's meal numbers to the kitchen.
examples.filled: Ward 4 has 28 meals today, 4 of them soft. Send the numbers to the kitchen?

move words.trigger: The kitchen's cut-off for numbers is near and the ward or class list in her record differs from what was last sent.

move words.card: The school needs 30 more lunches for the trip day. Order from the central kitchen?
move words.note: Ordering inside one organisation; not a sale.

examples.card: Order meals from your organisation's kitchen.
examples.filled: Your school needs 30 packed lunches for Friday's trip. Order them from the central kitchen?

move words.trigger: Numbers for a coming day in her record are above what the day's supply covers.

move words.card: Lunch is over at Hillside School. Note how many ate, and how many were turned away?
move words.note: How many people you actually fed or who came, and how many you turned away: the number a scheme, a client or next week's cooking is planned and paid on.

examples.card: Count the people you fed.
examples.filled: Lunch is over at Hillside School. Note how many ate, and how many were turned away?

move words.trigger: A meal, service or event she runs has ended.

move words.card: Mrs Bell ate a third of her lunch and drank a cup of tea. Her care plan says a full meal. Do you tell the nurse in charge, or offer her something else at three?
move words.note: What each person ate and drank, in your own words or a fraction of the plate, where a care plan or the law asks for a food and fluid chart.

examples.card: Note what each ate.
examples.filled: Mrs Bell ate a third of her lunch and drank a cup of tea. Her care plan says a full meal. Do you tell the nurse in charge, or offer her something else at three?

examples.card: Note what each ate.
examples.filled: Mr Wu refused the soup but ate all the pudding. You wrote it on the chart. Do you put the soup back on his menu tomorrow?

examples.card: Note what each ate.
examples.filled: Mrs Diaz ate nothing at tea and was asleep. You left the tray in her room. Do you look in again at seven?

move words.trigger: A meal round has been served in a care home, hospital or school to residents with a signed diet order or a weight-loss flag, and the person serving has not noted what each ate.

move words.card: Tomorrow's chicken curry cannot be made: the chicken did not come. 84 people chose it, 3 eat halal and 2 are vegetarian. Swap to vegetable curry for all, or choose for each?
move words.note: Changing a dish on a menu that is already out, telling everyone who chose it, and checking the new dish against each person's signed diet before it goes out.

examples.card: Change a dish on a menu already out, and tell those who chose it.
examples.filled: Chicken curry swapped to vegetable curry; 84 people told; the 3 halal and 2 vegetarian checked.

move words.trigger: A delivery fails, an oven breaks, or a supplier changes an ingredient after the menu is out.

you do this when: You run the meals of a school, hospital, care home or prison: the menu, the diets, the numbers, the round. Not eating from it.

name: Keeping a shopping list
card: Oats, onions, bin bags; Sam added milk. Start your shop on the way home?
note: You keep one standing list the household adds to and ticks off in the shop. You start it, anyone in the home you share it with can add to it, and you tick things off as you buy; it can be paused and ended. A rule that adds things when they run out is one you set, and the list shows what it added. Kept apart from Buying and selling food to use (the trip itself); Planning what to eat (a plan of meals, which makes the list); and Planning how much to make (what a seller makes to sell). It usually starts when something runs low, a recipe needs things you lack, a week's plan is made, you are on the way to the shop, or you have added the same item by hand again and again.

examples.card: Make a shared shopping list from what is running low.
examples.filled: Sam and Jo can add to the list: oats, onions, bin bags. Keep it as the household list?

examples.card: Check a recipe against what you have and list only what is missing.
examples.filled: You have six of the eight things. Buy cream and lemons?

examples.card: Add something when it runs out.
examples.filled: The rice is nearly finished. Add it to the flat's shared list in Kraków?

you do this when: You keep one standing list the household adds to and ticks off in the shop.

name: Observing a fast
card: You missed 3 Ramadan fasts. Plan to make them up on Mondays?
note: You keep a fast set by a calendar, a vow or a doctor: Ramadan, Lent, Yom Kippur, Ekadashi, a fast before surgery or a blood test. It is a set period with a daily clock, often kept together with family or a community. The dates come from the calendar or sighting your community follows, cited. You start it, note each day, pause it when you cannot fast, and end it with the feast. Days missed are owed, with a date to make them up, or a payment in their place (fidya), as your tradition says. Kept apart from Setting a diet (a rule you choose, such as an eating window); and Setting a goal (a target). It usually starts when the date arrives (a moon sighting, a calendar date) or a doctor sets one.

examples.card: Keep a fast with its daily times.
examples.filled: Suhoor before 4:52, iftar at 6:42. Set those times?

examples.card: Make up the fasts you missed.
examples.filled: 3 missed Ramadan fasts to make up. Fit them on Mondays?

move words.note: Settling owed fast days by giving, as your tradition allows (fidya, a gift in place of a day). It opens Giving to a cause with the cause and the amount yours to choose.

name: Setting your terms of trade
card: Eid falls on Thursday and your Bradford stall is open 8 to 6; 3 orders are booked for after 2. Close at 2pm and move them?
note: You set when you are open or available: your weekly hours and days, market days, school terms, a worker's days, and dated closures for Eid, Christmas, a funeral or a holiday. You choose the times and customers can read them. A change that breaks promises already made (bookings, accepted orders, subscriptions) shows them, so you can move each one. Hours that the law or a market sets (licensing hours, market days) are limits you cannot set past. Setting your credit terms: You set when people may pay you later and what that costs: who gets a tab, how big, how long, any discount for paying early and any charge for paying late. Every sale on credit reads it, and you change it when you like. Setting your deposit and cancellation terms: You set what backs a booking or an order: the deposit, the no-show fee, how late someone may cancel, what is returned and when. A deposit is held, not yours, until your terms say so. Every booking and order reads these terms, and you change them when you like; a change applies to new bookings. Setting your refund terms: You set what you give back when something is not right: money back, a replacement, or shop credit, and how long people have to ask. Every sale reads it, and you change it when you like; a change applies to new sales. Kept apart from Setting what, how much and where you sell (how many, not when); Selling on credit (one customer's tab); Setting what you accept in payment (in what, not when); Setting prices (how much); Taking table bookings (one booking); Returning something (one return); and Complaining and putting it right (one complaint). It usually starts when a holiday nears, your season changes, or you want to take a day off; as Setting your credit terms, when customers ask to pay later, when unpaid tabs pile up, or when your own suppliers change their terms; as Setting your deposit and cancellation terms, when people fail to turn up, when large orders are cancelled late, or when you start taking bookings; as Setting your refund terms, when you open, when a refund dispute happens, or when your supplier changes what they give back.

name: Keeping a want-to-try list
card: Ramen Kazan from your list has a table at 7. Book it?
note: You keep a list of places, dishes and drinks you want to try, alone or together, until you go. You add to it, change it, pause it, and end it when you have tried everything or no longer want to. A list stays on your device unless you share it with someone, who can then add to it. Kept apart from Posting an offer or a want (telling sellers what you want); Logging (you look back at what you tried); Keeping a shopping list (it is things to buy, not places to try); and Finding a place to eat (it looks for where to eat now). It usually starts when a friend recommends somewhere, you see a dish you do not know, you plan a trip, or a place on the list has a table free.

examples.card: Save a place you want to try.
examples.filled: Ramen Kazan, Tomás said the broth is the best in town. Add it to your list?

name: Paying it forward
card: Add €4 for a stranger's lunch?
note: You pay now for a coffee or meal that the next person who asks for one can claim: a suspended coffee, a meal on the board. The café holds your money until someone claims it, and what happens to one nobody claims (it stays, goes to a named fund, or comes back) is the café's stated term. Who may claim is the café's or the claimant's own say; FoodOS judges nobody. You add it, the café records it, and someone claims it. Kept apart from Giving and receiving food (spare food); Giving to a cause (money to a cause); Giving cash for food (cash to households); and Donating surplus (a business gives surplus to a charity). It usually starts when you pay your bill at a café that offers it, or when its board has meals waiting.
no mirror: a named third: the place holds what you paid until a stranger takes it, and the stranger's side is Getting free food, with that place

examples.card: Pay for a meal for someone in need.

name: Donating surplus
may the holder use it: yes, only for what was agreed
card: Your farm in Kent has 2 tonnes of carrots too small for the supermarket. Offer them to the food charity?
note: You are a business, a farm or a food bank giving surplus food to a food bank or charity. You offer it, the charity accepts what it can store and use (it may say no), you hand it over at a collection slot with the time and temperature noted, and you keep a record. Some places require shops to offer unsold food or forbid destroying it, and the card says so. A receipt or tax relief is separate from the gift. A charity reading the same offer sees it beside its own cold space and temperature log, and takes all, part or none. Kept apart from Giving and receiving food (spare food for anyone nearby); Running a community kitchen (a kitchen feeding a community); Selling spare food (sold cheap instead); and Handing out food parcels (parcels for people in need). It usually starts when it is closing time and stock is left, a collection slot is near, or a charity's posted needs match what you have.

name: Making an offering
card: It's the 1st of the lunar month. Set out oranges and tea at the altar?
note: You set out food for gods or ancestors: naivedya at a shrine, an ancestor altar, an ofrenda for the dead. Nobody receives it and nothing comes back. You choose the food, set it out, and it can repeat on every holy day or be paused. Sharing the food afterwards is Giving and receiving food or Eating and drinking, not this act. Kept apart from Giving and receiving food (food to monks or holy people who receive it). It usually starts when a date in the calendar comes, such as a new moon, a festival, an anniversary of a death, or a morning ritual.
no mirror: none: an offering to gods, ancestors or monks

name: Running a community kitchen
card: Saturday's langar: 400 expected and dal stock for 300. Ask the regulars for 10 kg?
note: You run a free kitchen for anyone who comes: a langar, a soup kitchen, a weekly community meal, iftar for the neighbourhood. You plan the number to cook for, line up stock and volunteers, cook and serve, and it runs each week until you end it. What you lack you ask for in Asking for donations or Asking for volunteers, and someone may sponsor a day. It is open to anyone, with no list and no proof of need. Cooking for the public carries the food-safety rules of the place. Kept apart from Giving and receiving food (food you will not use, to one or two people); Running a canteen (meals those people are owed); Handing out food parcels (a registered list); and Running a community fridge (a shelf people use unattended). It usually starts when it is the day it runs, when stock or volunteers fall short of the numbers expected, or when someone offers to pay for a day.

name: Finding a recipe
card: A 45-minute lasagne uses the mince and spinach in your fridge; you need lasagne sheets. Cook it tonight?
note: You look for something to cook: by what you have, a diet, a craving, a dish you ate somewhere, or what is in season. FoodOS suggests recipes with what each uses up, what you still need and how long it takes, and you pick. Making up a new dish is Developing a recipe, and asking a friend for theirs leads to Sharing a recipe. Kept apart from Choosing between products (cooking against ordering in); Checking one food (naming a food); and Finding a place to eat (a meal out). It usually starts when it is around dinner time, when ingredients need using up, after you ate something you liked, or when a season changes.

examples.card: Find a recipe for what you have.
examples.filled: A lasagne using the mince and spinach in the fridge. Cook it tonight?

name: Switching to a better deal
card: Your card reader costs €49 a month. Another posts €14 a month, tied in for 24 months, with €60 to set up. Switch?
note: You start from something you already pay for and find another you may prefer: cheaper, nearer, healthier, more local, by your own settings. FoodOS compares what you pay now with what is on offer, and shows the saving beside the catch: what leaving the old one costs (the sum for leaving early, fees, deposit), what the new one costs to leave early, and what switching costs once. You decide whether to switch; ending the old deal is that deal's own move. Kept apart from Finding someone to deal with (a supplier you do not have yet); Checking market prices (what things go for today); Choosing between products (picking now); and Running a trial (testing a change). It usually starts when a bill arrives, a cheaper price shows nearby, a contract is up for renewal, or a new option appears.

examples.card: Switch to a nearer or more local supplier.
examples.filled: A flour mill 30 km from your Durban café sells the same flour as your current mill, which is 140 km away. Switch mills?

examples.card: Switch to a cheaper phone or data plan for the shop.
examples.filled: You found a cheaper mobile-money plan for your kiosk in Dhaka. Switch plans?

name: Labelling food
card: 3 soups made today have no labels. Print them with celery marked?
note: You put the name, the date, the allergens and the ingredients on the pack, the shelf or a sheet, and check them against the rules for what you say about it, such as gluten-free or organic. You work out what is in the food, put the facts on it, change the label when the recipe or date changes, and keep it up for as long as you sell it. FoodOS shows what it checked against (the recipe, your supplier's sheet, the rules of your place) and will not let you say something it can show is false, such as gluten-free on a loaf with wheat in it. The rules are those of the place it is sold, so a new country can mean a new label. For a drink, the label's strength is checked against your test, with sulphites and other allergens the drink makes. When a recipe or a supplier's sheet changes, what is already packed or on shelves with the old words shows, with where it is: relabel it, stop selling it, or recall it. Kept apart from Posting an offer or a want (an offer shown to everyone, not the facts on the pack); Making a batch (putting the label on each batch); Recalling food (pulling a batch back); Sending proof (giving papers to a buyer); and Getting or giving a certificate (judging and issuing a certificate). It usually starts when something is made or packed, a recipe or supplier changes, a new product is added, or a rule about what you say changes.

name: Sending proof
card: The new buyer wants your hygiene certificate and last water test. Send both?
note: You send a buyer the papers they ask for: a hygiene certificate, a lab result, a spec sheet, an organic licence, a clean water test. You choose what to send and check it is still current. You send it with its date, to that buyer only, for as long as you say; once sent it cannot be unsent. Papers an authority demands are Inspecting a food place or Reporting to an authority. The proof can come from a record you already keep (where a catch was landed and with what gear, where a plot is and when it was picked), sending only the parts asked for. Kept apart from Reporting a problem to someone who can act (saying what is wrong at work, not proving what you sold); Labelling food (facts on the pack); Posting an offer or a want (shown to everyone); Getting or giving a certificate (the body that issues the certificate); and Vouching for someone (money of yours behind a person). It usually starts when a new buyer asks for papers, a certificate is renewed, a result comes back clean, or you want to win trust or a better price.

name: Reporting a problem to someone who can act
card: 3 people from your office were sick after the same lunch. Report it to the council?
note: You tell the council, and if you choose the people who bought it too, about food that made you ill or looks unsafe, or a place you saw that was dirty. You write what happened, and photograph the lot code on the pack, which lets a recall find it. What you ate, when, and how you were ill go to the council only if you allow it; what is made public is kept apart. It is done when the council has it, and you keep the receipt. The seller can answer beside your report. Telling the seller first, warning other buyers or writing a review are other choices, each its own act. A business the law makes report uses Reporting to an authority. Raising a problem at work: You take a problem at work to someone outside the job who can act: a union, a labour inspector, an ombudsman. Unpaid wages, tips taken, unsafe work, harassment. You write what happened, add your own records (hours, tips, countersigned shifts) if you choose, and send it; it stays between you and them, and they can ask and answer. Raising it with whoever runs your work is a button on the job itself. Work through an app counts too: pay for waiting, tips not passed on, being treated as self-employed while the app sets your hours, or an account closed with no reason. A union or a labour inspector can act on it. Kept apart from Complaining and putting it right (telling the seller you want it put right); Warning people nearby (a heads-up to neighbours); Recalling food (the seller pulls a batch back); Speaking up about a food rule (a rule being made); Sending proof (showing a buyer what you sold is what you said); Giving your word on something (it is public, while this is told only to whoever can act); and Asking for a ruling on a dispute (a case with two sides and a decider). It usually starts when you are ill after a meal, or you find something wrong with a product; as Raising a problem at work, when a problem raised at work goes unanswered, when pay is short, when a danger is seen, when something is done to you at work, or when a problem you raised has no answer by the date the terms give.

examples.filled: You found a swollen lid on a tin of fish in Leeds. Tell the council and others?

examples.filled: The walk-in fridge door at your kitchen in Johannesburg does not open from inside. Tell the labour inspector?

examples.card: Raise unpaid wages with a union.
examples.filled: You're missing two weeks' wages at the packhouse in Murcia. Tell your union?

examples.card: Take a problem at work to an ombudsman.
examples.filled: Your supervisor at the hotel in Dubai keeps your passport. Report it to the labour ministry in confidence?

examples.card: Take it further when an answer is late.
examples.filled: You raised short pay on 20 September and the agency promised an answer within 7 days. It is 12 days. Take it to the labour inspector, ask again, or let it rest?

examples.card: Raising a problem at work
examples.filled: You're missing two weeks' wages at the packhouse, and the manager has not answered. Tell your union?

you do this when: You tell someone who can act about unsafe food or a wrong at work: the council, a union, a manager. Not warning your neighbours or partners, not a report the law makes you give.

name: Paying tax on what you earned
card: Your quarterly tax payment in Lisbon is due on the 20th and the figure is ready. Pay it?
note: You pay tax on what you earned: income tax, a simpler scheme for small traders, a farm's yearly return. You gather the figures, send the return by the deadline, and pay, sometimes in instalments. The figures follow the law's meaning of what you earned. You can appeal if you think the bill is wrong. Tax taken from your pay that you did not owe is asked back through Claiming back from a scheme. Kept apart from Handing over tax you collected (VAT or wage tax you held for the state); Paying a fine or levy (a set charge); Choosing how your tax is counted (picking the scheme); and Contesting a charge (disputing one). It usually starts when a return is due, a quarter or year ends, or the figures are ready.

examples.card: Pay the tax your return shows.
examples.filled: Your income tax of £1,240 is due Friday. Pay it?

examples.card: File a yearly return as a small farm.
examples.filled: Your farm's annual return in Bavaria is ready. File it today?

examples.card: Declare takings from a market stall.
examples.filled: Your stall's quarterly takings in Lima are ready for the simplified tax regime. Send the declaration?

move words.card: Income tax of £1,240 is due Friday and your tax pot holds £1,300. Pay it?
move words.note: Tax on what you earned: nothing comes back and it is not a choice; the authority demands it under a law. The money half of the return.

examples.card: Pay tax, duty or a levy when it's due.
examples.filled: VAT due Friday from your tax pot.

move words.trigger: Tax or duty is due soon on her record, such as a VAT payment with the date in a week, and her tax pot or accounts hold enough to cover it.

you do this when: You pay tax on what you earned: income tax, a small trader's scheme, a farm's yearly return. Not a fine, not tax you collected for others.

name: Paying a fine or levy
card: The county market fee is KSh 50 and the officer comes at 10. Pay by M-Pesa and keep the receipt?
note: You pay what an authority sets: a fine for something done or said to be done, or a fee that is a condition of trading (a county market fee, a pitch fee, a charge on produce moved along a road). You pay and keep the receipt as proof. A fine paid early may cost less; the dates show. If you think it is wrong, you contest it in its own act. A charge with no rule or receipt behind it is Paying someone who demands it. Kept apart from Contesting a charge (disputing it); Paying tax on what you earned (tax worked out on earnings); and Renting something (rent for a pitch from a private owner). It usually starts when a notice arrives, a trading day with a fee begins, or a due date or early-payment date nears.

examples.card: Pay a market fee and keep the receipt.
examples.filled: The county officer wants the KSh 50 daily fee. Pay it and keep the receipt?

examples.card: Pay a fine.
examples.filled: A parking fine came for the delivery van. Pay it, or appeal?

examples.card: Pay a posted charge to carry produce past a checkpoint and keep the proof.
examples.filled: The produce charge at the Kano road checkpoint is posted at ₦1,500 a load, with a receipt. Pay it by transfer and keep the slip?

examples.card: Pay a hygiene fine.
examples.filled: Leeds council fined your takeaway £200 for a missing hand-wash sign. Pay within 14 days for the discount?

examples.card: Pay the landing fee at the jetty and keep the receipt.

examples.card: Pay the beach levy on what you landed.
examples.filled: The beach management unit charges KSh 5 a kilo landed. Pay it from this morning's landing and keep the slip?

you do this when: You pay what an authority sets for something done, or a fee that is a condition of trading. Not tax on earnings.

name: Inspecting a food place
card: Mill St Café is due a visit; last rating 3, two fixes outstanding. Book it for Tuesday?
note: You inspect a food place for an authority: a visit to a kitchen, shop, stall or farm, the findings, a rating, and a re-visit to check fixes. The law gives you the right to enter, sometimes without notice. You visit, write down your findings and the rating and sign them, and come back if fixes are outstanding. The place can answer a finding and appeal. Getting inspected: You are inspected by an authority under law and act on what it finds: a council hygiene visit, a veterinary inspection, a border check of your premises. You cannot refuse it. The inspection is booked or arrives, you keep the report, you fix the faults by the dates set and mark each one fixed with a photo and the contractor's receipt or word, and you ask for a re-inspection. Showing the score in your window may be required. Food ordered destroyed is Following an official order, and a finding you dispute is Contesting a charge. Kept apart from Getting or giving a certificate (an audit against a standard someone chose, ending in a certificate); Reporting a problem to someone who can act (a buyer's warning); and Logging food safety checks (the records an inspector reads). It usually starts when a place is due a visit, when illness reports or complaints come in, or when a past rating left fixes outstanding; as Getting inspected, when an inspector books a date, a fix-by date nears, or a complaint triggers a visit.

examples.card: Inspect a food place and give its rating.
examples.filled: Three illness reports came in about a grill in Manchester. Book your visit?

examples.card: Check a market's stalls before opening day.
examples.filled: Opening day is Saturday at the Lagos market. Start your round of the fish stalls' cold storage?

examples.card: Come back to see that fixes were made.
examples.filled: A Cape Town café was rated 3 with two fixes outstanding. Book your re-visit?

examples.card: Inspect a school canteen.
examples.filled: A school canteen in Seoul is due its check. Book your visit?

examples.card: Have an inspector check your place or food and keep the result.
examples.filled: The council hygiene inspection for your new kitchen is due this month. Book a date?

examples.filled: Fix the three faults in the report by the 20th. Start on the fixes?

examples.filled: Request a rescore after fixing the faults on your 2-star report. Request it now?

examples.card: Show the score on your window.
examples.filled: Your hygiene score is 4 stars in Leeds. Put the sticker in the shop window?

examples.filled: Inspection Tuesday. Open items: probe calibration and the pest log. Book the probe check for Monday?

move words.card: Someone from the council came into the kitchen this morning and left no paper. Note who came and what they said?
move words.note: Your own note of an official visit: who came, what they looked at, what they said, any date they gave, a photo of their badge if you took one. It is your word, never their finding; a paper that comes later sits beside it.

examples.card: Note a visit.
examples.filled: Someone from the council came into the kitchen this morning and left no paper. Note who came and what they said?

move words.trigger: She says someone from the council or an inspector came (or a visit shows in her day) and no report is in her record; also when a fix-by date was given by word only.

you do this when: An authority inspects a food place under law and you act on what it finds, or you are the inspector. Not an audit you chose for a mark.

name: Getting or giving a certificate
card: Hill Farm's organic audit passed with 1 minor finding. Issue the certificate?
note: You judge a farm, product or place against a standard and issue, renew or suspend a certificate: an organic body, a halal authority, or growers inspecting each other for a group's mark. You start the audit, note what you find, let the one certified answer each finding, then issue, renew or suspend. The certificate is your signed word, with an end date and a way to take it back. Usually the one certified pays you, and that is said first. A circle can certify a place: it signs each lot under its written rule, so anyone may say 'Nyeri-style' but only the circle can sign as the circle, and a false origin inside a sale wrongs the buyer. When growers inspect each other, each visit is a signed observation of what the visitor saw, and each inspector signs that she takes nothing else from the one she inspects and swaps no favours with her, with money behind that promise. Getting certified: You get a mark that a certifier signs and buyers may pay more for: organic, halal, kosher, Fairtrade, GlobalG.A.P. You apply, change how you farm or make if you need to, an auditor checks you, you pay, and you keep the mark until it is renewed or taken away. The certificate is the certifier's word, and you decide who sees it. Changing over can take years in which you follow the standard before you can use the mark, so the card shows that time, the fees, and selling without the mark as the other choice. A higher price is shown only when a buyer or co-op has signed it. A group can hold a mark for its members (they audit each other, or one audit covers all); the group decides to apply, and each member keeps their own records. Whether a mark allows a way of growing, such as without soil, can differ by country, and the card shows the rule that applies. Kept apart from Inspecting a food place (a visit the law requires); Sending proof (the one certified showing it); Getting a permit or registration (the state's permission); and Taking out insurance (cover against loss). It usually starts when someone applies, a certificate is close to renewal, or a finding comes in; as Getting certified, when conversion ends, a buyer asks for the mark, a renewal is near, or an audit window opens.

examples.card: Certify a farm, a product or a place against a standard.
examples.filled: Hill Farm's organic audit passed with one minor finding. Issue the certificate?

examples.card: Peers inspect each other for a shared mark.
examples.filled: Your growers' group in Kerala inspects each other's plots for its organic mark. Sign off this plot?

examples.card: Suspend a certificate when a finding is not fixed.
examples.filled: A coffee co-op you certify hasn't fixed its findings. Suspend its fair-trade mark until it does?

examples.card: Sign a lot under the circle's rule.
examples.filled: The Nyeri growers' circle has checked this lot of coffee against its written rule. Sign it as "Nyeri" for the circle?

examples.card: Sign what you saw on a visit.
examples.filled: You walked a neighbour's plot in Kerala on the 12th and saw no sprays and a clean compost heap. Sign a visit note, and promise to take nothing else from her?

examples.card: Get a certificate buyers ask for.
examples.filled: The halal certificate in Leicester ends in 6 weeks and the audit takes that long. Book the renewal?

examples.card: Get a fair-trade mark through a co-op.
examples.filled: Your coffee co-op in Huila wants Fairtrade certification for next harvest. Apply?

examples.card: Get ready for a farm assurance audit.
examples.filled: Your Suffolk dairy's yearly audit is in three weeks. Three records are missing: fill them from the milking log?

examples.card: Getting certified
examples.filled: Your 2 acres finish organic conversion in March, and the co-op pays 18% more for organic. Book the £600 audit?

you do this when: A body issues, renews or suspends a mark against a standard: you seek it or you issue it. Not the state's permission.

name: Reporting to an authority
card: Your cow in Devon gave birth on Monday. Report the calf's birth to the cattle tracing office before the 27th?
note: You give an authority what the law makes you report: animal births, deaths and movements, a disease among your animals or plants, an injury at work, water meter readings, your emissions, a stock return, a survey, or a theft or crop loss that the police, an extension officer or a disaster office records. You gather the figures from your record, send them by the deadline once you say yes, and keep the receipt or reference number. What a report may lead to (a disease report can bring a cull, with whatever pay the rules give) is shown before you send. Kept apart from Paying tax on what you earned (money owed); Reporting a problem to someone who can act (food that harmed people); Warning people nearby (neighbours, not an authority); and Following an official order (the authority tells you what to do, rather than you telling it). It usually starts when a birth, death or movement is logged, a reporting date is near, or a meter reading falls due.

examples.card: Send a water meter reading.
examples.filled: Your farm's meter near Fresno reads 4,812. Send the reading to the water board by the 1st?

examples.card: Report a disease among your animals.
examples.filled: Three of your hens in Tamil Nadu died overnight with swollen heads. Report to the animal health office today?

examples.card: File a ration shop's stock return.
examples.filled: The ration shop you run in Dhaka needs its monthly stock return by the 7th. Send the counts from your log?

examples.card: Report animals you moved.
examples.filled: You moved 40 sheep to the mart in Hereford on Tuesday. Report the movement before Friday?

examples.card: Send a landing declaration from your catch log.
examples.filled: Your trawler landed at Peterhead this morning. Send the landing declaration, 340 kg of mackerel, before the deadline?

examples.card: Send the weekly lice counts.
examples.filled: You counted cage 6 at your farm in Loch Fyne this week. Send the counts to the regulator by Friday?

examples.card: Send the month's feeding figures.

examples.filled: Your yearly report of medicines given to the cattle is due on 31 January and your record holds 11 treatments. Send it from them?

you do this when: You give an authority what the law makes you report: animal movements, a disease, an injury, readings.

name: Warning people nearby
card: The river at Kisumu will pass the bridge by dawn. Tell the 14 farms downstream tonight?
note: You warn the people a danger reaches: a rising river, a fire, a locust swarm, a disease nearby, dirty water. You say what, where, when, and what you saw or read that tells you so. The warning stands until you say all clear. People can answer: seen it too, all clear. FoodOS sends no warning it cannot show a reason for. Kept apart from Posting an offer or a want (an offer, not a danger); Reporting to an authority (what the law makes you report); Reporting a problem to someone who can act (food that harmed people); and Recalling food (a batch you sold, pulled back). It usually starts when you see a danger or a public notice names one near you.

examples.card: Warn people downstream of a rising river.
examples.filled: The river at Kisumu will pass the bridge by dawn. Warn the 14 farms downstream tonight?

examples.card: Warn neighbours of a swarm or a fire.
examples.filled: A locust swarm has settled on the hills above Marsabit. Warn the nearby herders now?

examples.card: Warn people that the water is contaminated.
examples.filled: The well in your village near Oaxaca smells of diesel. Tell the households that use it?

examples.card: Warn other cage farms of bad water.
examples.filled: Green scum and fish at the surface at your cages on Lake Victoria. Warn the 6 cage farms nearby?

examples.card: Warn the other sellers of a raid.
examples.filled: You saw council vans park at the end of your lane at 2:40. Warn the sellers in your lane group?

examples.card: Warn drivers of a road hazard.
examples.filled: The bridge on your route is closed. Warn drivers within 100 km?

you do this when: You warn the people a danger reaches, and the warning stands until you say all clear: a river, a fire, a swarm. Not a report to an authority.

name: Returning something
card: The blender can go back until Friday for £49. Return it?
note: You send back something you bought because you changed your mind or it did not suit: you check the return window, send or take it back, and get your money back. The window is the law's or the seller's own policy, and the card says which; fresh food is often left out. Who pays the postage and any restocking fee is shown before you send it. A refund is money; store credit is a claim on the seller with its own end date, and the card shows the difference. Accepting a return: You take back what you sold because the buyer changed their mind or it did not suit, and refund them by your policy or the law's. You check it is within the window and in the state your terms say, take it back, and refund money or give credit, as they choose where the law says. Kept apart from Complaining and putting it right (it was wrong or faulty and the seller puts it right); Claiming on a warranty (a fault after some time); and Returning containers (empties for their deposit). It usually starts when the return window is about to close or you find you have no use for something; as Accepting a return, when a customer brings something back or asks to.

examples.card: Return something you bought for a refund.
examples.filled: The blender, back by Friday for £49. Return it?

examples.card: Send back a machine that does not suit your kitchen.
examples.filled: The pasta machine bought in Bologna is too big for your counter. Return it by the 20th?

examples.card: Return clothes that did not fit.
examples.filled: The apron you ordered online in Lagos is too big. Return it by Monday, with the courier collecting for ₦1,500?

examples.card: Hand stale or damaged stock to the supplier's van.
examples.filled: The bread van in Kisumu took back 14 stale loaves and left a credit slip. Note what he took?

examples.card: Send back near-dated stock the supplier takes back.
examples.filled: You hold 28 packs of biscuits dated 12 November and sell about 3 a week. Put them on offer, or ask the distributor to take them back?

examples.card: Take back a return within the window.
examples.filled: A customer in Lisbon returns a pan bought last week, unused. Refund €30?

examples.card: Offer credit or money back.
examples.filled: A customer returns a cookbook in Leeds. Offer money back or credit, their choice?

examples.filled: The return in Austin is 40 days after sale, past your 30. Explain and decline?

examples.card: Accepting a return
examples.filled: A customer brings back the blender within your 14 days, unused. Take it back and refund £49?

you do this when: Something goes back and the price comes back: a purchase you changed your mind on, or you are the seller who takes it back. Not empties for their deposit, not a fault.

name: Returning containers
card: 14 kegs and 6 crates are due back to the brewery, worth £420 in deposits. Send them on Thursday's drop?
note: You return bottles, crates, kegs, gas cylinders, jars or trays for the deposit you paid on them: bottles into the shop machine, kegs to the brewery, crates to the dairy. The deposit is money you are owed by whoever took it, paid back in money or credit, sometimes by a time limit; some places make the scheme law. Kegs, crates and cylinders often stay the brewery's or dairy's, so you hold them and may owe for one you lose. You gather them, take or send them back, and the deposit comes back. Taking containers back: You take back the empties you sold with a deposit, and pay the deposit back: milk bottles, beer crates, gas cylinders, deposit cans at a machine, the jars your jam came in. Each deposit was the customer's money held by you, so it is owed to them on return. You check the empties, pay the deposit, and send them to be washed or refilled. The card shows how many deposits are still out. Each sale that carries a container writes the container into the sale, so the deposits still out are counted from sales and not from memory. Kept apart from Returning something (a refund on what you bought); Getting rid of waste (what nobody wants); Ordering stock (the order the empties came with); and Buying and selling food to use (food, not empties). It usually starts when empties pile up, when a delivery that can take them back is booked, or when a deposit nears its time limit; as Taking containers back, when customers bring empties back, when you are short of bottles or crates, or when the deposits you still owe pile up.

move words.card: You have 38 kegs out at pubs, and the Anchor has had 6 of them for 11 weeks. Do you want to ask them for the kegs back this week?
move words.note: A keg or cask is the brewery's biggest piece of unlisted kit and it walks. The maker's side of the deposit already exists; what is missing is the move for the gap between what went out and what came back, closed by the collector's count.

examples.card: Chase the empties.
examples.filled: You have 38 kegs out at pubs, and the Anchor has had 6 of them for 11 weeks. Do you want to ask them for the kegs back this week?

examples.card: Chase the empties.

name: Fishing
card: Wind drops to 12 knots after 4am. Fish the north bank with 2 tonnes of quota left?
note: You fish for work, food or fun: from a canoe off the beach, a trawler on quota, a rod on a river. You plan around grounds, weather, fuel, crew, any quota or licence and price, go out, land the catch and keep the log: how much, of what, from where, in how many hours. Quota and licences come from the state, and each catch uses some up. A crew paid in shares of the catch is the crew's own rule. Fuel and ice are Ordering stock, and what you sell is Selling at auction, Selling and buying in bulk or Selling spare food. Landing declarations, logbook returns and harbour dues the law requires are their own acts. Nobody answers, because it is from nature. Kept apart from Foraging (wild plants and shellfish on the shore); and Hunting (land game). It usually starts when the wind or tide suits, when a season or a quota opens, when the price is good, or when fuel and crew are ready.
no mirror: none: nature

examples.card: Line-fish from the shore on a calm day.
examples.filled: The sea is flat at dawn off Cape Coast. Take the canoe out for 4 hours?

examples.card: Run a small boat's trip and land the catch at the market.

examples.card: Fish for pleasure within local limits.
examples.filled: Salmon season opens on the river Tay. Book a day on the water for Saturday?

examples.card: Plan a fishing trip against quota and weather.
examples.filled: Your Cornish crab boat has 800 kg of quota left, a gale on Thursday and the best price on Friday. Sail Wednesday?

move words.card: You landed 340 kg of mackerel. Share it out as your crew agreed, a share each and one for the boat?
move words.note: You share a landing out by the crew's rule or the community's custom: so many shares to each hand, one for the boat, one for the harbour fund. Each share is handed over and noted in the record.

move words.card: Your canoe has been back at Elmina since 11 and no landing is logged. Log what you brought in?
move words.note: The catch you bring ashore, in your own measure (kilos, baskets, crates or a count), by kind of fish, with where you fished and where it went: sold, kept, shared or put back.

examples.card: Land the catch.
examples.filled: Your canoe has been back at Elmina since 11 and no landing is logged. Log what you brought in?

move words.trigger: A trip she planned or said she was starting has passed the time she gave for coming back, or she says she is back, and no landing is logged for it.

move words.card: Your pots brought up 22 lobsters under the legal size and 3 carrying eggs. Log them as put back?
move words.note: Fish you put back or lost before they came ashore: undersize, carrying eggs, protected, over quota, taken by seals, spoiled for want of ice. You count them as you count the rest. Some places ask you to record what you put back, and sending it is Reporting to an authority. Food binned on shore is Log what you throw away.

examples.card: Throw some back.
examples.filled: Your pots brought up 22 lobsters under the legal size and 3 carrying eggs. Log them as put back?

move words.trigger: A landing is logged with a kind of fish that has a size limit, a closed season or a quota already used up by an open fact, or she says she put some back or lost some before landing.

move words.card: You hauled 90 kg of sardines off the north bank and the shoal was still thick when you left. Tell the 6 boats in your group?
move words.note: Telling the boats you choose where the fish are: the ground, the hour and what you took, as your own word. It goes only to the circle you pick, and they can answer: seen it too, nothing there. You never owe it, and nothing about your grounds goes further without your yes.

examples.card: Tell the others.
examples.filled: Kofi asked where you fished yesterday. Tell him only the bank, not the depth?

examples.card: Record a loss.

examples.card: Record a loss.
