move words.card: A gale is posted for your ground. Do you go out, or are you not out today?
move words.note: A day she did not trade, with her own word for why. It keeps the days worked and the days lost in her record, which she carries and can share. It does not close anything and does not judge.

examples.card: Not out today.
examples.filled: The boats went out at 5 and you stayed in. Note why: the weather, the engine, or family?

move words.trigger: It is later than her usual start on a day she normally sells (from her own past days), and she has not started or counted anything; or she tells FoodOS it is raining or she is ill.

move words.card: You kept 4 kg of the catch for the house and gave 2 to the crew. Note it apart from what you sold?
move words.note: Stock that left because you used it yourself: grain for the house or the hens, seed kept back, feed for your own animals, diesel, flour taken home. Sales, waste and gifts are recorded by their own acts.

examples.card: Keep part of the catch for home.
examples.filled: You kept 6 kilos of the catch for the family. Note it as taken out?

move words.trigger: Her count of a store is lower than what came in less what went out by her records, and a sale, a loss she logged or a spray, feed or sowing record does not explain the remainder.

you do this when: You fish from a canoe, a trawler or a river bank, under any quota or licence, and keep the log of the catch. Not gathering or hunting.

name: Hunting
card: Deer season opens Saturday and your tag is valid. Book the day on the estate?
note: You hunt or trap under a licence, a tag or a customary right: deer on an estate, rabbits on a farm, springbok under a permit. A tag lets you take one animal, and the season and the landowner's yes are its conditions. You check them, go out, and it is done when you return. You say what you took (the animal, where, and its weight dressed), or that you came back with nothing or lost a wounded animal. Tag returns, check stations and disease reports the law requires are their own acts, and where hunting is forbidden FoodOS shows the law. Butchering is Preparing food for sale, and selling game has its own rules. Nobody answers, because it is from nature. Kept apart from Foraging (wild plants and mushrooms); Fishing (from water); and Controlling pests (killing pests, not hunting for food). It usually starts when a season opens, a tag is valid or custom allows it, or permission is given.
no mirror: none: nature

examples.card: Hunt or trap with a licence and permission.
examples.filled: The season is open and you have a tag. Go on the deer stalk on the estate on Saturday?

examples.card: Trap small game for the pot where the law allows.
examples.filled: Rabbit season is open on the farm in Tasmania. Set snares at dusk with the landowner's yes?

examples.card: Take a licensed animal for the family.
examples.filled: Your elk tag in Montana is valid until Sunday. Book the hunt?

examples.card: Hunt for food in the bush by custom and permit.
examples.filled: Your uncle in Namibia has a permit for a springbok this month. Go with him on Saturday?

move words.card: You brought back a springbok. Share it by your family's custom, elders first, then the rest of the household?
move words.note: You share a landing out by the crew's rule or the community's custom: so many shares to each hand, one for the boat, one for the harbour fund. Each share is handed over and noted in the record.

examples.card: Share a hunt out by community custom.
examples.filled: You and 3 others took an eland in northern Namibia. Give the elders' and widows' shares first, then split the rest among you?

examples.card: Share a deer between the people who hunted.
examples.filled: Your group stalked a red deer on a Scottish estate. Split the meat four ways and send a joint to the landowner?

move words.trigger: A hunt is logged in her record with the people who went and a sharing custom or rule she wrote, and no shares are handed out yet.

move words.card: You say you took a roe doe in the lower wood. Mark your tag for it now?
move words.note: Notches the tag in her record with date, place and species; feeds the legal return and the larder.

examples.card: Mark your tag.
examples.filled: You say you took a roe doe in the lower wood. Mark your tag for it now?

move words.trigger: She holds a valid tag and says (or her phone shows she is out and reports) that she took an animal.

move words.card: The rabbits are thick on the lower field at Hill Farm and the season is open. Ask the farmer for his yes, or hunt the common instead?
move words.note: You ask whoever holds the right to a tree or a site before you gather from it. It may be the landowner, the village or a family. They can say yes, no or name a limit.

examples.card: Ask the owner.
examples.filled: The rabbits are thick on the lower field at Hill Farm and the season is open. Ask the farmer for his yes, or hunt the common instead?

move words.trigger: She holds a valid licence or tag, a season is open, and the place she picked is land that is not hers or her group's.

move words.card: What did you bring home, and when was it shot and gutted?
move words.note: What you brought home: kind, count or weight, where, when it was shot, when it was gutted and chilled, and who took it. It starts the clock that decides whether the meat can be sold.

examples.card: Note what you brought home from a hunt.
examples.filled: One roe deer, 18 kg, shot at 6:40, gutted by 7:10, chilled by 9.

move words.trigger: She comes back from a hunt with an animal.

move words.card: You gave a haunch to your neighbour and kept the rest. Note what was kept and given?
move words.note: Stock that left because you used it yourself: grain for the house or the hens, seed kept back, feed for your own animals, diesel, flour taken home. Sales, waste and gifts are recorded by their own acts.

examples.card: Keep part of a kill for home.
examples.filled: You kept the haunch for the family and gave the rest to the dealer. Note it as taken out?

move words.trigger: Her count of a store is lower than what came in less what went out by her records, and a sale, a loss she logged or a spray, feed or sowing record does not explain the remainder.

you do this when: You hunt or trap under a licence, a tag or a customary right, in season and with the landowner's yes. Not fishing or gathering.

name: Planning what to grow or feed
card: The long rains start in March near Nakuru. Plan which fields go to maize and which to beans?
note: You decide a season's crops: what to grow where, the planting calendar, the rotation. Seed and work go in now and the harvest comes months later, so the plan shows what is tied up and when, and you write down what you expect each crop to yield and fetch. Land you rent and water you have rights to set its limits. How many crops you rely on is yours to choose. You plan, change it, invite others in, and finish it when the season is set. Planning feed: You plan the season's feed against the animals you keep: grass, hay, silage, bought feed, the grazing you have a right to, and by-products you take for free or cheap such as spent grain, bread or whey. You set out each way to close a gap (buy now, buy later, sell some animals), with what each costs and when, and you write down what you expect, such as grass by mid-April. A free load can stop when its giver changes plans, and the plan shows that. If spring comes late, you see it in the numbers; FoodOS does not guess for you. You change the plan as numbers or the weather change, and finish it when the season is covered. Kept apart from Planning how much to make (what a seller makes); Planning what to eat (meals); and Growing to a buyer's contract (a crop sold before it grows). It usually starts when a season ends, seed catalogues arrive, a bed is empty, or the first sowing date nears; as Planning feed, when winter or the dry season nears, the herd grows or shrinks, hay comes in, or feed prices move.

examples.card: Decide what to grow or raise this season from last year.
examples.filled: Beans gave 4 kg a square metre in bed 3 last year. Move them to bed 1 and put squash in bed 3?

examples.card: Plan the planting calendar so things ripen in turn.
examples.filled: Sow lettuce every three weeks from March so you never get thirty at once?

examples.card: Work out how much land you need to feed your household or fill an order.
examples.filled: For two adults and salads all year you need about 60 square metres. Plan for that?

examples.card: Spread the risk across more than one crop or buyer.
examples.filled: Your coffee smallholding in Kenya could add macadamia and a second buyer, so one bad season cannot sink the year. Plant the macadamia?

examples.card: Plan feed against your animals for the season.
examples.filled: Your 60 cows have hay until 2 March and grass comes in April. Order more hay?

examples.card: Buy feed early while it is cheaper.
examples.filled: Hay is £45 a bale now and was £70 last February. Buy early and store it?

examples.card: Plan the dry season against the herd.
examples.filled: Your 40 goats in Kajiado need 3 months of feed before the rains. Buy dry fodder, or sell some goats?

examples.card: Order layer feed before the shed runs out.
examples.filled: Your 200 layers in Kumasi finish a bag of mash every two days and the shed holds six. Order from the feed store before Friday?

examples.card: Plan feed against the weight of fish in the water.
examples.filled: Batch 7 catfish are on day 120 of 190. Buy the 18 tonnes of feed in three loads, or wait for the two-tonne price?

examples.card: Planning feed
examples.filled: 410 bales feed your 60 cows until 2 March, and grass comes mid-April. Buy more bales, or sell some of the herd?

you do this when: You decide the season ahead for land and animals: what to sow, how to feed your herd; the subject is one fact. Not planning meals or a batch, not doing it.

name: Looking after a pet
card: Biscuit is 0.6 kg over the vet's target. Cut to a level scoop each meal?
note: You feed and care for a pet and know what is safe for it to eat. It cannot answer, so you answer for it, with the vet's advice on its side. You start the care, change the food or amounts, note what happened, ask someone to sit, and end it when the pet is gone. A sitter you pay is Doing or getting a job for pay. Kept apart from Raising animals (kept for food, fibre or sale); and Looking after someone's animals (animals that are not yours). It usually starts when you bring a pet home, its weight or the vet's advice changes the feeding, you are about to go away, or a food in the house could harm it.

examples.card: Feed and care for a pet, and know what is safe for it to eat.
examples.filled: Your dog in Toronto has been scratching since you changed her food. Go back to the old one for a week?

examples.card: Keep a pet to its target weight.
examples.filled: Biscuit the spaniel in Dublin is 0.6 kg over the vet's target. Cut to a level scoop each meal?

examples.card: Arrange care for a pet while you are away.
examples.filled: You are two weeks away from Mumbai. Book the neighbour to feed the cat twice a day?

examples.card: Keep a pet away from a food that could hurt it.
examples.filled: Your rabbit's salad in Kyoto has chives in it. Keep them off its plate?

examples.card: Book a pet check-up and vaccinations.
examples.filled: Your dog's vaccination in Buenos Aires runs out next month. Book the clinic?

you do this when: You feed and care for a pet and know what is safe for it.

name: Looking after someone's animals
card: Your neighbour in Hawes is away for two weeks and asks you to feed her 30 ewes. Do it for £150?
note: You keep animals that belong to someone else: grazing heifers, boarding someone's horse, herding a family's cows, raising a company's chickens or pigs on contract. The animals and what they gain stay the owner's. You agree the pay (per head per day, or a share of the milk or calves as a term), who pays when an animal is ill or dies, and how either side ends it. On a contract, the company's chicks and feed stay theirs while your housing and work are yours, often bought on a loan, so the card shows how pay is worked out and what you have at stake. Moving animals onto your land brings reports the law requires. When you take your share of the milk or the calves as pay, you say so and the owner answers, so the pay in kind is written down. Kept apart from Doing or getting a job for pay (a job for pay where no animals stay with you); Looking after land for pay (land kept to a standard); and Having food processed (food milled or pressed). It usually starts when a farm needs grazing for young stock, a grazing season opens, a contract is offered, or animals arrive or are due to go home.

examples.card: Graze another farm's young stock for a fee.
examples.filled: Tait's wants 40 heifers grazed May to October at £1.10 a head a day. Take them?

examples.card: Raise broilers on contract.
examples.filled: A poultry company in Brazil offers a contract for 20,000 chicks. Take it?

examples.card: Herd cattle for a family.
examples.filled: A family near Maasai Mara asks you to herd their cows. Take them?

examples.card: Keep your own count of chicks, feed and deaths beside the company's.
examples.filled: The company's feed ticket says 12 tonnes and the bin in your broiler house near Chapeco took about 11. Photograph the ticket and the bin and write both down?

move words.card: Month end. Send the owner the count of births, deaths and weight for his herd?
move words.note: Sending the owner the record of what you did to what is theirs: the kill sheet with weights and grade, the treatment with its waiting days, the count of births, deaths and weight for animals you keep, the bags in store. It is your signed word and your proof of the work.

examples.card: Send the owner the herd's record.
examples.filled: This month: 2 calves born, one cow treated for mastitis, the herd counted at 46. Send it to the owner?

move words.trigger: A load of animals has been counted in on the act and the weights out are written, or the inspector's call is noted, and the owner has not yet been sent the sheet.

you do this when: You keep animals that belong to someone else for pay: grazing, boarding, herding.

name: Having someone keep your animals
card: Your 40 heifers at the Tait farm gained 0.6 kg a day, short of the 0.7 agreed. Ask why, or bring them home in May?
note: You have your animals kept or grazed by someone else for a season or longer: a grazier, a herder, a keeper, a mafisa arrangement. You agree what they are paid (per head per week, or a share of the milk or calves), what they may use (milk yes, sale no), who bears losses from theft, drought or disease, and what bringing them home early costs. You hand them over counted and marked, get the keeper's record of births, deaths and weight gain, and take them back the same way. Movement permits and health papers the law asks for are part of the job. Kept apart from Moving animals (you move them yourself); Raising animals (you raise them yourself); and Renting land or a place to trade (you rent ground, not care). It usually starts when your own pasture is short, a grazing season opens, a herder offers space, or animals are ready to move on.

examples.card: Send young stock to a grazier.
examples.filled: Send 40 heifers to Tait's farm for the summer?

examples.card: Send cattle to a herder for the dry season.
examples.filled: The Fulani herder near Kaduna will take 25 cows for the dry season at ₦2,000 a head a week. Send them?

examples.card: Send sheep to summer pasture.
examples.filled: The summer pasture in Asturias takes 60 sheep from June at €1 a head a week. Send them?

move words.card: Your 25 bags at the warehouse have not been counted since September. Ask them to count with you?
move words.note: Asking whoever holds what is yours to count it, or to show the count behind what they paid you: the animals with a keeper, the bags in a store, the jars on a shop's shelf, the portions made under your recipe. Their count is their signed word; you can ask to be there for it.

examples.card: Ask the keeper to count your animals.
examples.filled: Your 12 goats have been with the herder since June. Ask him to count them with you on Sunday?

move words.trigger: No count from the holder for longer than the agreed or usual gap, or a statement you are paid on looks low against your own record.

you do this when: Someone else grazes or keeps your animals for a season or longer.

name: Renting out land
card: The neighbour asks to rent your 2 back acres for a season at KSh 15,000, paid at planting. Agree?
note: You rent out a field, grazing, a vineyard, water or quota for money, by the season or for years. You offer terms, they accept, you hand over the land, they pay (before planting, or at harvest, so you wait to be paid), and it ends at the season's end; ending it sooner costs the sum agreed. The tenant bears the crop's luck. What happens to a standing crop or an improvement they made (a tree planted, a well dug) if it ends early is agreed up front, and tenancy laws of the place apply. Where land is held by a family or village, your right to let it is their rule. Quota and water rights are rights the state gave you, with their own terms. Paying in a share of the crop instead of rent is Farming land on shares. Kept apart from Lending and borrowing something (free, and things); Renting something (kit and rooms); and Running a market (pitches for many sellers). It usually starts when a neighbour asks for ground, when a season nears and a field lies empty, or when a lease is about to end.

examples.card: Rent out spare grazing for a season.
examples.filled: A herder in Kenya's Laikipia asks to graze 50 cattle for two months. Rent it at KSh 100 a head?

examples.card: Lease an orchard or vineyard to a grower.
examples.filled: A winemaker in Tuscany wants to lease your old vines for 5 years. Offer it at €2,000 a hectare?

examples.card: Lease out spare quota.
examples.filled: Your unused 20 tonnes of quota could be fished by another boat this season at £1,100 a tonne. Lease out 10?

examples.card: Lease out unused water rights.
examples.filled: Your water right on the canal in Mendoza is unused this season. Lease it to a neighbour?

examples.card: Set the guest nights a lodge counted beside your gate log.
examples.filled: A lodge on your land pays by the guest night. Its signed count for September is 612; your gate log shows 655. Put the two side by side and ask about the 43?

you do this when: You rent out a field, grazing, a vineyard, water or quota by the season or for years, and you wait to be paid. Not kit or a place to trade.
mirror: Renting land or a place to trade

name: Opening to visitors
card: A school in Bristol asks to bring 40 children to see the cows. Host them on the 12th at £3 a child?
note: You open your farm for visitors to pick their own or see it working: pick-your-own, farm tours, open days, harvest weekends, most often for a season. You set the price per basket or ticket and the slots, visitors book or turn up, agree your rules for the field, pick or look round, and pay. Booked slots, what happens if weather cancels, and cover if a visitor is hurt are said up front. Rooms for the night are Renting something. Paying and walking in are one moment, so the day's tickets are the day's count of people. A visitor can sign what he saw: a buyer's agent, a lender's messenger or a certifier writes 'on the 3rd, her stall open, about 20 sacks', his name to its truth. It is only what he saw from where you let him stand, never inside your place without your yes. Kept apart from Running a food event (a one-off food event); Selling at a stall, a gate or a screen (a stall on market day); and Buying and selling food to use (guests seated for a meal). It usually starts when a crop ripens, a season for visits opens, a holiday or weekend nears with good weather, or a booked group is due.

examples.card: Invite a group to visit or pick on your land.
examples.filled: Strawberries peak next week. Open pick-your-own Saturday at £5 a basket?

examples.card: Hold an open day.
examples.filled: Lambing begins in March. Hold an open day for families?

examples.card: Offer farm tours to travellers.
examples.filled: Tour groups from Munnar ask to see your tea estate on Sundays. Open it for tours at 400 rupees a head?

examples.card: Let a buyer's agent sign what he saw.
examples.filled: A lender's messenger asks to see your drying yard in Kisumu before he signs for a loan. Let him in, and let him sign what he sees from the gate?

move words.card: The farm open day has closed. Note how many came, and how many paid at the gate?
move words.note: How many people you actually fed or who came, and how many you turned away: the number a scheme, a client or next week's cooking is planned and paid on.

examples.card: Count the visitors.
examples.filled: The open day closed at 5. Note how many came in?

move words.trigger: A meal, service or event she runs has ended.

you do this when: You open your farm to visitors: pick-your-own, tours, open days, usually for a season.

name: Training your staff
card: Sam starts Monday. Book his allergen training before his first shift?
note: You make sure the people who work for you are trained for their work: induction, allergen and hygiene training, chemical handling, and whatever else the law asks for. You teach it yourself or book a course, they take it, and it is signed off; it repeats when a certificate runs out. The law makes some of this compulsory. It is paid time, so the card shows the hours. A training bond (repaying a course if they leave early) is agreed up front. The certificate goes on the worker's own record. Kept apart from Teaching a food skill (teaching with no legal sign-off); Doing an apprenticeship (years of work and teaching); and Getting trained for work (the worker getting their own certificate). It usually starts when a new person is about to begin, a certificate is about to lapse, new kit or a new chemical arrives, a season of risky work comes round, or a certificate held for someone on your staff nears its end date.

examples.card: Train a new starter before their first shift.
examples.filled: Sam starts on Monday. Book the allergen and hygiene induction?

examples.card: Train people before risky seasonal work.
examples.filled: The spraying season is near. Book the chemical training?

examples.card: Renew a team's food handling training before it lapses.
examples.filled: The food handling cards of your four stall staff at the Pune market run out in March. Book the group course?

examples.card: Train a new worker on a dangerous machine.
examples.filled: A new hand starts on your farm in Saskatchewan. Show them the grain auger guard before first use?

you do this when: You make sure your own staff are trained for their work, as the law asks: induction, hygiene, chemicals. Not a class anyone takes for fun, not one person's certificate.

name: Getting trained for work
card: Your food hygiene certificate runs out on 4 May. Book the renewal?
note: You get the certificate your work needs, and keep it current: food hygiene, allergens, a licence course. You find the course, book it, take it, and the certificate is kept as your own: issued by the body that ran it, with its end date, yours to carry to any employer. You renew it before it runs out. Some courses are required by law or by a licence. The card shows the fee and the day it takes. Kept apart from Learning a food skill (it is learning for its own sake with no certificate your job demands); and Getting a permit or registration (it is permission to trade, not a course certificate). It usually starts when you take a food job, when a certificate nears its end date, when a licence asks for a course, or when the law changes.

examples.card: Get a food hygiene certificate and keep it as your own.
examples.filled: Book the level 2 hygiene course in Leeds for your new café job?

examples.card: Renew a certificate before it runs out.
examples.filled: Your allergen awareness certificate in Auckland runs out in June. Book the half-day renewal?

examples.card: Take the course a licence needs.
examples.filled: The Bangkok district office wants a food handler course before it licenses your street food pitch. Book the next one?

you do this when: You get the certificate your work needs and keep it current: food hygiene, allergens, a licence course. Not a class you take for pleasure.

name: Doing an apprenticeship
card: The kitchen at Marlow Street offers a 2 year apprenticeship at £9.20 an hour with college on Fridays. Accept it?
note: You work for a master, a kitchen, a farm or a business while they teach you. You agree the wage or fee and when it is paid, the training plan, who assesses you, and what leaving early costs on either side. Often the teaching comes first and you pay for it with your work at a lower wage, so you owe the teacher until the work has repaid it. Your logged hours and sign-offs are yours. Either side can end it on the agreed terms. Each shift your teacher signs lowers what you owe them, shown on both sides. Taking on an apprentice: You take someone on to learn your trade by working beside you: a baker's, butcher's, cheesemaker's or chef's apprentice. You agree how long, what they will learn, what they will be paid or pay you, what they do in return, and whether they may set up nearby when done. You teach as they work, sign off what they have learned, and end it with a certificate or a word on their record. Either side can end it on the terms agreed. Kept apart from Working for someone (pay, no teaching); Getting trained for work (a certificate course); Teaching a food skill (a teacher, no work); Training your staff (people who already work for you); and Employing someone (work bought, nothing taught). It usually starts when a place offers an apprenticeship, you leave school, or you want to move into a trade; as Taking on an apprentice, when someone asks to learn from you, when you need help and can teach, or when a stage of the apprenticeship is done.

examples.card: Join a farm as a learner for a season.
examples.filled: A dairy near Cork will teach you cheesemaking for a season in return for 30 hours a week. Start in March?

examples.card: Pay a master baker to take you on.
examples.filled: A baker in Fez will teach you for a year and asks 2,000 dirhams up front. Pay and begin on Monday?

examples.card: Sign off a stage of training.
examples.filled: Your master in Osaka has logged 400 hours of your 800 for knife work. Ask for the first sign-off?

examples.card: Take on an apprentice on agreed terms.
examples.filled: A young man in Lyon wants to learn butchery with you for 3 years. Take him on?

examples.card: Sign off a skill your apprentice has learned.
examples.filled: Kwame can now run the oven alone in Kumasi. Sign it off on his record?

examples.card: End an apprenticeship with a certificate.
examples.filled: Lucía's 2 years end Friday in Valencia. Sign her certificate?

examples.card: Taking on an apprentice
examples.filled: Amina wants to learn baking with you for 2 years. Take her on?

you do this when: You work beside a master while they teach you, for years: you learn or you take someone on. Not a class, not a wage only.

name: Picking orders
card: Mrs Shah's and the Lees' orders are on the same aisle. Pick them together?
note: You gather the items for each order: click-and-collect, a dark store, a warehouse pick list. You start the pick, change the route or batch of orders, note what was found, pass it to a packer, and mark it done. A substitute needs the buyer's yes, or the limits they set beforehand (same size, no allergen change, not dearer); it repeats through the day. Kept apart from Stocking shelves (it fills shelves, not orders); and Moving food to someone (it takes finished orders to the customer). It usually starts when an order arrives, when a pick window opens, or when several orders sit in the same aisle and can be picked together.

examples.card: Pick the items for one customer's order.
examples.filled: Pick 12 items for Mrs Shah's order at your corner shop in Leicester. Start picking?

examples.card: Pick several orders together in one walk.
examples.filled: Two orders at your dark store in Jakarta are on the same aisle. Pick them together before the courier arrives?

examples.card: Substitute an item that is out.
examples.filled: Your warehouse in Johannesburg is out of the usual oil. Offer the buyer the same size of another brand?

examples.card: Pick for a collection slot.
examples.filled: Your food hub in Lyon has 30 boxes for Thursday's collection window. Start packing?

examples.card: The weight on the scale
examples.filled: Order 4417 for Tariq's Kebabs asks for 20 kg of lamb shoulder and the three boxes you picked weigh 21.4 kg. Do you send all three as weighed, or open a box to get closer to 20 kg?

examples.card: The weight on the scale
examples.filled: The cheese order asks for one 8 kg wheel and the nearest you have weighs 9.1 kg. Do you send it at its weight?

examples.card: The weight on the scale
examples.filled: The fish order is 15 kg of hake and your fillets scale at 14.2 kg. Do you send short or add a fillet?

examples.card: Which lot went to which customer
examples.filled: The school order is 10 cases of yoghurt and you hold two lots. Do you send the older lot, which they use up first?

you do this when: You gather the items for each order from stock. The same hand with no order is Stocking shelves.

name: Running a pickup point
card: Saturday at the hall: 12 boxes from 3 sellers. Send the slot times?
note: You host a spot where sellers or givers drop food and people collect it: a local group-chat swap, a harvest-share drop site, your shop, your home. You ask or offer to host, accept who joins, check each box in, hand each box to the person it is for, and chase what is left; it runs until ended. What happens to a box left past its day (back to the seller, to a food bank) is agreed up front. A fee or a free box for hosting is a term. Kept apart from Moving food to someone (moving food to people); and Picking orders (gathering an order). It usually starts when sellers announce a drop, the collection time arrives, or a box is left uncollected.

examples.card: Run a pickup point where sellers drop food and people collect it.
examples.filled: 12 member boxes arrive Saturday at the village hall in Dalarna. Host the pickup?

examples.card: Host a CSA drop site at your home.
examples.filled: Your garage in Brisbane could receive the farm's Tuesday boxes for 14 families. Host them?

examples.card: Run a group-chat swap for local sellers.
examples.filled: Your car park in Helsinki could host the weekly REKO swap at 6pm. Host it?

examples.card: Give each seller the pickup times.
examples.filled: Three sellers drop at your church hall in Nairobi on Saturday. Send them the 3pm drop time?

move words.card: 4 bags from 2 bakers arrive at 5pm. Check them in?
move words.note: Signing for what a seller drops off; holding it is not owning it.

examples.card: Sign for boxes dropped at your point.
examples.filled: 4 bags from 2 bakers at 5pm.

move words.trigger: A seller's drop is due at the pickup point by the slot she set up, or a box has just arrived that she has not yet signed for.

move words.card: Sam is here for his veg box. Hand it over?
move words.note: Handing each box to the person it is for.

examples.card: Hand a box to the person collecting it.
examples.filled: Sam's veg box at 6:20pm.

move words.trigger: A person with a box waiting in her record has arrived or the collection slot they booked has opened.

move words.card: 1 box from yesterday is still here. Message Sam?
move words.note: A box left past its time: remind, then tell the seller.

name: Dealing with a dead animal
card: A ewe died overnight in the top field. The collection service can come tomorrow for £45. Book it and log the death?
note: You deal with a farm or working animal that died: fallen stock collected by a licensed service, or out on the range a photo of the body or the hide, the ear or tag kept, and a fellow herder's word. Burial or burning only where the law allows, a sample for testing when the death is unexplained, and the death written in the herd or flock record. Where the herder keeps another's animals, the keeper's signed word and the hide are the proof. You keep the body safe from other animals until it is collected, book the collection, pay the fee, and log it; a death the law must hear about goes on to Reporting to an authority, and a claim goes to Taking out insurance or Insuring each other. A die-off of many fish or shellfish at once is the same steps at a larger scale, counted in kilos or tonnes and written once as a loss; a report or a claim may follow. Kept apart from Getting rid of waste (food and rubbish nobody wants); Slaughtering an animal (killing an animal for food); and Reporting to an authority (telling the authority, which may follow). It usually starts when an animal is found dead, a sensor shows an animal down, a collection the law requires is overdue, or a herd is hit by drought.

name: Preparing food for sale
card: 46 quarter-kilo sugar bags sold this week, 6 left. Bag up the new 50 kg sack tonight?
note: You break a sack, tin or carton into small packs a customer can afford: a quarter-kilo of sugar, oil in small bags, dal in 250 g packets, single eggs. You start, choose the pack size, count the packs, and mark it done. It repeats whenever the small packs run out. You say how much went in and how many packs came out, so spillage and short measure show. Cutting meat or fish: You break a carcass or a whole fish into cuts: trimming, jointing, filleting, gutting, as a butcher, a fishmonger or a home cook with a whole chicken. You choose the cuts, do the cutting, write down what you got (the weight of each cut, and of the trim, bone and fat), and which carcass or lot it came from, so a cut can be followed back, and mark it done. It repeats with every delivery. Kept apart from Making a batch (it makes a product, not repacks one); Grading produce (it sorts by quality); and Slaughtering an animal (the animal is alive, not yet food). It usually starts when the small packs on the shelf are nearly gone, when a new sack arrives, or when payday brings customers who buy small and often; as Cutting meat or fish, when a whole carcass or catch arrives, stock of a popular cut runs low, or a busy day such as a weekend or festival is ahead.

name: Storing food with someone
card: Your cold room has 8 pallets free next week. Offer them, at a daily price you set?
note: You hold other people's goods in your cold room, store or warehouse for a fee. Their own pallets stay theirs and you may not use them; grain mixed in a silo is owed back as the same amount, not the same grain. You give a receipt for what you hold, which they can pass on or borrow against. Who bears loss, spoilage or pests is agreed, your temperature log is the proof, and you may hold goods until the fee is paid if the terms say so. Goods left past their term cost the fee signed. Records a licensed chain requires are compelled. Weight and moisture are read when goods come in and again when they go out, and both are signed, so a loss in between can be traced. Storing food with someone: You pay a cold store, grain warehouse or village granary to look after your goods: you book space, hand the goods in, get a receipt, and take them out when you choose. The goods stay yours. The receipt shows what you put in, and you can sell it or borrow against it. Who pays if goods spoil, shrink or get eaten by pests is agreed first. In a bonded store, tax on imported goods is paid on the day they leave. Kept apart from Lending and borrowing something (free); Renting something (kit or rooms); Renting out land (ground); Storing a harvest (you keep it in your own store); Waiting to sell for a better price (the bet on price); Borrowing against stored stock (a loan on the receipt); and Renting land or a place to trade (ground). It usually starts when space frees up, when a harvest or a glut means farmers need storage, or when goods stay past their date; as Storing food with someone, when a harvest comes in, a glut needs cold, or your home or shop space runs out.

name: Importing food
card: Thai jasmine rice lands in Dar es Salaam at TSh 3,100 a kilo with duty. Order a container?
note: You buy food from abroad. It takes weeks: you ask, the exporter offers, you accept and pay on the agreed terms, the goods are shipped, cleared through customs and received. The delivery terms say when the goods become your risk and who holds them on the way. The card shows what it costs you delivered to your door, line by line (price, freight, insurance, duty, port charges, exchange rate), and what you expect it to sell for. Duty is paid in Clearing goods through customs; a price fixed ahead is Agreeing a price for later. Kept apart from Buying to sell on (bought at home to sell elsewhere); Ordering stock (on account from a supplier at home); and Catering for an occasion (made for a date). It usually starts when local supply runs short, when the exchange rate moves, when a shipping season opens, or when a container is due.

name: Exporting food
card: The Dutch buyer wants 2 containers of avocados in April at $28 a box. Accept?
note: You sell food abroad: the buyer's specifications, certificates, delivery terms, currency and payment. It covers a smallholder co-op sending a pallet as much as a grower filling containers. The buyer asks, you agree specs, price and delivery terms, get the papers and inspection, hand the shipment over and are paid. Who goes first (an advance, open account, a letter of credit) and what backs the buyer's promise are agreed, and payment in another currency means you carry the exchange rate until it arrives. Export levies and inspection fees show apart from the price, and the border itself is Clearing goods through customs. Kept apart from Supplying on contract (a standing supply at home); Running or answering a tender (a public contract); and Selling and buying in bulk (the same shape at home). It usually starts when a foreign buyer asks, a sailing or flight date nears, a harvest is ready for a buyer's season, or a certificate runs out.

name: Running a market
card: The Saturday market in Lima has 6 empty pitches and 9 traders asking. Offer them in order of asking?
note: You run a market for the people who sell there: pitches, fees, hours, rules, keeping it clean and safe. You offer pitches, traders accept and pay, you hand the pitch over each market day, and it runs until ended. How scarce pitches are shared (a queue, a draw, seniority, an auction) is your rule, shown to everyone in advance. A fee you collect for the council is shown apart from your own pitch fee. Your rules bind the traders who join; they never stop a trader selling elsewhere or another market opening nearby. Hygiene and weights rules of the place apply. Kept apart from Renting land or a place to trade (one place let to one trader); Running a shared shop (one online shop for many producers); Renting something (one thing to one renter); Renting out land (a field); and Storing food with someone (a store). It usually starts when it is market day, when fees fall unpaid, or when pitches are free.

name: Making compost
card: Your bin in Leeds has been turning for 8 weeks and reads 18 degrees. Turn it today, or leave it to finish?
note: You turn your own food scraps, manure and green waste into compost for your own beds or plot, or tend a heap that neighbours or a garden group bring their scraps to. It can be a heap, a bin, a wormery or a bokashi bucket. You add scraps and dry material, turn the pile, watch the heat, and write down when it will be ready to use. Kept apart from Getting rid of waste (that sends it away, this keeps it); Selling and buying in bulk (that sells it on); and Growing crops (that uses the finished compost). It usually starts when the scrap bucket is full, the heap has gone cold, or a bed is bare and waiting.

name: Keeping the power on
card: Power cut 6 to 10pm on the schedule. Run the generator for the two freezers only?
note: You keep the power on for the food that needs it: a generator, solar or a battery through a power cut, so the freezers stay cold. You start the plan, change it as the supply changes, note the fuel or charge, hand it to someone, and mark it done. Selling power and water by the meter you make is Selling power and water by the meter. Kept apart from Keeping equipment and places in order (the machine itself, not its power); Keeping food fresh (the food, not the power); Using power when it is cheap (choosing the hour, not getting through a cut); and Getting ready for an emergency (the whole plan for a storm or flood). It usually starts when a power cut is announced or begins, a battery runs low, or a freezer starts to warm.

name: Guarding against scams
card: This M-Pesa text says KSh 4,500 came in, but your balance hasn't changed. Hold the sacks until it shows?
note: You check that money or a person is real before you hand anything over: a payment text that is not yet a payment (your balance is), a changed bank account on an invoice, a fake buyer or supplier, a message or machine pretending to be someone. You start the check, confirm it by a way you already trust (your balance, the number you already have), note what you confirmed, and mark it done. How much you let a new buyer take before paying is your own call, from your own record. Kept apart from Checking who you are dealing with (reading someone's record); and Guarding against theft (things taken, not tricks). It usually starts when a payment text arrives, a new buyer or supplier appears, an invoice says the bank account has changed, or someone asks for money or goods before checks are done.

name: Making water safe to drink
card: Your town in Kent is under a boil notice until Thursday. Boil 4 litres now and fill the clean jug?
note: You make water safe to drink and cook with: boil it under a boil notice, filter it and change the cartridges, add chlorine tablets, keep clean water covered and stored. You do it once when a risk appears, or on a schedule. Kept apart from Cleaning (a space or its kit); Fetching water or fuel (getting it); Selling water or fuel by the load (buying it); Keeping equipment and places in order (the filter as kit); and Checking one food (food). It usually starts when a boil notice or flood warning is issued, a filter cartridge is due, your clean water runs low, or illness repeats in your household and its water is untreated.

name: Going out alone, with someone watching
card: Joaquín said he'd be back from the boat by 6, and it is 7:15 in Valparaíso. Call him now?
note: You keep watch over someone who has gone out alone to fish, hunt, herd, forage or travel, and who told you when they would be back. They chose to share it with you and who may be told. Nothing about where they are goes further without that. If they are overdue you check in first, then tell their family, then call a search party if the first calls go unanswered. The watch ends when they say they are back. Going out alone: You go out to work alone, or in a small crew, and let someone you trust watch until you are back: fishing alone or with two crew before dawn, a night delivery, a long drive to market, foraging far from home. You say where, when you will be back, who is aboard, who may see where you are and until when. You go, they see what you allowed, and it ends when you say you are back. If you are late, what you agreed says who they call. Kept apart from Checking on someone (how a person is eating); Keeping people safe at work (a workplace's drills and gear); Sharing a record (a share that stays open); and Getting ready for an emergency (a plan for the whole household). It usually starts when someone tells you they are going out and when they will be back, or the time they gave has passed; as Going out alone, when you leave for something risky, when you work late or far from anyone, or when your trips after dark rise in a week.

name: Acting on a recall
card: The oat milk you bought in Leeds is recalled for glass pieces, batch L2207. Stop using it and ask for your £1.80 back?
note: You act on a recall notice that matches food, seed, an input or a machine your own record shows you bought or hold. You stop using it, check where else it is, tell the people you gave or sold some to (the law may ask this of you), and return or dispose of it for what the seller owes you: money, a replacement or a fix, by the date they set. If you heard of it by a poster, the radio or a message and kept no receipt, you say what you bought and from whom, and FoodOS shows what in your stock and past buys could match. Kept apart from Checking one food (date, smell and look); Returning something (a return by choice); and Complaining and putting it right (a fault in one order). It usually starts when a recall notice matches something in your record, a supplier tells you a batch was pulled, or you hear of a recall by word of mouth.

examples.filled: The tinned fish recalled this week went out in last Thursday's parcels to 38 households. Tell them now?

examples.card: Act on a border refusal that names your supplier.
examples.filled: Two loads of sesame from your supplier were refused at a port, and you hold 400 kg from them. Hold it, test it, return it, or tell your buyers?

move words.card: Hill Dairy recalled the yoghurt you handed to 4 neighbours on Saturday. Tell them now?
move words.note: Every holder tells the people they gave or sold it to.

examples.card: Pass a recall on to everyone you gave food to.
examples.filled: 4 neighbours told about the yoghurt.

move words.trigger: A supplier or maker she bought or received from has recalled a batch, and her record shows she handed some of it on.

you do this when: A recall notice matches food, seed or a machine your record shows you hold, and you act on it.

name: Keeping your record safe
card: Your record lives on one phone in Accra and has no second copy. Add a copy on your laptop?
note: You keep your own record safe and yours: a second device, a copy where you choose, a recovery contact, and checking you can restore it. Each copy lives where you put it and nowhere else. You pick where copies go, test that one comes back, and change the places when you like. Kept apart from Moving your record (leaving a host); Getting back in after losing your phone (after a loss); Sharing a record (who sees it); and Getting your record back (bringing records in). It usually starts when you set up, a copy has not been tested for months, or you change phone.

examples.card: Add a second copy of your record.
examples.filled: Your record is on one phone in Glasgow. Keep a second copy with your sister?

examples.card: Name a recovery contact.
examples.filled: If you lose your phone in Glasgow, no one can help you restore. Name your brother as a recovery contact?

examples.card: Test that a copy restores.
examples.filled: Your last copy was made 8 months ago in Pune and never tested. Restore it on the spare phone now?

you do this when: You keep copies of your own record, a recovery contact, and check you can restore it.

name: Handing out food parcels
card: Thursday: 84 households booked, 6 new referrals, tins short. Make 12 parcels smaller or call the depot?
note: You give food to registered households in an organised way: a food bank, a relief centre, a ration distribution. You decide who is on the list by your own rule (a referral, proof of need, or in some places anyone who comes, with a name, a number or nothing), take referrals, set what goes in a parcel, run the distribution day, and record that each household collected theirs or, where no names are kept, a tally of the households and people who came and any who left with less or nothing. The list is personal. Each household keeps control of its own details and can leave, and how a household is removed is said when they join. Each parcel keeps the batch codes of what went into it, noted at intake, so a recall reaches only the households who took that batch. Kept apart from Giving and receiving food (guests you invite); Bringing meals to someone (friends cooking for one household); Running a community kitchen (a cooked meal, no list); Running a community fridge (an open shelf, no list); Giving food vouchers (vouchers to spend in shops); and Donating surplus (stock sent on). It usually starts when the distribution day nears, new referrals arrive, or stock does not match the households booked.

examples.card: Fit new referrals into the distribution day.
examples.filled: 84 households are booked for Thursday and 6 new referrals came in. Book slots for the 6 at the end of the afternoon?

examples.card: Give out a fixed ration to registered families and record who collected.
examples.filled: Your relief centre in Mogadishu hands out monthly rations to 600 families. Scan each family's card at the gate?

examples.card: Take on a referred household and book a time to collect.
examples.filled: A health visitor in Manchester refers a mother of three to your food bank. Register her and book Friday morning?

examples.card: Hold parcels for people who did not come.
examples.filled: Thursday: 78 of 84 collected. Keep the other parcels until Friday morning for those who missed it?

examples.card: Count who came to a pantry that keeps no names.
examples.filled: Saturday's open pantry in Dayton: 63 households, 211 people, 9 left with less. Save the tally?

examples.card: A parcel collected for a housebound household
examples.filled: You collected Mrs Hall's parcel at the food bank for her. Rice, tins and a loaf. She cannot get to the door quickly. Do you leave it with her neighbour?

examples.card: Hand out part of the ration when the shipment is late.
examples.filled: The April shipment is delayed. The store holds 9 days of maize. Hand out part now and the rest when it arrives, or hold the day?

examples.card: Hand a parcel to someone collecting for a household that cannot come.
examples.filled: Mrs Banda in Lusaka cannot walk to the hall, and her neighbour Joy collects with her say. Hand it to Joy?

move words.card: A new family was referred by the school. Register them for Thursday?
move words.note: Taking someone onto the list, by referral or need.

examples.card: Register a household for parcels.
examples.filled: A family referred by the school.

move words.trigger: A referral has arrived, or a household has asked to join and is not yet on the list for the next distribution.

move words.card: Thursday 2 to 4 has 6 slots left. Book the Okafors for 2:30?
move words.note: A time to collect, so the queue is short.

examples.card: Book a parcel collection slot.
examples.filled: Thursday 2:30.

move words.trigger: A distribution day is coming and a registered household has no time to collect, or one slot is filling up while others sit empty.

move words.card: 84 parcels ready; 6 households haven't come. Hold them until 5?
move words.note: Handing each parcel to the household it is for, with proof.

examples.card: Hand out parcels on the day.
examples.filled: 78 of 84 collected.

move words.trigger: The distribution day has started or its hours are running out, and parcels are ready that the households they are for have not yet collected.

move words.card: Today's pantry is over: 64 parcels went out and 9 people were turned away. Note them?
move words.note: How many people you actually fed or who came, and how many you turned away: the number a scheme, a client or next week's cooking is planned and paid on.

examples.card: Count the people you fed.
examples.filled: Today's pantry is over: 64 parcels went out and 9 people were turned away. Note them?

move words.trigger: A meal, service or event she runs has ended.

move words.card: Over six Thursdays, 31 households put back the lentils. Change what goes in the parcel?
move words.note: What a household put back or did not take at hand-out, counted by item. It is the plainest sign of what people value.

examples.card: Note what a household put back at hand-out.
examples.filled: Six households put back the lentils today.

move words.trigger: A household leaves or puts back an item at hand-out.

move words.words: Take a household off the list
move words.card: Eight households have not collected for four weeks. Take off those who left, keep them until you hear, or visit?
move words.note: Taking a household off the list when they have moved or stopped coming, by the rule they were told when they joined. The other side of Register a household.

examples.card: Take a household off the list when they have moved.
examples.filled: Three households who moved away taken off, by the rule they were told.

move words.trigger: Households long absent, or who said they moved.

move words.words: Tell them it is held up
move words.card: Thursday's delivery has not come; the hand-out starts at 10. Do you tell the 46 booked households it will start at 11, or give out what you have?
move words.note: A breakdown on the road is the main moment the shipper loses the load's story. The driver says where, why and for how long; the shipper sees it where the load is and decides.

examples.card: Tell people a hand-out is late.
examples.filled: The van from the depot is stuck and Thursday's hand-out starts at 2. Tell the households it is held up?

move words.trigger: Shows when the pickup or arrival time has passed with no handover recorded, when the driver reports a fault on the truck, or when he taps it himself.

you do this when: You give food to a registered list of households in an organised way.

name: Asking for donations
may the holder use it: yes, only for what was agreed
card: Pasta is down to 2 days. Ask the supermarket's collection point and the parish for pasta this week?
note: You ask others for food, goods or money to pass on: a food drive, a collection point, a harvest festival appeal, a zakat collection, a shop agreeing to pass you its surplus. What you collect is kept for its purpose and counted. You ask, they offer, you accept, they hand it over, and you thank them. Kept apart from Raising money from your community (money for your own venture or need); Applying for a grant (a funder judges applications); Claiming benefits (an entitlement); and Giving and receiving food (food for you). It usually starts when stock runs low, when a festival or season of giving nears, when a shop agrees to pass on surplus, or when a collection point is empty.

examples.card: Ask for food donations when stock runs low.
examples.filled: A pasta appeal at two collection points. Open it?

examples.card: Ask someone with spare food to give it to someone who can use it.
examples.filled: Your shelter is short of bread. Ask the bakery to pass its extra to you?

examples.card: Run a harvest collection at a place of worship or a school.
examples.filled: The school in Auckland has a harvest festival Friday. Ask each class for tinned food?

examples.card: Collect zakat in food for families who need it.
examples.filled: Ramadan begins in a week in Karachi. Ask the mosque's donors for flour and oil for 200 families?

examples.card: Count what a shop-door collection brought in.
examples.filled: Saturday's collection at the supermarket door in Bristol: 6 crates of tins and 3 of pasta. Save the count against the appeal?

you do this when: You ask others for food, goods or money to pass on to people in need.

name: Screening for malnutrition
card: Amina's arm measure is 11.2 cm, under 11.5. Refer her to the clinic's feeding programme today?
note: You measure people against a line and refer those under it: arm-tape checks, growth checks for under-fives, a nutrition screen when someone is admitted. The line comes from the programme and shows its source. You measure, FoodOS records it and marks who falls under the line, and you refer them, with the person's own yes, or for a child the parent's own yes to their own part, or under a programme rule that is shown. A measurement is the person's own health record. It repeats on a schedule. Kept apart from Finding out who is hungry (a household's or community's need); Checking on someone (a carer noticing one person); and Treating malnutrition (the feeding that follows). It usually starts when it is a clinic day, you are at a school or feeding point, a bad harvest or flood has happened, or someone is admitted to care.

examples.card: Screen children and refer those under the line.
examples.filled: Monthly arm-tape checks for 120 under-fives at your clinic in Niger: Amina's measure is 11.2 cm, under 11.5. Refer her today?

examples.card: Check a school's pupils for growth.
examples.filled: You're the school nurse in Odisha weighing every child this term. Refer the two under the line to the feeding programme?

examples.card: Screen older people on admission to care.
examples.filled: Your care home in Glasgow screens new residents. Refer the two flagged residents to the dietitian?

examples.card: Screen after a flood or poor harvest.
examples.filled: You're checking children in flood-cut villages in Bangladesh. Refer the flagged children for feeding?

you do this when: You measure people against a line and refer those under it.

name: Treating malnutrition
card: Amina left half her sachet at lunch. Offer the rest in an hour, with clean water beside it?
note: You feed a child or an adult back to health on a clinic's or dietitian's plan until they leave it: sachets of therapeutic food, tube feeding, a dietitian's plan. A parent or carer feeds and agrees for a small child, and the child's record of weights is theirs, held by the carer. You give the food as the plan says, note how it goes, bring them to each check, and the plan ends when the clinic discharges them. You are not charged, and reports to the programme go under its stated terms. The food left shows beside the day of the next check, so a shortage is seen before the food runs out. Kept apart from Running a malnutrition programme (the health worker's side: weighing, admitting, handing out and discharging); Feeding your children (a normal feed); and Feeding someone you care for (daily food for a dependent adult). It usually starts when a clinic or dietitian gives a plan, a weekly check comes round, or the food supply is about to run out.
no mirror: none: the patient receives care, and a small child signs nothing, so a parent makes their own promise

examples.card: Follow a dietitian's plan for someone who cannot eat enough.
examples.filled: The hospital in Leeds put Mr Thomas on a tube-feed plan after surgery. Raise the rate as the dietitian wrote?

examples.card: Give therapeutic food at home as the plan says.
examples.filled: Amina's plan says 2 sachets a day. Give the second one after her afternoon nap?

examples.card: Bring a child to the weekly check.
examples.filled: Amina's weekly check at the Kitgum clinic is Thursday morning. Walk her in with her record book?

examples.card: Count the sachets left for the weekly check.
examples.filled: Amina's plan in Kitgum says 2 a day and 3 are left from the 14. Bring the count to Thursday's check?

examples.card: Say a sachet was shared.
examples.filled: The sachet in Kitgum was split with her brother. Tell the health worker?

examples.card: Say the child would not eat it.
examples.filled: Amina left her sachet today in Kitgum. Tell the health worker on Thursday?

you do this when: You feed a child or adult back to health on a clinic's plan until they leave it.

name: Giving cash for food
card: 312 transfers ready; 9 SIMs failed last month. Send to the rest and call those 9?
note: You give people money to buy food themselves, by mobile money, bank or card, in place of giving the food: a charity, an agency or a government programme paying many households. You set who is on the list by your own stated rule, send each transfer on the day, and see which failed; you can pause, change the amount or end it. What it costs the household to turn the money into cash is shown. A transfer tied to a condition (a clinic visit, school attendance) states the condition up front. Each household's number stays theirs. Kept apart from Giving pocket money (a child's allowance); Giving food vouchers (spent only at listed shops); Sending money home (family supporting family); Giving to a cause (money to an outfit); and Giving a gift (a personal present). It usually starts when it is payment day, when a new household is added, or when a transfer fails.

examples.card: Send cash for food to registered households.
examples.filled: 312 transfers of KSh 3,000. Send them?

examples.card: Send a monthly cash top-up to people on a food programme and follow up on failures.
examples.filled: In Lima, 9 transfers to the soup-kitchen families bounced last month. Resend and call those 9?

examples.card: Give pupils' families a food allowance instead of a school meal.
examples.filled: Schools are closed for a month in Lagos. Send each family on the list the lunch money?

examples.card: Hand cash to a household and keep their word that they took it.
examples.filled: Your parish hardship fund gives an envelope of cash to a family at Thursday's session. Save that they took it?

you do this when: You give many households money to buy food themselves, in place of the food: a charity or a programme, by your own stated rule. Not an entitlement claimed.

name: Finding out who is hungry
card: Ward 3's survey shows 40% of households eat one meal a day. Put Ward 3 on next month's distribution?
note: You find out who is hungry, where and why, before you plan help: a phone or door-to-door survey, a warning about bad rains, or a check after a handout on who still ran short. People answer only what they agree to, and answers are counted, never named; anything given for answering (airtime, a coupon) is said up front. The result is your programme's own estimate, and the card shows who else would get less if you act on it in one place. You start it, note what you learn, and close it when you have enough. Kept apart from Screening for malnutrition (one person's body); Checking how things are going (your own results); and Checking one food (one thing). It usually starts when a distribution is planned, a harvest or rains report comes in, prices rise suddenly, a crisis hits, or a handout has finished.

examples.card: Survey who is short of food.
examples.filled: Phone survey of 400 households in Ward 3. Start calling?

examples.card: Check whether a distribution reached the people it was meant for.
examples.filled: A week after the maize handout in Turkana, call 60 households to ask who still ran short. Start the calls?

examples.card: Read an early-warning report before planning help.
examples.filled: The rains forecast for northern Ghana is poor. Plan seed and food help for the lean months?

examples.card: Ask neighbours who skips meals, and why.
examples.filled: Your tenants' group on a Glasgow estate wants to know which families skip meals before the school holidays. Start the count?

you do this when: You find out who is hungry, where and why, before you plan help.

name: Finding out what the rules are
card: Selling cakes from home in Leeds needs council registration 28 days before your first sale. Start the registration?
note: You find out which rules apply to what you want to do with food, where you are: what you need before selling from home, what a label must say, what a buyer's country asks for, which taxes and permits apply, what an allergen rule means for your menu, what a market or co-op allows. FoodOS reads the rules for your place and your plan and sorts them into what the law compels (taxes, fees, registration, reports) and what is your own choice (standards, schemes), each with its source, date and deadline, its fee, and any exemption that applies with its limits. You decide what to do next. Kept apart from Checking how things are going (your own results); Getting a permit or registration (getting one); Checking one food (a label in front of you); and Speaking up about a food rule (answering a rule being changed). It usually starts when you plan to sell something new or somewhere new, when a rule changes, when a buyer or inspector asks for something you have not heard of, or when a new rule that fits your record comes into force.

examples.card: Find out what a buyer's country asks for before exporting.
examples.filled: Shea butter to Germany needs an EU importer and a product safety report. Ask the Accra exporters' group for an importer?

examples.card: Find out what a label must say.
examples.filled: Your chutney sold in Ontario must show a French name and a best-before date. Update the label template?

examples.card: Find out which permits a market stall needs.
examples.filled: A weekend stall at Mercado Roma needs a delegación permit and a health card. Book the health card course?

you do this when: You find out which rules apply to what you want to do with food where you are.

name: Working out what went wrong
card: The bread didn't rise again, and both times the kitchen was under 18°C. Try it somewhere warmer tomorrow?
note: You work out why something went wrong: a loaf that did not rise, a sauce that split, a cow whose milk dropped, a crop that wilted, takings that fell, an order that keeps arriving late. FoodOS lays out what was different from the times it went right, from your record, readings and photos ('both failures were under 18°C; the six that rose were over 21°C'), and puts each possible cause beside the test that would show it wrong. A single failure is not enough to say why. You decide what to try, often in Running a trial. Kept apart from Checking one food (naming a thing); Checking how things are going (results, not causes); and Logging (writing down what happened). It usually starts when something fails twice, a number drops against its usual, a customer complains, or a batch, animal or crop does not do what it normally does.

examples.card: Work out why a bake failed.
examples.filled: The bread didn't rise again, and both times your Dunedin kitchen was under 18°C. Try it in a warmer room tomorrow?

examples.card: Work out why an animal's yield dropped.
examples.filled: Daisy's milk fell 4 litres since the new hay arrived in Nakuru. Go back to the old hay for a week?

examples.card: Work out why takings fell.
examples.filled: Saturday takings at your Porto café fell £40 on the two days the card reader was down. Keep a cash float for the next time it fails?

examples.card: Work out why a crop is failing.
examples.filled: The tomato leaves in your Chiang Mai beds curl only where the hose water pools. Water at the roots instead?

you do this when: You work out why something failed: a loaf, a crop, falling takings. Causes, not results.

name: Seeing your food life
card: Your record from 4 apps is in: sourdough on 61 different days, and Friday at 7 is when your food life gathers. See the rest?
note: You see your own food life, read from your whole record: what you keep coming back to, when you eat and buy, your places, the people you eat with, how your eating has changed, and what changed most against your own past. It runs when your record first comes in and again as it grows. Every line says which records it counted. If one is wrong you say so and FoodOS reads it again. It is private to you. Showing it to anyone is Sharing a record, and you choose each line you show. Kept apart from Checking how things are going (results against a yardstick you chose, not who you are); Logging (your own ranking of meals and places); and Getting your record back (bringing the record in, not reading it). It usually starts when your record comes in from the apps that held it, at the end of a season or year, or when you ask what FoodOS knows about you.

examples.card: See how your eating has changed.
examples.filled: Since March you cook at home in Toronto twice as often and order half as much. See what changed most?

examples.card: See where and with whom your food life happens.
examples.filled: Three places hold most of your meals in Nairobi, and you eat with others on 4 days in 10. Show it on your card?

examples.card: See the one thing that surprised FoodOS.
examples.filled: You buy mangoes in every month, even out of season in Lyon. Show this line on your card?

examples.card: Look back at your year in food.
examples.filled: The year is ending. Collect your best meals of 2026, with the photos?

you do this when: You see your own food life read from your whole record: habits, places, people, change.

name: Guaranteeing someone's loan
card: Wanjiru asks you to guarantee KSh 10,000 of her SACCO loan; she has repaid on time for 2 years. Guarantee it?
note: You promise to pay someone's loan only if they do not. You are asked, you agree to a set amount, until a date, alone or jointly with others; you watch the loan being paid down, are called on if they default, and are released when it is repaid. In a group loan, you each borrow and each stand for the rest, by one rule you agree together: who is in, the most each may borrow, and what happens if one cannot pay. If you pay, you step into the lender's place and are owed by the borrower. You cannot walk out of a loan already drawn unless the lender releases you. The card shows what you could lose and what you could not borrow meanwhile, and what you have seen of their repayments, never a probability. Kept apart from Vouching for someone (you stand behind a person for any deal they fail, up to a cap, and here you stand behind one loan); and Letting someone act for you (authority, not a promise to pay). It usually starts when someone asks you to back a loan, a payment of theirs is missed, or the loan is repaid.
no mirror: none: a promise to the lender, standing behind the borrower

examples.card: Back a friend's loan from a savings group.
examples.filled: Your friend Esi in Tamale asks you to back GH₵2,000 of her group loan. Guarantee it?

examples.card: Back a new trader's first credit order from a supplier.
examples.filled: Wanjiru has a first KSh 20,000 order from the mill. Guarantee it?

examples.card: Guarantee a family member's loan to open a shop.
examples.filled: Your brother in Mumbai is borrowing Rs 3 lakh for a tea stall. Guarantee half?

examples.card: Back a farmers' group's loan for a shared machine.
examples.filled: Your co-op in Peru wants a loan for a dryer. Guarantee S/5,000 of it?

examples.card: Form a group that answers for each other's loans.
examples.filled: The microfinance bank in Dhaka lends only to groups of 5, each standing for the others. Form one with your neighbours?

examples.card: Agree what happens when a member cannot pay.
examples.filled: Grace in your Kisumu group missed two payments. Cover them this month as your rule says?

you do this when: You promise to pay one named loan only if they do not. Not a cap over any deal.

name: Running a community fridge
card: Fridge at the café: 3 yoghurts past date, 12°C at 2pm. Clear them and check the seal?
note: You host a fridge, a shelf or a crate that anyone can leave food in or take from. What you give is the space and its upkeep; the food passes straight from whoever leaves it to whoever takes it. You check dates and temperature, clear what is past it, clean it and keep its rules, which you set openly; the food-safety rules of the place show where they apply. Nobody is barred from taking. It runs until you close it. When you clear what is past its date, that is written down as lost, with what it was and how much. Kept apart from Giving and receiving food (leaving food in it); Donating surplus (a business leaving food in it); and Running a community kitchen (cooked meals). It usually starts when it is the daily check, when a warm reading comes, when food is past its date, or when a donation arrives.

examples.card: Keep a community fridge safe and stocked.
examples.filled: Daily date check and clean of the fridge outside the café. Do it now?

examples.card: Turn your porch into a surplus point for neighbours.
examples.filled: Porch fridge: 6 portions from 2 neighbours, followed by 14 people. Keep it open?

examples.card: Close the fridge while you are away.
examples.filled: You are away from 3 to 10 June. Ask Dana to keep the café fridge going, or close it for the week?

examples.card: Host a shared shelf in a village or block where people leave what they can spare.
examples.filled: Your community crate by the village shop in Kerala has been empty since Monday. Ask the market growers for greens?

examples.card: Ask shops nearby when the fridge empties early.
examples.filled: Your fridge was empty by 11 am on 5 of the last 7 days, and three shops post spare food. Ask them?

move words.card: The fridge has 6 items past their date. Do you clear them now?
move words.note: Writing down what you bin builds the picture of what you waste, so you can buy or make less.

examples.card: Log what you clear and why.
examples.filled: You cleared 6 bags of bread past their date this week. Log them?

examples.card: See what is thrown away most.
examples.filled: Bread past its date was cleared 4 times this month. Ask donors for less?

move words.trigger: Her record shows food she binned in the last weeks, enough to see a pattern such as the same loaf going stale by day three, or it is bin day, the fridge is being cleared, or a delivery or donation is being sorted.

you do this when: You host a fridge or shelf anyone can leave food in or take from, unattended.

name: Taking turns to work for each other
card: Saturday is Kahindi's turn: 8 of you plant his maize at 7. Go?
note: You and other households run a work group that goes round: each household works the others' fields or builds their houses in turn, feeds the workers on its own day, and keeps count of days owed. Its names include mweria, minga, ayni, debo, nnoboa and bayanihan. You ask others to come, they accept, you work the turn, and the days owed stay on record; it runs until ended. Whether days owed can be paid in cash or passed on, and what happens when someone leaves, is the group's rule. The host's meal is part of the swap. Each turn ends when the host signs who came, so the days owed come from those signatures, not from memory. Kept apart from Planning who works when (a rota inside one household); Doing your share of communal work (everyone turns out for a shared thing, not a turn at someone's own field); Saving in turns (a turn at money, not work); and Sharing a machine (a shared tool, not days owed). It usually starts when it is a member's turn, at the start of a season of sowing or harvest, or when the days owed are out of balance.

examples.card: Work each member's field in turn and track days owed.
examples.filled: Tuesday is Juan's field in the Andes, and six of you are going. You owe him 2 days. Will you come?

examples.card: Help a neighbour raise a house.
examples.filled: A bayanihan in Cebu carries a family's house to its new site on Sunday, with lunch from the owner. Will you come on Sunday?

examples.card: Take turns at harvest across households.
examples.filled: A group in Ghana works each member's cocoa harvest in turn, a day each, led by the oldest. Will you work Kofi's day on Wednesday?

examples.card: Transplanting with your buffalo
examples.filled: Rina's field is ready to plant on Thursday. Do you bring three women from your house?

examples.card: Transplanting with your buffalo
examples.filled: You bring your buffalo to plough. Do you ask that it counts as two days?

examples.card: Transplanting with your buffalo
examples.filled: You cannot work your day. Do you send your daughter in your place?

you do this when: Households run a work group that goes round: each works the others' fields in turn and keeps count of days owed.

name: Settling up with trading partners
card: You owe Hassan's shop KSh 48,000 and he owes you 31,000. Settle the 17,000, or send 2 sacks of rice?
note: You cancel what you and another trader owe each other, so only the difference moves. It can be a running two-way balance settled now and then, or a ring (the baker owes the miller, the miller owes the farm, the farm owes the baker) where everyone says yes and every debt is cancelled together, or none is. Debts due on different dates are not the same, so the card shows the dates. The difference is paid in money, in goods at a price you both agree, or by handing over someone's IOU (a written promise to pay); if the person you hand it to is not paid, you still owe them. One side offers a figure, each accepts or changes it, and the debts clear. Kept apart from Trading with community credits (balances in a circle's own unit); Asking for a ruling on a dispute (a disagreement about what is owed); Splitting costs (one bill); and Lending money (no netting). It usually starts when it is month end, two traders each owe the other, you spot a ring of debts, or cash is short and goods would do.
no mirror: self: every party settles the same way

examples.card: Settle a running balance with a trading partner.
examples.filled: You and Hassan each owe the other this month. Net it and pay him KSh 17,000?

examples.card: Clear a ring of debts so no cash moves.
examples.filled: The baker, miller and farm each owe KSh 8,000 in a ring. Cancel all three together?

examples.card: Pass an IOU on to clear a debt.

name: Shopping for others
card: Your elderly neighbour in Glasgow sends her list for Friday. Do her shop, up to £30?
note: You shop, order and collect for someone for a small fee: a neighbour who is not online, someone housebound, a busy family. They tell you what, the most to spend and by when, and you act only within that. Money they hand you first is spent only on their list; if you pay first, they owe it to you until they pay you back. You buy it, hand it over with the receipt, and they pay. They can change the list or cancel. Kept apart from Leading a group buy (you gather many orders for a cut); Carrying for pay (you carry orders others have placed); and Doing a favour (unpaid). It usually starts when a neighbour needs food and cannot get it, a co-op drop day comes, or a weekly shop agreed with someone is due.

mirror: Buying and selling food to use

name: Leading a group buy
card: 18 families on your street in Nairobi want a sack of rice each from the wholesaler. Place the order?
note: You gather your neighbours' orders for a cut. You post the deal, people ask and pay, you place one order, split it when it arrives and hand it out. Your cut is shown to every neighbour before they order, and the money they pay you is theirs until the order is placed. If the order only goes ahead above an amount, the card says so, and the money comes back if it is not reached. At collection the neighbour signs for the goods and the money in one moment, so each share shows as paid. Kept apart from Buying together (friends or your own household, unpaid); Shopping for others (one person's list, not a shared order); and Running a pickup point (the drop itself). It usually starts when a supplier offers a better price for a bigger order, a weekly drop day nears, neighbours ask for the same thing, or an order arrives and needs splitting.

examples.card: Lead a neighbourhood group buy for a cut.
