you do this when: You gather your neighbours' orders for a cut, place one order and split it when it arrives. Not one person's list, not buying together with no leader.

name: Saving with a collector
card: The collector comes by at 10. Put in your GH₵20 for today? Her fee is one day in 31.
note: You give a small amount each day or week to a collector you trust and get it back at the end of the cycle, less a fee, often one day's deposit: Ghana's susu, Nigeria's alajo, India's pigmy deposit. It keeps money out of reach until you need it, without a bank. The collector comes round, you pay in and both sign each deposit, and you are paid out at the end. Whether the collector may use your money meanwhile says whether it is held for you or lent to them; you are exposed until payout, and the card shows the fee in plain days, as one day in 31. Leaving mid-cycle follows the terms agreed at the start. Your count of deposits sits beside the collector's book, so a missing day shows. Collecting savings for others: You go round a market each day taking small deposits from traders and pay each back at the end of the cycle, less your fee, often one day's deposit: Ghana's susu collector, Nigeria's alajo, India's pigmy agent. Each deposit is signed by both sides. Whether you may use the money meanwhile is said up front: if not, you only look after it; if so, the savers are lending to you and are exposed until payout. What backs you (your own deposit, a guarantor, the market association) is shown. Paying someone out early is a term. A licence may be needed where you work. It runs until one side ends it. Kept apart from Keeping money with a bank or wallet (a bank or app holds it); Saving in a group (a group fund); Saving in turns (each takes the pot in turn); Putting money aside (you keep it yourself); and Borrowing money (a loan for yourself). It usually starts when a collector comes by on a market morning, or when the cycle ends and payout is due; as Collecting savings for others, when the first deposit comes on a market morning, or when the cycle ends and payout is due.

name: Letting someone use your place
card: A neighbour's delivery robot asks to cross your side gate on weekdays from 5 to 7pm for nothing. Allow it until the end of March?
note: You let someone enter, cross or use your place, and it stays yours: a delivery robot through your side gate, a neighbour's drone over your field, a herder's cattle crossing to water, a van parking in your yard. You set the times, how often, the end date and any fee, and who pays if something is damaged: the owner of the robot or drone, or the herder. A free permission you can stop when you like; a paid or fixed one ends as agreed. A path the law or custom already opens is not yours to grant or refuse. Whoever uses your place signs each time, and any fee is worked out from those signs. Using someone's place: You ask to use a place that is someone else's without renting it: crossing a field with cattle, parking a food van on a forecourt, flying a drone over a farm, drawing water from a neighbour's well. You agree what, when, for how long and at what price, if any, and what you must leave as you found it. You use it on those terms, and either side can end it as agreed. Kept apart from Renting out land (ground to farm); Lending and borrowing something (a thing handed over); Letting someone act for you (a job done for you); Renting land or a place to trade (you hold the land for a season); Renting something (you take a thing away); and Sharing a commons (land your group shares by its own rule). It usually starts when someone asks to cross or park, a season of movement begins, or a regular route runs through your land; as Using someone's place, when your route, pitch or water is cut off, when a season needs a crossing, or when the agreement is up for renewal.

examples.card: Let herders cross to water.

you do this when: Someone crosses, parks or draws water on a place that stays the owner's, for a fee: you let or you use. Not renting land.

name: Running a shared kitchen
card: Your kitchen is idle 6pm to 6am and 3 makers nearby have asked for time. Open it to them by the hour?
note: You run a kitchen that several small makers share: slots booked by the hour or the day, shared ovens and cold storage, house rules for hygiene and cleaning, and a check that each maker holds what the law asks. You open the kitchen, makers ask for slots, you agree hours and a fee, they cook and clean down, you take payment, and it runs until you close it. The next person to use it signs that it was left clean and whole, so cleaning and damage are on record. Kept apart from Renting something (one thing to one renter); Running a market (pitches for sellers); and Sharing a machine (co-owners booking shared kit). It usually starts when your kitchen stands idle for long hours, makers ask for time, or a new kitchen is fitted out to share.

examples.card: Open an idle kitchen to makers by the hour.
examples.filled: Your kitchen in Leeds is idle 6pm to 6am and 3 makers have asked for time. Open it to them by the hour?

examples.filled: Your shared kitchen in Lagos has 4 makers and a new one wants Tuesdays. Give her Tuesday 6am to noon after her hygiene check?

move words.note: Offering the space left on a trip, in a store or in a kitchen that is already going, to anyone, at a price you set. It is tied to that trip or slot, and only you know there is room.

examples.filled: The kitchen is free from 2 to 6 on Wednesday. Offer the time?

name: Insuring each other
card: Kofi's stall burned. The circle's pot is GH₵3,200. Approve his GH₵600 claim?
note: You and a circle pay in every month and the pot pays out only to whoever suffers a loss: a dead cow, a stall fire, a funeral, sick days. The pot can pay only what it holds, so the most it pays per claim, any waiting time for new members, who judges a claim and how fast it pays are said up front. Members decide each claim by the group's rule, and help can be in kind (groceries, a cow, tents, cooks for a funeral). Every payment in and out is shown to every member. What a leaving member takes is agreed when they join. A claim begins with the loss you record, and whoever saw it signs. Help in kind is counted when it is handed over and received. Twenty farmers each pay £50 a year, and a member whose cow dies is paid £800 when the vet they all named signs that it happened. Each member pays in what she chose, never forced equal. A payout never goes past what the pot holds, and the pot's own signed rule says who is paid first if it runs short; with no such rule, a payout past the pot counts for nothing. What voids a payout (a member's own neglect) is that member's signed promise. A bigger party can stand behind the pot with a vouch. It pools only a class of loss that nobody's choice decides: whether one person pays is a case, and is never pooled. Kept apart from Taking out insurance (cover bought from a company); Splitting costs (a bill); and Pooling money (a pot spent for the group, with no claims). It usually starts when a member is hit by a loss, a monthly payment is due, or a new member asks to join.

name: Sharing a machine
card: Your 6 hours on the shared combine are Thursday. Kofi wants Wednesday instead. Swap?
note: You co-own a combine, a mill, a robot or a van, book hours, log use, and split upkeep and repairs by use. You ask for hours, others offer or swap them by the group's rule, you pay your share, and it runs until ended or paused. Your part of the machine is yours to sell or pass on, how a leaving owner is bought out is agreed up front, and letting outsiders use it needs the owners' yes. Each use starts from the last reading, signed by the next person to use it, so upkeep splits by real use. Kept apart from Buying together (the buying of it); Renting something (renting it to outsiders); Lending and borrowing something (a one-off loan from a neighbour); Sharing a place (a place or pitch, not equipment); and Taking turns to work for each other (labour, not a machine). It usually starts when the machine is needed in a season, a slot is free, a repair bill arrives, or a member wants to swap hours.

name: Getting back in after losing your phone
card: Your phone was stolen. Ask Ana and Joseph to confirm this new phone is you, and cut off the old one?
note: You get back into your record after losing a phone. The people you named in advance confirm that the new phone is you. When enough have, and after the waiting time you set, the new phone speaks for you and the old one is cut off. If the old phone still works, it can say 'this is not me' during the wait. The new phone gets exactly what the old one had. The friends who confirm see nothing of your record, and no company can reset it for you. Kept apart from Naming who can confirm it is you (setting them up beforehand); Keeping your record safe (copies to prevent loss); and Getting your record back (history held by outside companies). It usually starts when a phone is lost, stolen or broken.
no mirror: none: people you named in advance confirm it is you

name: Subscribing
card: You have skipped your Friday veg box 3 weeks running. Pause it, or cancel it?
note: You join a seller's fixed offer that comes regularly: a veg box, a bread round, a milk delivery, meals for someone you look after. You ask, they accept, you pay, and it comes each time until you stop. You can skip a delivery, pause it or cancel. If you pay ahead, the seller holds your money until they deliver, and the card says what you are owed if they stop. Kept apart from Paying ahead for a share of the harvest (you share the season's luck); Buying a voucher or pass (you use it when you like); Ordering stock (a business orders on account); and Buying and selling food to use (paid for there and then). It usually starts when you buy the same thing again and again, when someone you look after needs regular meals, or when a seller offers a plan.

name: Visiting where food comes from
card: Hill Farm near Bath has pick-your-own strawberries on Saturday at 9am for 4.50 a punnet. Book 2 places?
note: You pay to visit a farm or a maker for a day: pick-your-own, an open day, a farm tour, a harvest festival, a cheesemaker's cellar. You book a place, go, pick or take part, and pay for what you take. Kept apart from Giving and receiving food (you pick what is left, for nothing); Learning a food skill (learning on your own); and Buying and selling food to use (a shop, not a farm). It usually starts when a farm posts a day, a crop comes into season nearby, or a free weekend lines up with one.

name: Buying someone's know-how
card: The bakery that closed on Mill St is selling its sourdough method for £6,000. Ask to see it first?
note: You buy a recipe, a process or a plant variety outright: a closing bakery's loaf, a retiring cheesemaker's method, a breeder's variety. Knowledge is copied, not handed over, so what you really buy is the right to use it, the records, any training, and the seller's promise not to use or sell it again. You ask to see it under a promise not to use it if you do not buy, agree a price, receive it with its records, and pay, sometimes in stages. An idea is not property (Kinsella), so nothing changes owner when a method is bought: you get the seller's signed word that you may use it and that they will not, and a copy of what they know. Kept apart from Letting someone use your recipe or brand (you use it for a while under their terms); Selling a brand (the name, not the method); and Developing a recipe (you work it out yourself). It usually starts when a maker retires or closes, a method you need comes up, or working it out yourself would take too long.

name: Saving in turns
card: Your merry-go-round's KSh 45,000 is Wanjiru's this month. Send your KSh 3,000?
note: You join a rotating savings group: everyone pays in on a schedule and each takes the whole pot in turn, by order, lot or bid: a merry-go-round, susu, esusu, tanda, ekub, hui, chit fund, tontine or partner. Taking the pot early is borrowing from the others until your payments catch up; taking it late is lending to them, and a bid for an early pot is the price of that, said plainly. Who is exposed if an early taker stops paying, and what backs it (a guarantor, new members taking late turns), is agreed. You pay in on the date, take the pot on your turn, and can swap turns with another member as the group allows. Every payment in and out is shown to every member, and leaving mid-round follows the terms agreed at the start. Kept apart from Saving in a group (a fund that grows); and Pooling money (a pot a holder spends). It usually starts when the payment date comes round, when it is your month, or when a member needs money out of turn.

you do this when: Everyone pays in on a schedule and each takes the whole pot in turn: susu, tanda, chit fund.

name: Pooling money
may the holder use it: yes, only for what was agreed
card: The flat kitty is down to £6 and the shop is Saturday. Ask the other 3 to top it up?
note: You and others put money into one pot and a named person spends it for the group: a flat kitty, a house fund, siblings paying in monthly for their parents' food. You agree who looks after it and what it may be spent on, members pay in, that person spends, and everyone sees every payment in and out. They may spend only on what was agreed, and what leaving takes out is agreed up front. It ends when the group ends it. The person who holds the pot counts the cash beside the group's balance, and a second member signs. A pot can also pay out only for a loss: each member pays in what she chose, never forced equal; a confirmer all of you named says a loss happened; a payout never passes what the pot holds; what voids a payout is each member's own signed promise; and what backs the pot (a bigger party's vouch) is shown to every member. That is Insuring each other. Kept apart from Splitting costs (dividing a bill after it is spent); Chipping in (a one-off whip-round for a gift or a treat); Insuring each other (the pot pays out only when someone is hit); and Contributing to a collection (a pledge recorded and returned in kind). It usually starts when a household forms, when the balance is low, when a shop or bill is due, or on the payment date.

examples.card: Pool money with friends, family or your team and spend or share it by an agreed rule.

move words.note: Each member's payment into the pot.

you do this when: People put money into one pot and a named person spends it for the group: a flat kitty, a house fund.

name: Selling vouchers
card: Mother's Day is in 3 weeks. Sell £20 afternoon-tea vouchers at your café in York?
note: You sell vouchers, gift cards or passes for what you supply: a signed promise to give food later for money now. A voucher can carry a name or be for whoever holds it, and it says which. The card shows the discount beside when vouchers are usually used. You offer them, buyers pay, and when one is shown you supply what it promised, in part or whole. You owe what is unspent, and the card shows the total. Kept apart from Running a loyalty scheme (rewards you give, not credit they pay for); Selling subscriptions (food sent on a schedule); and Trading with community credits (credit many members accept). It usually starts when buyers trust you and you need money ahead, when a season is slow, or when a holiday brings gifts.

move words.note: Vouchers for what you will supply: a signed promise anyone holding one can redeem.

examples.card: Issue vouchers for what you supply.
examples.filled: 50 bread vouchers worth KSh 100 each.

move words.trigger: Buyers keep coming back to her in her sales history, and she has a planned cost to fund or a slow season ahead in her calendar.

move words.note: Supplying what a voucher promised; part of one can be redeemed.

examples.filled: KSh 100 of bread for Ama's voucher.

move words.trigger: A voucher she issued is presented, or its holder has asked to use it, and its balance in her record covers what is asked.

you do this when: You sell vouchers, gift cards or passes for what you supply: a signed promise of food later for money now.

name: Advising someone on their eating
card: Mrs Adeyemi's glucose logs since March are shared with you until the 30th. Send her the questions before Wednesday's visit?
note: You advise a person on their eating as a dietitian, nutritionist, doctor or community health worker. You take the booking, read the records they chose to share, give a plan, and follow up. It may be paid, or free in a public service. You only see what they share, for the time they set. Your notes are yours and they can ask for their copy; your qualifications are on your record, signed by the body that gave them. A plan paid ahead or at the end says so. Seeing a health worker: You see a dietitian, doctor, nutrition clinic or community health worker for advice on your eating. You book, or are referred, share the records you choose (which ones, until when, and whether they may keep a copy), get a plan, and follow up. What the clinic writes is theirs, and you can ask for your copy. It may be paid, or free at the door in a public service; the card shows the price, the travel and the wait. Kept apart from Teaching a food skill (a skill for anyone, not advice about one person's body); Treating malnutrition (a feeding programme, not a one-to-one plan); Advising someone on their work (food production, not eating); Setting a diet (the plan once you have it); and Logging (the readings you take). It usually starts when someone books you, a client's follow-up date comes round, or a client shares new records; as Seeing a health worker, when a test result or a diagnosis comes in, a doctor refers you, or your own record shows a worry that is not settling.

name: Selling under a scheme
card: A woman pays with a WIC voucher for milk and eggs, 6 items allowed. Accept it?
note: You sell food at the till under a public or aid scheme: a ration shop's quota, food stamps, WIC, e-vouchers, school and relief vouchers, a farmer's input voucher. The scheme says who may buy, what, and often the price, which binds you while you are in it. You check the customer's entitlement (they share only the answer), sell, and record what the scheme owes you. You collect that in Claiming back from a scheme. Each voucher you take is a line of what the scheme owes you, and you note those you had to turn away. Kept apart from Selling subscriptions (a plan the buyer chose); Buying and selling food to use (an ordinary sale); Handing out food parcels (free food); and Selling vouchers (your own vouchers). It usually starts when a customer shows a card or voucher, or a new scheme lists your shop.
no mirror: none: the customer spends a benefit they claimed (Claiming benefits)

examples.card: Take a customer's food voucher at the till.
examples.filled: A man at your stall in Detroit pays with food stamps for rice and beans, with the allowed items listed. Accept them?

examples.card: Join a relief voucher round.
examples.filled: The aid office in Dadaab will pay shops 400 shillings per voucher this month. Join the round?

name: Supplying workers from an agency
card: The farm outside Valencia needs 12 pickers from Monday for 3 weeks at €11 an hour. Send your 12?
note: You supply your agency's workers to farms, kitchens or factories. The workers are employed and paid by you. You check the client's licence, agree the numbers and the rate, send the workers, and settle each period. You pay workers every week while clients may pay in 30 days, so you carry that credit. You agree who loses out if a worker does not come or a client does not pay. Any fee a worker pays is shown to them before they sign, and the place's rules on such fees apply. A hidden fee, or a debt that ties a worker to you, is not allowed. Each worker is paid against the hours or pieces counted, with every deduction written as a line. Getting workers from an agency: You buy work from an agency or labour contractor who supplies people: pickers for a harvest, kitchen staff for a busy week, packers for a rush. The agency is their employer and you pay the agency. You agree how many, for how long, the rate and what the agency pays them, then they come, work, and you pay the agency. The card shows what the workers are paid as well as what you pay, if the agency tells you. Kept apart from Employing someone (the business is the employer); Working for someone (the worker's side); Finding someone to deal with (searching, not supplying); Hiring help for a day (one person, paid by you); and Doing or getting a job for pay (a finished job, not hours). It usually starts when a farm or kitchen asks for hands, a season opens, or a gap opens in your list of workers; as Getting workers from an agency, when a harvest or a season is near, when orders jump, or when staff are off.

examples.card: Place pickers on a farm for the season.

move words.note: Each shift's hours, signed by the worker and received by you, keep pay right and within the law. Where work is paid by the piece, the count (crates, kilos) is signed the same way as hours.

examples.card: Check hours worked.
examples.filled: The agency's sheet shows 14 workers on Tuesday; you counted 12 at the gate. Pay the sheet, pay your count, or ask the agency?

you do this when: An agency supplies people and stays their employer: you buy the workers or you supply them. Not your own hire.

name: Selling your know-how
card: A sauce company offers £40,000 once for your chilli sauce recipe. Ask for a cut of each sale instead, or sell outright?
note: You sell what you know how to make or grow: a recipe, a method such as a brew schedule or a cure, a plant variety you bred. You still know it afterwards, so what you really sell is the buyer's right to use it, and your promise not to use or share it yourself. You agree where and for how long that holds, and the price: once, in parts, or a cut of each sale. You hand over the method, your notes and your trials, and you are paid. An idea is not property (Kinsella), so nothing changes owner when a method is sold: the buyer gets your signed word that they may use it and that you will not, and a copy of what you know. Kept apart from Letting someone use your recipe or brand (they use it for a while and you keep it); Selling a brand (the name, not the method); and Sharing a recipe (no sale). It usually starts when a buyer makes an offer, you are retiring, a method has outgrown your kitchen, or you need money for something bigger.

examples.card: Sell a recipe outright.
examples.filled: A sauce company in Leeds offers £40,000 once for your chilli sauce recipe. Ask for a royalty instead, or sell outright?

examples.card: Sell a plant variety you bred.
examples.filled: A seed company wants to buy your drought-tolerant millet line in Rajasthan outright. Ask what they will pay?

examples.card: Sell a process you worked out.
examples.filled: A brewery in Portland wants to buy your sour beer schedule and stop you brewing it. Ask for an offer?

you do this when: You sell what you know how to make or grow: a recipe, a method, a variety, with your word not to use or share it yourself. Not use for a while.

name: Selling a brand
card: You closed your juice bar, and 400 people looked up its name on your page last month. Offer the name to the café that asked?
note: You sell what you can sign over of a name customers know: a brand, a label, a shop name, its logo and trademarks, with or without the recipes. You agree what passes (the name, the trademarks, accounts on other platforms by their rules), the price, whether you may use the name again or say 'formerly', and who answers for products already sold under it; then you hand it over and are paid. Reviews and vouches stay with those who wrote them, and the brand's followers go with it. Vouchers sold under the name are the buyer's to honour if agreed. An idea is not property (Kinsella), so no one owns a name: it is a reputation. What you sell is your signed word that the buyer may use it and that you will not, and the things that really can be handed over (the registered mark, which is the state's grant, the accounts on other platforms, your stock). Buying a brand: You buy the signed right to use a name customers already know: a brand, a label, a shop name, with or without the recipes behind it. You check what you get (the registered marks, and accounts on other platforms, which pass only by those platforms' rules) and what you take on: vouchers, points and stamp cards given out under the name become yours to honour. You agree a price, pay now or partly from later sales, and receive it. Old reviews and vouches stay with the old owner; the name shows who stands behind it from the day it changes. An idea is not property (Kinsella), so no one owns a name: it is a reputation. What you buy is the seller's signed word that you may use it and that they will not, and the things that really can be handed over (the registered mark, the accounts on other platforms, the stock). Kept apart from Selling your know-how (the method); Selling your business (the whole going concern); Letting someone use your recipe or brand (use for a while); Buying someone's know-how (the method, not the name); and Buying a food business (the whole business). It usually starts when a buyer asks, you close or retire, or a name is worth more to someone bigger; as Buying a brand, when a known name comes up for sale, a maker retires, or a name would open doors faster than your own.

examples.card: Sell a brand you no longer use.
examples.filled: You closed your Accra juice bar, and 400 people looked up its name on your page last month. Offer the name to the café that asked?

examples.card: Sell a label to a bigger maker.
examples.filled: A grocer chain wants to buy your Kerala pickle label and keep your recipe with you. Ask what they offer?

examples.card: Sell a shop name when you retire.

examples.filled: A beloved bakery name in Lyon is for sale after the owner retired. Offer for the name and its social accounts?

examples.card: Buy a label to put on your own product.
examples.filled: A defunct coffee brand in Bogotá still has loyal fans. Buy the name for your roastery?

examples.filled: A closed jam maker in Cork is selling its name and labels for €3,000. Ask what comes with it?

you do this when: You sign over the use of a name customers know, with or without the recipes: you buy or you sell. A name is not owned, so what is sold is your word, not the name. Not the method, not the whole business.

name: Contributing to a collection
may the holder use it: yes, only for what was agreed
card: Otieno's mother's funeral harambee is Saturday. At your father's, he gave KSh 3,000. What will you pledge?
note: You pledge to a collection someone raises, then pay what you pledged: a funeral, a wedding, a neighbour's hospital bill, school fees, a church roof. This is harambee, koden, moi virunthu, abuloy and funeral dues. The pledges are read out in front of everyone, held to, and returned in kind at your own occasion. You are asked, you offer a pledge, it is recorded, then you pay before the day. The treasurer holds the pot for its stated purpose. You can change or withdraw a pledge; what that costs among people is yours to weigh. Your record shows what you gave and what was given to you, and FoodOS puts no fair sum on it. Whoever holds the pot signs for each gift as it comes in, and everyone who gave keeps the list, so at your own occasion it shows what you were given. Kept apart from Giving a gift (given freely, with no list and nothing owed); Giving to a cause (money to an outfit); Pooling money (a one-off kitty, no list kept); and Saving in turns (a standing circle where each takes the whole pot in turn). It usually starts when an occasion is announced, a date for paying nears, or your own occasion is due and what others gave you is on record.

examples.card: Pledge and pay toward a family occasion.
examples.filled: KSh 3,000 to Otieno's mother's funeral. Pledge it?

examples.card: Pledge toward a neighbour's hospital bill.
examples.filled: KSh 1,000 to Akinyi's surgery harambee on Sunday. Pledge it?

examples.card: Give toward a church or temple project and have it written in the book.

name: Giving pocket money
card: It's Friday. Send Leila her £5 pocket money to her card?
note: You give a child or teenager a regular allowance: cash in a jar, mobile money, or a child's card. You set the amount and the day, send it when it is due, and change it as they grow. A spending cap or a savings goal is your rule and they can see it; as they grow, the money becomes freely theirs. What they buy is their own record. Money for a job they did is Doing or getting a job for pay. Kept apart from Giving a gift (one present); Giving cash for food (aid for households); and Working for someone (a job). It usually starts when the day you set comes round, a savings goal is close, or a child starts buying their own food.
no mirror: none: the child simply receives it, and your promise to them is your own

name: Bringing meals to someone
card: The Okafors had a baby on Monday. Six friends in Enugu have each offered a night. Set up a rota, one meal per evening this week?
note: You and others take turns cooking for a household that cannot cook right now: a new baby, a death, an illness or an operation. One person sets up the rota with the household's yes, and each person takes a night. The household's food needs and allergies show on every night while they choose to share them. The household can change days or stop it, labels say what is in each dish, and containers go back. Meals go to the door, and the rota ends after the stretch you set. Being brought meals: You are brought meals for a while by friends, family or neighbours: after a birth, an illness or a death. You say yes or no, which days, what you can and cannot eat, and where to leave it, and you share only what you choose. Meals come, you take them, and the containers go back. You can change the days, pause or stop it, and thank people when it ends. Kept apart from Feeding someone you care for (one carer, day by day); Asking for volunteers (you ask for time, not cooked food); Giving and receiving food (they come to you, not you to them); and Getting meals from a canteen (an institution feeds you). It usually starts when someone you know has a birth, a death or an illness, or a friend asks who can help; as Being brought meals, when a baby is born, after an illness, an operation or a death, when friends offer, or when you need a break from cooking for a while.

examples.card: The first week home from hospital
examples.filled: You live on your own and came home with a cast on your arm. A friend from church will bring lunch on Tuesdays. Do you say yes?

examples.filled: Friends want to bring you dinner each night this week after the birth. Say yes, and which nights?

you do this when: You take meals to someone who cannot cook for now, again and again on a rota, or you are the one brought them. Not a one-off meal, not a canteen.

name: Giving a customer a treat
card: Ama has just had her 100th flat white here. Give her the next one free?
note: You give one customer a treat you chose for them, once: a slice on their birthday, something for their 100th coffee, a thank-you when a first-timer comes back, the extra handful in the bag (the yapa, the baker's dozen), or the best of the catch held back for a regular. You decide, give it, and that is the end of it; they can take it or leave it. A birthday is used only if the customer chose to share it with you. Kept apart from Giving and receiving food (guests at your table); Giving a free sample (to win a trade buyer); Running a loyalty scheme (a standing scheme with rules for everyone); Complaining and putting it right (putting a mistake right, not a treat); Giving a gift (a present to someone you know outside the shop); and Running a canteen (meals for a whole place, every day). It usually starts when a customer you know comes in on their birthday or a milestone, a first-timer comes back, you have the best of something and a regular you know wants it, or a regular has not come in for longer than their own usual gap.

examples.card: Give a regular a treat on their special day.
examples.filled: It is Thandi's birthday and she has come in every week to your café in Cape Town. Give her a slice of cake?

examples.card: Thank a first-time customer who comes back.
examples.filled: The woman who tried your empanadas last Tuesday in Buenos Aires is back. Add one free for her?

examples.card: Add a little extra for a regular.
examples.filled: Mama Rose buys tomatoes from your Kampala stall every market day. Add two extra to her bag?

examples.card: Hold the best of something for a regular.
examples.filled: The best snapper of the morning landed in Kochi, and Mr Nair buys it every Friday. Hold it for him until 10?

examples.card: A barista's free drink within the owner's rule
examples.filled: The delivery rider is soaked. Give him a coffee from your allowance?

examples.card: Hold a usual table for a regular who has gone quiet.
examples.filled: A guest came every second Thursday for a year and has not come for 7 weeks. Hold her usual table this Thursday?

move words.card: Mama Rose is at the stall again. Add two tomatoes to her bag?
move words.note: The extra handful given to a regular: the yapa, the ñapa, the baker's dozen.

examples.card: Add a little extra for a regular.
examples.filled: Your regular in Lima is buying bread again. Add a roll for her child?

move words.trigger: A customer her own sales record shows as a regular is buying now.

move words.card: The best snapper is in and Mr Nair buys it every Friday. Hold it for him until 10?
move words.note: Keep the best of something back for a regular who usually wants it, for a time you say.

examples.card: Hold the best of something for a regular.
examples.filled: The first figs at your Izmir stall are perfect, and Selin buys them every week. Keep a box until noon?

move words.trigger: Something a regular buys often by her record has just come in, and it usually sells before they arrive.

you do this when: You give one customer a treat you chose for them, once: a birthday slice, the yapa, the baker's dozen. Not a present between friends, not a tip.

name: Giving a free sample
card: People slow down at your stall but only 1 in 10 buys. Put out tasters of the new chutney?
note: You give a small free taste to anyone passing, to tempt them to buy: a cheese cube at a stall, a sip of cider at the farm gate, a tasting tray in a shop. You set out the tasters, note how many tried and how many bought after, and stop when the tray is empty. What is in each taster is said truly, allergens included. Sending samples: You send a free sample to one trade buyer you want to win: a chef, a shop, a merchant, an importer. You choose who and what, and send it with what they need to know. You ask how it went after a while, and it ends when they order or say no. The cost of the sample and the postage is yours. Kept apart from Running a community kitchen (meals for anyone, no sale); Donating surplus (food handed to a charity); Giving and receiving food (food given to feed someone); Giving a customer a treat (a treat for someone who already buys); Running a food event (a tasting people pay for); and Posting an offer or a want (an offer to everyone). It usually starts when a product is new, people stop at the stall but walk on, or a market day is quiet; as Sending samples, when you have a new product, when a buyer you want to supply asks to try, or when a sample sent has had no answer.

examples.card: Put out free tasters of a new product.
examples.filled: Your new mango chutney is out at the Saturday market in Durban. Put out 40 tasters?

examples.card: Offer a taste when people stop but do not buy.
examples.filled: People stop at your honey stall in Ljubljana but most walk on. Offer a spoonful of each kind?

examples.card: Offer tasters to people waiting in a queue.
examples.filled: The queue at your Brick Lane bagel stall is 15 deep. Hand out halves of the new rye?

examples.card: Send a sample to a chef you want to supply.
examples.filled: The head chef at a Lisbon restaurant asked about your olive oil. Send her a litre?

examples.card: Ask how a sample went.
examples.filled: The shop in Nairobi got your honey 2 weeks ago. Ask what they thought?

examples.card: Send samples to an importer.
examples.filled: An importer in Rotterdam wants to try your coffee. Send 2 kilos by courier?

examples.card: Send a sample with your price list to a shop.
examples.filled: A delicatessen in Seoul has never stocked your kimchi. Send a free jar with your price list?

examples.card: Sending samples
examples.filled: The deli in Leeds might stock your chutney. Send them 3 jars to try?

move words.card: The tasting is over. Note how many tried it, and how many bought?
move words.note: How many people you actually fed or who came, and how many you turned away: the number a scheme, a client or next week's cooking is planned and paid on.

examples.card: Count who tried it.
examples.filled: The tasting table is packed away. Note how many people tried the new cheese?

move words.trigger: A meal, service or event she runs has ended.

you do this when: You give a free taste or sample to win a sale: to anyone passing, or to one trade buyer.
no mirror: none: whoever tries it simply receives it, and a trade buyer answers with an order

name: Running a prize draw
card: Your bakery turns 10 on the 1st. Run a free draw for a year of Saturday loaves, winner drawn on the day?
note: You give a prize to someone drawn by chance, with free entry: a year of bread for your tenth birthday, a guess-the-weight cake, a hamper for everyone who signs up. You set the prize, how to enter and the draw date, people enter, the winner is drawn in a way anyone can check, and you hand over the prize. If the prize is food to be collected later, say what happens if you close before then. FoodOS never picks the winner. Kept apart from Running a raffle (people pay for tickets); Running a competition (a judge picks the winner); Giving a customer a treat (a treat you choose for one person); and Running a loyalty scheme (rewards earned by buying). It usually starts when an anniversary, a fair or a launch is coming.
no mirror: none: entrants answer by entering, and the winner is drawn, never chosen

examples.card: Run a free prize draw for an anniversary.
examples.filled: Your bakery in Nairobi turns 10 on the 1st. Draw one customer to win a year of Saturday loaves?

examples.card: Draw a winner from entries at your stall.
examples.filled: Your stall at the Taunton Harvest Festival is Saturday. Draw one name from the entry box to win your giant marrow?

examples.card: Run a free draw for people who sign up.
examples.filled: Your café in Melbourne opens a second site. Draw one free brunch from everyone who signs up this week?

you do this when: You give a prize to someone drawn by chance, with free entry. Not tickets sold.

name: Doing your share of communal work
card: Canal clearing is Saturday 7am; missing it costs KSh 500. Go, or send Otieno in your place?
note: You turn out with everyone on one day to work on a shared thing: clearing the canal, mending the dam or the fence. Attendance is counted and those who miss it pay a fine, under a rule they signed or, where the state sets the day, because the law requires it. If you send someone in your place, you pay them for it. Its names include faena, tequio, umuganda, shramdaan, gotong royong and a working bee. You are asked, you accept or decline (or send someone in your place), you work, and it is done when the work is finished; it can repeat each season. Kept apart from Taking turns to work for each other (a turn at one member's own field); Asking for volunteers (people give time freely for a cause, no fine); and Pooling money (money, not work). It usually starts when the community sets the day, a season is coming (canals before the rains), or damage such as a storm has happened.

examples.card: Turn out for communal work on the shared thing.
examples.filled: Your village in Rwanda has set umuganda for Saturday 7am to clear the canal. Turn out?

examples.card: Mend a shared fence or dam.
examples.filled: Your hill village in Nepal needs the terrace wall mended after the monsoon. Turn out to help?

examples.card: Clean the common land before a festival.
examples.filled: Your neighbourhood in Yogyakarta has gotong royong this morning to clear the lane before the festival. Join in?

examples.card: The river is rising
examples.filled: The river is rising and the drum is calling. Do you go to the dyke?

examples.card: The river is rising
examples.filled: You cannot go. Do you send your son and pay him?

examples.card: The river is rising
examples.filled: The dyke held. Do you add the names of those who came?

move words.card: The canal cleaning is done. Note who turned out, and who sent someone in their place?
move words.note: How many people you actually fed or who came, and how many you turned away: the number a scheme, a client or next week's cooking is planned and paid on.

examples.card: Count who turned up for the work.
examples.filled: The canal clean-up is done. Note who came?

move words.trigger: A meal, service or event she runs has ended.

you do this when: Everyone turns out on one day to work on a shared thing: clearing the canal, mending the dam.

name: Sharing ownership with your team
card: You retire from the trattoria in 3 years and your 4 cooks run it. Pass them shares over those 3 years, or sell to an outside buyer?
note: You pass part or all of the business to the people who work in it: shares they earn over time, shares they buy, a trust that keeps it for them, a sale paid from future takings, or turning it into a workers' co-op. You set the share, the rule and the dates; shares earned over time pass on a date, and a sale paid later means you are lending to them, with interest and the risk they cannot pay. What happens to a leaver's share is agreed up front. They accept and the shares pass. The law taxes shares. Offering it to your team, an outsider, or no one is your choice. Kept apart from Sharing profit with your team (a share of profit, not of the business); Putting money into a business (to outside backers); and Running a group (a co-op founded together). It usually starts when you plan to retire or step back, key people might leave, or the team asks for a say.

examples.card: Hand the business to the workers as you retire.
examples.filled: Start passing shares to the 4 cooks at your Bologna trattoria over the 3 years before you retire?

examples.card: Turn the business into a workers' co-op.
examples.filled: The 9 pickers and packers at your farm near Valencia asked for a say. Offer them shares, or turn the farm into a workers' co-op?

examples.card: Sell the business to your team, paid from future sales.
examples.filled: Your 5 staff in Leeds offer to buy the café over 6 years from its takings, at 4% a year. Agree?

you do this when: You pass part or all of the business to the people who work in it: shares, a trust, a workers' co-op. Not a profit share only.

name: Bargaining for your members
card: The county wants the daily market fee at KSh 80. You speak for 400 traders. Put a counter-offer to your members first?
note: You speak for your members, as a union, a farmers' group or a market association, and agree terms with an employer, a buyer or a council. You work within what they asked of you (a lowest price, until a date). You put the terms to them before you agree, and the terms cover only the members who gave you this job. One side asks or offers, the other counters, and both accept or one walks away. A fee that an authority sets is answered in Speaking up about a food rule. Kept apart from Working for someone (your own rise); Asking for a ruling on a dispute (one clash); and Striking together (action that backs up a bargain). It usually starts when a contract or price is due to renew, a buyer or council changes its terms, or members ask the group to speak for them.

examples.card: Agree terms for all your members.
examples.filled: The processor wants to renew the milk price for the season. You speak for 140 farms. Open talks?

examples.card: Agree the daily market fee for all traders.
examples.filled: The county wants a daily market fee of KSh 80. You speak for 400 traders. Counter at 60?

examples.card: Agree pay and hours for all pickers.
examples.filled: Your pickers' union in Valencia can agree an hourly rate with the growers for the harvest. Open talks?

examples.card: Ask for one posted fee with receipts.
examples.filled: 13 members recorded payments at the same roadblock this quarter. Back the group's ask for a posted fee with receipts?

you do this when: You speak for members (a union, a farmers' group) and agree terms for them all with an employer, buyer or council. Not one member's quarrel.

name: Striking together
card: The processor cut the milk price 3p. 140 members vote to hold milk for 3 days with strike pay at 50%. Join?
note: You and others hold back your own work, produce or market day together to press your case: riders logging off, a milk hold, a market shut. The group decides by its own rule, or each person signs the same pledge once enough others do. Then each holds back their own part, strike pay comes from the group's own pool, and you agree when to go back. The card shows the pledge count, the grievance and the date, and any deal the hold would break with what leaving it costs; what holding back costs you is yours to judge. Kept apart from Boycotting together (refusing to buy); Deciding as a group (the vote); and Bargaining for your members (the talks). It usually starts when a buyer cuts the price, terms are refused, or a council changes market rules.

examples.card: Hold back your produce together with your members.
examples.filled: 3-day milk hold, strike pay at 50%. Join the hold?

examples.card: Close the market for a day together.
examples.filled: Traders at the Oaxaca market vote to stay shut on Monday over a new stall fee. Will you stay shut on Monday?

examples.card: Hold back your work together with others.
examples.filled: The riders in Bogotá plan to stop deliveries on Friday over a pay cut. Stop with them?

move words.card: Riders in your zone are pledging to log off Friday if 200 sign. 140 have. Add your pledge?
move words.note: A pledge that counts only once enough others have signed; until then it binds nobody, and you can take it back.

examples.card: Pledge to act only if enough others do.
examples.filled: Milk farmers near Cork pledge to hold milk for 3 days if 120 farms sign. 95 have. Add yours?

move words.trigger: A group she belongs to has an open pledge with a count and a date, and she has not answered it.

you do this when: You and others hold back your own work or market day together to press your case. Not a boycott of buying.

name: Running a shift
card: Table 6's mains are 4 minutes behind and grill is free. Move the steaks to grill and hold table 8's starters?
note: You run a team minute by minute within work already agreed: calling the pass, sending riders out, a line lead moving people. Each call goes to one person, who says yes, no, or hands it on, and says when it is done. The card says what a move costs (table 8 waits three minutes more). What each person did goes on their own record too. Before it you brief the team (the specials, what has run out, who has an allergy), and at the end you pass it to the next shift with what they need to know; both are notes the whole team sees. It lasts one shift. Kept apart from Planning who works when (the rota, set before the shift). It usually starts when service is about to open, an order slips behind, a rider frees up, or someone is missing.

examples.card: Call the pass during service.
examples.filled: Table 8 is waiting and the grill is free. Move the steaks to grill and hold table 8?

examples.card: Tell each person what to do next.
examples.filled: Sam has been on fries for three hours and the grill is short. Swap Sam and Ama for the rush?

examples.card: Send riders to the next orders.
examples.filled: Two orders are ready in Jakarta and rider three has just dropped off. Send her to Jalan Sabang?

examples.card: Cook tickets in the order they came in.
examples.filled: Five pad thai tickets are up at your Bangkok street stall; the oldest has waited eight minutes. Wok that one first?

examples.card: Pass to the next shift: drawer counted at handover
examples.filled: You hand the bar to Sam at two. Drawer counted together; oat milk is low. Pass it on now?

move words.card: Bream is off and table 6 has a nut allergy. Brief the team at 5:30?
move words.note: What the team needs to know before or during the shift: the specials, what has run out, who has an allergy, a change on the day. Everyone on the shift sees it, and you see who has read it.

examples.card: Tell the team what the shift needs to know.
examples.filled: Rain is due on your farm in Andalusia. Tell the crew which rows to pick first?

examples.card: Tell the team what the shift needs to know.
examples.filled: The bream is off and table 6 has a nut allergy. Brief your Cape Town kitchen team at 5:30?

move words.trigger: A shift of hers is about to start or is under way, and something on the day has changed.

move words.card: The stock is half done and needs 30 more minutes before use. Pass it to the morning team?
move words.note: Handing the shift on with what the next team needs to know.

examples.card: Hand the shift on with what is unfinished.
examples.filled: You're the night cook in Seoul: the stock is half done and needs 30 more minutes before use. Pass it to the morning team?

move words.trigger: Her shift is ending and another shift follows.

move words.card: Line 2 stopped at 10:40 at the Leeds unit. Wait for the fitter, move the crew to line 3, or call it for the day?
move words.note: Downtime is where a factory loses its day and it is never written. The supervisor says when and why in her own words; FoodOS adds nothing.

examples.card: Note a stoppage.
examples.filled: Line 2 stopped at 10:40. Wait for the fitter, move the crew to line 3, or call it for the day?

examples.card: Note a stoppage.
examples.filled: The mill has no cartons for the afternoon. Change the run to bulk bags, send the crew home early, or ask Hamid for cartons today?

examples.card: Note a stoppage.
examples.filled: The power cut at 08:15 stopped the press. Run the generator for the press, or wait for the grid?

move words.trigger: A shift is open and a batch is running, and for longer than the line's usual gap no reading or pack count has been added.

you do this when: You run a team minute by minute within work already agreed.

name: Keeping track of special days
card: Diwali is in 2 weeks and your family cooks for 30. Start planning the feast?
note: You keep the dates that bring food with them: birthdays, anniversaries, festivals, holy days, a death you remember each year, a regular customer's celebration. FoodOS remembers them in pencil from what people told you, your calendar, the faith or place calendars you follow, and your own sales, and never asks you to add one. The list is yours: you add a date, correct one or say forget it in your own words, and say once how far ahead you want to know. A regular's date read from your own sales stays yours and is never shown to them or anyone. A remembered death stays private. When a date nears, it points you to the act it invites: a cake, a feast, a gift, a fast. A rest day you keep is one FoodOS stays quiet on; whatever happened comes in afterwards, in your words. A date that follows a moon sighting or a local calendar may move by a day or more; it shows in pencil with the source it follows until your community confirms it. Kept apart from Keeping a shopping list (things to buy); Planning what to eat (meals); and Observing a fast (the fast itself). It usually starts when a date you keep comes near, someone tells you a date, a new year begins, a festival calendar is published, or a date that needs money nears: school fees, a loan payment, rent.

examples.card: A friend's birthday is near.
examples.filled: Ana's birthday in São Paulo is on Saturday. Bake her a cake?

examples.card: A remembered death brings a family meal.
examples.filled: Your father's anniversary is in 10 days and the family meets in Hanoi for a meal at the altar. Start planning what to cook?

examples.card: A regular's yearly occasion is near.
examples.filled: Mr Okafor's 14 June is in 3 weeks. Ask if he wants a cake for his wife again?

you do this when: You keep the dates that bring food with them: birthdays, festivals, a death you remember.

name: Getting ready for an emergency
card: A cyclone warning is out for Beira on Friday. Stock up on water and tinned food today?
note: You get ready before a storm, flood, power cut, war or drought: what to store (food, water, fuel, cash), a grab bag, what to move, where to go and who to tell. You do it once for the event, or on a schedule. Prices often rise before a storm; the card shows today's price beside what waiting costs. An evacuation order is not your choice and shows as such. Kept apart from Buying and selling food to use (usual needs); Keeping the power on (energy only); Keeping food fresh (stock you hold); Storing a harvest (food kept through lean months); and Warning people nearby (telling neighbours). It usually starts when a forecast or warning is issued, or your stores fall below the days you set.

examples.card: Stock up before a storm that is forecast.
examples.filled: A cyclone warning is out for Beira on Friday. Buy 20 litres of water and 3 days of tinned food today?

examples.card: Prepare for a long power cut.
examples.filled: Eskom shows 6 hours of load-shedding tonight in Pretoria. Fill the cool box and charge the lamps before 5?

examples.card: Plan where to go and who to tell.
examples.filled: A flood warning covers your street in Dhaka. Move the rice to the upper floor and message your sister?

you do this when: You get ready before a storm, flood, power cut or drought: store, move, tell.

name: Registering your land
card: Your plot near Kisumu has no mapped boundary. Ask two neighbours to walk it with you?
note: You get the land you hold recorded: its boundary mapped, your ownership or right to use it registered, or a right by custom backed by elders and neighbours. You gather the proofs (a survey, neighbours' and elders' signed word, old papers), send them in, wait out any time for objections, and keep what comes back. The card says what becomes public, such as a map of your plot, before you send it. A registered right is the registry's record that the land is yours. It can back a loan or a sale, or show a buyer where food was grown. Kept apart from Buying land, water or quota (buying it); Inheriting something (it passes to you); and Getting a permit or registration (permission to trade). It usually starts when a buyer or lender asks for proof, a neighbour disputes a boundary, or you take on a plot.
no mirror: none: the registry or authority that records it

examples.card: Map a boundary with neighbours.
examples.filled: Your plot near Kisumu has no mapped edge, and two neighbours have agreed to walk it with you on Saturday. Book the surveyor for 1,500 shillings?

examples.card: Back a customary claim with elders.
examples.filled: Three elders in your village near Kumasi can vouch for your family plot. Ask them to sign this month?

examples.card: Register your ownership before a sale.
examples.filled: The buyer for your field in Ohio wants the title registered first, which costs 120 dollars. Start the filing today?

you do this when: You get the land you hold recorded: boundary, ownership or a right by custom.

name: Entering a competition
card: The cheese show in Bristol closes entries on 3 March, with a fee of £25 for each cheese. Enter your washed rind?
note: You enter a food competition or award: a cheese or wine show, a young chef award, a bake-off, a best street food award or a creator award. You enter by the closing date, send or bring your entry, are judged, and may win a prize or an award you can show. The card shows the whole cost: fees, postage, samples and time. An award records who judged it and whether you paid to enter, so it reads as what it is. Kept apart from Applying for a grant (money given to you for a purpose); and Getting or giving a certificate (a standard you keep). It usually starts when entries open, a closing date nears, or you have something new you are proud of.

examples.card: Enter a young chef award.
examples.filled: The young chef award in Singapore takes entries until 15 June from cooks under 26. Enter with your lamb dish?

examples.card: Enter a street food prize.
examples.filled: The night market in Taipei runs a best street food prize, with a NT$500 entry fee. Enter your stall?

examples.card: Enter a home bake-off.
examples.filled: The church bake-off in Ohio is on Saturday, and it is free to enter. Enter your lemon cake?

you do this when: You enter a show, bake-off or award, usually for a fee. The organiser's side is Running a competition.

name: Claiming on a warranty
card: The blender is 14 months old and has a two-year warranty. Claim a replacement with the receipt?
note: You claim on a warranty or guarantee when something you bought fails later: a mixer, a fridge, a tractor part, a coffee machine, a pump. A warranty is a promise from whoever gave it: what it pays out (repair, replace, refund), until when, and whether it passes to a new owner. The law may give a floor of its own. You check it is still covered, find the receipt, send the claim to the seller or the maker with photos, they repair, replace or refund it, and you keep the record. A warranty you bought separately is Taking out insurance. When something fails, you note the date and what it was doing, so the claim has the day it began. Kept apart from Complaining and putting it right (something wrong when it arrived); Repairing and treating for pay (paying someone to fix it); and Returning something (sending it back by choice). It usually starts when a machine fails while its cover runs, or the cover is near its end and a fault keeps coming back.

examples.card: Check if equipment is still under warranty and claim.
examples.filled: The blender is 14 months old and has a two-year warranty. Claim a replacement?

examples.card: Claim a repair on kit that failed within its cover.
examples.filled: The cold room compressor at your Kampala shop failed at month 10 of 24. Send the claim to the maker with the log?

examples.card: Claim before a warranty ends.
examples.filled: Your oven in Melbourne has tripped twice and its cover ends in 3 weeks. Claim now?

you do this when: Something you bought fails months later and you claim on the promise of whoever gave the warranty: repair, replace or refund. Not a wrong order, not a return by choice.

name: Selling on credit
card: Mrs Mensah's tab is GH₵ 340 and 6 weeks old. Ask her to settle it before she takes more?
note: You let customers you trust take food now and pay later: the khata book, the slate, a trade account with 30 days to pay. You open a tab for someone with a limit and a day to pay, write each thing they take, and they settle all or part. A tab can run the other way: money a customer left with you ahead, or small change you owe them, is a line on the same page. A customer who has FoodOS sees each line, and what they owe is their own word. A customer who does not signs or thumbs the page and you photograph it. You can stop more credit at any time, and what is owed is still owed. Your money is out while you wait, so you may charge for the wait, and the card shows how old each tab is and what it would cost you to wait longer. Who you trust and how much is yours to set. You can also note a customer you turned down for credit. You choose how the thing is sold, and nothing is chosen for you: 'it's his now, and he owes the price', or 'he holds it now, and it becomes his when he has paid in full', so the holding moves today and the owning moves on the last payment by a condition you both signed. If his business folds first, your record already shows the thing was never his. A tab can also fall due on an event instead of a date, such as 'when it is sold', 'when his customer pays' or 'at harvest'. Buying on a tab: You buy from a shop that trusts you to pay later: the udhaar at the kirana, the fiado at the bodega, the ardoise at the café, 'pay me on Friday'. You open the tab, take food on it day by day, and settle it all or in part on the day you agreed. Either side can close it, and what is owed is still owed. When you pay, your own balance sits beside the shop's book, and the tab closes on the number you both signed. Kept apart from Buying and selling food to use (they pay at the counter); Lending money (you lend money, not goods); Selling subscriptions (they pay you first); Setting your terms of trade (your standing limits, not one tab); Selling to be paid when they are paid (the price is due when someone else pays him, or when he returns what is unsold); Borrowing money (you are lent money, not goods); and Subscribing (you pay first and the food comes later). It usually starts when a regular asks to pay later, when a tab passes its limit or its day, or when money you are owed is holding up your own buying; as Buying on a tab, when money runs short before payday, when a shop you use often offers a tab, or when the tab reaches the limit you set or the day it is due.

examples.card: Open a tab for a regular customer.
examples.filled: Auntie Ama buys from your stall in Kumasi every day. Let her pay weekly, up to GH₵ 200?

examples.card: Ask for payment on a tab that is past its day.
examples.filled: The café in Leeds owes you £420 for 5 weeks of bread on 30-day terms. Remind them today?

examples.card: Add a charge for paying late on a trade account.
examples.filled: Three restaurant accounts in Nairobi pay 20 days late. Add a charge for late days from next month?

examples.card: Take a customer's advance and draw it down.
examples.filled: Priya left KSh 500 with you at your Nakuru duka last week and has KSh 180 left. Take today's flour off it?

examples.card: Read a regular her page and note what she says.
examples.filled: Auntie Ama's page in your Kumasi shop shows GH₵ 86 over three weeks and she has no phone. Read it to her on Saturday and note what she says?

examples.card: Note small change you owe a customer.
examples.filled: You owed Mr Banerjee 4 rupees at your Kolkata kirana. Put it on his page for next time?

name: Paying ahead for a crop
card: A trader offers KSh 2,600 a bag now for your maize at harvest. Your own sales last harvest were at 3,400. Take the money now?
note: You sell your crop or catch before it is ready and are paid now, all or part: the standing crop sold to a trader, an advance from a coffee buyer, the cash you need in the lean months. You agree the price, amount, quality and day, and what happens if the harvest is short. You take the money, grow, and deliver. The card shows this price beside the harvest prices you can find signed, and beside what you expect. What is sold ahead can also be a herd's young, its wool or a season's milk, on the same terms. If the harvest falls short, you say what happened and why, with a photo while it can be shown, so the shortfall is read as a loss with its cause. Buying a crop before harvest: You pay a grower now, all or part, for a crop they will deliver at harvest: a standing field of rice, the coffee cherries, a boat's catch next season. You agree the price, the amount, the quality, the day and what happens if the harvest is short. You pay the advance, wait, and receive the crop. The card shows this price beside today's price, and you record what you expect the crop to be worth when it comes. What is bought ahead can also be a herd's young, its wool or a season's milk, on the same terms. Kept apart from Selling and buying in bulk (the crop is ready); Buying growing supplies (inputs paid for from the harvest, not money for the crop); Borrowing money (you owe money, not a crop); Buying and selling food to use (it is there to buy today); Supplying on contract (a standing deal without an advance); and Agreeing a price for later (nobody pays until delivery). It usually starts when the lean months before harvest come, when school fees or a bill fall due, or when a buyer comes offering advances; as Buying a crop before harvest, when growers need cash before harvest, when you need to be sure of supply, or when a season's price looks likely to rise.

name: Agreeing a price for later
card: The mill will fix wheat at £210 a tonne for March delivery. Fix 50 tonnes at that price?
note: You and the other side agree today the price of something that changes hands later: wheat in March, milk for six months, a menu price held for a season, coffee at a set price next year. Nobody pays or hands over anything yet. You agree the price, the amount, the date, and what each side puts up to back it. On the day you both do your part at the price you fixed. Either side gives up the chance of a better price to be sure of this one, so the card shows the price, the date and the price you wrote down as your own guess. Leaving the price to be fixed later: You and the other side agree to buy and sell now but leave the price open. It will be what a reading says on delivery day (a price posted by readers you both named), or what one side calls within a window (the seller picks the day to fix it, or the buyer does), with a lowest and a highest price if you want them. Until it is fixed the deal shows 'price unfixed'. Nothing is filled in: if no one calls by the end of the window it stays unfixed, the deal shows it, and only you two or your judge can settle it. A call after the window counts for nothing, and the window ends by a clock you both chose. Kept apart from Paying ahead for a crop (one side pays now); Supplying on contract (a standing supply deal); Setting prices (your own price for anyone); and Adding a weather clause (the amount can drop, not the price). It usually starts when a price swings, when you plan a season and need a cost you can count on, or when a buyer or supplier offers to hold a price; as Leaving the price to be fixed later, when a trader offers the going rate on delivery day, when a season starts and prices swing, or when a window to call is closing.

no mirror: self: both sides do the same thing

name: Paying ahead for a share of the harvest
card: Last year 32 people bought veg shares. Open shares for next season?
note: You sell people a share of what your farm, boat or herd will yield before the season, and they share its luck with you: community-supported agriculture, a herd share, a catch share. You set how many shares, the price, what a share is and how it is delivered; people buy, you grow and send each share as it comes. Their money is paid ahead, so you say who holds it until the food is delivered and what anyone gets back if they leave or the season fails. When a share is smaller than promised, you record what was lost and why. Buying a share of the harvest: You pay a farm, boat or herd before the season for a share of whatever it yields: a vegetable share, a herd share, a catch share, a share of an olive harvest. You agree the price, the share and how it is delivered, then you pay, and the farm sends your share as it comes. A good year means more and a bad year less, so you share the grower's luck as well as the food. You are paying ahead, so the card says who holds your money until it is delivered and what you get back if you leave. Kept apart from Selling subscriptions (a fixed box at a fixed price); Putting money into a business (a share of the business itself); Paying ahead for a crop (a set amount to one buyer); and Subscribing (a fixed box at a fixed price). It usually starts when you need money for seed and wages, when last year's members ask about next year, or when you have more land or boat time than buyers; as Buying a share of the harvest, when farms sell shares in late winter, when a grower you know asks for support before the season, or when your share ends.

examples.card: Open shares of next season's harvest.
examples.filled: Open summer veg shares from your farm near Totnes?

examples.card: Tell members what this week's share holds.

name: Selling a debt
card: The supermarket owes you £8,400 in 60 days. A lender will pay £8,150 today for the invoice. Sell it?
note: You sell money someone owes you, to get cash today: an unpaid invoice from a supermarket, a hotel or a council, a receipt for grain in store, a buyer's promise to pay at harvest. You offer it, the buyer checks who owes it, pays you a little less than the full amount, and collects it when it falls due. The gap is the price of having the money now, and the card shows it as a yearly rate so you can set it beside borrowing. You agree up front whether you still answer if the one who owes never pays. A debt can be marked 'not to be passed on', and then selling it counts for nothing; a payment the debtor made to you before he saw the sale still counts, and you hold it for the buyer. Kept apart from Borrowing money (you owe it back); Borrowing against stored stock (the stock backs a loan); Selling on credit (you give credit, not sell it); and Handing on what you are owed (you pay a creditor with it, or hand it back to the one who owes it). It usually starts when a large buyer pays slowly, when wages or stock must be paid before the money comes in, or when a financier offers to buy invoices.

examples.card: Sell an unpaid invoice for cash now.
examples.filled: The hotel group in Cape Town owes you R36,000 in 45 days. A lender pays R35,100 today. Sell it?

examples.card: Compare selling an invoice with a loan.

examples.card: Agree who bears it if the buyer never pays.

examples.card: Sell what a brand owes you.
examples.filled: A brand owes you 2,400, due in 75 days, and a buyer posts an offer for invoices like it. Sell it, wait, or ask the brand to pay sooner?

you do this when: You sell money someone owes you to get cash today.

name: Waiting to sell for a better price
card: Maize is KSh 2,800 a bag now. March prices over the last 5 years ran from 3,100 to 4,000. Hold 20 bags until March, or sell now?
note: You keep stock you could sell now because you expect a better price later: grain after harvest, onions into winter, cheese, timber or coffee held for the season to turn. You decide what to hold, until when or until what price, and you record what you expect. The card shows what holding uses (storage, loss, the money tied up) next to the price you expect. When the day or the price comes you sell, keep holding or let it go. When you sell, keep holding or let it go, you count what is left against what you put in, so what was lost in store shows as a loss and not a guess. Kept apart from Storing a harvest (keeping food safe to eat or sell); Ageing food or drink (it gets better as it waits); and Agreeing a price for later (the price is agreed now). It usually starts when prices are low at harvest, when a store has room, or when the price or the date you set comes.

examples.card: Hold grain after harvest for a later price.
examples.filled: Rice in Tamale is GH₵ 420 a bag after harvest and was 600 in May. Hold 30 bags until May?

examples.card: See what holding stock costs you.
examples.filled: Holding 10 tonnes of onions in Nashik until January costs storage and some rot. Keep holding?

examples.card: Sell when the price you set comes.
examples.filled: Maize reached KSh 3,600 a bag in Kitale, the price you were waiting for. Sell the 20 bags?

examples.card: Decide to let it go.
examples.filled: The onions in your Nashik store are starting to rot and the price has not moved. Sell what is left now?

you do this when: You keep stock you could sell now because you expect a better price later.

name: Borrowing against stored stock
card: Your 40 bags in the warehouse can back a loan of GH₵9,000 at 2% a month. Borrow it and keep the grain?
note: You borrow money against grain or coffee you have stored in a warehouse, so you can pay bills without selling at harvest prices. The warehouse gives you a receipt, the lender keeps it until you repay, and you get the money. When you sell the stock, the loan and its interest are paid first. If you do not repay, the lender sells the stock. Kept apart from Borrowing money (nothing is held back); Selling a debt (you sell what is owed to you outright); and Waiting to sell for a better price (you wait without borrowing). It usually starts when prices are low at harvest and bills are due, or when a warehouse and a lender offer receipts and loans.

examples.card: Borrow against grain in a warehouse.
examples.filled: The warehouse in Dodoma holds 25 bags of your maize. Borrow TSh 1.5m against them until March?

examples.card: Repay a loan against stock when you sell.
examples.filled: You sold the 40 bags in Kumasi. Repay the GH₵ 9,000 and its interest from the sale?

examples.card: Compare borrowing with selling now.
examples.filled: Selling now gives you ₦480,000; borrowing ₦300,000 against the stock costs ₦27,000 to April. Which one?

you do this when: You borrow money against grain or coffee you have stored in a warehouse, on the receipt. Not an ordinary loan.

name: Holding money until a deal is done
card: Kofi and Esi ask you to hold GH₵ 6,000 for a cow until it is delivered healthy. Hold it?
note: You hold money for two sides until both say a deal is done: an elder holding a cattle price, a market master holding a deposit, a lawyer holding a land payment, a platform holding pay until delivery. Both sides name you and agree when you let it go and to whom. You take the money, keep it apart, do not use it, and pay it out when the condition is met, or back if it fails. A fee, if any, is agreed first. The release can run on a clock both sides chose: 'to Amara if Joe has not arrived by 9, back to Joe if he has'. The two conditions are read on the same clock, so a late arrival cannot win by being signed first, and no receipt from that clock by the time counts as no arrival, because that is the term both signed. Both sides can also agree to release early. Kept apart from Asking for a ruling on a dispute (deciding who is right); Saving with a collector (one person's savings); Keeping money with a bank or wallet (it is yours to call back); and Putting up a bond (the money is one side's own penalty for a promise). It usually starts when two people who do not know each other trade something large, when a deposit must sit with someone neither side controls, or when the condition for release arrives.
no mirror: none: each side names the holder in their own deal

examples.card: Hold the money for a deal between two people.
examples.filled: A buyer and a seller of 20 goats in Maasai Mara ask you to hold KSh 160,000 until delivery. Hold it?

examples.card: Release held money when the deal is done.
examples.filled: The cow arrived healthy and both sides say so. Release the GH₵ 6,000 to Kofi?

examples.card: Return held money when a deal fails.
examples.filled: The land sale in Mbale fell through and both sides agree. Return the deposit to the buyer?

examples.card: Hold a bond on a clock both chose.
examples.filled: Joe the caterer puts £200 with you: it goes to Amara if he has not arrived by 9 on the clock you all named, and back to him if he has. Hold it?

examples.card: Release early when both agree.
examples.filled: Kofi and Esi both sign that the cow arrived healthy, two days before the date. Release the GH₵ 6,000 to the seller now?

you do this when: You hold money for two sides until both say a deal is done: escrow.

name: Keeping money with a bank or wallet
card: Your takings are KSh 48,000 in cash. Put them in your mobile wallet tonight, or the SACCO account that pays 6%?
note: You keep money with a bank, a mobile-money wallet, a SACCO or a trusted shopkeeper, and take it back when you want it. If they hold all of it, it is yours on demand. If they use or lend it, it is a loan to them: they pay you back when you ask, in the order people ask, while they have it. You put money in, take it out, and close the account when you choose. The card names who holds it, what they pay or charge, how fast you can take it out, and what covers it if they fail. Each fee shows in the provider's own words, with what is free and the date a fee on a small or idle balance starts. Kept apart from Holding money until a deal is done (whoever keeps it may not use it); Saving with a collector (someone collects from you each day); and Lending money (you lend it for a time to someone who needs it). It usually starts when takings pile up, when cash at home or in the till is a risk, when a provider pays or charges more, or when you need the money back.
no mirror: none yet: the bank or wallet publishes its own act

examples.card: Bank the day's takings.
examples.filled: R6,400 is in the till at close in Soweto. Deposit it at the agent before 7pm?

examples.card: Move savings to a place that pays more.

examples.filled: Your village bank in Mwanza has no deposit cover. Keep only a month's takings there?

examples.card: Open an account for the business.
