you do this when: You keep money with a bank, mobile-money wallet or SACCO and take it back when you want.

name: Buying a voucher or pass
card: The bakery sells 10 coffees for the price of 9. Buy the card for £27?
note: You pay now for food or a service later from one seller: a coffee card, a meal pass, a gift voucher, a canteen balance, a top-up on a shop wallet. You pay, then spend it a bit at a time until it runs out or ends. You pay first, so the card shows the discount beside when you will use it. Kept apart from Joining a loyalty scheme (you earn it as you buy); Subscribing (food is sent to you on a schedule); and Receiving a gift (someone else paid). It usually starts when a seller you use often offers a card or pass, when you want to give one as a present, or when a balance runs low.

examples.card: Buy a pass from a place you use often.
examples.filled: Your lunch spot in Melbourne sells 10 lunches for A$150, valid 3 months. Buy it?

examples.card: Top up a canteen or shop balance.
examples.filled: Your canteen card in Bengaluru has ₹40 left. Top up ₹1,000?

examples.card: Buy a voucher as a present.
examples.filled: Your sister loves the dumpling place in Taipei. Buy her an NT$1,000 voucher?

examples.card: Buy a pass for classes or courses.
examples.filled: Your cookery school in Cape Town sells 5 classes for R1,500, valid 6 months. Buy the pass?

examples.card: Buy a pass for a market or food hall.
examples.filled: The food hall in Mexico City sells MX$500 of credit for MX$450. Buy it?

you do this when: You pay now for food or a service later from one seller: a coffee card, a gift voucher.

name: Joining a loyalty scheme
card: The supermarket scheme gives back 1p in each £1 and keeps a record of what you buy. Join it?
note: You join a shop's or a group's scheme that gives back as you buy: stamps, points, a member price, cashback. You see the terms first: what you earn, what it pays out in, when it runs out, whether you can pass it on, and what the scheme keeps about you and who it shares that with. You join, earn as you buy, and leave when you like, keeping your own record of what you bought. What you earn is owed to you by the shop, and you pay with it on any purchase. What you earn is written into each purchase, and if a purchase should have earned something and did not, you note it. Kept apart from Buying a voucher or pass (you pay for it); and Taking part in a group (members share a plan). It usually starts when a shop you use asks you to join, when a scheme changes its terms, when you stop using a shop whose scheme you are in, or when points or credit you hold near their end date.

examples.card: Join a shop's scheme after reading its terms.
examples.filled: The bakery in Lisbon gives a free loaf after 9. Join with your number?

examples.card: Leave a scheme you no longer use.
examples.filled: You haven't used the Delhi grocer's points in a year. Leave and take your record?

examples.card: Read what a scheme keeps about you.
examples.filled: The supermarket app shares your shopping with its partners. Join anyway, or join without the app?

you do this when: You join a shop's scheme that gives back as you buy (stamps, points, a member price). Its keeper's side is Running a loyalty scheme.

name: Trading with community credits
card: The circle gives you 300 credits for the bread you sold Rosa. Spend them on Ali's vegetables?
note: You trade with other members of a circle that keeps its own unit: you sell to one member and earn credits, buy from another and spend them, and the balances net out. Time banks, LETS, Sardex, Sarafu and village credits work this way. You join under the circle's rules, which say who may go how far below zero, what a credit buys, whether it can be turned into money, and what happens if someone leaves owing. You sell, buy and settle, and leave when you like. A credit is not money. It is only worth what other members will give you for it. Kept apart from Swapping with someone (one swap between two people); Saving in a group (money pooled in one pot); and Settling up with trading partners (debts netted between named partners). It usually starts when cash is short in a place, when traders nearby start or join a circle, or when your balance runs far above or below zero.

examples.card: Join a circle that trades in its own credits.
examples.filled: Thirty traders in Kangemi trade in Sarafu. Join and accept it for half of each sale?

examples.card: Spend credits you have earned.
examples.filled: You have 420 circle credits in Sardinia. Spend them on cheese from a member?

examples.card: Bring a balance back towards zero.
examples.filled: You are 600 credits below zero in the Bristol circle. Sell a member some bread, or leave it for now?

examples.card: Take the circle's vouchers for what you sell.
examples.filled: Every shop in your village in Bolivia takes the circle's food vouchers. Take them for your bread this week?

you do this when: You trade with members of a circle that keeps its own unit, and the balances net out.

name: Claiming back from a scheme
card: You took 64 food vouchers this month worth R5,120. Claim them back from the scheme today?
note: You ask a scheme to pay you back for food you already gave under it: vouchers and benefit cards taken at the till, school meals served under a public contract, a subsidy on milk for children. You gather what was taken, send the request with its proof, and the scheme checks and pays, or asks questions. You gave the food first, so the scheme owes you until it pays. The card says when payment is due and what you are owed so far. A refund the state owes is claimed the same way: tax on goods sent abroad, duty on drink destroyed or sent back, tax taken from pay under a temporary code, or the tax relief on gifts a donor declared. Once sent, a claim can be sold as Selling a debt. Kept apart from Selling under a scheme (taking the voucher at the sale); Claiming benefits (a person asking for themselves); and Applying for a grant (money you ask for before you act). It usually starts when a month or claim period ends, when vouchers or meals pile up unclaimed, or when a claim is late or questioned.
no mirror: none: the scheme

name: Selling animals
card: A farmer in Nyeri wants 6 of your in-calf heifers at KSh 95,000 each. Sell them?
note: You sell live animals to another keeper, a dealer, a butcher or an abattoir: weaners to a fattener, in-calf heifers, day-old chicks, spent hens at the end of lay, a ram after the season, goats before a festival. You agree the price, the animals, their papers and health, and when they move. Whether the price is by the head, by live weight, or by carcass weight and grade is part of the deal; by carcass, the kill sheet settles it. An animal still inside the waiting time of a medicine you gave is shown with its date beside the sale date; moving the sale or telling the buyer is yours to decide. You hand them over with their records and the movement report the law asks for, and they pay. What you say about the animals' health is your signed word, so the card shows what their records say. If an animal dies or goes missing before it moves, you record it, so the count at handover matches and the price follows what moved. Kept apart from Selling at a stall, a gate or a screen (any goods on a market day); Selling at auction (the price is bid); and Slaughtering an animal (for meat). It usually starts when animals reach the age or weight buyers want, before a festival when prices rise, when feed runs short, or when a keeper you know asks to buy.

examples.card: Sell young animals to another farmer.
examples.filled: A fattener in Nakuru wants 20 weaners at KSh 6,500 each. Sell them this week?

examples.card: Sell goats before a festival.
examples.filled: Eid is in 3 weeks and buyers in Kano pay more for rams. Sell 8 now?

examples.card: Send animals with their records.
examples.filled: The 12 heifers leave for the buyer in Devon on Monday. Send their movement papers and test dates?

examples.card: Sell by the head at a water point.
examples.filled: A trader at the well offers 2,300 a head for 6 goats, cash now. Sell?

move words.card: The ewe you are selling was dosed 10 days ago; the label says 28. Hold her back until the date?
move words.note: Keep something back from going out until someone says it is fine: a batch on hold until a test, milk or eggs inside a treatment's waiting days, an animal not yet clear to sell. Release it when the result or the date comes.

examples.card: Hold back animals inside a medicine's waiting days.
examples.filled: Two lambs are inside the 28 days after their wormer. Hold them back from Friday's sale?

move words.trigger: A reading or a result on a batch of hers is outside the limit in its spec, or an open problem is recorded against it.

you do this when: You sell live animals to a keeper, dealer, butcher or abattoir.

name: Repairing and treating for pay
card: A farmer 4 km away has a cow down after calving. Go now for your call-out fee of KSh 1,500?
note: You treat other people's animals for a fee: a vet, a community animal-health worker, a farrier, a vaccinator going farm to farm. You are asked, agree a fee or a visit price, examine and treat, and record what you found and gave. The animal's record belongs to its keeper. Medicines have a waiting time before the milk or meat can be sold, and you write it on the record. A disease the law names must be reported, which is its own act. Getting something repaired: You have someone else fix kit you own: a fridge, oven, tractor, till or coffee machine. You ask, they look and quote a fixed price or an estimate, you accept, they repair it and say it is done, and you pay. If the kit goes to their workshop they hold it and answer for it until it comes back. The card shows the repair beside replacing it, renting, or waiting, and the warranty on parts and work. A price above the quote needs your yes. Fixing it yourself is Keeping equipment and places in order. Calling the vet: You call a vet or animal-health worker to visit, diagnose and treat your animal, or to do the routine checks that keep a herd healthy. You ask, they offer a time and a fee (a call-out, a night rate, sometimes paid in kind), you accept, they treat, and you pay. The treatment, and the days you must wait before selling its milk or meat, go on your animal's record, which is yours. Tests and vaccinations the law requires are shown as required. A disease the law names is reported in Reporting to an authority. When the vet leaves medicine for you to give later, their note of the course and the waiting days goes on the animal's record, and each dose you give is yours to note. A vet's note on the cause of a death is theirs and can go to an insurer with your photo of the ear tag. Repairing for others: You fix other people's kit for pay: a fridge engineer, a tractor mechanic, a pump repairer, someone who mends mills or knives. You are asked, look at it, say what is wrong and what it will cost, and they agree. You repair it, hand it back, and say how long your work is guaranteed. A quote is a promise, so a change in the price needs their yes. Kept apart from Doing or getting a job for pay (any piece of work); Looking after someone's animals (keeping them, not treating them); Reporting to an authority (telling the state); Buying equipment (you replace it); Having food processed (your own food goes in and comes back changed); Testing samples (a lab test of a sample); Looking after a pet (a pet's care at home); Keeping equipment and places in order (your own kit); and Selling equipment (you sell the kit). It usually starts when a keeper calls with a sick animal, when a vaccination round is due in an area, or when a herd you treat needs a check-up; as Getting something repaired, when something breaks or a sensor shows it heading that way, when a service is due, or when a warranty is about to end; as Calling the vet, when your record shows an animal off its feed or its milk dropping, an injury or a birth is going wrong, or a routine date comes (vaccination, TB test); as Repairing for others, when someone's kit breaks, when a season is about to start and machines need checks, or when a repair you did comes back under its guarantee.

move words.note: Sending the owner the record of what you did to what is theirs: the kill sheet with weights and grade, the treatment with its waiting days, the count of births, deaths and weight for animals you keep, the bags in store. It is your signed word and your proof of the work.

you do this when: Someone mends your kit or treats your animal for a fee: you call them or you do the work; kit or animal is the one fact. Not a general job for pay, not advice.

name: Commissioning something new
card: A designer quotes ₹45,000 for your new labels, and you keep the rights. Commission her?
note: You pay someone to make something new for you: a logo and labels, photos of your dishes, a recipe developed for your menu, a website, a mural, a song for your shop. You write down what you want, agree the price, the stages, how many changes and who may use the result, then they make it, you pay in stages, and you take it. You also agree who may use it, and whether the maker may show it in their own portfolio. An idea is not property (Kinsella), so you do not own a design or a recipe, you hold the maker's signed word about who may use it; a photo file or a printed label you do own. Kept apart from Doing or getting a job for pay (a job that leaves nothing new to own); Buying someone's know-how (something that already exists); and Getting your product made (copies of your product). It usually starts when you start or rename a business, when a menu or pack changes, or when an event needs something made for it.

examples.card: Commission a design and keep its rights.
examples.filled: A designer in Lagos quotes ₦250,000 for your new pack design, with all rights to you. Commission it?

examples.card: Agree the stages and changes before you start.
examples.filled: The photographer in Lisbon offers 20 photos in 2 rounds of changes for €600. Agree?

examples.card: Pay the last stage when the work is done.
examples.filled: The chef finished the 6 new dishes for your menu in Mexico City. Pay the final MX$8,000?

you do this when: You pay for something new that you then own: a label, photographs, a recipe developed for you.

name: Awarding a grant
card: Your co-op fund has £12,000 and 9 applications. Award grants to the 4 you rank highest?
note: You give money for a purpose to people who apply: a co-op's development fund, a town's food grant, a foundation's prize, a farmers' union fund. You say what it is for, who may apply and by when, read the applications and choose by the rules you set, then pay in one go or in stages and ask for a report. Conditions and what happens if the money is not used as agreed are stated up front. Your rules and your choices are signed so applicants can see how you decided. Kept apart from Sending money home (family support); Giving cash for food (money to households, nobody applies); Putting money into a business (you want a share back); and Lending money (it is paid back). It usually starts when a fund opens, when applications come in, when a stage's report is due, or when the year's money must be given out.

examples.card: Open a round of grants with clear rules.
examples.filled: Your union's fund has R80,000 for young farmers in Limpopo. Open applications until June?

examples.filled: The Accra school garden sent photos and receipts for stage 1. Pay stage 2 of GH₵ 4,000?

you do this when: You give money for a purpose to people who apply, choosing by your own published rule. Not cash to every household on a list.

name: Collecting waste for others
card: Six restaurants on your route have food waste on Tuesdays. Collect it for KSh 300 a bin?
note: You collect what others throw away and take it where it is used or disposed of: a waste picker sorting plastic and metal, a scrap dealer buying old kit, a compost service taking food waste, a collector taking used oil. You agree what you take, when, and who pays whom: they pay you to take it, or you pay for something worth selling. You collect, sort, and sell or dispose of it as the law asks. Kept apart from Selling and buying in bulk (one load bought to use); Getting rid of waste (the giver's side); and Making compost (what you do with it after). It usually starts when businesses near you have regular waste, when scrap prices rise, or when a collection day comes.
no mirror: none fixed: who pays whom varies, so the giver's side, Getting rid of waste, is matched by the deal's terms

name: Running a competition
card: Entries for your county show's best cheddar open next week. Name the 3 judges and publish the rules today?
note: You run a contest people enter with their food: a bake-off, a produce show, a cheese award, a chef's competition. You set the rules, the classes, the entry fee, the prizes and who judges, and publish them before anyone enters. Entries come in, the judges judge by the rules and sign their verdicts, and you give the prizes and titles. Who judged, and whether entrants paid, is said beside every title, so everyone can see what a medal means. Kept apart from Running a prize draw (winners by chance); Running a food event (people come to eat); and Getting or giving a certificate (a standing mark). It usually starts when a show or festival season comes, when you want to find or honour good makers, or when entries close.

examples.card: Publish the rules and judges before entries open.

name: Paying to be shown
card: The food podcast offers a read-out for your hot sauce for £300, labelled as paid. Sponsor an episode?
note: You pay someone to show your name or your food: a creator's video, a local football kit, a school fair, a food festival stage. You agree what they show, where, how often, and that it is labelled as paid, then you pay and they show it. What they say about your food stays their own words. Paying for adverts: You pay a place to show you to its users: an advert in an app, a promoted listing, a radio spot, a signboard, a flyer through doors. You agree where, who will see it, how long and the price, then pay and it runs. A customer who comes from an advert can say so, and each sale then shows which advert it came from; sales that rose while it ran went together with it, which is not the same as because of it. Kept apart from Giving to a cause (you give and ask for nothing back); Commissioning something new (you own what is made); Posting an offer or a want (free); and Offering customers a deal (a lower price, not an advert). It usually starts when a creator or event asks for sponsors, when you launch something, or when a season of an event ends; as Paying for adverts, when you open or launch something, when a quiet season comes, or when an advert ends.

you do this when: You pay a creator, an event or a platform to show your name or food. Not a free post.

name: Taking a sponsorship
card: A flour brand offers £800 to use its flour in 2 videos, labelled as paid. Take it?
note: You are paid to show someone's name or food: a creator using a brand's flour, a festival naming a sponsor, a team wearing a café's name. You agree what you show, how often, and that it is labelled as paid, then you show it and are paid. Your own words stay your own, and anything paid is shown as paid. Pay can be a fee, free product, or a share of what sells through your link; whatever the pay, every post says it is paid. A promise to keep rivals off your channel for a time is a term of the deal. Kept apart from Paying to be shown (you pay for the name); Publishing food content (nothing paid); and Doing or getting a job for pay (work done for someone, not shown). It usually starts when a brand asks to work with you, when you look for money for an event or channel, or when a sponsored piece is due.

name: Working a day for pay
card: A farm 3 km away pays KSh 600 for a day of weeding, paid at sunset. Take it?
note: You sell a day of your work and are paid for that day: a harvest day, a Saturday in a kitchen, a day as a market porter, a shift found on a group chat. You agree the work, the hours, the pay and when it is paid, and keep your own record of the hours. You work the day and are paid. You owe nothing after, and they owe you what was agreed. The pay can be by the day, the hour or the piece (a crate, a bucket, a kilo), or in goods; whichever it is, it is agreed before you start, and you keep your own count. Your pay is received against the count it was for, so a short count shows. Kept apart from Working for someone (a job that runs until ended); Doing or getting a job for pay (a finished piece of work, not a day); and Volunteering with food (unpaid). It usually starts when a farm or kitchen near you needs hands, when you have a free day, or when the day ends and pay is due.

examples.card: Clock in.

move words.card: You picked beans from 7 until the sun was high and the farmer is paying by the bucket. Add your 34 buckets to Tuesday?

examples.card: Log hours worked.
examples.filled: You weeded at the Nashik farm from 7 to 4. Log it?

move words.card: The farmer paid KSh 450 and you agreed KSh 600. Raise it with him?

examples.card: Raise a problem.
examples.filled: The farmer paid KSh 450 and you agreed KSh 600. Raise it with him?

move words.card: It is 41 degrees and the shade and water for the crew are not here. Stop work until it is put right?
move words.note: Taking yourself out of a danger at work (heat with no shade or water, a field inside its spray wait, a machine with no guard), with the time, the reason and a photo if you have one. What the law of your place allows is shown as a fact. It is not a strike; others carry on as they choose.

examples.card: Take yourself out of danger at work, on record.

move words.card: No work at the gate this morning. Note it as a day not out?
move words.note: A day she did not trade, with her own word for why. It keeps the days worked and the days lost in her record, which she carries and can share. It does not close anything and does not judge.
