examples.filled: It is past nine and you have not started. Is today a rain day, a sick day, a day for the family, or something else you will say?

move words.trigger: It is later than her usual start on a day she normally sells (from her own past days), and she has not started or counted anything; or she tells FoodOS it is raining or she is ill.

you do this when: You sell a day of your work and are paid for that day, keeping your own tools and say. Not the hirer's side.

name: Hiring help for a day
card: You need 4 extra hands to get the maize in before Thursday's rain. Hire them for KSh 600 a day?
note: You pay someone for a day of work: hands for the harvest, a porter on market day, an extra cook for a Saturday. You agree the work, the hours, the pay and when it is paid, then they work and you pay that day. Nothing goes on after, and you record what you paid. Kept apart from Employing someone (a job that runs until ended); Supplying workers from an agency (the agency is the employer); and Doing or getting a job for pay (a finished job). It usually starts when work piles up for a day or two, when weather forces a rush, or when someone is off.

examples.card: Hire people for a day of harvest.
examples.filled: The tea is ready in Kericho. Hire 6 pluckers for tomorrow at KSh 500?

examples.card: Hire an extra cook for a busy night.
examples.filled: You have 120 booked on Saturday in Lisbon. Hire a cook for the night for €100?

examples.card: Pay the day's help before they leave.
examples.filled: Three porters worked your stall in Kano today. Pay them ₦3,000 each now?

examples.card: Book a helper for one busy day.
examples.filled: A Lagos buka needs a kitchen porter this Saturday for a wedding order. Post the shift?

examples.card: Call in extra help when it gets busy.
examples.filled: The queue at your Manila lunch counter is out of the door. Message your three on-call helpers?

examples.card: A porter paid per trip
examples.filled: The trolley man made 3 trips today. Do you pay per trip or a day rate?

examples.card: Porters are paid by the sack you counted
examples.filled: Four porters unloaded 300 sacks of onions at your Wakulima market shed and you tallied them in chalk. Do you pay them by your tally tonight, or wait for the weighing tomorrow?

examples.card: Agree the rate per crate with the help.
examples.filled: You need 10 pickers tomorrow for the grapes. Tell them the pay per crate and how you will count before they start?

examples.card: Example: pickers by the kilo
examples.filled: Three women picked pods for you today. What did each bring, and what did you pay?

move words.card: Tom says he worked from three until midnight at the wedding and asks for 15. Do you want to agree?
move words.note: Each shift's hours, signed by the worker and received by you, keep pay right and within the law. Where work is paid by the piece, the count (crates, kilos) is signed the same way as hours.

examples.card: Check hours worked.
examples.filled: Tom says he worked from three until midnight at the wedding and asks for 15. Do you want to agree?

examples.card: Check hours worked.
examples.filled: Your washer-up says she left at ten, not midnight. Do you want to agree her hours?

move words.trigger: A hired day has ended and the worker has noted hours or asks for pay, and she has not yet said yes.

you do this when: You pay someone for a day of work and direct it: hands for the harvest, a porter. Not a standing job.

name: Sharing profit with your team
card: Your year closes on 31 March. Pay your 6 staff their share by the rule you set?
note: You give the people who work for you a share of what the business makes, by a rule you state in advance: a share of profit or a bonus pool. You set the share, who is in it and how it is divided, and say it before the work is done. When the period ends you show the figures it rests on and pay each person their part. Changing the rule needs the team's notice. Kept apart from Sharing ownership with your team (they own part of the business); Employing someone (a wage only); and Splitting takings (dividing what a group earned together). It usually starts when you want staff to share in a good year, when someone you want to keep might leave, or when a period ends and shares are due.

examples.card: Set a profit share before the year starts.
examples.filled: Tell the 5 cooks in Mexico City they get a share of what is left after costs, by hours?

examples.card: Pay out shares at the end of a period.
examples.filled: The boat's season in Kerala is over and the crew's share rule is set. Pay each crew member their share?

examples.card: Show the figures the share rests on.
examples.filled: Staff in Melbourne asked how the bonus pool was worked out. Send them the year's takings and costs?

examples.card: Share profit with the team by an agreed rule.
examples.filled: Your 6 staff at a Bristol bakery have been with you 4 years. Offer them a share of profit by hours worked?

you do this when: You give the people who work for you a share of what the business makes, by a rule stated in advance.

name: Taking a share of your workplace
card: The owner offers you 5% of the bakery, and you earn a bit more of it each year for 4 years. Say yes?
note: You are offered part of the business you work for, or part of what it makes: shares, a profit share, a stake that grows each year you stay. You see the terms: what you get, when it becomes yours, what it pays, what happens if you leave, and whether you can sell it. You say yes or no, and if yes it is yours and recorded with your work. Kept apart from Putting money into a business (you pay money for it); Working for someone (a wage only); and Taking part in a group (a group whose members share one plan). It usually starts when an owner offers staff a stake, when a profit share is set up, or when you are about to leave and need to know what is yours.

examples.card: Read a share offer before you say yes.
examples.filled: The co-op in Lisbon offers you a member share after a year. Say yes?

examples.card: Accept a profit share.
examples.filled: The farm in Kent offers 3% of the yearly profit to each of its 6 staff. Accept?

examples.card: Check what you keep if you leave.
examples.filled: You leave the café in Austin in June. Take the part of your stake that is yours now, or wait?

you do this when: You are offered part of the business you work for, or of what it makes, and see the terms. Not giving the share.

name: Showing your machine how you do a task
card: Your new kitchen robot can learn your dough. Show it how you fold and proof, step by step?
note: You teach a machine you own how you do something: a kitchen robot your fold, a milking robot your cows' order, FoodOS how you like your shop done. You show it, step by step, correct it, and say when it is right. What it learned stays yours: it leaves you only if you allow it. Kept apart from Teaching a food skill (a person learns); Letting someone act for you (authority given, not know-how); and Letting someone use your recipe or brand (others may use it). It usually starts when you get a new machine, when it does a task differently from you, or when you change how you do it.

examples.card: Show a new machine how you do a task.
examples.filled: The new bread robot in Lyon is ready. Show it your shaping for 3 batches?

examples.card: Correct a machine that does it differently.
examples.filled: The robot folds your dumplings with 14 pleats; you do 18. Show it again?

examples.card: Keep what your machine learned as yours.
examples.filled: The robot's maker asks to copy what it learned from you. Keep it yours?

you do this when: You teach a machine you own how you do something: a kitchen robot, a milking robot, FoodOS.

name: Taking table bookings
card: A party of 8 wants Saturday at 8. Hold the table, with the deposit in your terms?
note: You promise a table for a time: a booking, a waitlist place, a private room for a party. You say yes or no, hold the table, and the guests come or cancel. Your deposit, no-show fee and how late they may cancel are your own terms, said before they book, and a deposit is held, not yours, until the terms say so. When they arrive the booking ends and the meal begins. When the guests sit, the booking ends and you count how many came. If they do not come, you note it with the time, so a no-show fee has something behind it. Kept apart from Buying and selling food to use (looking after guests once they sit); Taking orders in advance (food made ahead for a date); and Setting your terms of trade (the standing terms, not one booking). It usually starts when someone asks for a table, when a cancellation frees one, or when a party is late.

examples.card: Hold a table for a party.
examples.filled: A party of 6 asks for Friday at 7:30 in Lisbon. Hold the corner table?

examples.card: Offer a freed table to the waitlist.
examples.filled: The 9pm table for 4 just cancelled in Melbourne. Offer it to the first couple on the waitlist?

examples.card: Keep a no-show deposit as your terms say.
examples.filled: The party of 10 didn't come and didn't cancel. Keep the £100 deposit as your terms say?

examples.card: Move a booking to another time.
examples.filled: A guest in Mumbai asks to move their table for 4 from 8 to 9pm. Say yes?

examples.card: Note a booking turned away.
examples.filled: You turned away a party of 6 for Saturday at 19:30 because the house is full. Put them on the waitlist, or note it as a missed booking?

move words.card: The 8 o'clock booking for 8 came as 5. Note how many came?
move words.note: How many people you actually fed or who came, and how many you turned away: the number a scheme, a client or next week's cooking is planned and paid on.

examples.card: Count the booked guests who came.
examples.filled: Saturday's service is over. Note how many of the 64 booked guests came?

move words.trigger: A meal, service or event she runs has ended.

you do this when: You promise a table for a time: a booking, a waitlist place, a private room.
mirror: Buying and selling food to use

name: Running a shared shop
card: Twelve farms sell through your Friday shop. Open orders until Thursday 8pm?
note: You run one shop that sells for many producers: a food hub, a shared online shopfront, a co-op shop window, a market box scheme from several farms. You set the order window, the fee, or share of each sale, each producer pays, who holds the food between drop-off and pickup, and when producers are paid. You open orders, producers deliver, customers collect, and you pay each producer their part. Each producer's prices are their own. For each drop-off the shop counts what came in, what sold, what went back and what was lost, and the producer is paid on those numbers. Kept apart from Running a market (pitches where each seller trades for themselves); Selling through an agent (one grower's produce); and Leading a group buy (buyers gathered, not sellers). It usually starts when producers near you want one place to sell, when an order window is due to open or close, or when a producer's pay is due.
no mirror: none: each producer sells through it in Selling through an app

examples.card: Open an order window across several producers.
examples.filled: Your hub in Bristol has 14 farms on it. Open orders until Wednesday noon?

examples.card: Agree each producer's cut before they join.
examples.filled: A cheesemaker wants to join your Leeds shop. Offer it at 15% of sales?

examples.card: Pay each producer after the pickups.
examples.filled: Saturday's pickups are done in Austin. Pay the 9 producers their share?

examples.card: Tell customers what is missing this week.
examples.filled: Two of the farms on your Kigali co-op shelf have no vegetables this week. Tell customers before they order?

move words.card: 8 producers are in for Saturday's drop. Open orders until Thursday 8pm?
move words.note: A shared ordering window across several sellers, with a cut-off.

examples.card: Open a shared order window for several producers.
examples.filled: Orders open until Thursday 8pm.

move words.trigger: Producers have signed up for the next drop and the order window for it has not yet opened, or it is due to open.

you do this when: You run one shop that sells for many producers: a food hub, a shared online shopfront.

name: Running a raffle
card: Tickets for the school fair hamper are £1. Sell them until 3pm and draw at 3:30?
note: You sell tickets for a chance to win a prize: a hamper at a fair, a lamb at a village show, a year of coffee for a cause. Each ticket is a chance in a fair draw. You set the prize, the price, how many tickets, where the money goes and when the draw is, and the law of the place says whether you may. People buy, the draw is made in a way anyone can check, the winner gets the prize, and the takings go where you said. FoodOS never picks the winner. Kept apart from Running a prize draw (entry is free); Running a competition (entries are judged); and Asking for donations (people give with no chance of a prize). It usually starts when a fair, a show or a cause is coming, when a prize is given, or when the draw time comes.
no mirror: none: people buy tickets in Doing the shopping

examples.card: Sell raffle tickets for a cause.
examples.filled: Sell £2 tickets for a lamb at the Brecon show, with the money to the air ambulance?

examples.card: Draw the raffle where everyone can check it.
examples.filled: It's 4pm at the Kumasi church fair. Draw the hamper ticket in front of everyone?

examples.card: Say where the takings went.
examples.filled: The raffle raised R6,200 for the school kitchen in Durban. Post the total and the receipt?

examples.card: Raffle a prize for your club.
examples.filled: Your supporters' club in Kampala wants to raffle a goat for the new kit. Set the ticket price and the draw date?

you do this when: You sell tickets for a chance to win a prize and a cause gets the money. Not a free draw.

name: Asking customers for a review
card: 34 people bought from your stall this week. Ask them all for a review, by email?
note: You ask customers to say what they thought: on a review site, an app or your own page. You ask everyone, or by a rule you set, never only the ones you think liked it. If you give anything for a review, you say so beside it. What they write is theirs. Kept apart from Giving your word on something (answering one that exists); and Posting an offer or a want (an offer). It usually starts when a new product is out, a busy week has passed, or you have few reviews.

examples.card: Ask everyone who bought this week.
examples.filled: 34 people bought from your Lisbon stall online this week. Ask them all for a review?

examples.card: Ask by a rule, not by who liked it.
examples.filled: Ask every 10th order in Austin for a review, whatever they ordered?

examples.card: Say when a review earns something.
examples.filled: You give 10% off for a review. Say so on the ask and beside each review?

examples.card: Ask the people you feed what they thought, and fix what was wrong.
examples.filled: Ask last night's guests how the new dish was. Send the ask?

examples.card: Ask a customer after a catering job.
examples.filled: The wedding you catered in Galway was last Saturday. Ask the couple for a review?

you do this when: You ask customers to say what they thought, before any review exists.

name: Introducing two people
card: Ana sells goat cheese and Ben's café wants some. Point each of them to the other?
note: You put two people in touch who could trade or help each other: a farmer and a chef, a worker and someone hiring, a buyer and a grower. One tap sends each of them a note that points to the other, with the word that person signed (what Ben wants, what Ana sells), so neither has to explain themselves again. A word posted to anyone can be pointed to freely; a word someone told only you is theirs, so you ask them before it goes. You sell nothing and step back, and what they do next is theirs. A finder's fee, if there is one, is for the two of them to agree with you, and FoodX takes nothing. Their deal points back to the introduction, so the introductions that ended in a signed deal build your own record as a connector, and whoever reads it decides what it is worth. Kept apart from Handing a request on (one request goes to someone who can meet it, and you drop out); Giving your word on something (a word to one person); Vouching for someone (money of yours behind a person); and Selling through an agent (you make the sale). It usually starts when you know two people who want what the other has, when someone asks if you know anyone, or when both have said yes.

examples.card: Ask both sides before you introduce them.
examples.filled: A grower in Kiambu has avocados and an exporter you know is short. Ask both if you may connect them?

examples.card: Introduce a worker to someone hiring.
examples.filled: Your old sous-chef is looking and a bistro in Lyon is hiring. Introduce them?

examples.card: State a finder's fee to both.
examples.filled: You take 2% for linking buyers and sellers in Kano. Tell both before you connect them?

examples.card: Introduce two people who could trade.
examples.filled: A cook in Kochi asked if you know a spice grower. You know one in Kerala. Ask both if you may introduce them?

examples.card: Link a household to an adviser who can help with benefits.
examples.filled: A mother of three at your Manchester food bank may qualify for free school meals. Ask her and the council's welfare adviser if you may introduce them?

examples.card: Point a buyer and a seller of eggs to each other.
examples.filled: Tom wants eggs for the weekend, Rose keeps hens in the next village, and you know them both. Point each to the other?

examples.card: Point two cafés to a supplier one of them has.
examples.filled: The bakery down the road has lost its flour supplier, and your café has bought from Hill Mill for two years. Point the bakery and Hill Mill to each other?

examples.card: Point someone you care for to a seller who can help.
examples.filled: Mrs Okafor, whom you care for, has asked who sells soft food, and a neighbour runs a weekly veg box round her street. Point them to each other?

examples.card: Point a trader with a gap to a grower with a glut.
examples.filled: A trader in Kumasi wants onions and a grower in Bolgatanga has more than she can sell. You know both. Point each to the other?

examples.card: Point a driver with spare hours to a shop that needs one.
examples.filled: A rider you know is free on Fridays and a bakery in Leeds posted that it needs a Friday driver. Point each to the other?

examples.card: Point a buyer to the farm that grows what yours does not.
examples.filled: Your robot farm grows lettuce only, a kitchen has posted that it wants basil every week, and the farm down the lane grows basil. Point each to the other, under your grant?

move words.card: Tom wants eggs and Rose sells eggs. Introduce them?
move words.note: The tap that sends both notes. It is your signed word that each of them could meet the other's word, and it binds only you. It is done when they have read it.

examples.card: Introduce two people who could trade.
examples.filled: A chef in Lyon posted that she wants walnuts and a grower in Périgord posted that she sells them. Introduce them?

examples.card: Introduce a carer to a seller.
examples.filled: A man you care for wants fresh fish on Fridays and the van that parks on his road sells it. Introduce them?

examples.card: Introduce a farm to a farm.
examples.filled: Two robot farms on the same estate each grow what the other's kitchen buyers want. Introduce them?

move words.trigger: Two words in her record that fit each other (one person wants what the other offers), both signed by people she knows, and no introduction between them yet.

move words.card: Ana and Ben's café agree to give you 5% of their first order if you bring them together. Sign it?
move words.note: The two people you put in touch, or the one you handed a request to, offer you a share if a deal comes of it. It is their choice, it is a signed offer to you with its own terms, and FoodX takes nothing. The deal they make points back to the introduction.

examples.card: Offer the connector a share of the first order.
examples.filled: Rose and Tom agree 2% of their first egg order for Agnes, who put them in touch. Sign it?

examples.card: Thank someone who handed you a request.
examples.filled: Sam wins the café's onion order that Agnes handed on. Offer her KSh 300 a delivery for the first month?

examples.card: Agree nothing, and say so.
examples.filled: A neighbour put you in touch with a baker and wants nothing for it. Note that no fee was agreed?

move words.trigger: A signed introduction or a request handed on points two people to each other, and nothing signed yet says whether the one who connected them is paid.

you do this when: You put two people in touch who could trade or help each other.

name: Setting what you accept in payment
card: Customers at your stall keep asking to pay by M-Pesa. Take it from Monday?
note: You set what you take as payment and on what terms: cash, card with an extra charge said up front, mobile money, vouchers at the value printed on them, a local savings circle's unit, swaps. You say it once and every sale reads it, and you change it when you like. Kept apart from Setting prices (how much, not in what); and Setting your terms of trade (when people may pay later). It usually starts when you open, when customers ask to pay another way, when a fee changes, or when a scheme or circle near you starts.

examples.card: Start taking mobile money.
examples.filled: Customers at your Kisumu stall keep asking to pay by M-Pesa. Start taking it?

examples.card: Add a surcharge for card, said up front.
examples.filled: Card fees cost you money in Lisbon. Add a card charge, shown at the till, or keep taking card free?

examples.card: Accept a local scheme's vouchers.
examples.filled: The council's food vouchers start in Leeds next month. Accept them at your shop?

examples.card: Change how you take cash on delivery when it is refused.
examples.filled: 17 of your last 118 cash-on-delivery orders were refused at the door, against 2 of 94 paid ahead. Ask for a deposit on first cash orders, take cash only from past customers, or leave it?

examples.card: See what each way of paying costs you.
examples.filled: Last month 38 percent of payments came by card at 1.6 percent, 41 percent by mobile money at 1 percent, and the rest by bank transfer with no fee. Change what you accept?

you do this when: You set what you take as payment and on what terms: cash, card, mobile money, vouchers, swaps. Not the price, not your credit terms.

name: Clearing goods through customs
card: Your container is at Mombasa port. Hand in the customs papers and pay KSh 186,000 duty?
note: You get goods across a border: the customs papers, the certificates, the duty and fees, and the inspection. The state requires it and holds the goods until it is done. You, or a broker you pay, hand in the papers, pay what is due, answer questions, and the goods are let go. The days goods wait, what an officer takes or keeps, and any storage charge that builds while they wait are written down as they happen, in your own words or with a photo. The duty is not a choice; the broker is. Money asked beyond the published fee is Paying someone who demands it. Kept apart from Importing food (the deal with the seller); Exporting food (the deal with the buyer); Inspecting a food place (a visit to your own place); and Testing samples (a sample sent to a lab). It usually starts when goods reach a border or port, papers are missing or questioned, or duty is due.
no mirror: none: the state

examples.card: Hand in the papers for goods at the border.
examples.filled: Your onions are at the Busia border. Send the customs papers and certificates?

examples.card: Pay the duty to release a shipment.
examples.filled: The olive oil at Felixstowe owes £1,240 duty. Pay it and release the pallets?

examples.card: Answer customs when they ask.
examples.filled: Customs in Lagos asks for the health certificate for the fish. Send it now?

examples.card: Use a broker.
examples.filled: Your broker in Rotterdam quotes €240 to clear the pallets of dates. Hire her?

examples.card: Small trader crossing on foot
examples.filled: You carry sacks of dried fish from Kasenyi across to Bunagana most weeks. Which posts do you pass and what do you pay at each?

examples.card: Broker's bill
examples.filled: Your broker's bill for the cocoa shipment lists one sum for port and papers. Do you ask him to split it so you can set it against the official receipts?

examples.card: Count the free days at the port.
examples.filled: Your container is on day 7 of 5 free days and the inspector wants a lab paper. Pay a broker, courier the paper, or move the goods to a bonded store?

examples.card: Ask the supplier for an origin paper that cuts the duty.
examples.filled: Duty on your rice is 12 percent, or nothing with an origin paper from a country in a trade deal, and the supplier has not sent one. Ask for it?

move words.card: Your container of avocados has been at the port since Tuesday and has not been let go. Do you log the hold, with the date it began and the notice if you have one?
move words.note: The wait costs money and time and is the core of many disputes, with no step now to start the clock.

examples.card: Log a hold.
examples.filled: Your container of avocados has been at the port since Tuesday and has not been let go. Do you log the hold, with the date it began and the notice if you have one?

move words.trigger: Goods have reached the border or port and no release date has been recorded.

move words.card: The officer opened your load of maize at the Busia post and kept a sample. Do you record what was taken and what you were given for it?
move words.note: Samples, seizures and shortfalls leave no receipt; her own tally and photo make the loss hers to prove.

examples.card: Record what was taken.
examples.filled: The officer opened your load of maize at the Busia post and kept a sample. Do you record what was taken and what you were given for it?

move words.trigger: Goods are held or opened at a border and she says something was taken or removed.

you do this when: You get goods across a border: papers, certificates, duty, inspection. The deal with the seller is Importing or Exporting.

name: Writing a food-safety plan
card: You've added raw fish to the menu. Add its hazard, safe limit and check to your plan?
note: You write down how your kitchen or plant keeps food safe: the hazards (what could make food unsafe), the safe limits (the lines you must not cross), what you check, how often, and what you do when a check fails. Most places' law requires it, but what goes in it is yours. You write it, keep it with your checks, review it when something changes, and show it when asked. Kept apart from Logging food safety checks (the checks themselves); Setting house rules (your own house rules); and Inspecting a food place (the inspector's visit). It usually starts when you open, when you add a dish, a process or a supplier, when a check fails, or when an inspection is due.

examples.card: Write the plan for a new kitchen.
examples.filled: Your café in Leeds opens next month. Write the plan from your menu and kit?

examples.card: Add a new process to the plan.
examples.filled: You start making cured salmon in Oslo. Add its hazards and checks?

examples.card: Review the plan after a check fails.
examples.filled: The cold room went over 8°C twice this week. Review that part of the plan?

examples.card: Keep the plan short and in your own words.
examples.filled: Your Cape Town sauce kitchen now cools sauces in an ice bath, faster than before. Change the cooling rule in your plan?

you do this when: You write down how your kitchen keeps food safe: hazards, safe limits, checks, what to do when one fails.

name: Following an official order
card: The vet's order says your flock must be culled by Friday, and the law pays £4 a bird. Book the cull team?
note: You do what an authority orders, that the law backs: a cull for bird flu, crops destroyed for a disease, food seized or condemned at an inspection, stock held at a border, animals kept indoors, a field taken for a road. You read the order, ask what it rests on and what pay the law gives, carry it out or let it be carried out, and ask for what you are owed. Recording it as it happened is yours, and you can contest it in its own act. An order to keep birds indoors can, after a time the law sets, change what their eggs may be called; that is Labelling food. Where the officer will, they countersign what was taken; otherwise your own count and photo stand, marked as yours. Kept apart from Paying a fine or levy (money only); Contesting a charge (disputing it); and Dealing with a dead animal (one fallen animal). It usually starts when an order arrives, when an inspector condemns food, or when pay is due.

examples.card: Carry out an order and ask for the pay the law gives.
examples.filled: Your 3,000 hens in Lancashire must be culled under the bird flu order. Book the cull team and ask for the pay?

examples.card: Record what an inspector took.
examples.filled: The inspector in Nairobi condemned 40 kg of fish. Record what was taken and why?

examples.card: Ask what an order rests on.
examples.filled: The council orders your stall moved by Monday in Accra. Ask which rule it rests on?

examples.card: Work out what a letter or notice about food asks you to do.
examples.filled: A photo of a council letter: two things to fix by the 20th, one to reply to. Start with the reply?

examples.card: Stop taking shellfish from an area that was closed.
examples.filled: The council closed your oyster lease in Carlingford after a toxin test and gave no date to reopen. Hold the harvest and tell your buyers?

examples.card: Only a part is condemned, and why
examples.filled: Three livers were condemned for fluke. Do you write them with the reason?

examples.card: Load turned back at the gate
examples.filled: The officer at the gate said your honey load needs a certificate in the local language. Do you note what was missing and when?

examples.card: Only a part is condemned, and why
examples.filled: A head was condemned for cysts. Whose loss is it, the owner's or yours?

examples.card: Ask for a place when your lane is cleared.
examples.filled: The city posts that your street is to be cleared by 30 June for a bus lane, and a relocation zone is posted. Ask for a place there, or contest the order?

examples.card: Keep a few hens in under a housing order.
examples.filled: A bird flu housing order covers your county from tomorrow, and you keep 6 hens and 2 ducks. House them from the morning?

you do this when: An authority orders something the law backs (a cull, seized food, a field taken) and you do it.

name: Contesting a charge
card: The tax office says you owe £2,300 more. Your records say not. Appeal before the 30-day limit?
note: You challenge a charge an authority made: a fine, a tax bill, a fee, food taken from you, a batch they ruled unfit to sell, a refused licence. You gather what your own records show, write why it is wrong, send it by the deadline, and a reviewer or a court decides. You may win, lose, or settle, and money paid may come back. Kept apart from Asking for a ruling on a dispute (a disagreement with a trading partner); Paying a fine or levy (paying it); and Following an official order (doing what was ordered). It usually starts when a charge arrives that your records do not support, when a deadline to appeal is near, or when a decision on an appeal arrives.
no mirror: none: the authority answers in its own act

examples.card: Appeal a fine your records don't support.
examples.filled: The council fined your stall in Leeds for a dirty pitch on a day you weren't trading. Appeal?

examples.card: Challenge a tax assessment.
examples.filled: The revenue says you owe ₦420,000 on sales your books don't show. Send your records and object?

examples.card: Ask for food seized to be returned.
examples.filled: Police took 12 crates of tomatoes at a Lagos checkpoint with no order. Ask for them back in writing?

you do this when: An authority made a charge (a fine, a tax bill, seized food, a refused licence) and you challenge it. Not a quarrel with a trading partner.

name: Registering your brand
card: Nobody has registered 'Mama Ayo's' for sauces in Nigeria. Ask the state for a monopoly on it for ₦120,000?
note: You ask the state for a monopoly on a name, logo or design, so that it will force everyone else not to use it. A name is a reputation, an idea, so no one owns it: what the registry gives is a privilege the state grants and enforces by force, and it is compelled, never consent, however politely the form is filled in. It is not a licence: a licence lets you do what you could not, this stops everyone else doing what they could. You check nobody already holds the name, apply, pay the fee a law sets, and the office says yes or no. It covers certain things, in certain places, until a renewal date. What you can then sign over is your word about who may use the name (see Selling a brand and Letting someone use your recipe or brand). A protected place name for a regional food is the same grant. Kept apart from Getting a permit or registration (permission to trade); Selling a brand (selling it); and Letting someone use your recipe or brand (letting others use it). It usually starts when you name a product or business, when someone copies your name, or when a renewal is due.
no mirror: none: the registry

examples.card: Register the name you trade under.
examples.filled: Your granola sells in 40 shops in Lisbon under 'Bom Dia'. Register the name?

examples.card: Renew a registration before it lapses.
examples.filled: Your trademark in Kenya ends in 2 months. Renew it for KSh 15,000?

examples.card: Protect a regional name for your food.
examples.filled: Your cheese from the hills near Arta has a place name that others use. Apply to protect it?

you do this when: You register a name or design so the state will back you if someone copies it.

name: Paying someone who demands it
card: The man at the bridge wants ₦2,000 to let the truck through. Pay, and record it as a demand?
note: You pay, in money, goods or a free service, what someone with power over you demands that no law or deal gives them: a toll at a roadblock, a 'fee' to an official, protection money at a market, a free plate each day, a share of your ration to a gatekeeper. You can pay, refuse, or go another way, and you record it as what it is, never as a fee or a purchase. Your record is yours and leaves you only when you choose, so you can share it with others on the route, a trader group or a court when you choose. Kept apart from Paying a fine or levy (a charge the law sets); Following an official order (an order under law); and Contesting a charge (challenging a lawful charge). It usually starts when your route has roadblocks, when an official asks for money to do their job, or when a group you trade with asks who has been paying.
no mirror: none: the one demanding it

examples.card: Record a payment at a roadblock as it is.
examples.filled: You paid KSh 500 at 3 roadblocks between Kisumu and Nairobi. Record them as demanded payments?

examples.card: Share what was demanded on a route.
examples.filled: Ten traders on the Kano road share their roadblock records. Add yours, without your name?

examples.card: Take another route to avoid a demand.
examples.filled: The bridge at Onitsha costs ₦2,000 a crossing in demands. Take the longer road?

examples.card: Record a demand paid in fish.
examples.filled: The man at the jetty took 2 fish from each of your baskets. Record it as a demand, in fish?

examples.card: A checkpoint on the highway
examples.filled: A man at the checkpoint outside Machakos wants money to let your lorry through, and gives no slip. Do you pay, say no, or take the other road?

examples.card: An officer at the door of a brewer
examples.filled: An officer came to your yard and said he would break your pots unless you gave him 500 shillings. Do you want to pay, refuse, or move the brewing to another day?

examples.card: Overload on the road
examples.filled: A police officer on the Mombasa road took 2,000 shillings for your overload and gave no receipt. Do you record it as demanded?

examples.card: Set what you were charged beside the posted fee.
examples.filled: The county posts a slaughter fee of 200 a head; your last three receipts show 350. Contest the charge?

you do this when: You pay what someone with power over you demands where no law or deal gives them the right: a toll, protection money. Force, named as force, never called consent.

name: Handing over tax you collected
card: You collected £3,140 VAT this quarter. Send the return and pay it by 7 May?
note: You hand the state the tax you collected for it: VAT or sales tax on what you sold, tax taken from your staff's wages, or the duty on drink you let out of your brewery or cellar for sale. That money was never yours; you held it for the state until the day it is due, so the card shows it apart from your takings. You add it up from your own records, send the return, and pay. For drink, the duty comes from the batches and bottlings you wrote down and what you sold, at the rate your place sets for a maker your size. The sum comes from what you recorded, and says so. Kept apart from Paying tax on what you earned (tax on you); Paying a fine or levy (a set charge); and Logging (your own books). It usually starts when a quarter or month ends, when the money held grows large, or when a deadline nears.

examples.card: Send a sales tax return and pay it.
examples.filled: Your food truck in Austin collected $1,860 sales tax in March. File and pay by the 20th?

examples.card: Keep the tax you hold apart from your takings.
examples.filled: ₦380,000 of this month's takings in Lagos is VAT. Move it to a separate pot?

examples.card: Pay over tax taken from wages.
examples.filled: You took R4,200 tax from your 3 staff's pay in Cape Town. Pay it over by the 7th?

examples.card: Pay VAT as a small shop.
examples.filled: Your sweet shop in Pune collected ₹46,000 GST this month. File the return and pay it by the 20th?

you do this when: You hand the state tax you held for it: VAT, wage tax, drink duty. Not tax on your own earnings.

name: Leaving something in a will
card: Your will names nobody for the allotment and the bees. Add who gets them?
note: You say who gets what when you die: the farm, the business, the house, your recipes and record, your animals, and who looks after children or land until then. You write it, have it witnessed as the law asks, keep it safe, and change it when you like until the end. Where custom or law fixes some shares, the card shows them. It is signed by you alone and read only when you die. Kept apart from Handing something down (while you are alive, often over years); Settling an estate (the person who sorts out what was left); Choosing who decides for you (someone to act for you while you live); and Giving a gift (now, to someone you choose). It usually starts when a child is born, when you buy land or a business, when someone named dies or falls out, or when your health changes.

examples.card: Make a will for the farm and the animals.
examples.filled: You own the farm in Wales and 60 ewes but have no will. Write one?

examples.card: Leave your recipes and record to someone.
examples.filled: Your café's recipes and its record would go nowhere. Leave them to your daughter?

examples.card: Change a will after a change in the family.
examples.filled: Your son married and moved to Nairobi. Change who gets the shamba?

examples.card: Leave a share of the business to a worker.
examples.filled: Your four cooks have run the trattoria for 10 years. Leave each of them a share in your will?

you do this when: You say who gets what when you die and keep it safe until then. Not handing down while alive, not inheriting.

name: Settling an estate
card: Your father's farm owes the co-op KSh 120,000. Pay it from the estate before sharing the land?
note: You look after what someone left when they died until it is shared out. You may be named in the will, appointed by a court, or be the family member the custom names. You hold the farm, stock, money and debts, which are not yours to use. You find out what is owed and to whom, pay the debts and any tax the law asks for, finish or end the open deals, and share out what is left by the will or the law. It ends when everything is handed on. Those who may be owed state their claim in their own signed word, and relatives state what they hold of the deceased's. Kept apart from Inheriting something (receiving your share); Leaving something in a will (writing it); and Holding money until a deal is done (one deal's money). It usually starts when someone dies, when a creditor asks to be paid, when a will is read, or when the last share is ready to hand on.
no mirror: none: each heir and creditor answers in their own act

examples.card: List what someone left and what they owed.
examples.filled: Your aunt's bakery in Accra has stock, a lease and a GH₵ 8,000 loan. List them before anything is shared?

examples.card: Finish the open deals of someone who died.
examples.filled: Your father had 3 open orders with the mill in Iowa. Finish or end them?

examples.card: Share out what is left.
examples.filled: The debts are paid. Share the remaining 12 acres in Muranga as the will says?

you do this when: You look after what someone left when they died until it is shared out.

name: Taking over a family farm or business
card: Your father offers you the dairy over 5 years, a third each year. Agree the steps with him?
note: You take over a farm or business from family while they are alive, often in steps over years: the herd this year, the land later, the name and its record at the end. You agree the steps, what you owe them (money, a share of the harvest, a home or care), and who carries the debts. Debts only move to you if the lender says yes. Either side can pause or end it on the terms you agreed. The elder can sign the years you worked, and at the takeover that backs what is owed. Kept apart from Inheriting something (after a death); Buying a food business (from someone outside the family, for a price); and Employing someone (you work there without owning it). It usually starts when a parent wants to slow down, when you are ready to take on more, or when a step in the handover is due.

examples.card: Agree the steps of a handover.
examples.filled: Your mother wants to hand you the bakery in Lyon over 3 years. Agree the steps and what she keeps?

examples.card: Take on the debts with the lender's yes.
examples.filled: The farm in Iowa has a $90,000 loan. Ask the bank to move it to your name?

examples.card: Take the next step in a handover.
examples.filled: This year the 40 acres in Kiambu pass to you. Sign it over with your father?

examples.card: Take over a family farm or business.
examples.filled: Your dad's farm could pass to you over 5 years, along with its debts. Say yes to the plan?

you do this when: You take over a farm or business from family while they are alive, often in steps.

name: Giving food vouchers
card: 180 families on your list can get a KSh 2,000 voucher for the shops in Kibera this month. Send them?
note: You give people vouchers to get food at shops you name: a charity's voucher, a school holiday voucher, an aid agency's e-voucher, a council scheme. Which shops take it is said. You list who gets one, send them, see which were spent, and pay the shops that took them. Kept apart from Giving cash for food (money they can spend anywhere); Handing out food parcels (the food itself); and Selling vouchers (sold, not given). It usually starts when a programme pays out, when school holidays come, when a disaster hits, or when shops ask to be paid.

examples.card: Send vouchers to families on a list.
examples.filled: The school holidays start in Leeds. Send £30 vouchers to the 220 families on free meals?

examples.card: Pay the shops that took vouchers.
examples.filled: Seven shops in Mzuzu took 410 vouchers this month. Pay them?

examples.card: Add shops that will take your vouchers.
examples.filled: Families in Kibera say the two shops are far. Ask two nearer shops to take the vouchers?

examples.card: Pay a food voucher to families after a disaster so they can buy what they need.
examples.filled: Floods hit Sylhet. Send 1,500 taka of e-vouchers to the 240 flooded families on the list?

move words.card: A family says the shop on Mill Road would not take their voucher. Note it and ask the shop?
move words.note: Short weight, spoiled or wrong food, a scoop that was not full, being turned away, or no distribution at all. Your word, with a photo or your own weighing if you have one, goes to the giver, who can answer beside it. If you cannot agree it can go to Asking for a ruling on a dispute.

examples.card: Say what went wrong with a voucher.
examples.filled: Two families say the shop on Main Street would not take your vouchers on Monday. Note it and ask the shop why?

move words.trigger: The giver's step for a distribution day shows less than the entitlement, a day passes with no distribution, or she says she was refused.

you do this when: You give people vouchers to get food at shops you name.

name: Cooking together
card: Friends are coming Sunday and everyone wants to cook. Split the dishes between you?
note: You cook one meal with others and share it: a family cooking Sunday lunch together, friends making dumplings around a table, a potluck where each brings a part, a cook-along online. You agree who makes what and who brings what, cook, and share what you made. Nobody is the host and nobody is paid. Kept apart from Cooking a meal (you cook alone); Giving and receiving food (you cook for guests); and Running a community kitchen (feeding others for a cause). It usually starts when people are coming over, when a festival needs a lot of food at once, or when friends want to learn a dish together.
no mirror: none: one group, one plan

examples.card: Plan who cooks what for a shared meal.
examples.filled: Six of you are making dinner together in Taipei. Split the 6 dishes between you?

examples.card: Make a big festive dish together.
examples.filled: Tamales for Christmas in Oaxaca take all day. Cook them together with your sisters on the 23rd?

examples.card: Cook along with friends far away.
examples.filled: Your friends in Berlin and Lagos want to cook jollof together on a call. Pick Saturday at 6?

examples.card: Write who made a dish and what is in it.
examples.filled: Your lentil dahl is going to the temple potluck in Leicester. Add a card with your name and that it has milk?

examples.card: Name the dishes on a shared table.
examples.filled: Eleven dishes are on the iftar table in Dearborn. Label each with its cook?

examples.card: Keep the sign-up for next time.
examples.filled: Eleven families brought a dish to the Passover supper in Brooklyn. Save who brought what?

you do this when: You cook one meal with others and share it: Sunday lunch, a potluck, a cook-along.

name: Taking turns at home
card: Four of you eat at home this week. Set a cooking night each, you, Sam, Ali and Jo?
note: You and the people you live with take turns at the jobs of the house: whose night to cook, whose week to shop, who does the bins, who feeds the dog. You agree the turns, write them down, swap when someone can't, and change them when life changes. Nobody is paid and nobody is the boss. Kept apart from Planning who works when (a business's staff); Splitting costs (money, not turns); and Taking turns to work for each other (between households). It usually starts when someone moves in or out, when the turns stop working, or when a swap is needed.
no mirror: none: one household, one plan

examples.card: Set the cooking turns for the week.
examples.filled: Four of you share the house in Manchester. Each cook one night, takeaway on Fridays?

examples.card: Swap a turn when you can't.
examples.filled: You work late Wednesday. Swap your cooking night with Ali?

examples.card: Share the shopping by week.
examples.filled: Take turns doing the big shop each week with your two flatmates in Toronto?

examples.card: Take turns at the other jobs of the house.
examples.filled: Jo has moved in. Add Jo to the rota?

you do this when: You and the people you live with take turns at the jobs of the house: whose night to cook, whose week to shop. Not a business's staff rota.

name: Making food last when money is short
card: ₹600 left and 9 days to payday. Plan meals from the rice, dal and onions you have, and buy only eggs?
note: You make the food you have, and the money left, last until more comes: a plan for the days to payday, the lean months before harvest, or a hard week. You see what you hold and what is left to spend, choose meals that stretch it, and change the plan as the days go. FoodOS shows what you hold and what each meal uses, and never judges what you choose. Kept apart from Planning what to eat (meals for an ordinary week); Giving and receiving food (food given); and Setting a budget or how you need to be served (a limit you set ahead). It usually starts when money runs short before payday, when the lean season begins, or when something costly happened.

examples.card: Stretch what you have to payday.
examples.filled: £18 and 6 days left in Leeds. Plan dinners from the pasta and tins, buying only milk?

examples.card: Plan the lean months before harvest.
examples.filled: Two sacks of maize and 10 weeks to harvest in Malawi. Plan how much to use each week?

examples.card: Change the plan when something comes in.
examples.filled: Your brother sent KSh 2,000. Add beans and eggs to the week?

examples.card: The store counted in tins
examples.filled: You have 4 tins of maize and 2 of beans in the store, and the harvest is nine weeks off. Your sister has a spare sack. Do you want to ask her for it now?

examples.card: Note the meals you skipped to make the food last.
examples.filled: You skipped lunch twice this week in Kisumu so the maize lasts to Friday. Keep it in your private record?

examples.card: Plan the sack to the next distribution.
examples.filled: You hold what is left of the sack and the distribution is 12 days away. Plan meals to last until then?

examples.card: Redo the plan after a cut.
examples.filled: The agency says April's ration is smaller. Redo your plan from what you hold?

you do this when: You make the food and money you have last until more comes.

name: Comparing offers
card: Two buyers want your maize: KSh 3,200 a bag now, or 3,600 in 60 days. Which one?
note: You lay offers you already have side by side before you sign: two buyers, three loans, a supplier's terms, a cash price against instalments. You see the price, when each side's part arrives, what backs it, what leaving costs, and what each costs a year, so time and credit are visible. Then you choose, or ask for better. Kept apart from Choosing between products (things in front of you on a shelf or menu); Finding someone to deal with (looking for offers); and Switching to a better deal (leaving what you have now). It usually starts when two or more offers arrive, when one offer has hidden terms, or before you sign anything with credit in it.

examples.card: Compare two buyers' offers with time in them.
examples.filled: The mill pays ₹2,100 a quintal now; the trader ₹2,300 in 3 months. Compare them?

examples.card: Compare loans side by side.
examples.filled: The SACCO, the bank and the app each offer KSh 50,000. See what each costs a year?

examples.card: Compare paying now with paying in instalments.
examples.filled: The oven is £4,000 cash or £190 a month for 2 years. Compare them?

examples.card: Set a programme's posted price beside the markets.
examples.filled: The county buys goats at 2,000 until the 20th; one market posted 1,700 and another 2,300, two days' walk away. Sell to the county, take them to market, or hold?

examples.card: Lay a loan tied to a sale beside one that is not.
examples.filled: The agent advances 38,000 if you sell him all your landings at the price of the day; the group lends 38,000 with no tie, repaid from takings. Which do you take?

you do this when: You lay offers you already hold side by side before you sign.

name: Checking who you are dealing with
card: A new buyer wants 2 tonnes on 30 days' credit. Read what they've chosen to show of their record first?
note: You look at what someone has chosen to show before you deal with them: how long they have traded, the deals they kept or broke with people who say so, who vouches for them, and what you have seen yourself. FoodX gives no score; you read what others signed and decide. You ask, read, and note what you found. A supplier can look at a buyer too, a big one included, before going first on long credit. When someone has no record, that is said plainly and only what they sent is shown. Kept apart from Guarding against scams (checking a payment or a message is real); Sharing a record (asking them to share more); Vouching for someone (your own money behind them); and Checking on someone (someone you care for). It usually starts when someone new offers a deal, when a deal asks you to go first or give credit, or when you hear something about someone you deal with.

examples.card: Read a new buyer's record before giving credit.
examples.filled: A hotel in Mombasa wants fish on 30-day terms. Read what it shows of paying other suppliers?

examples.card: See who vouches for a broker.
examples.filled: A broker in Kano offers to sell your sorghum. See who has vouched for him?

examples.card: Check a seller before you pay first.
examples.filled: A seller online wants payment before sending a grain mill. See how long they have traded and with whom?

examples.card: Check a supplier's papers before you buy.
examples.filled: Your restaurant in Cádiz has a new fish supplier. Check their hygiene and traceability certificates before the first order?

examples.card: Unknown rider
examples.filled: You are handing 3 crates to a rider you have never met. Do you note his plate and phone number first?

you do this when: You look at what someone has chosen to show before you deal with them: how long they traded, who vouches.

name: Looking back at what you expected
card: You expected the new oven to add 40 loaves a week. It added 26. See why, and what you'd do next time?
note: You lay what you expected beside what happened once something you tried has run: a crop, a new product, a machine, stock held for a price, a market you tried. Your expectation was yours, in your words, from when you started. You see the gap, note what you learned, and carry it to the next time. It closes only after a stock count, and what was never counted shows as not counted, never as zero. Kept apart from Checking how things are going (how things stand now); Working out what went wrong (one failure); and Logging (your money). It usually starts when a harvest is in, a product has run a season, stock held is sold, or a deal you expected something from ends.

examples.card: Compare a harvest with what you expected.
examples.filled: You expected 22 bags of maize from the field in Kitale; you got 17. Look back at why?

examples.card: Look back at a new product after a season.
examples.filled: You expected the chilli jam to sell 50 jars a week in Leeds. It sold 31. Note what you learned?

examples.card: Look back at stock held for a price.
examples.filled: You held the onions until January in Nashik expecting ₹30 a kilo. They sold at ₹24. Look back?

you do this when: Something you tried has run and you lay what you expected beside what happened.

name: Checking stock against your records
card: You should hold 48 bags of rice and you counted 44. Look at where the 4 went?
note: You compare what you should hold with what you counted: what you started with, plus what came in, less what went out, against the shelf, the store or the pen. A herd or flock counts the same way: births and buys in, sales, deaths and the pot out, against the head count. What you already noted on the way (thrown away, sold cheap, given, taken home, sent back, lost) is taken off first, so the remainder is only what nobody wrote down. You say where it went in your own words: eaten at home, eaten by staff, given on the house, trimmed, dried out, spoiled, broken, stolen, sitting in another bay, or miscounted; FoodOS never picks a cause for you. At a stall with no till, what went out is also how you know what you sold. You carry the counts forward. A cause you name that is a home draw (eaten at home, taken home) is written as Logging, so the stock count and the books agree. Kept apart from Logging (the count itself); and Guarding against theft (stopping it). It usually starts when a count is done, when a gap shows, or at the end of a day, a month or a season.

examples.card: Find a gap between stock and the count.
examples.filled: You should have 120 bottles of oil in the Lagos shop and counted 112. Look at where 8 went?

examples.card: Note the cause of a gap.
examples.filled: Six of the missing loaves went to staff at close in Leeds. Note it as given?

examples.card: Reconcile at the end of a month.
examples.filled: It's month end at your food bank in Detroit. Compare what came in and went out with the count?

examples.card: Spot a gap in perishables.
examples.filled: Your Kumasi stall is 12 kg of tomatoes short with no sale to match. Look at where they went?

examples.card: Check grain in and out against the bins.
examples.filled: You weighed 1,840 tonnes of wheat in and 1,500 out, so the bins should hold 340, and you count 320. Look at where 20 went?

examples.card: Work out what is missing from a pond at harvest.
examples.filled: You stocked 5,000 in pond 3, counted 420 dead and harvested 3,900. 680 are not accounted for: birds, theft, escape or dead you missed. Write down where you think they went?

examples.card: Note small goods given as change.
examples.filled: You gave sweets for change at your Lagos shop most days this week. Note it as a known use of the sweets?

examples.card: Empty shelf, stock on the record
examples.filled: The record says 6 cases of rice. The shelf is bare. Did the cage get missed?

examples.card: Set what your sales say you used beside what you counted.
examples.filled: By what you rang up this week your recipes used 52 litres of milk. You took in 61 and counted 3 left. About 6 litres are not accounted for. Look into it now?

examples.card: Set pints drawn beside pints rung.
examples.filled: The keg you changed on Friday drew 88 pints by the line meter; the till shows 79. Work out where the 9 went?

you do this when: You compare what you should hold with what you counted.

name: Finding what people want that nobody sells
card: 14 people near you posted wanting gluten-free bread this month and nobody nearby sells it. Look into baking it?
note: You look for things people near you want that nobody sells yet: posted wants, questions in your own shop, what your regulars ask for and you do not have. FoodOS reads open wants and your own record, and shows what it found with where it came from. What to do about it is yours. Kept apart from Finding someone to deal with (buyers for what you have); Checking market prices (prices); and Developing a product (making the new thing). It usually starts when you have time or kit to spare, when customers keep asking for something, or when wants posted near you go unanswered.

examples.card: See what people near you want that nobody sells.
examples.filled: Wants posted in your part of Accra this month include 9 for fresh tilapia at night. Look closer?

examples.card: Count what customers asked for that you lack.
examples.filled: Your till notes show 22 asks for oat milk in Leeds. Look into stocking it?

examples.card: See unanswered wants in a market.
examples.filled: Three people at the Saturday market in Lima asked for cut fruit cups, and no stall has them. Look closer?

you do this when: You look for things people near you want that nobody sells yet.

name: Adding your own records
card: Your order book from 2019 to 2024 is in a spreadsheet. Bring it into your record?
note: You bring your own old records into your record: photos of receipts, a paper order book, a spreadsheet of sales, a chat where you took orders. FoodOS reads them in pencil, and each entry is marked as your own evidence, from your own file. You are never asked to check what it read: where it is wrong, you say so in your own words whenever you notice, and the reading changes. It is not only old files: tonight's page of the tab book, today's milk slip or the care book can come in as you go, by a photo. Kept apart from Getting your record back (asking a company for what it holds about you); and Logging (a count now). It usually starts when you join, when you find old files, or when you want to show a history you kept yourself.

examples.card: Bring in a paper order book.
examples.filled: Your catering order book from Accra covers 3 years. Photograph it and bring it in?

examples.card: Bring in a spreadsheet of sales.
examples.filled: Your market sales from Bath are in a spreadsheet. Bring them in?

examples.card: Bring in orders from a chat.
examples.filled: You took orders on WhatsApp for 2 years in Lagos. Bring them in from the chat export?

examples.card: Bring in photos of receipts.
examples.filled: You have 200 photos of supplier receipts from 2023 on your phone in Lyon. Bring them in?

examples.card: The exercise book of who owes you
examples.filled: Six pages of your exercise book are in. Do you chase those owing since September?

examples.card: The paper production sheet from the line
examples.filled: Here is the photo of line 3's sheet from last night. Want it kept with the batch it belongs to?

examples.card: Photograph the stamped page of your savings book.
examples.filled: Your passbook from the VSLA in Kisumu has 14 stamps this cycle. Photograph the page and bring it in?

examples.card: The paper production sheet from the line
examples.filled: This is the notebook page of the pressing day. Keep it with Tuesday's run?

you do this when: You bring your own old records into your record: receipts, an order book, a sales sheet.

name: Naming who can confirm it is you
card: Name 5 people you trust, any 3 of whom can confirm a new phone is you?
note: You choose, before anything goes wrong, the people who can confirm it is you if you lose your phone or key: how many you name, how many must agree, and how long to wait before it counts. Each person is asked and says yes. You change them when you like. No company can reset your record, so this is how you get back in. Kept apart from Getting back in after losing your phone (using them after a loss); Choosing who decides for you (someone to act for you); and Vouching for someone (your money behind someone else). It usually starts when you set up your record, when someone you named moves away or falls out, or when you add a new device.

examples.card: Name the people who can confirm it is you.
examples.filled: Name your sister, two friends and your neighbour, any 3 of them to confirm?

examples.card: Replace someone you named.
examples.filled: Your friend Tom left the country. Replace him with your cousin?

examples.card: Set how long to wait before it counts.
examples.filled: Make a recovery wait 2 days, so you can stop it if it isn't you?

move words.card: Ana thinks someone is trying to take over your record. Freeze every grant and recovery until you confirm, as any of your confirmers may?
move words.note: Any one named confirmer may pause every grant and every recovery at once; it only narrows, and only she, or her confirmers by her own rule, can resume.

examples.card: Freeze a friend's record when something looks wrong.
examples.filled: Kofi's account is asking people for money in his name. Freeze his record until he confirms?

move words.trigger: Someone she confirms for appears to be acting strangely, or she has lost her own phone.

move words.card: You want to swap Ben for Esi as a confirmer. The change counts after your 7-day wait, and all your confirmers are told. Make it?
move words.note: A change to the confirmers or their number waits the same time a recovery does, and every confirmer is told, so a stolen phone cannot quietly replace them.

examples.card: Swap one confirmer for another.
examples.filled: Your brother moved abroad and is hard to reach. Replace him with your cousin, after the wait?

move words.trigger: Someone she named has moved away, fallen out or not answered, or she wants a different number to agree.

you do this when: You name beforehand the people who can confirm it is you if you lose your phone: how many, how long to wait.

name: Choosing how your tax is counted
card: Your place lets small traders count tax on cash in and out, or on invoices. Which will you use?
note: You choose the ways your place's tax law lets you count: cash or invoices, a simple scheme or the full one, how your stock is valued, which month your year ends. You choose once, change it when the law allows, and your books and returns follow it. The choices come from the signed rules for your place. A line the law draws by sales, staff or size shows beside your own twelve-month figure, with its source and date, and nothing says how near is too near. Kept apart from Paying tax on what you earned (the return); Handing over tax you collected (VAT held); and Logging (the books themselves). It usually starts when you start trading, when your takings cross a line the law sets, or when a new tax year begins.

examples.card: Choose cash or invoice counting.
examples.filled: Small traders in the UK can count on cash. Count your stall's tax that way, or on invoices?

examples.card: Join a simplified scheme.
examples.filled: Your takings in Kenya allow the turnover tax. Choose it instead of the full return?

examples.card: Choose how stock is valued.
examples.filled: Count your year-end stock in Lisbon at what you paid, or at what it would cost now?

you do this when: You choose the way your place's tax law lets you count: cash or invoices, a simple scheme or the full one.

name: Moving your record
card: A co-op in Lisbon will host your record for €2 a month. Move it there, with your keys?
note: You move your whole record and keys to another host, or to your own machine, and leave FoodX's hosting: the open format and your keys go with it, and everyone you deal with keeps reaching you. You choose the new host, check what they charge and keep, start the move, check it all arrived, and end the old hosting. Nothing stays behind that is yours. Kept apart from Keeping your record safe (copies, not a move); Getting your record back (from companies that hold your data); and Sharing a record (letting someone read it). It usually starts when another host suits you better, when you want your record on your own machine, or when you are unhappy with FoodX.
no mirror: none yet: the new host publishes its own act

examples.card: Move your record to a host you choose.
examples.filled: Your union in Nairobi runs a host for its members. Move your record there?

examples.card: Move your record to your own machine.
examples.filled: You have a home server in Austin. Move your record and keys onto it?

examples.card: Check everything arrived before ending the old host.
examples.filled: The move to the new host is done. Check every deal and record arrived before closing the old one?

examples.card: Move your record to another host.
examples.filled: Your host in Berlin charges €4 a month; another charges nothing and keeps no second copy. Move your record there this week?

you do this when: You move your whole record and keys to another host and leave FoodX's hosting.

name: Enforcing your group's rule
card: Peter took water out of turn twice. Under your rule that's a warning, then a fine. Warn him?
note: You and your group act when a member breaks a rule they signed: a warning, a fine, a lost turn, removal. The rule says what each step is. The member hears what they are accused of and answers before anything is decided, and may ask for it to be looked at again. The group decides by its own rule and writes it down. Kept apart from Deciding as a group (any choice the group makes); Asking for a ruling on a dispute (between two sides as equals); and Running a group (the group's whole life). It usually starts when a member breaks a rule, when another member reports it, or when an appeal is asked for.

examples.card: Warn a member under the rule.
examples.filled: Grace sold outside the co-op twice this season in Kitale. Send the warning your rule says?

examples.card: Hear the member before deciding.
examples.filled: Ali is accused of missing 3 work days in Kigali. Ask him to answer before the meeting?

examples.card: Remove a member as the rule allows.
examples.filled: Tomas has broken the fishing limit 3 times in Galicia. Remove him as your rule says?

you do this when: A member broke a rule they signed and the group warns, fines or removes them.

name: Boycotting together
card: The big mill in Eldoret still pays farmers late. Pledge to stop buying its flour if 500 others do?
note: You and others agree to stop buying from someone until something changes: a chain that pays late, a supplier that broke its word, a product made in a way you object to. Each person pledges, often only if enough others do. You stop buying, and you stop the boycott when the change comes or when you choose. A plain shared refusal needs no cause: farmers who hold out together for a price, or customers who stop buying from a chain, are each using their right not to deal. A refusal that names a person has guards: it rests on a deal he did not keep, which the card names; the creditor sent him a notice first; it names only the one who signed that deal, never his family or fellow members; and it counts only signers who hold a role in the circle, so free keys swell nothing. It lifts the moment he settles, the creditor withdraws her note, or the deal's judge rules the note wrong. Kept apart from Striking together (you hold back your own work or produce); Deciding as a group (the vote); and Giving your word on something (one person's word). It usually starts when a buyer or seller wrongs many people, when a group calls for one, or when what you asked for is done.

examples.card: Pledge to stop buying if enough others do.
examples.filled: Pledge to stop buying from the mill in Eldoret until it pays farmers, if 300 others do?

examples.card: Stop a boycott when the change comes.
examples.filled: The supermarket now pays dairy farmers in 30 days. End your boycott?

examples.card: Add your pledge to a boycott that is still open.
examples.filled: 412 people in Leeds have pledged to stop buying the eggs, and the aim is 500. Add your pledge?

examples.card: Stop buying from one supplier together.
examples.filled: A hundred cafés in Melbourne stop buying from a roaster that broke its promise. Will you stop buying too?

examples.card: Refuse a trader who did not settle.
examples.filled: A trader in Kano owes Anna 40 since 4 October and she sent him a notice. Add your refusal to deal with him until he settles, once 10 of your market have signed?

examples.card: Lift your refusal when he pays.
examples.filled: The trader in Kano has paid Anna, and she has withdrawn her note. Lift your refusal today?

examples.card: Refuse together with no cause needed.
examples.filled: Thirty farmers near Eldoret will not sell milk below KSh 45 a litre this month. Sign that you hold out with them?

you do this when: You and others stop buying from someone until something changes, each pledging, often only if enough others do. Not a strike.

name: Paying what you can to everyone you owe
card: You owe 6 suppliers KSh 180,000 and can pay 120,000. Offer each of them two-thirds?
note: You offer everyone you owe the same share of what you can pay: a stall that cannot pay everyone after a fire, a café closing. You list who you owe and how much, offer each the same share, and each says yes or no. The offer holds only for those who say yes. The rest can still ask you for all of what you owe them. The list of who is owed comes from claims that creditors sign themselves, beside what is recorded. Kept apart from Settling up with trading partners (cancelling what you owe each other); Settling an estate (after a death); and Borrowing money (a new loan). It usually starts when you cannot pay everyone you owe, when a business closes, or after a loss.
no mirror: self: each creditor accepts or not

examples.card: Offer everyone the same share.
examples.filled: You owe 4 suppliers £9,000 and can pay £6,000. Offer each two-thirds?

examples.card: See who has accepted.
examples.filled: 3 of 5 suppliers in Nairobi accepted 60%. Pay them now and keep talking to the others?

examples.card: Pay those who accepted.
examples.filled: The 4 who accepted in Lagos are owed ₦600,000 in all. Pay them today?

examples.card: Tell them what you can pay.
examples.filled: A fire closed your stall in Lagos. You owe 5 suppliers ₦900,000 and have ₦540,000. Write to all five with the same offer?

examples.card: Share out what you can pay at home.
examples.filled: Pay is in and you owe five: a shop tab, your sister, the electricity, a catalogue and a lender. Offer each the same share?

you do this when: You cannot pay everyone in full and offer every creditor the same share (a fire, a closing café).

name: Telling others a price
card: You paid KSh 3,200 a bag for maize in Kitale today. Share the price, with no names, for others to read?
note: You share a price you paid, or one you were quoted, with no names, so others can read it: in a shop, a market, a deal. You choose what to share, how close to you the place is said to be, and whether it is once or every time until you stop it. Kept apart from Giving your word on something (a verdict on a place or thing); Posting an offer or a want (your own offer); and Checking market prices (reading prices others shared). It usually starts when you pay or are quoted a price.

examples.card: Share a price you paid, with no names.
examples.filled: Tomatoes cost you KSh 80 a kilo at Wakulima this morning. Share it?

examples.card: Share prices under a standing grant.
examples.filled: Share every price you pay for flour, no names, until you stop it?

examples.card: Share a price you were quoted but did not take.
examples.filled: The trader in Kano asked ₦52,000 a bag and you said no. Share the ask?

you do this when: You share a price you paid or were quoted, with no names, so others can read it.

name: Ageing food or drink
card: The 2023 cheddars are 18 months old. Sell some now, or age them to 24?
note: You keep food or drink so it gets better with time: wine and spirits in a cellar, cheese, hams, miso, vinegar. You start it, check it, turn it, taste it, and decide when to open or sell. The card shows what waiting uses (space, time) next to selling now. It closes with a count when it is opened, sold or picked. Kept apart from Keeping food fresh (stopping it going off); Waiting to sell for a better price (the price changes, not the food); and Preserving food (making it keep). It usually starts when a batch is made, when you check or taste it, or when the time you planned arrives.

examples.card: Decide when to sell aged cheese.
examples.filled: Your goat cheeses in Rioja are at 10 months. Sell some now and age the rest?

examples.card: Check something ageing.
examples.filled: The miso in your Kyoto store has been 6 months. Taste and turn it?

examples.card: Open what you laid down.
examples.filled: The 2018 wine you laid down in Porto is ready by your notes. Open a case?

examples.card: Cut a wheel that is ready.
examples.filled: Your gouda wheels are at two years. Cut one for the market stall this Saturday?

examples.card: Green fruit ripening in the back room
examples.filled: Your 6 hands of green bananas are turning. Put them out Saturday or hold another day?

examples.card: Hanging beef or ham and weighing the loss
examples.filled: A side of beef went into the chill for dry-ageing. Do you write the day and the weight?

examples.card: Hanging beef or ham and weighing the loss
examples.filled: A ham has hung in the cellar since November. Weigh it?

move words.card: The 2025 Syrah in barrel 4 has lost about a hand's width to the angel's share. You have 9 litres of the same wine in a demijohn. Do you want to top up barrel 4 with it?
move words.note: In wine, cider and spirits the wine moves several times before it is sold and each move loses some. Where the law keeps a register of movements the maker writes it by hand.

examples.card: Move or blend it.
examples.filled: The 2025 Syrah in barrel 4 has lost about a hand's width to the angel's share. You have 9 litres of the same wine in a demijohn. Do you want to top up barrel 4 with it?

examples.card: Move or blend it.
examples.filled: Tank 3 has stood on its lees since harvest and the March racking is due. Do you want to rack it into tank 5 this week?
