examples.filled: Tanks 3 and 5 taste good together. Do you want to blend them before you bottle?

move words.trigger: A barrel or tank has been standing as long as she usually leaves it before racking, or she says she topped up, racked or is about to blend two lots.

you do this when: You keep food or drink so it gets better with time: wine, cheese, hams.

name: Sharing a commons
card: Your water turn on the canal is Tuesday 4am to 8am. Swap it with Ruth for Thursday?
note: You share something with the others who use it, under the rules you all agreed (a commons): water turns on a canal, grazing days on common land, a fishing ground's quota, a forest you gather in. The rules say who may take how much and when, how turns are swapped, and what happens to someone who breaks them. Where the rule allows it, one turn can also be sold once, for money or for a share of the crop. You take your turn or share, swap it, sell one, give it up, and help keep the rules. When a turn ends, the next in line takes over by counting what is left. Kept apart from Sharing a place (a shelf or pitch inside one place); Sharing a machine (equipment); and Letting someone use your place (one owner says yes). It usually starts when a season or turn comes round, when someone wants to swap or buy a turn, or when a rule is broken.

examples.card: Take your turn of water.
examples.filled: Your canal turn in Punjab is 2am to 6am tonight. Open the gate on time?

examples.card: Swap a turn with another member.
examples.filled: Ruth can't take her grazing day on the common. Swap with her for Thursday?

examples.card: Give out water turns to farmers on a canal.
examples.filled: Your water users' group in Kathmandu is at the start of the dry season. Hand out the irrigation turns?

examples.card: Share out quota among boats.
examples.filled: Your fishing co-op in Newfoundland has 18 tonnes of quota left and 6 boats. Allocate 3 tonnes each?

examples.card: Report a boat fishing inside a closed zone.
examples.filled: A trawler fished inside the 3-mile line off Takoradi at night. Send the committee the photo and the time?

examples.card: The guard posts the week's turns
examples.filled: The guard of your canal posted next week's turns by inlet. You farm the second inlet. Do you keep your Tuesday 10pm hour or swap with your neighbour who wants morning?

examples.card: Report blast or poison fishing.
examples.filled: Two blasts on the reef near Kilwa this morning. Report to the village committee with the time?

examples.card: Report a net below the legal mesh.
examples.filled: A small-mesh beach seine is being hauled on Lake Victoria. Tell the beach management unit with a photo?

move words.note: Asking for a share when one frees up.

examples.card: Join a waiting list for a share.
examples.filled: Allotment waiting list.

move words.note: Letting your share go back to the group.

examples.card: Give up your share.
examples.filled: Plot 14 back to the society.

move words.card: 18 tonnes of quota left and 6 boats. Allocate 3 tonnes each?
move words.note: Giving out shares by the group's rule: plots, quota, water turns.

examples.card: Allocate shares by the group's rule.
examples.filled: 3 tonnes of quota per boat.

move words.trigger: A season begins or a share has become free, and the group's rule says it is time to give shares out.

move words.card: The octopus are spawning. Close the reef for 3 months?
move words.note: Closing a shared resource for a season, by the group's rule.

examples.card: Close a shared resource for a season.
examples.filled: Reef closed for 3 months.

move words.trigger: A season in the group's rule has come, or a public notice or a sensor reading shows the resource must rest.

move words.card: Cattle grazed the closed field last night. Report it to the committee?
move words.note: Telling the group someone broke its rule; what happens to them is decided together.

examples.card: Report someone breaking the group's rule.
examples.filled: Cattle in the closed field.

move words.trigger: Her record or a public notice shows a use that the group's rule forbids, such as grazing a closed field.

move words.card: Your turn at the upper gate was 5 to 8 this morning. Do you tell the group how much water you got?
move words.note: Closes the hole between 'you take your turn' and what happened. A tail-end farmer who lost the transplanting window finally has a dated record to back a complaint or a request to the guard.

examples.card: Log your turn.
examples.filled: Your turn at the upper gate was 5 to 8 this morning. Do you tell the group how much water you got?

move words.trigger: The hours of her turn have passed, or she says the water came late, short or not at all

you do this when: You share something with others who use it under rules you all agreed: canal water, common grazing.

name: Farming land on shares
card: A young farmer wants your 5 acres for half the crop. Agree, with you paying half the seed?
note: You let someone farm your land for a share of what it grows: half the crop, a third of the olives. Both of you share the season's luck. You agree the share, who pays for what (seed, fertiliser, water, work), who decides what to grow, how the crop is weighed and split, and how either of you can end it. They farm it, and you take your share at harvest. It closes only with a harvest weight both sides sign, and the shares follow from it. Farming land on shares: You farm someone else's land and give them a share of what it grows: half the rice, a third of the yams, a share of the calves. You agree the share, who pays for what, who decides, how the crop is split, and how either side ends it. You farm, harvest, split, and keep your share. If the season is bad you both get less. It closes only with a harvest weight both sides sign, and the shares follow from it. Kept apart from Renting out land (for money); Lending and borrowing something (things, not land); Having someone keep your animals (animals, not land); Renting land or a place to trade (you pay money); Working for someone (a wage); and Taking turns to work for each other (labour swapped, not land). It usually starts when you cannot farm all your land, when a neighbour asks to farm it, or when the harvest is shared out; as Farming land on shares, when you need land, when a landowner offers it on shares, or when the harvest is in.

examples.filled: Ramesh wants your 3 acres in Bihar for half the rice, with you paying for half the seed. Agree?

examples.filled: The olives on your Puglia land are in. Weigh them together and take your third?

examples.filled: Neighbour Lee wants to grow beans in your plot for half the crop. Agree?

examples.filled: A landowner near Patna offers 2 acres for half the wheat. Agree?

examples.filled: Your aunt in Oaxaca cannot farm her 3 hectares any more. Farm them and give her a third of the maize?

examples.card: Counted at the threshing floor
examples.filled: The landowner and you will count the sacks at the floor. Do you set the day?

examples.filled: Mr Okoro's palms give you about 60 litres a day. You and he agreed a third for him. Do you want to bring him his share on Friday?

examples.card: Counted at the threshing floor
examples.filled: Half is his by the deal. Do you both sign the count?

examples.filled: Mr Okeke will let you farm his 4 acres for a third of the yams. Agree?

you do this when: Land is farmed for a share of what it grows: you farm it or you let it. Not rent in money.

name: Lending and borrowing food or seed
card: Your neighbour needs a bag of maize until harvest. Lend it, to be repaid in kind?
note: You lend food or seed that will be eaten or sown, so it comes back as the same kind, not the same thing: a cup of sugar, a sack of maize until harvest, seed from a seed library, starter for someone's bread. You agree how much comes back and when, and whether a little extra comes with it. You hand it over and they repay in kind. Borrowing food or seed: You borrow food or seed and give back the same kind: an ingredient from a neighbour, a sack of grain until harvest, seed from a seed library to return from your crop. You agree how much goes back and when. You take it, use it, and repay in kind. Kept apart from Lending and borrowing something (the same thing comes back); Giving and receiving food (nothing comes back); Selling growing supplies (a trade on terms); and Buying growing supplies (a trade on terms). It usually starts when a neighbour runs short, in the lean season, or when the seed library opens; as Borrowing food or seed, when you run out of something, in the lean season, or at sowing time.

examples.card: Lend grain until harvest.
examples.filled: Your neighbour in Malawi is out of maize. Lend her some, to be repaid in kind after harvest?

examples.card: Lend seed from your seed library.
examples.filled: Someone wants your heritage tomato seed. Lend some, and ask for seed back after harvest?

examples.card: Ask for food lent to be repaid.
examples.filled: The 2 bags of rice you lent in Tamale were due last month. Ask for them?

examples.card: Rice bank

examples.card: A village grain bank
examples.filled: The group lends grain to its members. What was borrowed and what comes back?

examples.card: Rice bank
examples.filled: You have a spare sack. Do you give it to the bank?

examples.filled: You need one more onion for tonight in Lyon. Borrow one from next door?

examples.filled: Your store in Mzuzu is empty 2 months before harvest. Borrow 2 bags from your uncle?

examples.filled: The seed library in Oakland lends bean seed. Borrow a packet and return seed in autumn?

examples.filled: Your cooking oil ran out and the shop is shut in Dhaka. Borrow a cup from the flat upstairs?

examples.filled: Your neighbour lends you a cup of meal until Saturday's distribution. Repay it then?

name: Answering for someone
card: Your father named you in 2024 for his food and money. Act for him now his doctor has signed?
note: You act for someone who can no longer answer for themselves, on what they signed while they were well: a parent with dementia, someone very ill. It rests only on their own earlier signed word naming you; nobody signs as them without it. It covers only the parts of life that word names, such as food, money or health. Their record stays theirs, and their own yes or no counts whenever they can give it. It ends when they can answer again, when what it rests on ends, or when they narrow it. A child has no one who signs for them: a parent makes their own promise to the child (Feeding your children), and the child signs their own words once they can. Kept apart from Choosing who decides for you (naming your own person in advance); Letting someone act for you (a job you hand over while you can still answer); and Feeding someone you care for (the daily feeding). It usually starts when a diagnosis comes, or the person is ready to answer for more.
no mirror: none: the person acted for is the other side, and their own yes counts when they can give it

examples.card: Hand a part back as they can answer more.
examples.filled: Your father is well again and wants to pay his own bills. Hand that part back to him?

examples.card: Act for a parent with dementia, on their earlier grant.
examples.filled: Your father named you in 2024 for his food and money. Start acting for those now his doctor has signed?

examples.card: Cover only part of life, such as food shopping.
examples.filled: Your mother's carer in Leeds does her shopping. Let the carer act for her food shopping only?

you do this when: You act for someone who can no longer answer for themselves, on what they signed earlier: a parent with dementia.

name: Pledging something as security
card: The SACCO will lend KSh 50,000 if you pledge your motorbike. Pledge it until the loan is repaid?
note: You let a lender or a seller hold something of yours until a promise is kept: gold, a cow, a motorbike's papers, a warehouse receipt, a title deed. It stays yours. They may not use it. It comes back when the promise is kept, and if it is not kept it is theirs to sell as you agreed. You agree what is pledged, for what, and what happens if you miss a payment. Kept apart from Borrowing against stored stock (grain in a warehouse); Guaranteeing someone's loan (your promise, not a thing); Lending and borrowing something (they may use it); and Pledging something for a loan (the thing becomes theirs if you miss the date). It usually starts when a loan or a big order needs security, or when the promise it backs is kept or missed.

examples.card: Pledge something to back a loan.
examples.filled: The lender in Kumasi wants your gold bracelet for GH₵ 3,000. Pledge it?

examples.card: Get a pledge back when a loan is repaid.
examples.filled: You repaid the SACCO in Kisumu. Ask for your bike papers back?

examples.card: Pledge a title deed.
examples.filled: The bank in Kampala wants your land title for a UGX 10m loan. Pledge it?

examples.card: Let a shop hold a card until a tab is paid.
examples.filled: The shopkeeper at Dadaab wants to keep your card until your tab is paid. Let him hold it, and write down the date it comes back?

you do this when: You let a lender hold something of yours until a promise is kept; it stays yours and comes back. Not handed to them to keep on a miss.

name: Connecting an app or account
card: Suppliers write to you on WhatsApp. Let FoodOS read those chats and draft replies, keeping only orders and prices, until you disconnect?
note: You let FoodOS read an app or account you already use (email, WhatsApp, SMS, a mobile-money statement, a till) so it can bring what matters into your record. Before you say yes it shows what it will read, what it will keep, what it can send (nothing without your tap unless you say so), and how to disconnect. You connect, it reads, and you disconnect when you like; what it kept stays yours. Kept apart from Getting your record back (asking a company for what it holds); Adding your own records (files you already have); and Letting someone act for you (a person who acts for you). It usually starts when you set up, when you start using a new app, or when you want to stop one.

examples.card: Connect your email to bring in receipts.
examples.filled: Let FoodOS read receipts in your email from food shops and apps, and nothing else?

examples.card: Connect a mobile-money statement.
examples.filled: Let FoodOS read your M-Pesa statement to log sales and stock buys?

examples.card: Connect a till to bring in sales.
examples.filled: Let FoodOS read the sales from your shop till in Lagos and nothing else?

move words.card: FoodOS reads your till in Lagos. Disconnect it?
move words.note: Stops FoodOS reading that app or account from now on; what it already kept stays yours.

examples.card: Stop FoodOS reading an app you connected.
examples.filled: FoodOS has read your WhatsApp orders since March. Disconnect it?

move words.trigger: An app or account of hers is connected.

you do this when: You let FoodOS read an app or account you already use so it can bring what matters into your record.

name: Growing to a buyer's contract
card: The packer will take all your peas at £280 a tonne if you sow their variety. Sign the contract?
note: You agree before sowing to grow a crop for one buyer: peas for a freezer plant, barley for a maltster, tomatoes for a cannery, chickens for meat for a processor. You agree the variety, the area, the standard, the price or how it is set, when they take it, and what they advance you. You grow it, deliver it, and are paid. Seed, feed or money they advance is a loan against the crop, and what selling elsewhere costs is said up front. Kept apart from Taking orders in advance (customers order what you already make); Selling and buying in bulk (a crop already grown); Paying ahead for a crop (paid up front for the crop); and Supplying on contract (a standing supply of what you already make). It usually starts when buyers offer contracts before sowing, when the price of an open market swings, or when a delivery date comes.

examples.card: Sign a contract before sowing.
examples.filled: The maltster offers £230 a tonne for 50 acres of spring barley. Sign before sowing?

examples.card: Agree what selling elsewhere costs.
examples.filled: The cannery's contract in Sinaloa forbids selling elsewhere. Ask what it costs if you do?

examples.card: Deliver what you grew under contract.
examples.filled: The peas are ready on 12 July. Book the packer's harvesters?

examples.card: Sign for a long-term crop.
examples.filled: A tea factory in Kericho offers a fixed price for leaf from your new bushes for 5 years. Sign?

move words.words: Tell them it will be short
move words.card: The hail has taken part of the tomatoes you agreed to deliver in August. Do you want to tell the cannery now, with your loss record?
move words.note: Telling the buyer, with your dated record of the loss, that you cannot deliver all you agreed. What happens next is what the deal said, or what the buyer answers.

examples.card: Tell them it will be short.
examples.filled: A flood took the lower field you promised to the maltster. Do you want to tell them you will be short?

examples.card: Tell them it will be short.
examples.filled: The drought cut your cotton. Do you want to tell the buyer before the delivery date?

move words.trigger: A loss was recorded on a crop that this contract covers.

you do this when: You agree before sowing to grow a crop for one buyer. The sale comes before the crop.

name: Growing trees and vines
card: Plant 200 avocado trees that fruit in 4 years, or keep the field in maize?
note: You plant and keep trees, vines and bushes that bear for years: an orchard, a vineyard, a coffee or cocoa farm, olives, dates, nuts, berries. Some you tap for sap every day instead of picking a fruit once a season: palm wine, toddy, maple, rubber. They may be yours or trees you rent for the tapping. It is years before the first crop, so you note what you expect and the card shows what the land could grow meanwhile. You plant, prune, graft, feed, protect, and pick or tap each season, and replace old trees when they decline. Before the pick, you read the sugar or taste the fruit to choose the day. Kept apart from Growing crops (sown and harvested within a season); Looking after land for pay (paid to keep land to a standard); Planning what to grow or feed (the plan, before you plant); and Foraging (trees you did not plant). It usually starts when you plan a long crop, when trees get old, or when a season's pruning, harvest or tapping comes.

examples.card: Plant a long crop.
examples.filled: Plant 300 coffee trees in Huila that bear in 3 years?

examples.card: Replace old trees.
examples.filled: 40 of your olive trees in Jaén yield half what they did. Replant them this winter?

examples.card: Prune before the season.
examples.filled: The vines in Stellenbosch are dormant. Prune them this month?

examples.card: Plant a tree anyone can pick from.
examples.filled: The community garden in Medellín has room. Plant three apple trees for anyone to pick from?

examples.card: Pick the crop when it is ripe.
examples.filled: The coffee cherries on your Huila farm are ripening unevenly. Pick the red ones this week?

move words.card: A frost warning is out for tonight and your Conference pears are in blossom. Run the fans from 2 a.m., or wait for the cold to reach the valley floor?
move words.note: Frost, hail, heat or a wet spell you saw, what you did about it, for how long, and a photo of any damage. Any public warning is shown beside it as its own word.

examples.card: Note the weather.
examples.filled: You ran the fans in the top block from 1 a.m. to 7 a.m. and it fell to minus 2 by your thermometer. Note the night, with the block and a photo of cut buds?

move words.trigger: A frost, hail or storm warning for the place, bud-burst or bloom time, or a hard night just passed

move words.card: The pruning crew finished eleven rows of the Syrah block today. Log the rows done, and let the crew leader sign the same count?
move words.note: The rows or trees pruned, grafted, thinned, tied or trained, by whom, and the pay per vine or per row if it is by piece. The crew leader or a pruner signs the same count.

examples.card: Prune or graft.
examples.filled: Tom's crew has pruned rows 1 to 14 of the old Pinot. Log the rows and sign Tom's count?

move words.trigger: Winter pruning season, a crew has come to the block, or thinning or tying time arrives

move words.card: You picked the lower block of the cocoa farm today. How many kilos of wet beans came off it, and will you ferment them at home or sell them fresh?
move words.note: Picking or cutting a crop when it is ready: each picking is a Note with its weights; Done is the last harvest of the crop. Grading is Grading produce; milk, eggs, honey and shearing are words on Raising animals.

examples.card: Harvest food.
examples.filled: Third pass of coffee on the north slope. How many kilos of cherry did you pick, and do you take them to the pulper tonight?

examples.card: Harvest food.
examples.filled: Leaf plucked on Tuesday from the three rows by the stream. How many kilos did you take to the buying centre?

move words.card: The label on the copper spray you used on the cherry block says 7 days before picking. Do you pick on Friday for the delivery or hold the round until Monday?
move words.note: Product, dose, block and weather; the harvest interval starts here. A spray keeps the label's waiting days before picking and before people go back in, so a booked pick or crew is checked against them.

examples.filled: You spread fertiliser around the young cocoa trees on the lower plot. Which product and how many bags?

move words.trigger: She logs spraying, or a picking day comes within the waiting days of a spray she logged.

move words.card: You found leaf rust on 12 coffee trees in the east block. Do you spray now, cut the worst trees, or call the extension officer?
move words.note: What was found walking the field: pests, disease, weeds.

examples.card: Weed or scout.
examples.filled: Swollen cocoa shoots on 3 trees. Do you report them or cut them out now?

move words.trigger: She walks the farm in the wet season, or a neighbour tells her of a disease nearby.

move words.card: You planted 120 coffee seedlings in the top block with the society's free stock. How many went in, and how many do you plan to replace in the next rain?
move words.note: Seed, rate, block and date, each time.

examples.card: Sow or plant.
examples.filled: You grafted 40 cocoa trees onto old stumps. How many took after six weeks?

move words.trigger: Planting time, or a nursery or society hands out seedlings.

move words.card: You tapped the 14 palms on the ridge this morning and at dusk yesterday. Do you want to write down the litres you got from each visit?
move words.note: Tapping is a daily flow, not a harvest, and the trees are often not the tapper's. Palm wine, toddy, pulque, rubber and maple all work this way.

examples.card: Collect the sap.
examples.filled: You tapped the 14 palms on the ridge this morning and at dusk yesterday. Do you want to write down the litres you got from each visit?

examples.filled: Mr Okoro's palms gave less than usual last week. Do you want to rest the eastern trees for a fortnight?

examples.card: Collect the sap.
examples.filled: The agave field is in its eighth year and three plants are ready to scrape. Do you want to collect the aguamiel at dawn and again at dusk?

move words.trigger: She keeps trees that are tapped (palm, coconut, date, maple, agave) and has not written a collection for a day, or she says she is going up the trees.

move words.card: Frost is forecast tonight and 12 tomato plants went out on Saturday. You have 2 sheets of fleece. Cover them, bring them in, or leave them?
move words.note: Covering, shading, netting, heating or watering a crop against frost, hail or heat, with what you did, where, when and what it used.

examples.card: Cover or shade a crop against the weather.
examples.filled: Nets over the young cherries before Thursday's hail.

move words.trigger: A frost, hail or heat warning for her place while plants are tender, in bloom or ripening.

move words.card: A buyer wants to know where this cocoa was grown. Walk the edge of the plot with your phone?
move words.note: Walking the edge of a plot with your phone to record where it is. A buyer may ask for it as proof of where food grew; it stays yours until you share it. Registering the land is a longer act of its own.

examples.card: Walk the edge of a plot to record where it is.
examples.filled: The cocoa plot by the river walked and mapped: 1.2 hectares.

move words.trigger: A buyer asks for origin proof, or a plot is added.

you do this when: You plant and keep trees and vines that bear for years: orchard, vineyard, coffee.

name: Selling power and water by the meter
card: Your solar sends 900 kWh a month you don't use. Sell it to the grid at 12p, or to the farm next door at 18p?
note: You sell power you make: solar, biogas, wind or a small hydro, to the grid, a neighbour, or a village network. You agree the price per unit (a set tariff, if the grid sets one), how it is metered, when you are paid, and how either side can end it. The power flows and you are paid by the meter. What you sell can be heat, warm water or the gas your boiler makes, metered or by an agreed amount. Payment and the meter reading are one moment, signed by the buyer reading the meter. Paying for power and water: You buy the power, water and gas your kitchen, farm or home runs on: mains power and water, piped gas, prepaid tokens, a solar company's monthly fee. You choose a supplier or plan, pay by bill or by token, and change or end it as its terms allow. The card shows what you use and what a change of plan or time of use would cost. Kept apart from Selling and buying in bulk (things, not power); Keeping the power on (your own supply); and Selling water or fuel by the load (a tank or a sack at a time). It usually starts when you put in generation, when a tariff changes, or when a neighbour or grid offers to buy; as Paying for power and water, when a token runs low, when a bill comes, when prices change, or when you move or open.

examples.card: Sell spare solar power to the grid.
examples.filled: Your dairy's panels in Devon export 1,200 kWh a month. Sign the grid's export tariff?

examples.card: Sell power to a neighbour.
examples.filled: Your biogas makes more than you use in Kiambu. Sell it to the school next door?

examples.card: Compare buyers for your power.
examples.filled: Two energy companies offer different export prices in Ireland. Compare them?

examples.card: Sell spare heat to a neighbour.
examples.filled: Your boiler made more heat than the glasshouse needed on 40 nights, and a pool nearby posts that it wants heat. Offer it at a price a unit, metered?

examples.card: Top up a prepaid meter.
examples.filled: The meter at your Lagos kitchen has 4 units. Top up ₦10,000?

examples.card: Switch to a cheaper plan.
examples.filled: Night power is half price in Lisbon and your cold room can run at night. Switch plans?

examples.filled: The water bill for your café in Cape Town doubled. Check the meter readings?

examples.card: The prepaid gas card for an older person who cannot top it up
examples.filled: Your mother's gas card is down to 1.40 and it is cold this week. Do you top it up from here, or ask the neighbour to take her to the shop?

examples.card: The prepaid gas card for an older person who cannot top it up
examples.filled: Dad's electric key was topped up at the post office on Thursday by Mr Fonseka. Do you pay Mr Fonseka back or leave it as a favour?

examples.card: The prepaid gas card for an older person who cannot top it up
examples.filled: The meter ran out last night and the oven went off with the stew half done. Do you ring the supplier or the daughter?

examples.card: Paying for power and water
examples.filled: Your token meter has 6 units left and the cold room uses 9 a day. Top up KSh 1,000 now?

move words.card: Your power meter reads 48,213 on the first of the month. Note it?
move words.note: A meter or gauge read by hand, kept with the time, so use and cost can be worked out later.

examples.card: Read a meter by hand.
examples.filled: Your power meter reads 48,213 on the first of the month. Note it?

move words.trigger: She has read a meter or gauge.

you do this when: Power or water is bought by meter and sold by the maker on standing terms: you pay or you sell.

name: Buying a debt
card: A farmer offers you a KSh 40,000 invoice the café owes in 60 days, for KSh 36,000 now. Buy it?
note: You buy money that someone else is owed, for less than it will pay: an unpaid invoice, a warehouse receipt, a buyer's promise to pay at harvest. You check who owes it, when, what backs it, and whether the seller still answers if it is never paid. Then you pay, tell the one who owes it to pay you, and collect when it falls due. Kept apart from Lending money (you lend, they repay); and Buying a voucher or pass (bought from its issuer). It usually starts when someone offers you what they are owed at less than it pays.

examples.card: Buy an invoice at a discount.
examples.filled: A grower in Eldoret offers the school's KSh 80,000 invoice, due in 30 days, for KSh 76,000. Take it over?

examples.card: Buy a warehouse receipt.
examples.filled: A grower in Kano offers her receipt for 10 bags of maize in the store for ₦380,000, below the market. Buy it?

examples.card: Tell the one who owes it that you are the one to pay.
examples.filled: You took over the café's invoice. Tell them to pay you on the 30th?

you do this when: You buy money someone else is owed, for less than it will pay: an unpaid invoice or a warehouse receipt.

name: Selling nature credits
card: Your hedges and woodland earned 120 verified credits. Sell them at £25 each to the buyer who asked?
note: You sell credits your land earned: carbon stored in soil or trees, or nature credits for wildlife or clean water. A verifier checks the land and signs for each credit, and a registry records who holds it. You get the land checked, offer the credits, a buyer pays, and the registry moves them to the buyer. What you promised to keep doing on the land, and for how long, stays your promise. FoodX gives credits no quality score; buyers read what the verifier signed. Plastic or recycling credits a verified scheme records for a collector's weighed tonnes are sold the same way. Kept apart from Looking after land for pay (paid for the care itself); Selling and buying in bulk (things you make); and Selling land, water or quota (the land or right itself). It usually starts when credits are verified, when a buyer asks, or when the price changes.
no mirror: none yet: the buyer publishes its own act

examples.card: Sell verified credits to a buyer.
examples.filled: Your soil carbon in Iowa earned 340 verified credits. Sell them to the brewery at $30?

examples.card: Get credits verified before selling.
examples.filled: Your new woodland in Wales is 5 years old. Book the verifier?

examples.card: Compare buyers for your credits.
examples.filled: Two buyers in Kenya offer different prices for your 200 tree credits. Compare them?

examples.card: Sell credits from planted trees.
examples.filled: Your mangrove planting in Khulna has been measured and signed off. Offer the credits to the buyer who asked?

you do this when: You sell credits your land earned: carbon, wildlife or clean water.

name: Running an auction
card: Thursday sale: 120 lambs in, 18 buyers registered. Open the bidding?
note: You run a sale where the price is found by bidding: a livestock ring, a fish auction, a tea or coffee auction. You take in the lots, publish the rules (reserve prices, your commission, when buyers pay and collect), take the bids, knock down each lot, collect the money and pay the sellers. Sealed bids stay unread until the close. Kept apart from Selling at auction (a seller's side); Buying at auction (a buyer's side); and Running a market (pitches, not bids). It usually starts when sale day comes, sellers bring lots, or buyers register.
no mirror: none: sellers sell in Selling at auction and buyers buy in Buying at auction

examples.card: Open a sale with its rules.
examples.filled: The fish auction at Peterhead opens at 7. Publish today's lots and your fee?

examples.card: Knock down a lot and record it.
examples.filled: Lot 14, 20 boxes of haddock, last bid £48 a box. Knock it down?

examples.card: Pay sellers after the sale.
examples.filled: The buyers have paid for Thursday's cattle in Pelotas. Pay the 9 sellers less your commission?

you do this when: You run a sale where the price is found by bidding: the ring keeper's side, not the lot owner's.

name: Advising someone on their work
card: A farmer near Eldoret asks why her maize yellows. Visit Friday for KSh 1,500?
note: You advise someone on how to grow, raise or make food for pay: an agronomist, an extension worker, a food scientist, a master brewer. You are asked, agree a fee or a visit, look and listen, and give your advice, which is your signed word; what they do with it is theirs. Getting advice on your work: You ask someone who knows to advise you on growing, raising or making food: an agronomist, an extension worker, a food technologist. You ask, agree the fee if there is one, they look and advise, and you decide what to do with it. An adviser can say, in their own signed word, who pays them and whether they sell what they advise; it shows as a plain fact beside the advice. Kept apart from Advising someone on their eating (a person's diet); Teaching a food skill (teaching how, not advising on one case); Selling your know-how (a recipe or process you sell for good, not advice on one case); Testing samples (a lab result); and Learning a food skill (learning for yourself). It usually starts when a crop or batch goes wrong, before a season, or when a new product needs a recipe for scale; as Getting advice on your work, when a crop, a herd or a batch goes wrong, before a season, or before scaling up.

examples.card: Visit a farm to advise.
examples.filled: A grower in Mbale asks about wilting beans. Visit on Tuesday for USh 40,000?

examples.card: Advise a maker on scaling a recipe.
examples.filled: A sauce maker in Lisbon wants her recipe safe for jars. Advise for €200?

examples.card: Follow up on advice given.
examples.filled: You advised on soil in March in Kitale. Ask how the crop did?

examples.card: Ask an agronomist to visit.
examples.filled: Your tomatoes in Arusha have spots on the leaves. Book the agronomist for TSh 30,000?

examples.card: Get advice before scaling a recipe.
examples.filled: Your chutney is going into shops in Leeds. Pay a food technologist to advise on jars and shelf life?

examples.card: Ask the extension worker.
examples.filled: The extension worker visits your village near Tamale on Thursday. Ask about the fall armyworm?

examples.card: Getting advice on your work
examples.filled: Your maize is yellowing in the lower field. Ask the agronomist to visit Friday for KSh 1,500?

you do this when: Someone who knows your trade tells you what to do on your farm or business for a fee: you ask or you advise. Not advice on a body, not teaching a skill.

name: Selling water or fuel by the load
card: Three homes on the hill want 5,000 litres each tomorrow. Deliver at KSh 3,500 a load?
note: You sell water or fuel a load at a time or an hour of your pump: a tanker of water, jerrycans from a kiosk, sacks of charcoal, gas cylinders, hours of your tubewell for a neighbour's field. You set the price, take orders, deliver or hand over, and are paid. Whether the water is safe and the load full is your signed word. Water by the hour from your tubewell or pump, and a turn at a canal outlet, are sold here too. Buying water or fuel: You buy water or fuel a load at a time or an hour of someone's pump: a tanker of water, jerrycans from a kiosk, a sack of charcoal, a cylinder of gas, a can of diesel, hours of a neighbour's tubewell for your field. You choose the seller, check the price and how clean or full it is, pay and take it. The card shows what you use and when the next load is needed. Water for animals at a borehole or a private well, paid by the head or by the day, is bought here too. Kept apart from Selling power and water by the meter (power by a meter); Carrying for pay (you carry for pay what is not yours); Selling and buying in bulk (what your work leaves over); Fetching water or fuel (you collect it yourself for nothing); and Buying and selling food to use (food). It usually starts when customers run low, the dry season comes, a regular round is due, or the fields need flooding; as Buying water or fuel, when a tank or store runs low, when the price changes, when the usual seller is out, or when the field needs flooding.

examples.card: Take orders for water loads.
examples.filled: Four farms near Nakuru want a tanker this week. Book them at KSh 3,500?

examples.card: Sell charcoal by the sack.
examples.filled: Cooking fires are busy in Lusaka this week. Sell 20 sacks of charcoal?

examples.card: Swap gas cylinders at your depot.
examples.filled: A customer in Accra brings an empty cylinder. Swap it for a full one at GH₵ 180?

examples.card: Sell water by the hour from your pump.
examples.filled: A neighbour asks to water an acre from your tubewell for 3 hours on Saturday, paying the fuel. Offer it, at your price an hour?

examples.card: Order a tanker when the tank runs low.
examples.filled: The farm tank in Nakuru is at 20%. Order 10,000 litres for Thursday?

examples.card: Stock up on fuel when you are low.
examples.filled: You have one bag of charcoal left in Lusaka and it is rainy season. Buy 4 bags now?

examples.card: Swap a gas cylinder.
examples.filled: Your stall's gas cylinder in Accra is empty. Swap it at the depot for GH₵ 180?

examples.card: Buy fuel at the fishermen's rate.
examples.filled: The co-op pump at Kochi sells fishermen diesel at the posted rate, 150 litres a week. Buy this week's 150 litres?

examples.card: Fuel with the kilometres on the clock
examples.filled: You filled the tank at the station in Eldoret. What does the clock say?

examples.card: Buy your ration at the landing site.
examples.filled: The fuel committee at Elmina sells each canoe 60 litres on Mondays. Buy yours?

examples.card: Fill the jerrycans for tomorrow's trip.
examples.filled: You have 2 jerrycans left for tomorrow. Buy 4 more from the kiosk at the jetty?

examples.card: Buy ice before a trip.
examples.filled: The ice plant at the jetty posts blocks at 150 each from 4 am; your usual kiosk sells crushed ice by the basket. Where do you buy for Thursday's trip?

examples.card: Buy a bigger lot together instead of by the tin.
examples.filled: You bought charcoal by the tin 20 times this season. The depot posts a 50 kg sack and two neighbours want one too. Buy a sack together?

examples.card: Buying water or fuel
examples.filled: The tank is a quarter full. Order a 5,000-litre load from the tanker for KSh 3,500?

you do this when: A load of water or fuel changes hands: you buy or you sell. Not metered.

name: Taking something as security
card: Juma offers his bike papers as security for a KSh 20,000 loan. Hold them until he repays?
note: You hold something of someone else's until they keep a promise: gold, a cow, a title deed, papers. It stays theirs; you may not use it, and you give it back when the promise is kept, or sell it by the terms if it is not, returning anything above what you are owed. Kept apart from Pledging something as security (the same, from the side that hands it over); Lending money (the loan itself); Storing food with someone (held for a fee); and Holding money until a deal is done (money for two sides). It usually starts when you lend or sell on credit to someone who offers security, or when the promise it backs is kept or missed.

examples.card: Hold security for a loan.
examples.filled: A trader in Lagos offers a gold chain for ₦200,000. Hold it until he repays?

examples.card: Return security when a promise is kept.
examples.filled: Akinyi repaid in Kisumu. Give back her bike papers?

examples.card: Sell security when a promise is missed, by the terms.
examples.filled: The loan is 3 months late in Kampala and the terms allow it. Sell the pledged goat and return the rest?

you do this when: Someone hands you something to hold until they keep a promise. The other side is Pledging something.

name: Claiming a farm payment
card: Your farm payment declaration in Castilla closes on 30 April and your parcels are the same as last year. File it?
note: You ask a public scheme for a payment tied to your land or what you farm: a yearly farm payment, a drought payment, a payment for planting trees. You check your parcels, make the declaration by its date, wait for any inspection, receive the payment, and keep proof. Kept apart from Claiming benefits (support for a person or household); Applying for a grant (a competed award); and Claiming back from a scheme (money for food you already gave under it). It usually starts when a declaration window opens, when your land changes, or when a payment is late.

examples.card: Say your land has changed before the deadline.
examples.filled: You bought a neighbour's 3 hectares in Kent this winter. Add the field to your payment declaration before 15 May?

examples.card: Ask about a late farm payment.
examples.filled: Your yearly payment in Poland was due in December and has not come. Ask the agency when it will pay?

examples.card: Apply for a payment for planting trees.
examples.filled: The scheme in Wales pays for hedges and trees planted this winter. Add your 400 metres of new hedge to the application?

examples.card: File a yearly parcel declaration.
examples.filled: Your farm payment declaration in Castilla closes on 30 April and your parcels are the same as last year. File it now?

no mirror: none: the scheme pays by its own published rule, so there is no one on the other side to answer
you do this when: You ask a public scheme for a payment tied to your land or what you farm: declared parcels, an inspection. Not benefits for a person.

name: Getting a place to trade
card: A stall pitch has opened at Saturday's market. Apply for it?
note: You ask for a place to sell or grow that someone else hands out: a market stall pitch, an allotment plot, a bench in a shared kitchen. You find who hands it out, apply, wait on a list or a draw, pay the fee if there is one (a set sum, a share of what you take, or both), and keep the place by turning up. A hawker's place often comes from a town vending committee, a zone list or a draw; a fee taken by someone with no receipt book is Paying someone who demands it, recorded as what it is. Kept apart from Renting land or a place to trade (a rent you agree with a landowner); Getting a permit or registration (permission to trade); and Applying for a grant (money or kit). It usually starts when a pitch opens, a waiting list moves, or you want a regular place to sell.

examples.card: Apply for a market stall pitch.
examples.filled: The Saturday market in Brixton has two pitches free from March. Apply for one?

examples.card: Join the waiting list for an allotment.
examples.filled: The council allotments in Bristol have a 3-year list and yours has moved up to 4th. Confirm you still want a plot?

examples.card: Book a bench in a shared kitchen.
examples.filled: The community kitchen in Nairobi has a bench free on Tuesdays. Ask for it?

examples.card: Plot rules and handover
examples.filled: The allotment society says your plot looks neglected. Do you send them a photo of the beds you dug this week?

examples.card: Plot rules and handover
examples.filled: Your plot rules say you may not sell produce. Do you give the extra away?

no mirror: none: the place is handed out by a list or a draw, and whoever hands it out answers by their own rule

move words.card: A plot list near you is open. Do you want to join it?
move words.note: Asking for a share when one frees up.

examples.card: Join a waiting list for a share.
examples.filled: Allotment waiting list.

move words.trigger: A share in a group she wants to be in has freed up, or she has asked for one and her place in the queue has come.

you do this when: You ask for a stall pitch, an allotment or a bench that someone hands out, not bargained rent.

name: Passing on a recipe
card: Gran's 30 recipes in Hyderabad could go to the grandchildren. Send them?
note: You pass on something that holds a family's food: Gran's recipes, the family starter, a way of making a dish. You choose who gets it and hand it over with the notes that go with it, and you can keep your own copy. They accept, and they can carry it on. An idea is not property (Kinsella), so a recipe is told, not handed over, and you keep yours; only the living starter or the book itself changes owner. Kept apart from Handing something down (a farm, a business or a herd); Giving a gift (one present); and Teaching a food skill (showing how, over time). It usually starts when a child leaves home, a grandparent is getting older, or a family gathering comes.

examples.card: Write down a family dish before it is lost.
examples.filled: Your aunt in Manila cooks the Christmas adobo by feel. Sit with her and write it down for the cousins?

examples.card: Give a family cookbook to the next generation.
examples.filled: Your mother's handwritten recipe book in Accra is falling apart. Copy it for each of your sisters?

examples.card: Share a family ferment or culture.
examples.filled: Your grandfather's kimchi crock in Busan has a culture older than you. Give a jar of it to your daughter?

examples.card: Hand down your recipes.
examples.filled: Gran's 30 recipes in Hyderabad, with her notes, could go to the grandchildren. Send them?

examples.card: Pass on a sourdough starter.
examples.filled: The 1974 starter in your Vienna kitchen could be split for your three children. Split it?

you do this when: You pass on what holds a family's food: Gran's recipes, the starter, a way of making a dish, with the notes that go with it. Not a single telling, not a farm or business.

name: Tipping someone
card: The rider brought your order in the rain. Add a tip?
note: You thank someone who served you with a little extra money or food: a waiter, a rider, a porter, a market boy. You decide whether to give anything and how much, and you pay by cash, card or app. They keep it, or share it the way their workplace does. It is not payment for the job, which is Buying. The person tipped may note cash tips at the end of a shift as their own count, building income they can show. Kept apart from Sending money home (supporting family far away); Giving a customer a treat (a gift from the seller); Giving a gift (a present to someone you know); and Giving to a cause (money to a group). It usually starts when a meal, delivery or errand is done well.

examples.card: Tip a rider who delivers in bad weather.
examples.filled: The barista in Melbourne remembered your order again. Leave a tip in the jar?

examples.card: Tip the person who served your meal.
examples.filled: The waiter at the Lisbon tasca looked after your table all evening. Leave something extra on the card?

examples.card: Tip someone who carries your shopping.
examples.filled: The porter at Nakuru market carried your four sacks to the matatu. Give him a tip?

you do this when: You thank someone who served you with a little extra money or food: a waiter, a rider, a porter. Not a present, not a customer's treat.

name: Renting land or a place to trade
card: The unit next to your bakery has been empty for 2 months and a florist has asked about it. Offer her a lease?
note: You rent a shop, stall space, café unit or kitchen to someone who will trade from it, often for years. You agree the rent, the deposit, rent reviews, what they may change, who repairs what, and how either side ends it. You hand over the keys, collect the rent, and take it back at the end. Renting land, water or quota: You rent a field, grazing, an allotment, a rooftop, water or a quota that is someone else's, by the season or for years. You ask, they offer, you agree the rent, when it is paid and how long, take it over, and it runs until the lease ends or one side ends it early, which costs the sum signed. Rent reviews, what you are paid for improvements you leave, and what happens to a standing crop are agreed up front. A lease may be a signed word and a witness where land is held by custom. A quota is a right to fish or grow a set amount, given by the state or a body. A waiting list may take years. Paying with a share of the crop is Farming land on shares. Renting a place to trade: You rent a shop, café, warehouse, stall or kitchen to trade from, often for years. You agree the rent, the deposit, rent reviews, what you may change, who repairs what, whether you can pass the lease on if you sell, and how either side ends it. You take the keys, pay the rent, and hand it back at the end. Kept apart from Renting something (a thing or a room by the day); Renting out land (fields); Running a market (pitches for many sellers); Farming land on shares (you pay in crop, not money); Lending and borrowing something (movable things); Storing food with someone (space to keep food); and Opening another site (the whole decision to open). It usually starts when a unit falls empty, a lease is about to end, or someone asks about a space; as Renting land, water or quota, when a lease is about to end, a season is coming and you need ground, or an allotment list opens; as Renting a place to trade, when you open or move, when a lease is up for renewal or review, or when the landlord changes the terms.

examples.card: Let a shop or café unit to a new tenant.
examples.filled: The corner unit in your building in Leeds is empty and a baker asks about it. Offer a 3-year lease?

examples.card: Agree a rent review with a tenant.
examples.filled: Your tenant in Mombasa has run the kiosk for 3 years and the lease is up for review. Offer a new rent?

examples.card: Let out a stall or kitchen space for the long term.
examples.filled: A caterer in Jakarta wants your spare kitchen for a year. Offer it on a one-year lease?

examples.card: Get a plot to grow on from the council or a landowner.
examples.filled: The council allotment list is open for your area. Join it with your family in Sheffield?

examples.card: Renew a lease before it ends.
examples.filled: Your grazing lease on Low Field in Wales ends soon. Ask to renew it for three years?

examples.card: Rent a small plot in the city to grow on.
examples.filled: A restaurant in São Paulo has a rooftop going spare. Rent it to grow herbs?

examples.card: Rent water or a quota with the land.
examples.filled: You could rent a field near Murcia with its irrigation turns. Take it?

examples.card: Record the state of a field on the day you take it.
examples.filled: You take Low Field on a three-year lease from 1 October. Photograph the gateways, drains and fences and note the soil test, so day one is on your record?

examples.card: Pay rent in grain and have the landowner sign.
examples.filled: Oksana's rent is 1.2 tonnes of wheat and 40 litres of sunflower oil, due by 1 December. Have her sign for it when she collects?

examples.card: Hand the field back and record how you left it.
examples.filled: Your lease on Hill Field ends on 30 September. Photograph the stubble and the ditches before you hand it back?

examples.card: Ask for a long lease where your fit-out cannot move.
examples.filled: The lease on the warehouse you grow in ends on 31 March, and the rent rose twice in 4 years. Ask for a 5-year term with a cap you set, or look at the two other units posted?

examples.card: Renting land, water or quota
examples.filled: Your grazing lease on Low Field ends in March. Ask to renew for 3 years?

examples.card: Take a lease on a shop.
examples.filled: A café unit in Leeds is £1,400 a month for 3 years. Take it?

examples.card: Agree a rent review.
examples.filled: The landlord in Nairobi asks 15% more from January. Agree, or ask for less?

examples.card: Hand a place back at the end.
examples.filled: Your lease in Lisbon ends in March. Leave on that date and book the check-out?

examples.card: Renting a place to trade
examples.filled: The shop on the corner is £1,800 a month for 5 years, with a 3-month deposit. Take the lease?

known as: Renting out a place to trade

sides.from: Renting out a place to trade

you do this when: A field, water, quota or a trading spot is rented for money for a while: you rent or you rent out. Not kit or a kitchen, not many tenants at one market.

name: Using power when it is cheap
card: Power is half price after midnight in Leeds. Run the dishwashers then from now on?
note: You move the work that needs power to the hours when it costs least: cooling a cold store before the dear hours, charging vans overnight, running grow lights through the cheap hours. You say it once, and after that it runs by itself each day, listed quietly in what FoodOS did for you; you are asked again only when a price or your own plan changes. Kept apart from Keeping the power on (getting through a cut); and Selling power and water by the meter (paying the bill). It usually starts when a cheaper hour is offered, a tariff changes, or your work changes what must run when.

examples.card: Run kit that can wait in the cheap hours.
examples.filled: Your cold store in Murcia can pre-cool overnight, when power costs least. Do that every night from now on?

examples.card: Charge vehicles when power is cheap.
examples.filled: Your bakery in Oslo has three e-vans. Charge them overnight on the solar battery from now on?

examples.card: A price change moves the cheap hours.
examples.filled: Your new tariff in the Netherlands makes power cheapest from 1 to 5, not midnight to 6. Move the greenhouse lights to the new hours?

examples.card: After a cut, the timers are wrong
examples.filled: The power came back at 4 and the cold store timer shows 12:00. Do you check the timers before the dear hours start?

examples.card: After a cut, the timers are wrong
examples.filled: The grow lights are on a plug timer and the cut was last night. Do you look at the clock on it?

examples.card: After a cut, the timers are wrong
examples.filled: The off-peak heater did not come on after the cut. Do you reset it and note when it ran?

examples.card: Be paid to pause at the peak.
examples.filled: Cold room 2 can go 90 minutes unpowered and stay under 5°C. An aggregator pays for a pause from 6 to 7:30 pm on up to 20 days a year. Join?

you do this when: You move work that needs power to the hours it costs least.

name: Brewing
card: Your ginger beer in Kingston is two days into its first ferment. Bottle it tomorrow?
note: You make a drink that needs time to ferment: beer, wine, cider, kombucha, ginger beer, palm wine, kvass. You mix it, let it work, taste it, bottle or barrel it, and wait. A batch started from a culture kept from an earlier one (yeast, a mother, a starter) names the batch it came from, so the chain can be followed. A batch closes with the bottled quantity counted against what went in; where your place's rules relieve duty on lost drink, a recorded loss lowers what is owed. Kept apart from Preserving food (food, not a drink); Ageing food or drink (it starts after the drink is made); and Making a batch (a run made to sell on a schedule). It usually starts when the fruit or grain is in, a bucket is free, or the season for it comes.

examples.card: Start a ferment.
examples.filled: The apples from your tree in Somerset are ripe. Press them and start cider this weekend?

examples.card: Bottle when it is ready.
examples.filled: Your kombucha in Seoul has fermented for nine days. Taste it and bottle it?

examples.card: Tap a drink at the right time.
examples.filled: The palm sap from your trees in Kisumu is bubbling by evening. Collect and share it tonight?

move words.card: The elderflower fizz has worked for 9 days and you have 40 clean bottles in the shed. Do you want to bottle it tomorrow?
move words.note: This is the moment drink becomes stock. No receipt exists for it.

examples.card: Bottle or barrel it.
examples.filled: The elderflower fizz has worked for 9 days and you have 40 clean bottles in the shed. Do you want to bottle it tomorrow?

examples.card: Bottle or barrel it.
examples.filled: Your 2025 red is 11 months in the tank. Do you want to barrel it or bottle it now?

examples.card: Bottle or barrel it.
examples.filled: Tuesday's palm wine is sitting in two jerrycans at the roadside. Do you want to fill the 25 calabashes for the evening?

move words.trigger: A batch has worked as long as she usually lets it, or she says the bottles are washed or the barrel is empty.

you do this when: You make a drink that needs time to ferment: beer, wine, cider, kombucha.

name: Lending a worker
may the holder use it: yes, only for what was agreed
card: Ana's shift is quiet on Tuesday and the cafe next door is short. Lend her for the afternoon?
note: You lend one of your own team to another business for a time. You agree who pays them, for how long, and what happens if they are hurt or the other business wants them longer. The worker agrees to go first. Kept apart from Supplying workers from an agency (an agency whose business is placing workers); Employing someone (hiring your own); and Working for someone (a worker's side). It usually starts when your shift is quiet, or a nearby business is short-handed.

examples.card: Lend a cook to a nearby kitchen on a quiet day.
examples.filled: Your Tuesday lunch is quiet and the bistro across the road is two cooks short. Lend Tomas for the afternoon?

examples.card: Send a worker to help a neighbour for a busy week.
examples.filled: Your neighbour's stall in Kisumu has a wedding order this week. Lend Achieng for three days?

examples.card: Take a worker from a friend's business for a short time.
examples.filled: The bakery next door offers Pedro for Saturday while your baker is away. Take him for the day?

examples.card: Lend one of your team to a nearby business on a quiet day.
examples.filled: Lend Ana to the cafe next door on Tuesday afternoon. Agree to it?

no mirror: none: the business that takes the worker is hiring help (Hiring help for a day), paying for work, not borrowing a person
you do this when: You lend one of your own team to another business for a time.

name: Warning your trading partners
card: Juma took 30 crates on credit and hasn't paid in 3 months. Warn your trading circle?
note: You tell the people you trade with about a trader who did not keep a deal you really had with him. It goes to your trading circle only, and he can answer beside it. You write what happened, send it, and can take it back if he puts it right. Kept apart from Vouching for someone (money of yours behind a person, on their record); Warning people nearby (neighbours, not partners); and Settling up with trading partners (getting paid). It usually starts when a deal has gone unpaid well past its date, or goods keep arriving short.

examples.card: Warn your circle about a trader who didn't pay.
examples.filled: Juma took 30 crates on credit in July and has not paid. Warn your trading circle?

examples.card: Warn buyers about a payment that bounced.
examples.filled: A café in Nairobi paid you with a cheque that bounced twice. Warn the traders in your circle?

examples.card: Warn buyers about a supplier who sends short loads.
examples.filled: A supplier in Kampala sent 40 kg short on three orders. Warn the buyers you trade with?

you do this when: You tell the people you trade with about a trader who did not keep a deal you really had, to your circle only. Not a danger to neighbours.

name: Running a malnutrition programme
card: Amina has gained 300 g in four weeks and her arm band reads 12.6 cm. Give this week's 14 sachets and book next week's check?
note: You run a programme that treats malnutrition: you weigh and measure each patient, admit them to treatment, hand out the week's therapeutic food, and discharge them when they are well. The programme's own admission and discharge rules decide, and FoodOS shows the rule beside each reading; you make the move. You start the plan, change the amount as the weight changes, note each check, hand over each week's food, and end it at discharge. The carer pays nothing, and reports to the funder go under the programme's stated terms. A plan ends in one of four ways, in the programme's own words: recovered, moved to another clinic, left, or died; a transfer takes the carer's record with her yes, and the ending is the health worker's signed word. Kept apart from Treating malnutrition (the carer's side: feeding at home); Screening for malnutrition (finding who needs help); and Handing out food parcels (food for households, with no treatment plan). It usually starts when there is a weekly weighing, an arm measurement, a new referral, or the stock of sachets runs low.

examples.card: Give therapeutic food by weight each week.
examples.filled: Amina is on week 4 of treatment. Hand over this week's 14 sachets?

examples.card: Check progress at a clinic and decide whether the child is ready to leave the programme.
examples.filled: Week 6 at the Niger clinic: his arm band reads 12.6 cm. Discharge him with a two-week ration?

examples.card: Get therapeutic food to families who live far from the clinic.
examples.filled: You have 10 sachets left for 3 children in rural Odisha. Request a refill before Friday?

no mirror: none: the patient receives care, and a small child signs nothing, so a parent makes their own promise

move words.card: Fatuma has missed two Tuesdays. Visit her at home on Thursday's round?
move words.note: Missed weeks are how children quietly drop out. The visit is what the health worker did and saw, and the result is her signed word in the programme.

examples.card: Visit at home.
examples.filled: Fatuma has missed two Tuesdays. Visit her at home on Thursday's round?

move words.trigger: A weekly weighing passes with no reading for a child still in the programme.

move words.card: This week's weighing day is over. Note how many children came, and who did not?
move words.note: How many people you actually fed or who came, and how many you turned away: the number a scheme, a client or next week's cooking is planned and paid on.

examples.card: Count who came for their check.
examples.filled: Today's clinic is over. Note how many children came for their weekly check?

move words.trigger: A meal, service or event she runs has ended.

you do this when: You run a programme that weighs, admits, feeds and discharges patients. The carer's side is Treating malnutrition.

name: Splitting takings
card: Saturday's landing is sold. By your share rule the crew get €925 each. Pay out?
note: You and others divide what a group earned: what a shared sale brought in, a boat's landing, the week's tips. The shares follow a rule agreed before the work, by hours, by points or half to the boat, and one person holds the money. When it is sold and the costs are known you work out each share and pay it. The law taxes tips. Everyone in the split sees the total it was made from (the buyer's signed sale, the pooled tips), the rule, and their own share, without having to ask. The holder counts the pot in front of the group, and each share closes when its receiver signs for it. Kept apart from Chipping in (each putting money in for one thing); Splitting costs (dividing what was spent); Sharing profit with your team (the owner choosing to give staff a share of profit); and Employing someone (a wage). It usually starts when a landing or sale is done, when the week's tips are counted, or when the stall closes after a fair.

examples.card: Split what a shared sale earns with the people who helped.
examples.filled: Split the stall takings with the three friends who baked, after a school fair in Cebu. Send the split?

examples.card: Share out a catch among the crew.
examples.filled: Saturday's landing made €8,400 and fuel and ice cost €1,000. By your share rule the boat takes half of the €7,400 and the 4 crew get €925 each. Pay out?

examples.card: Share out the week's tips.
examples.filled: This week's tips are £2,140 across 9 staff by points. Send each their share?

examples.card: Jar counted at close by two
examples.filled: You counted the jar at close with Priya. Share it by hours as agreed, or hold it till Friday?

examples.card: An envelope from the host for the staff
examples.filled: Mr Mensah gave you an envelope marked 'for the staff' with 300 in cash. There were nine of you. Do you want to share it by hours, or equally?

examples.card: Ask the crew leader to write down each picker's count before he pays out.
examples.filled: The leader was paid for the row of six pickers on Friday. Ask him to write each person's crates before he divides the money?

examples.card: Crew leader pays out a pruning crew
examples.filled: The estate paid you for 14 rows of pruning. Pay out the crew's shares by the rows each pruned?

examples.card: Write down the rule for sharing card tips.
examples.filled: Card tips of 842 came in October and there is no signed rule for sharing them. Share by hours, by points, or another way, and write it down?

examples.card: Agree a split before a shared fee comes in.
examples.filled: You and a friend are making a paid series together for 1,500. Agree the split before the brand pays?

move words.card: This week's tips are £2,140 across 9 staff by points. Send each their share?
move words.note: Sharing tips by the rule; the person who holds the tips is named in advance. A service charge added to a bill is part of the price, not a tip; where both are shared, each shows as its own line.
move words.trigger: The week's tips or tronc are tallied in her record and the day for sharing them by the agreed points has come.

examples.card: Share out the week's tips.
examples.filled: £2,140 across 9 staff.

move words.card: Saturday's landing made €8,400 and fuel and ice cost €1,000. By your share rule the boat takes half of the €7,400 and the 4 crew get €925 each. Pay out?
move words.note: Splitting a catch or harvest's earnings by shares.
move words.trigger: A landing or harvest has been sold and its costs are on record, so the shares by the rule on record can be worked out.

examples.card: Pay a crew by shares of the catch.
examples.filled: €925 each to 4 crew, after €1,000 of fuel and ice and the boat's half.

you do this when: You and others divide what a group earned, by a rule agreed before the work. Not costs, not a whip-round.

name: Chipping in
may the holder use it: yes, only for what was agreed
card: Priya is leaving. Chip in $5 for her cake with your 8 colleagues in Denver?
note: You and others each put in a small amount to buy one thing for someone or for the group: a leaving present, a wedding gift, a cake, a team meal. One person collects, tells everyone the amount, buys it, and shows what was spent. It ends when the thing is bought; leftover money goes back or to the person it was for, as agreed. Kept apart from Splitting takings (sharing out money you earned together); Pooling money (a lasting pot kept for the group); Contributing to a collection (a pledge recorded and returned in kind, as at a funeral); and Splitting costs (dividing a bill already paid). It usually starts when a colleague leaves, a birthday or wedding comes, or the team finishes a hard shift.

examples.card: Chip in with colleagues or friends for a cake, meal or treat for someone's occasion.
examples.filled: Priya is leaving. Collect $5 from 8 colleagues in Denver for her cake?

examples.card: Put in for a gift for a friend or neighbour.
examples.filled: A neighbour is getting married. Put in 50 rupees each from your street in Kolkata for a gift?

examples.card: Put in for a team meal.
examples.filled: The late shift is done in your Sydney kitchen. Put in $10 each for pizza?

examples.card: Put in for a leaving present.
examples.filled: A teacher at your school in Accra retires on Friday. Collect from the staff room?

move words.card: Priya's leaving cake: $5 each. Put in yours?
move words.note: Your part of the whip-round.
move words.trigger: A whip-round she belongs to has been called, with an amount per person, and her share has not yet been paid.

examples.card: Put in your share of a whip-round.
examples.filled: $5 for Priya's leaving cake.

you do this when: You and others each put in a small amount to buy one thing: a present, a cake, a team meal. Not dividing a bill or takings.

name: Handing a request on
card: A café asks you for 20 kg of onions and you have none, but Sam does. Hand the request on to Sam?
note: You get a request you cannot meet and send it to someone who can: a café asks for onions and you have none, a family asks a carer for a night she cannot take, a buyer asks for a lorry you do not have. One tap sends the request itself, the words its maker signed, to the one you pick, and tells the maker where it went. You do not take the request, promise anything or answer for it. The one you pick can say yes, say no or ignore it, and any deal is between them and the maker. A request posted to anyone can go on freely; one made to you alone is theirs, so you ask the maker before it goes. A finder's fee, if there is one, is for the two of them to agree with you, and FoodX takes nothing. Kept apart from Introducing two people (both sides are put in touch and both words travel); Giving your word on something (you send a name, not their request); and Selling through an agent (you take the goods and sell them yourself). It usually starts when someone asks for something you do not have, you know who has it, or a request lands while you are full or away.

examples.card: Hand a request you cannot fill to a neighbour who can.
examples.filled: A neighbour asks your farm for 30 dozen eggs for Saturday and your hens are laying half that. Rose has more. Hand the request on to Rose?

examples.card: Hand a café's order to the one who has the stock.
examples.filled: A café down the road asks you for 20 kg of onions. You have none, but Sam does. Hand the request on to Sam?

examples.card: Hand a booking you cannot take to another carer.
examples.filled: A family asks you for a Sunday night with their father and you are booked. Maria does Sundays and is free. Hand the request on to Maria?

examples.card: Hand a buyer's order to a trader with stock.
examples.filled: A buyer in Mombasa asks you for 50 sacks of maize and you are out. Halima has a store full. Hand the request on to her?

examples.card: Hand a delivery job to a driver with room.
examples.filled: A restaurant asks you to bring a pallet across town tonight and your van is full. Kofi's van is empty. Hand the request on to Kofi?

examples.card: Hand an order on from a robot farm.
examples.filled: Your robot farm is asked for 40 kg of basil this week and has 10. The farm next door grows basil. Hand the request on to it, under your grant?

move words.card: The café asked you for onions and Sam has them. Hand the request on?
move words.note: The tap that sends the request. It is your signed word that this request is one they could meet, carrying the maker's own words unchanged, and it binds only you. It is done when it has been read.

examples.card: Hand on a request you cannot meet.
examples.filled: A shop asks you for a case of oat milk you do not stock, and the wholesaler across the road does. Hand the request on?

examples.card: Hand on a request while you are away.
examples.filled: A buyer asks for your spare tomatoes while you are at a funeral, and your brother has a stall. Hand the request on to him?

examples.card: Hand on a request from a person you care for.
examples.filled: The woman you care for asked for a lift to the market and you cannot drive her. A volunteer driver can. Hand the request on to her?

move words.trigger: A request signed by someone else lands in her record, she holds nothing that meets it, and she knows someone whose own word says they do.

move words.card: Ana and Ben's café agree to give you 5% of their first order if you bring them together. Sign it?
move words.note: The two people you put in touch, or the one you handed a request to, offer you a share if a deal comes of it. It is their choice, it is a signed offer to you with its own terms, and FoodX takes nothing. The deal they make points back to the introduction.

examples.card: Offer the connector a share of the first order.
examples.filled: Rose and Tom agree 2% of their first egg order for Agnes, who put them in touch. Sign it?

examples.card: Thank someone who handed you a request.
examples.filled: Sam wins the café's onion order that Agnes handed on. Offer her KSh 300 a delivery for the first month?

examples.card: Agree nothing, and say so.
examples.filled: A neighbour put you in touch with a baker and wants nothing for it. Note that no fee was agreed?

move words.trigger: A signed introduction or a request handed on points two people to each other, and nothing signed yet says whether the one who connected them is paid.

you do this when: You get a request you cannot meet and send it to someone who can, then drop out.

name: Pledging something for a loan
card: You need KSh 8,000 until the 28th and a lender will take your gold chain. Pawn it, to be theirs only if you have not repaid by then?
note: You hand something of yours to a lender to hold while you borrow, and it becomes theirs only if you have not repaid by a date you both name: a gold chain, a sewing machine, a title deed, a heifer. Holding moves to them now; owning stays with you until the date passes unpaid. Repay in time and it comes straight back; miss the date and it is theirs, and that settles the loan. Nothing else of yours is at stake: the thing you named is the whole price of missing. They may not use it, and an animal that earns or a tool you work with is pledged only if you name it. The date is read on a clock you both chose, so a time written on a message changes nothing. Each of you is bound only by what you signed. Kept apart from Pledging something as security (the thing stays yours and is sold if you miss, with anything above the debt coming back to you); Lending money (the loan itself); Putting up a bond (money held by a third person that goes to the other side if you fail a promise); and Guaranteeing someone's loan (someone else pays, not a thing). It usually starts when you need cash against something you own, when the date is near, or when you repay.
no mirror: none yet: the lender's side is written when a lender publishes it

examples.card: Pawn something for a short loan.
examples.filled: You need KSh 8,000 until pay day on the 28th and a lender in Nairobi will hold your gold chain. Pawn it, to be hers if you have not repaid by then?

examples.card: Name the tool you earn with, or leave it out.
examples.filled: A lender in Kumasi offers GH₵ 1,500 against your sewing machine. Pawn the machine, or offer your wedding ring and keep the machine working?

examples.card: Repay before the date and get it back.
examples.filled: Your pawned bracelet comes back if you pay £420 by Friday. Repay today?

examples.card: Pledge an animal that does not earn.
examples.filled: A neighbour in Boyacá will lend 600,000 pesos against a heifer, not your milking cow, until harvest. Name the heifer only?

you do this when: You hand something to a lender while you borrow, and it becomes theirs only if you have not repaid by a date. Not held and returned.

name: Letting a debt go
card: Joe still owes you £30 from March and has lost his job. Let all of it go?
note: You say, in your own signed word, that someone no longer owes you what they owed: all of a debt, or only part of it. Only the person who is owed can do this, and only for what is hers to let go; a debt you have sold belongs to the buyer. You name the debt, how much you let go and the day. The one who owed does not have to say yes, and you cannot take it back. What you do not let go stays owed. Kept apart from Giving a gift (something handed over, not a debt dropped); Releasing each other (both sides end everything between them, with a list of the debts that stay); Paying what you can to everyone you owe (you are the one who owes); and Lending money (the debt itself). It usually starts when someone cannot pay and you choose to be kind, when only a small part is left, or when a late charge has piled up that you would rather not collect.
no mirror: none: the one who owed needs no yes, and answers in no act

examples.card: Let a whole debt go.
examples.filled: Amina owes you KSh 4,000 for fish from last season and her boat has sunk. Let all of it go?

examples.card: Let part of a debt go.
examples.filled: The café in Leeds still owes £90 of a £400 bill and says money is tight. Let £40 of it go and keep £50 owed?

examples.card: Let a late charge go.
examples.filled: Your supplier in Lagos owes ₦20,000 and a ₦3,000 late charge. Let the charge go and keep the debt?

you do this when: You say in your own signed word that someone no longer owes you, all or part.

name: Releasing each other
card: You and Hassan have traded for two years and the books are even except KSh 4,000 for the broken crate. Release each other from everything else?
note: You and someone you have dealt with each sign that you are settled: nothing more is owed between you, except the debts you list. Each of you lets go only of what is owed to you, so your release binds only you; if only one signs, only that side's claims end and the other side's stay. A debt you list stays owed exactly as it was. Nothing is wiped that you did not name: the release says which deals it covers. Kept apart from Letting a debt go (one debt, one side); Settling up with trading partners (netting what you owe each other into one payment, or a ring of debts); Paying what you can to everyone you owe (an offer of part to many creditors); and Having a business of your own (ending a whole business). It usually starts when a year or a season ends, when two traders stop dealing, when a partnership winds up, or when the books are even apart from a few items.
no mirror: self: each side lets go of its own claims

examples.card: Close the books with someone you traded with.
examples.filled: You and the miller in Eldoret have traded for three years. Sign that you are settled, except his KSh 12,000 for the sack that burst?

examples.card: Release a partner who is leaving.
examples.filled: Your cousin is leaving the juice stall in Accra. Release each other from everything but the GH₵ 2,000 he still owes you?

examples.card: End a group year with nothing owed.
examples.filled: Your chama in Kisumu closes its year. Sign that no member owes another, apart from the two loans you list?

you do this when: You and someone you dealt with both sign that nothing more is owed between you, except the debts you list.

name: Handing on what you are owed
card: Hassan owes you KSh 30,000 and you owe the miller 30,000. Hand the miller Hassan's debt in place of paying him?
note: You hand on money you are owed. You give it to someone you owe, in place of paying them, or you give it back to the person who owes it, so that two debts between you cancel. You sign the debt over, naming the deal it comes from.
