From then on the one who owed pays the new holder exactly what he signed and no more; a payment he made to you before he saw the handover still counts, and you pass it on. You may say you stand behind the debt up to a sum, and the one who takes it must say yes to that. Only the person who is owed can hand a debt on, and silence moves nothing. A debt can be marked 'not to be passed on', and then handing it on counts for nothing. Your own debts stay yours: you cannot hand your debt to someone else unless the one you owe says yes. Two people who owe each other can each hand their debt to the other, and both are settled up to the smaller sum; the rest stays owed. Kept apart from Selling a debt (you sell it to a buyer for cash, for less than it pays); Settling up with trading partners (everyone agrees to cancel together); Letting a debt go (you drop it and nobody gets it); and Paying what you can to everyone you owe (you are the one who owes). It usually starts when you owe someone and are owed by someone else, when the one who owes you also holds a debt of yours, or when a creditor asks to be paid in a debt.
no mirror: self: the one who takes the claim does the same act

examples.card: Pay a creditor with a debt owed to you.
examples.filled: The shop in Pune owes you ₹6,000 and you owe your flour supplier ₹6,000. Hand the supplier the shop's debt in place of paying?

examples.card: Hand a debt back to the one who owes it.
examples.filled: You owe Ravi £50 for a delivery and he owes you £80 for eggs. Each hand the other's debt back, so £50 is settled and £30 stays owed?

examples.card: Stand behind a debt you hand on.
examples.filled: You hand the miller Hassan's KSh 30,000 and offer to stand behind it up to 10,000. Hand it on with that?

you do this when: You hand on money you are owed, to pay a creditor with it.

name: Putting up a bond
card: You promise to be at the Saturday market by 9. Put £200 with Gita, to be Amara's if you are not there?
note: You put money with a third person as a penalty you choose in advance: if you do not do what you promised by a time, it becomes the other side's; if you do, it comes back to you. You, the other side and the holder sign three things first: what you promise, the time, and whose clock tells whether you were on time. Until that time passes the money is still yours. If you arrive in time, a receipt from the chosen clock shows it and the money goes back to you; if no such receipt exists by the time, the money goes to the other side, and that is a term you signed, so a message with an earlier time written on it does not save you. Both outcomes are read on the same clock, so a late arrival cannot win by being signed first. The bond is the whole penalty: it is what you put up, and your word reaches nothing else of yours, never your body. The holder signs that she holds it and may not use it. Kept apart from Holding money until a deal is done (the holder's side, money kept for a deal's two sides); Pledging something for a loan (a thing held against a debt); Pledging something as security (a thing held until a promise is kept, then returned); and Guaranteeing someone's loan (someone else pays if the borrower does not). It usually starts when a booking, a delivery or a job has a time that matters, when the other side asks for something behind your word, or when the time arrives.
no mirror: none: the one it pays is the other side, and the holder acts in Holding money until a deal is done

examples.card: Put money behind a promise to turn up.
examples.filled: Your catering for Amara's wedding in Lagos starts at 9. Put ₦40,000 with Gita, to go to Amara if you are not there by then?

examples.card: Back a delivery date with a bond.
examples.filled: You promise 200 kg of tomatoes to the hotel in Arusha by Friday noon. Put TSh 150,000 with the market master, to go to the hotel if you are late?

examples.card: Back a clean lab result with a bond.
examples.filled: Your lab reading may show a fault, and you promise a notice by Monday. Put £2,000 behind the notice, to be your buyer's if none is signed by then?

you do this when: You put money with a third person as a penalty you choose: it becomes theirs if you break your promise.

name: Naming a judge for a deal
card: You and the Kisumu grain buyer are agreeing a price for 30 tonnes. Name Mama Akinyi as your judge now, papers only, ruling within 5 days?
note: You and the other side, before any quarrel, write into your deal who will decide one if it comes, and how: the judge, and a backup if she stays silent for a time you set; whether she reads only papers or hears you; the date by which she must rule; a list of the facts you already agree on, so she need not rule on them; and who pays her fee, and whether the winner gets it back. You may name several judges and say how many must agree. A judge both of you named is the only one who decides; a side never judges itself. She is bound only by what she accepted when she took the role, and she never fills a gap: where nothing you signed covers a point she says 'no term', unless you both signed a clause that lets her read it by the trade. Kept apart from Asking for a ruling on a dispute (asking a judge to decide a quarrel that has begun); Settling a money quarrel by sealed bids (the two of you find a number, with no judge); and Trading under a rulebook (a whole circle's rules, with its own panel). It usually starts when you sign a deal where a lot is at stake, when the other side asks who would decide, or when a rulebook is named.
no mirror: self: both sides sign the same naming, and the judge acts in Ruling on a dispute

examples.card: Name the judge when you sign the deal.
examples.filled: You and a buyer in Tamale sign for 20 bags of shea. Name the market committee as judge, papers only, with a fee the loser pays?

examples.card: List the facts you already agree.
examples.filled: You and the caterer in Lyon agree the date, the 60 guests and the price. Write them down as agreed, so a judge only rules on the dessert?

examples.card: Name a backup judge.
examples.filled: Your judge may be away at harvest. Name a second one who takes over after 7 days of silence?

you do this when: Before any quarrel you write into your deal who will decide one if it comes, and how. Not asking a judge to rule on a quarrel that has begun.

name: Claiming for harm with no deal behind it
card: Your neighbour's spray drifted onto your organic carrots on the 3rd. Write the claim and name your judge?
note: You say, in writing that is sealed (only the people you name can read it), that someone crossed into your body, your place or your thing with no deal between you: a neighbour's spray drifting onto your organic carrots, a poisoned well, a stolen pot, a blow. You write what was crossed, who did it, the date and your evidence (photos, readings, witnesses), and you name the judge you want. The other person does not have to accept your judge; he can name his own, and whoever each judge's own offer (its `rulings` term) lets read sees that judge's ruling; that a ruling went unhonoured is public. A ruling moves nothing by itself and forces no one: it is a fact beside the record, and anyone who acts by force on a wrong ruling answers for it. Only the person harmed, or someone she handed her claim to (an heir, someone who bought it), can bring it; nobody brings it for 'society'. A rival's better bread, a lower price or a true review crosses nothing, so it is no claim. Kept apart from Complaining and putting it right (a deal went wrong); Asking for a ruling on a dispute (a judge both sides named); Claiming on a warranty (a fault a maker promised against); and Saying a signature was not your free word (about something you signed). It usually starts when your crop, stock or place is damaged by someone you have no deal with, while you can still show the evidence.

examples.card: Claim for spray that drifted onto your crop.
examples.filled: Your neighbour in Kent sprayed on a windy day and your organic strawberries are marked. Write the claim with photos and name your judge?

examples.card: Claim for a theft.
examples.filled: Someone took 12 crates from your stall in Lima overnight, and your camera shows the van. Write the claim and name your judge?

examples.card: Claim for fouled water.
examples.filled: A tannery upstream put waste in the stream your cattle drink from. Write the claim with the readings and name your judge?

you do this when: You say, in sealed writing, that someone crossed into your body, place or thing with no deal between you: spray drift, a stolen pot.

name: Saying a signature was not your free word
card: A market inspector made you sign that you paid the stall fee freely. Write beside it that you signed under force?
note: You write, beside something you signed, that it was not your free word, and why. There are three reasons: you signed under force (a threat of a blow or a seizure, not a hard bargain, a boss's order or a refusal to deal); the signature was not yours (your phone or key was taken and used); or you did not understand what you signed. You say what the threat was. It sits beside the signed thing for good: nothing is erased or unsigned, and it changes nothing by itself, because it is your word, a claim and not a verdict; only a judge the deal named can rule that the signed thing does not count. It is sealed, so only the people you name read it (a judge, a lender, a friend), it has no time limit, and only the person who signed can write it for herself. Kept apart from Claiming for harm with no deal behind it (an attack with no deal); Asking for a ruling on a dispute (a judge decides); Contesting a charge (answering an authority's demand); and Getting back in after losing your phone (getting your key back). It usually starts when you are made to sign, when you find something signed with a key that was taken, or when you later learn what you signed.

examples.card: Say you signed under force.
examples.filled: An officer with a stick made you sign "I paid the stall fee freely" at the market in Kisumu. Write that it was signed under force?

examples.card: Say it was not you.
examples.filled: Your phone was stolen and a loan of £300 was signed with your key. Write that it was not signed by you?

examples.card: Say you did not understand.
examples.filled: You signed a contract for 40 bags of seed in a language you cannot read. Write that you did not understand what you signed?

you do this when: You write beside something you signed that it was not your free word, and why.

name: Going into partnership
card: You and Nasra want to run the Saturday stall together. Write who puts in what and how you share it?
note: You and one or more people start a business or a job together and write down what each puts in (money, a van, a kitchen, land, your work), what share of the profit each gets, when it ends or how a partner leaves, and, because it can go badly, who loses what if it does. A quiet backer can sign too: she puts in money for a share, and the most she can lose is a sum she names. Each partner is bound only by what she signed. A promise of work binds only what she put up, never her person, and leaving is always open, at the cost she agreed up front. Where your terms say nothing about a loss, the card says 'not agreed' and fills nothing in. Kept apart from Putting money into a business (you put money into someone else's business and do not run it); Sharing ownership with your team (a share for the people who work there); and Having a business of your own (a business of your own). It usually starts when two people want to run a stall or a farm together, when a friend offers money for a share, or when a business has grown too big for one.
no mirror: self: every partner signs the same terms

examples.card: Start a stall together.
examples.filled: You and Nasra will run a juice stall in Mombasa, 60/40 on profit because she brings the blender. Write who puts in what and sign?

examples.card: Add a quiet backer.
examples.filled: Your aunt offers £3,000 for a share of the bakery in Leeds but wants no say. Sign her in as a backer who can lose at most £3,000?

examples.card: Say how it ends.
examples.filled: Two farmers in Punjab share a tractor and a field. Write when it ends, how one leaves, and who loses if the harvest fails?

you do this when: You and others start a business or job together and write down what each puts in, the shares, and who loses what if it fails.

name: Selling to be paid when they are paid
card: A trader in Kisumu wants 200 kg of dried fish. Sell it, with KSh 3,000 due the day Odhiambo pays him or when he returns what is unsold by the 20th?
note: You sell now and are paid when your buyer is paid, or when he gives back what he did not sell: fish to a trader who sells on, vegetables to a shop, bread to a kiosk. You write it plainly: 'my fish is yours now; your 3,000 is mine the day Odhiambo pays you, or when you return what is unsold by the 20th'. The goods are his from today unless you choose to keep the title until he has paid (see Selling on credit). The condition is another deal's payment, so you can read it only if the buyer lets you see that deal; if he does not, the card says 'cannot be read' and nothing is filled in. What he returns by the date is yours again, and what he keeps he owes for. If you signed no date, none is supposed. Kept apart from Selling on credit (the price is due on a day you set, whoever pays him); Selling through an agent (the goods stay yours and he takes a fee); Selling and buying in bulk (paid at handover); and Supplying on contract (a standing supply, paid on its terms). It usually starts when a trader asks to take stock before he has sold it, when he returns what did not sell, or when the one who pays him has paid.
no mirror: none yet: the buyer reads the same deal in Buying to sell on, with the pay-when-paid term

examples.card: Sell stock to be paid when the buyer is paid.
examples.filled: A stallholder in Nairobi takes 40 crates of tomatoes and will pay the day the hotel pays her. Sell on those terms?

examples.card: Sell on sale-or-return.
examples.filled: The kiosk near the school in Accra takes 100 loaves and will return what is unsold by Friday. Sell on sale-or-return, paid for what he keeps?

examples.card: See whether you can read his payment.
examples.filled: Your buyer in Dhaka will pay when his retailer pays but will not show you that deal. Sell anyway, or ask for a date instead?

you do this when: You sell now and are paid when your buyer is paid, or when he gives back what he did not sell.

name: Offering a friend a line of credit
card: Your cousin Wanjiru's shop in Embu often runs short before market day. Offer her up to KSh 50,000 for a month, if she is stuck?
note: You tell a friend or a regular: 'I will lend you up to 50,000 for a month if you are stuck.' You write the most you will lend (the cap), the dates it runs between, and that you may withdraw it for the future whenever you like; whatever she has already drawn stays owed. She draws when she needs to, and each draw is a loan she signs for. Nothing is owed until she draws. A line that is only said between kin binds nobody, so the cap is shown as a fact, and FoodOS never judges a family for asking. The lines open to you from others show beside it ('lines open to me: 3, total 150,000'). Kept apart from Lending money (money goes out now); Guaranteeing someone's loan (you pay someone else's lender); Setting your terms of trade (your rules for every customer); and Selling on credit (food now, money later). It usually starts when a friend or a regular is often short, when a season is about to start, or when a line is about to run out.
no mirror: none: the friend draws in Borrowing money

examples.card: Offer a friend a line for the lean weeks.
examples.filled: Your sister runs a stall in Cebu and is short each month before pay day. Offer her up to ₱10,000 until the end of March?

examples.card: Withdraw a line for the future.
examples.filled: Your line to Jomo is open until June, but his shop has closed. Withdraw it for any new draw and keep what he already owes?

examples.card: Cap the line low.
examples.filled: A neighbour asks for an open loan with no limit. Offer a line capped at KSh 20,000 for two months instead?

you do this when: You say 'I will lend you up to this much', for a period, and may withdraw it for the future.

name: Recording first use of a place
card: You have cleared the lower field and walked its edge with Kwame and Esi. Write down the first use and the boundary, sealed to the three of you?
note: You write down, as plainly as a price, that you put a place, or a use of it, to work first: the first clearing, a boundary walked with your neighbours, each planting, each water draw, each season fished, a spray or a smell you live with, a path you keep. You say what you did, the date, and the bounds of where and when, even the hours or the season. Neighbours can sign it with you. It is sealed: only you, the neighbours who signed and a judge you name read it, and it is never published as a map. It is evidence a judge reads, never title. A claim against a latecomer rests on a mark he could see (a fence, a path, a planted field, neighbours who saw it), so the card shows 'mark shown' or 'witnessed' apart from the sealed record, and 'use shown: none' means only none in what that reader holds. If you leave a field to rest you write 'resting until 2029': it is your word, and resting is not leaving, so the field stays yours until you let it go or hand it on in your own signed word. Kept apart from Registering your land (a public record with the authority); Keeping equipment and places in order (keeping it in repair); Logging (your own time); and Sharing a commons (rules among people who share a thing). It usually starts when you clear or plant new ground, when a water draw or a fishing season begins, when a neighbour asks where your boundary is, or when you rest a field.

examples.card: Write down the first clearing.
examples.filled: You cleared the scrub at the top of your plot near Eldoret in March and fenced it. Write down the first use with the date, sealed to the neighbours who saw?

examples.card: Walk the boundary with your neighbours.
examples.filled: Two neighbours will walk your plot's edge with you on Saturday. Write the boundary and ask them to sign as witnesses?

examples.card: Write down a water draw.
examples.filled: You have drawn water from the stream below Hill Farm at dawn since 2014. Write down the draw, with its hours and its season?

examples.card: Write that a field is resting.
examples.filled: Your lower field rests until 2029. Write "resting until 2029", so no one can read it as left?

you do this when: You write down that you put a place, or a use of it, to work first.

name: Getting a lot graded
card: Your coffee lot reaches the buyer in Mombasa and he says it is not the grade you sold. Ask the grader you both named, with 7 days to put it right?
note: You and the other side agree before delivery that a grader you both named will say only one thing about a lot: does it match what was described? She answers yes or no and nothing more; she does not say whose fault it is or what is owed. If it does not match, the seller has a window to replace the lot before anyone has broken their word. If you both signed it, she may instead give an allowance (keep it and take 5% off), which settles it. You agree beforehand the grader, the description, the standard she grades by (the glossary defines each grade word and how it is checked), the length of the window, whether an allowance is allowed, and who pays her. Only when the window passes with no fix does the delivery count as broken, and then your judge rules. Kept apart from Grading produce (sorting your own harvest before you sell it); Asking for a ruling on a dispute (a judge who decides fault and money); Naming a judge for a deal (who decides a quarrel); and Complaining and putting it right (you ask the seller to put it right). It usually starts when you trade by grade, as in coffee, cocoa, grain or fish, when a lot arrives that may not match, or when the window to fix it is running out.
no mirror: self: both sides sign the same grader and window

examples.card: Ask the grader whether a lot matches.
examples.filled: Your grain buyer in Lusaka says the maize is not the grade sold. Send the lot to the grader you both named and accept her yes or no?

examples.card: Take an allowance and keep the lot.
examples.filled: The grader says your cocoa is a grade lower than sold. Take 5% off and keep it, or give the seller 7 days to replace it?

examples.card: Replace the lot inside the window.
examples.filled: The grader says your maize is damp, and you have 5 days to replace it. Send a dry lot on Thursday?

you do this when: Before delivery you both name a grader who will say only whether a lot matches what was described: yes or no, no fault, no money.

name: Adding a weather clause
card: You sold 10 tonnes of maize for harvest and the rains are late. Add a clause: if under 300 mm falls by 15 March, you deliver 8 tonnes?
note: You and the other side add one clause to a deal for food not yet grown: if the rain (or heat, frost or wind) reads a certain way, the amount the seller must deliver drops by a quantity you wrote. You name the readers, two people or an operator you both trust, who each sign the public reading by a date they promised. A gauge or an office that signs nothing cannot make the clause fire. The relief is in quantity: the seller may deliver less, and he promises not to sell the withheld amount to anyone else; it is never a free cancellation. The card says plainly that a reading can fire when you lost nothing and stay quiet when you lost a lot. FoodOS offers the clause to a farmer selling forward and never adds it as a default; both sides sign it, or there is no clause. Kept apart from Agreeing a price for later (a price written today); Paying ahead for a crop (the sale itself); Taking out insurance (cover paid by a company); and Insuring each other (a pot that pays a loss). It usually starts when a farmer sells ahead of the season, when rains come late or early, or when the date for the readings comes.
no mirror: self: both sides sign the same clause

examples.card: Add a rain clause to a forward sale.
examples.filled: You sold 10 tonnes of maize in Eldoret for harvest. Add: if under 300 mm falls by 15 March, you deliver 8 tonnes?

examples.card: Name the readers.
examples.filled: Two rain-gauge keepers in your district sign a reading every Friday. Name them both as the readers of the clause?

examples.card: Promise not to sell the withheld maize elsewhere.
examples.filled: If the clause fires and you deliver 8 tonnes, the other 2 stay unsold to anyone else until the buyer agrees. Sign that promise?

you do this when: You add one clause to a deal for food not yet grown: if the weather reads a certain way the amount the seller must deliver drops. Not the sale itself, not insurance.

name: Trading under a rulebook
card: The Kisumu maize traders publish Lake Maize Rules v3. Trade this lot under it, naming it by its fingerprint?
note: You and the other side name a rulebook that a trade circle has published (grain dealers, a market's traders, a coffee co-op), by its fingerprint, which pins the exact version, so a later change to the rulebook never reaches a deal made under the old one. Both of you sign by naming it, so the weaker side never has to ask for protection and look difficult. Or you start one for your group: its terms, its panel of judges, its deadlines, its fee. Its glossary says what each trade word means and how it is checked ('a debe is 20 litres, against the clerk's tin'). A rulebook may set a cover price (damages are the gap to the lowest of three signed quotes, so nobody shows their margins), a judge who reads only papers on a deadline, and a window to fix a bad lot. It binds only those who signed it and never excuses an invasion of someone who did not. A judge never fills a gap: where nothing signed covers a point she says 'no term', unless both signed a clause that lets her read it by the trade. Kept apart from Running a group (starting the group itself); Naming a judge for a deal (the judge for one deal); Getting a lot graded (one grader and window); and Taking part in a group (joining a group's own rules). It usually starts when you trade in a circle's trade, when a circle writes its rules, or when a rulebook has a new version.

examples.card: Name a rulebook by its fingerprint.
examples.filled: Your sale of 40 bags to a trader in Kisumu can run under Lake Maize Rules v3. Name it by fingerprint, so a later version never changes this deal?

examples.card: Check a word against the glossary.
examples.filled: The rulebook says a debe is 20 litres, checked against the clerk's tin. Check your debe against the clerk's tin before you sign?

examples.card: Start a rulebook for your group.
examples.filled: Your coffee co-op in Nyeri trades by rules nobody has written down. Write them as a rulebook, with a panel of judges and a glossary, for the members to sign?

you do this when: You and the other side name a circle's published rulebook by its fingerprint, so later changes to it never reach this deal.

name: Getting paid on a code
card: Chidi will pay you £5 when you show him the four-digit code at his door. Take the delivery on those terms?
note: You are paid when you show a code, with no judge, no clock and no third party. The customer gives you a code (four digits at the door, a word, a number on a slip); when you show it to him, the money he signed for becomes yours. A pick-up works the same way: whoever shows the code collects the order. Any computer checks it alike, so nobody can argue about it. Anyone who learns the code can show it, but it pays only the person already named, and if no code is shown nothing is paid and the money stays his. Kept apart from Carrying for pay (the delivery job itself); Holding money until a deal is done (a person holds the money and decides); Moving food to someone (the collecting); and Running a pickup point (a point where many orders are collected). It usually starts when a delivery or a pick-up is about to be handed over, when the customer sends the code, or when the order is at the door.
no mirror: none yet: the payer writes his side when he publishes it

examples.card: Take a delivery paid on a code.
examples.filled: Chidi's £5 delivery in Leeds is paid when you show the four-digit code he gives at the door. Take the job on those terms?

examples.card: Hand a pick-up to whoever shows the code.
examples.filled: A customer's order is ready at your stall in Nairobi and the code is 4471. Hand it to whoever shows it?

examples.card: Ask for the code before you set off.
examples.filled: A customer in Jakarta has not sent a code for the Rp 90,000 order. Ask him for it before you deliver?

you do this when: You are paid when you show a code, with no judge, no clock and no third party.

name: Selling what you know before it is read
card: You hear tomorrow's price at the Kampala depot will be 15% higher. Offer it sealed to the trader who asked?
note: You sell something you know before the buyer has seen it: tomorrow's price at the depot, which road is shut, which field is ripe, a route, a season note. You post a signed line that says what kind of thing it is, and a sealed copy of it (locked, and only you hold the key). The buyer's payment is on a condition: it becomes yours when you show the opening, so that he can read it. The price is for being first: once read, it is anyone's, and you cannot sell the same reading to the same buyer twice. Whether it was true is for the judge the deal named, not for the system. You sell the reading of it, never a right to the fact, since an idea is not property, and the buyer is bound only by what he signed. Kept apart from Telling others a price (shared openly, with no names); Selling your know-how (a method, with a promise not to use it yourself); Posting an offer or a want (your goods or service, shown to everyone); and Giving your word on something (a verdict on a thing). It usually starts when you learn something before others do, when a trader asks what the price will be, or when the news would be worth less by tomorrow.
no mirror: none yet: the buyer's side is written when a buyer publishes it

examples.card: Sell tomorrow's price before it is public.
examples.filled: You know the Kampala depot will pay 15% more tomorrow, and a trader asks. Offer it sealed for UGX 20,000?

examples.card: Sell a route.
examples.filled: A back road to Mombasa port is open while the main road is shut. Sell it sealed to the haulier who asked?

examples.card: Show the opening once he has paid.
examples.filled: Wanjiku's trader paid KSh 500 for a sealed tip on the maize price. Show him the opening so the payment is yours?

you do this when: You sell something you know before the buyer has seen it: tomorrow's price, which road is shut.

name: Issuing paper notes
card: Forty of your regulars in the village have no phone. Print KSh 100 paper notes, held in full and paid when the code is shown?
note: You print slips for people with no phone. Each slip is your promise to pay a sum to whoever shows it: the holder needs no key, no phone and no account, and hands it on like cash. Each slip has a serial, and a code under a scratch strip is its key; whoever shows the code is paid, and each slip is paid once. You say first which of two kinds you issue. 'On demand' means the money behind the slips is held in full, so any holder can take it any time and you can show the money. 'On request, in the order people ask, while I have it' means you lend out some of what is behind, so holders are paid in the order they ask, and only while you have it. A slip never says 'on demand' unless the money is there. The slip is your word and the paper is never title. Kept apart from Selling vouchers (credit for what you supply); Keeping money with a bank or wallet (an account in a name); Trading with community credits (a circle's own unit); and Saving with a collector (someone collects from you each day). It usually starts when a group with no phones wants to trade, when your regulars ask to carry credit, or when you hold money for others.
no mirror: none: the holder needs no account, and shows the code in Buying a voucher or pass

examples.card: Print notes for traders with no phone.
examples.filled: A market in Kisumu has 60 traders with no phone. Print KSh 50 notes they can hand on, with the money held in full?

examples.card: Say which kind of note it is.
examples.filled: You lend out part of what backs your notes. Mark them "on request, in the order people ask" and not "on demand"?

examples.card: Pay a slip when the code is shown.
examples.filled: A trader shows slip 0417 with its code. Pay the KSh 100 once and mark it paid?

you do this when: You print slips for people with no phone.

name: Settling a money quarrel by sealed bids
card: You and the caterer disagree over a £600 bill. Each write a secret number and open them together?
note: You and the other side, stuck over how much one of you owes, each write a number in secret: the most you would pay, the least you would take. Each number is locked, with a date by a clock you both chose. When both are in, both locks open together. If the numbers overlap, the middle is shown, and you can settle there by an ordinary payment or ask your judge to confirm it; if they do not, you see only 'no overlap' and not the numbers. A number opened late counts for nothing. It binds only by what you both signed in the form, and nothing is forced. Kept apart from Asking for a ruling on a dispute (a judge decides); Naming a judge for a deal (a judge chosen before any quarrel); Releasing each other (ending everything between you); and Bargaining for your members (terms for many). It usually starts when a bill, a damage or a price is disputed and neither side wants to ask a judge.
no mirror: self: both sides do the same thing

examples.card: Each write your number in secret.
examples.filled: You say the supplier owes you KSh 40,000 for spoiled goods. Lock in the least you would take, while he locks in the most he would pay?

examples.card: Settle in the middle.
examples.filled: Your numbers overlap: you would take 30,000 and he would pay 36,000. Settle at 33,000?

examples.card: Learn only that there is no overlap.
examples.filled: He would pay at most 20,000 and you would take at least 30,000. Take it to your judge, having seen only "no overlap"?

you do this when: You two are stuck on how much one owes: each seals a number, the most you would pay and the least you would take, and no judge decides.

name: Trading futures and options
no mirror: self: both sides do the same thing
card: Cocoa for September delivery is $9,300 a tonne on the exchange and your buyers will want 40 tonnes then. Sell a futures contract to fix the price?
note: You fix today, on an exchange, a price for food you will buy or sell later, or you buy the right to. A futures contract binds both sides to buy and sell at the date; an option costs a premium, which is gone if you do not use it, and gives the right but not the duty. The exchange's clearing house stands between the two traders, so you deal with it and never with the other side, and it asks for margin: money you leave with it against a price move, topped up when the price goes against you, by a deadline, or it closes the position for you. Most contracts are closed by the opposite trade before delivery; few go to delivery of real food at a set grade, place and size. A hedge covers food you really hold or will make, so a loss on the contract meets a gain on the food; a bet with no food behind it is speculation and all of it is yours. What usually goes wrong is basis (your local price does not follow the exchange's), a contract size that does not fit your lot, a margin call you cannot meet, and a broker's commission you did not count. Kept apart from Agreeing a price for later (the two of you fix a price between yourselves, no exchange, no margin); Buying at auction (the price is found by bidding on the day, for food you can see); and Paying ahead for a crop (a real buyer pays for a real crop). It usually starts when you plant or buy stock whose price may move before you sell, a buyer asks for a fixed price months ahead, or a margin call is due.

examples.card: Hedge a crop you have planted.
examples.filled: Your maize in Zambia is planted and the price may fall by harvest. Sell futures on 50 tonnes to fix today's price?

examples.card: Buy the right to sell, not the duty.
examples.filled: Coffee is $2.30 a pound and you fear a fall before your June sales. Buy a put option for a premium of 6 cents?

examples.card: Meet a margin call.
examples.filled: Wheat moved against your hedge and the clearing house asks for $4,200 by 10 tomorrow. Pay the margin?

examples.card: Close a position before delivery.
examples.filled: Your September sugar futures are two weeks from delivery and you have no warehouse. Close them with the opposite trade?

you do this when: You fix a price for food on an exchange, through its clearing house and with margin; the two of you do not fix it between yourselves.

name: Opening a letter of credit
card: Your Rotterdam buyer will pay $48,000 for the coffee only when you ship. Ask his bank to open a letter of credit in your favour?
note: You ask a bank to promise a seller payment, in its own name, when the seller shows the papers the buyer named: a bill of lading, an invoice, a quality certificate, an insurance paper. The buyer asks his bank to issue it and pays the bank a fee and often leaves money or credit with it; the seller, who is the one paid, may ask a bank near her to confirm it, so she is paid even if the buyer's bank fails. The bank pays on the papers alone, never on the food: papers that differ from the credit by a word, a date or a weight are refused, so most losses are a mistake in the papers, a shipment a day late, or a credit that expires before the goods can leave. Check the credit's last date to ship, the last date to show papers, who pays each bank's fees, and whether it can be cancelled without your word (an irrevocable credit cannot). Kept apart from Exporting food (the sale itself, which the credit pays); Agreeing a price for later (a price, not a bank's promise to pay); and Selling a debt (a debt already owed is sold at a discount). It usually starts when a new buyer abroad wants to buy but you have never been paid by him, a big first order is agreed, or a buyer's bank offers one.

examples.card: Ask a buyer to open one for a first order.
examples.filled: A new importer in Dubai wants 20 tonnes of dates and you have never met him. Ask him to open a letter of credit before you ship?

examples.card: Check papers against the credit.
examples.filled: Your credit says shipment by 30 June and the bill of lading shows 1 July. Ask the buyer to amend it before you present the papers?

examples.card: Ask a local bank to confirm it.
examples.filled: The buyer's bank is in a country with little foreign money. Ask your bank to add its confirmation for a fee of 0.8%?

examples.card: Open one to buy abroad.
examples.filled: A Brazilian mill wants payment against papers for 100 tonnes of sugar. Ask your bank to open a credit of $62,000?

you do this when: A bank promises to pay on papers, in its own name; the sale it pays is a different deal.

name: Buying on lease-to-own
card: A solar pump costs $900 and the seller offers $40 a month for 26 months, yours at the last payment. Take the lease-to-own?
note: You use a machine from the day it is delivered and pay for it in parts; it becomes yours only with the last payment, or after a small final one. Until then the seller still owns it and can take it back if you miss payments, so you carry the wear and the breakage but not yet the title. Hire purchase, rent-to-own and pay-as-you-go devices (a pump or a freezer that stops until you pay) are the same shape. The price is the whole sum you will pay, not the monthly figure: add every payment, the deposit and the fees, and set it against the cash price. Check who insures it, who repairs it, what happens to the payments already made if you stop (some contracts keep them all), whether you may sell or lend it before it is yours, and whether the device can be switched off for a missed payment. Kept apart from Buying equipment (it is yours at once, paid in one go); Renting something (it never becomes yours); and Borrowing money (you get money, not the thing, and it is yours from the start). It usually starts when you need a machine that pays for itself over time, a seller offers instalments at the till, or your cash will not stretch to the cash price.

examples.card: Compare the lease with the cash price.
examples.filled: A walk-in cooler costs £2,400 cash or £95 a month for 30 months. Take the lease-to-own at £2,850 in all?

examples.card: Take a pay-as-you-go device.
examples.filled: A solar freezer comes for KSh 3,000 down and KSh 450 a week for a year, locked if you miss two weeks. Take it?

examples.card: Buy out the last payments early.
examples.filled: You have paid 20 of 26 months on your dehydrator. Pay the remaining £228 now and own it?

examples.card: Ask what happens if you stop.
examples.filled: Your contract says the seller keeps every payment if you stop. Ask for the payments to count towards a smaller machine instead?

you do this when: You use the thing now and own it only after the last payment; until then it is the seller's.

name: Getting paid early on a buyer's approved invoice

sides.from: Getting paid early on a buyer's approved invoice

card: A supermarket has approved your £18,000 invoice, due in 90 days. Get paid £17,550 now by selling it to its bank?
note: You are paid early on an invoice a big buyer has approved: the buyer approves it in its own system, and a bank or finance company the buyer works with pays the supplier at once, less a small discount, then collects the full sum from the buyer on the due date. It is sometimes called reverse factoring. Because the bank is paid by the big buyer, the discount follows the buyer's credit, not yours, so it is far lower than a loan to a small supplier would cost. It is only open for invoices the buyer has approved, so a buyer that disputes the goods, or never approves, leaves you without it. Check the rate as a yearly figure, whether you may refuse the early payment, whether the buyer may stretch its payment date (some use it to pay later and later), and whether the invoice is sold outright or the bank may come back to you if the buyer does not pay. Kept apart from Selling a debt (you choose the buyer of the debt and the discount is bargained, for an invoice nobody approved); Borrowing against stored stock (money lent against food in a store); and Selling on credit (you are the one waiting for the money). It usually starts when a large buyer offers the scheme, an invoice is approved and cash is short, or your payment terms with a buyer lengthen.

examples.card: Take the early payment on an approved invoice.
examples.filled: Your £18,000 invoice to a chain is approved for payment in 90 days. Sell it to its bank for £17,550 today?

examples.card: Compare the yearly rate.
examples.filled: The discount is 1.1% for 75 days against your overdraft at 14% a year. Take the early payment?

examples.card: Ask for a fixed payment date.
examples.filled: The buyer has moved its payment date from 60 to 90 days twice this year. Ask for the date to be written into your terms?

examples.card: Check who carries the risk.
examples.filled: The contract lets the bank claim the money back from you if the buyer does not pay. Ask for the sale to be outright?

you do this when: A bank pays you early because a big buyer approved your invoice, at the buyer's credit, and collects from the buyer.

name: Paying a retailer to list your product

sides.from: Charging a supplier to list its product
sides.to: Paying a retailer to list your product

card: A supermarket chain will stock your sauce in 60 stores for a listing fee of £6,000 and a promotion. Pay the fee?
note: You pay a retailer to put your product on its shelf: a listing or slotting fee for each store or each line, a fee to be in the leaflet or at the end of an aisle, a fee for a promotion, sometimes a rebate paid back at year end. The fee buys the chance to sell, not a sale: the retailer does not promise to buy more, and often takes the product off if it does not sell in a few weeks. Ask what you get for it: which shelf, how many facings, for how long, from which date, and what happens to the fee if the line is dropped early. Add the other costs a listing brings: free stock for the first order, returns of what does not sell, a delivery window you can be fined for missing, and payment terms of 60 days or more. Work out what each store must sell to cover the fee before you pay it. Kept apart from Paying to be shown (you pay to be seen, not to be on a shelf); Renting land or a place to trade (a pitch you run yourself); and Supplying on contract (a standing supply at a set price and volume). It usually starts when a retailer offers a listing, a buyer asks for a contribution to a promotion, or a new product is ready for shops.

examples.card: Weigh a listing fee against sales.
examples.filled: A grocer wants £6,000 to list your sauce in 60 stores. Each store would need to sell 24 jars a month to cover it. Pay the fee?

examples.card: Ask what the fee buys.
examples.filled: A chain asks KSh 150,000 to list your honey and says nothing of shelf or time. Ask for the facings, the weeks and a refund if it is delisted?

examples.card: Pay for a promotion.
examples.filled: A wholesaler offers a front-of-aisle display for ¥80,000 for two weeks. Pay for it?

examples.card: Take a rebate instead.
examples.filled: A buyer will list your cheese with no fee if you pay back 4% of sales each year. Take the rebate?

you do this when: You pay a retailer to be on its shelf, and nothing is promised about selling.

name: Forwarding freight and clearing customs for others

sides.from: Forwarding freight and clearing customs for others

card: A Kenyan avocado exporter has 12 tonnes for Rotterdam on Friday. Quote for booking the flight, the papers and the customs?
note: You arrange someone else's shipment from door to door without carrying it yourself: book space on a ship, plane or lorry, prepare the papers (invoice, packing list, bill of lading or airway bill, health and origin certificates), clear it through customs at each end as a licensed broker, arrange insurance, and chase it on the way. You act as the shipper's agent, so you answer for the papers being right and the duty being worked out right; the carrier answers for the goods in transit. Pass on the carrier's charges, duties and port fees at cost and show your own fee apart. Wrong codes for the food, a missing certificate or a late booking are what delay a shipment and make food spoil at a port. Keep every paper and its date for the years the customs authority asks. Kept apart from Carrying for pay (you carry the goods yourself); Clearing goods through customs (clearing your own goods); and Exporting food (selling the food). It usually starts when an exporter or importer has goods ready and no one to arrange the road, a new market needs papers the shipper has never seen, or a shipment is stuck at a border.

examples.card: Quote for a whole shipment.
examples.filled: A Kenyan exporter has 12 tonnes of avocados for Rotterdam on Friday. Quote for the flight, the papers and customs at both ends?

examples.card: Check the code for the food.
examples.filled: A shipper declares dried mango under a code with a lower duty than the one the officer used last time. Ask for the product sheet before you file?

examples.card: Chase a shipment stuck at a port.
examples.filled: A container of cocoa has sat at Antwerp for four days waiting for a plant health paper. Ask the exporter to send the certificate today?

examples.card: Show your fee apart.
examples.filled: The carrier's rate is $2,100, duties $640 and port fees $230. Send the shipper the bill with your fee of $180 on its own line?

you do this when: You arrange and clear a shipment for someone else without carrying it; the papers and customs are the job.

name: Breeding plants and saving seed
card: Your best tomato plants this year set early and resisted blight. Save their seed and mark the line?
note: You raise the next generation of plants on purpose: saving seed from the plants that did best, crossing two parents for a new kind, taking cuttings and grafts, or growing young plants in a nursery to sell on or to plant out yourself. Pick on what you need (earliness, yield, taste, resistance, keeping time), save from many plants rather than a few so the line does not narrow, label every lot with its parent, year and place, and dry and store seed cool, dark and dry, testing a sample for germination before you rely on it. Some crops cross with their neighbours, so they need distance or a barrier; hybrids do not come true from seed. Selling plants or seed is a sale of goods (Selling growing supplies). A new variety is know-how, an idea, which no one owns: you may sell your signed word about who may use it, and your own plants are yours. A plant variety right is a monopoly the state grants (Registering your brand has the same shape); where you live may restrict selling or swapping some seed. Kept apart from Growing crops (raising the food, not the next plants); Breeding animals (animals, not plants); Growing trees and vines (a long crop kept for fruit); and Raising animals (animals, not plants). It usually starts when a crop is ripening and the best plants show, sowing time nears, a neighbour asks for seed, or you want young plants for the next season.

examples.card: Save seed from your best plants.
examples.filled: Your bean rows in Ethiopia have three plants that held on through the dry spell. Mark them and save their seed?

examples.card: Test seed before sowing.
examples.filled: Your saved seed is two years old. Sow 50 on damp paper to see how many sprout before you plant the field?

examples.card: Run a small nursery.
examples.filled: Your greenhouse in Pune has 400 spare chilli seedlings and sowing is a week away. Pot them for the neighbours' farms?

examples.card: Take cuttings from a good vine.
examples.filled: One grapevine in the old plot fruits earliest. Take 30 cuttings in winter to plant out in spring?

you do this when: You raise the next plants on purpose, from seed, cuttings or crosses, before anything is sold.

name: Collecting from many small growers
card: A centre in Meru gets milk twice a day from 140 farmers and pays each by fat and cleanliness. Open the day's collection?
note: You run, or deliver to, a collection centre that takes small lots of milk, tea leaf, coffee cherry or vegetables from many small growers at one place and time, weighs and tests each lot in front of the grower, pays by a published quality schedule (fat and solids for milk, cleanliness and grade for produce), and sells the whole on to a processor or buyer. Each grower is paid for what was received and graded, with the weights and the test written in a book or on a slip they keep. The centre carries the price risk between collecting and selling, and cold milk, shade for leaf, and a quick sale are what stop loss. A rule for deductions (for transport, a levy, inputs bought on credit) is signed by those who join and binds only them. Pay on a set day and show every deduction; a grower with a doubt can ask for a retest. Kept apart from Buying to sell on (a trader buying from the market); Selling at a stall, a gate or a screen (growers selling for themselves); and Selling through an agent (an agent taking a cut on the day's price). It usually starts when growers are too small to sell alone, a processor wants steady volume, or a collection day comes round.

examples.card: Pay by quality.
examples.filled: A grower's milk tested at 3.1% fat and a bit sour this morning. Pay for the lot at the lower grade and show the test?

examples.card: Show every deduction.
examples.filled: At month end you took KSh 1,800 for transport and KSh 2,400 for feed on credit from a grower. Send her the slip with each line?

examples.card: Reject a lot with a reason.
examples.filled: A can of milk arrived warm after a long walk. Test it, write the result and tell the farmer why it is refused?

examples.card: Sell the day's bulk.
examples.filled: Your tank holds 3,400 litres and the processor's truck comes at 4. Weigh it and sell the lot?

you do this when: Many small growers deliver to one place and are paid by a signed quality schedule; you are not trading in a market.

name: Handling landings for others

sides.to: Landing a catch or load for handling

card: Three boats land at Elmina tonight with 2,100 kilos between them. Weigh, grade and record each catch for the owners?
note: You run the place where a catch or a load comes ashore or into a hall, and you handle it for the people who bring it: you weigh it on a scale they can see, sort or grade it, write down who brought what and when, keep it cold or shaded until it is sold or collected, and give each owner a slip that is theirs. You hold the goods only for the owner, never as your own, so you may not sell, mix or use them except as agreed, and a loss is yours to answer for as agreed. Your fee is a set rate per kilo or per lot, shown before, and a record kept honestly is the work: it is what a buyer, a bank and a regulator will read, and what a quota or a levy is counted from. Check the scale against a known weight each day, write the weight in front of the owner, and never let a lot with no owner's name go in. Kept apart from Running a market (you let out places to many sellers); Running an auction (you ring the bidding); and Storing food with someone (goods held for a stay against a receipt, not handled on the day). It usually starts when a boat or lorry arrives with a lot, a quota day opens, or a buyer asks for the day's weights.

examples.card: Weigh and record a catch.
examples.filled: A canoe landed 140 kilos of sardines at Tema, owner Kojo Mensah. Weigh them in front of him and write the slip?

examples.card: Keep a lot cold until collected.
examples.filled: A buyer collects at 5 and it is 28 degrees. Move his three crates of prawns to the cold room and note the time?

examples.card: Check the scale.
examples.filled: The scale reads 4.9 on a 5-kilo test weight. Fix it before the next boat and tell the two who weighed on it today?

examples.card: Report a quota count.
examples.filled: The week's landings from your site add to 18 tonnes against a 20-tonne limit. Send the count to the owners?

you do this when: You weigh, record and hold a lot for its owners at the place it comes ashore; you do not buy it or sell it.

name: Tracing a batch back and forward

sides.to: Tracing a batch back and forward

card: A customer was ill after your chicken pies. Which flour, eggs and filling went into batch 14 and who received the other pies?
note: You follow a batch one step back and one step forward: where each thing in it came from (the supplier, their lot number, the delivery date) and who got what you made (the customer, the date, how much), so that a fault can be found at its source and pulled before it spreads. Each food business keeps its own step: you write the lot numbers on what comes in and on what goes out, and you can show them within hours. When a problem is found, you ask each supplier and customer for their step, and the chain is read link by link; a missing or smudged lot number is a break, and the batch is treated as the widest it could be. It stops short of a recall: tracing finds the batch and its reach, and a recall is the pulling back that follows. It is also how a good name is proved: you can show a buyer where a thing came from. Keep the records as long as the law and your buyers ask, usually a year past the date on the pack. Kept apart from Acting on a recall (food is pulled back after the tracing); Labelling food (the words on the pack); and Logging (what you hold today). It usually starts when a customer is ill or complains, a supplier warns of a fault, a buyer or inspector asks where something came from, or you test your own records before they are tested.

examples.card: Trace a batch back to its supplier.
examples.filled: A pie from batch 14 had a stone in it. Which flour lot and which supplier went into it?

examples.card: Trace a batch forward to who got it.
examples.filled: A supplier warns that egg lot E-2291 may carry salmonella. Which of your batches used it and which customers have them?

examples.card: Test your records.
examples.filled: Pick one batch of salsa and find its tomato farm, the date it arrived and every shop that got a jar, in under an hour. Run the test?

examples.card: Ask a supplier for their step.
examples.filled: Your sesame lot has no origin on its invoice. Ask the importer for its lot and where it came from?

you do this when: You follow a batch back to its sources and forward to who got it; pulling it back is a different act.

name: Auditing your own supplier
card: A bakery chain buys your oats and wants to see your mill before it renews. Agree a date for it to audit you?
note: You are audited by a buyer, or you audit your own supplier: a buyer checks a supplier for itself, as a condition of buying, rather than leaving it to a state inspector or a certifier: it visits the farm, factory or kitchen, reads the records, looks at hygiene, traceability, workers' conditions or whatever its own standard names, and writes up what it found with a date to fix each fault. It is called a second-party audit. The supplier agrees to it in the deal, usually with notice, and the buyer's finding is the buyer's word, never a public mark: it may stop buying, ask for a fix, or buy on stricter terms. Ask for the checklist beforehand, who comes, what they may photograph, who pays (usually the buyer), and what happens to what they see (kept to the two of you). A supplier who has a certificate or has passed an inspection can show it, and a buyer may accept it instead of coming. Keep your own copy of the finding and what you fixed. Kept apart from Inspecting a food place (an authority, under law); Getting or giving a certificate (an outside body issues a mark that any buyer can read); and Checking who you are dealing with (looking at what someone chose to show). It usually starts when a buyer renews or starts a contract, a complaint points at a supplier, or a retailer's own standard asks for an audit each year.

examples.card: Agree a date for a buyer's audit.
examples.filled: The chain that buys your oats wants a two-day audit before it renews in March. Offer the 12th and 13th?

examples.card: Ask for the checklist first.
examples.filled: A buyer announces a visit to your mill and gives no list. Ask for its standard and what it will look at?

examples.card: Fix a fault by a date.
examples.filled: The auditor found no hand-wash sign at the packing door and gave you 14 days. Fix it and send a photo?

examples.card: Audit a supplier yourself.
examples.filled: You buy honey from a co-op in the hills and have never seen its store. Visit and read its records before you order again?

you do this when: A buyer checks its own supplier, at its own cost, with findings that stay between the two of them.

name: Receiving a patronage refund
card: Your co-op made a surplus of KSh 2.4 million and will return it by how much milk each member sold. Your share is KSh 38,000. Accept it?
note: You get back part of your co-op's yearly surplus, by how much you used it: a co-operative that trades with its own members returns its yearly surplus to them in proportion to how much each one used it, not how much each put in: a farmer by what she sold through it, a shopper by what he bought. It is a refund of what was charged too much or paid too little, not a profit on shares. The members decide at the yearly meeting how much goes back and how much stays to build the co-op, so it is only due once the board has proposed it and the members have voted. Often part is paid in cash and part is kept as shares or a credit in your name, which is yours but paid out later, on a date or when you leave. Keep your own record of what you sold or bought through the co-op, so the share can be checked. Ask what the cash and the credit parts are, when the credit is paid, and whether you are taxed on the whole in the year it is declared. Kept apart from Sharing profit with your team (workers sharing what the business earned); Splitting takings (a group dividing what it earned by a rule agreed before the work); and Putting money into a business (money put in for a share of the earnings). It usually starts when a co-op's year ends and the accounts show a surplus, a general meeting is called, or you leave and your credit falls due.

examples.card: Take a refund by your use.
examples.filled: Your co-op returns KSh 38,000 on the 9,500 litres of milk you sold through it. Accept it, half in cash and half as credit?

examples.card: Check your share.
examples.filled: The slip shows 6,200 kilos of coffee but your own book says 7,100. Ask the secretary to look at the weighing record?

examples.card: Vote on how much goes back.
examples.filled: The board proposes returning half of the surplus and keeping half for a new cold room. Vote at the meeting?

examples.card: Ask when the credit is paid.
examples.filled: £140 of your refund is a credit in your name. Ask the co-op the date it is paid out?

you do this when: A co-op returns its surplus to members by how much each used it, after its members voted.

name: Spending a group's fair-trade premium
no mirror: none: one group, one plan
card: Buyers paid $0.20 a pound extra on 31,000 pounds of coffee this year. Spend the $6,200 premium on the washing station roof?
note: You and your group hold and spend a fair-trade premium: a fair-trade or similar scheme makes buyers pay a premium on top of the price, and the premium goes to the group of growers or workers, not to each person. The group holds it in its own account and spends it by a rule it wrote and every member agreed to: a vote at a general meeting on what to spend it on (a school, a well, a processing machine, a loan fund, a bonus), a committee that keeps the books, and a report back to every member showing what came in, what was spent and what is left. Some schemes require a share to go to the community or to workers rather than the owners, and a certifier checks the spending. It is the group's money, held for the group, so no one member or buyer may spend it alone; keep it apart from the group's ordinary money, and keep the receipts. Kept apart from Pooling money (a standing pot the group chose to fill itself); Getting or giving a certificate (the mark that makes buyers pay it); and Receiving a patronage refund (a surplus returned by use). It usually starts when a sale with a premium is paid, the year's premium is known, or a general meeting is called to decide how to spend it.

examples.card: Vote on how to spend it.
examples.filled: This year's premium is $6,200. The meeting can fix the washing station roof or fund school fees. Put both to a vote?

examples.card: Show the books to every member.
examples.filled: The premium account has $1,150 left after the well. Print the receipts and read them at the meeting?

examples.card: Keep the premium apart.
examples.filled: The premium sits in the same account as the dues. Open a second account for it?

examples.card: Pass a share to workers.
examples.filled: The scheme asks that part of the premium go to hired pickers. Agree the share at the meeting?

you do this when: A group holds a premium that is the group's, and spends it by its own rule and vote.

name: Exhibiting at a trade fair

sides.from: Selling stands at a trade fair

card: A food fair in Cologne has a 9-square-metre stand for €4,200. Take the stand and show your pickles?
note: You rent a stand at a trade fair for a few days to show your food to buyers, press and other makers, and bring home leads. The fee is for the floor space, and the extras are the real cost: the stand's walls and lights, power and water, a fair's catalogue entry, travel, a sample stock, a lodging, and your own time. Samples may need a food permit for the fair's country, and a label in its language. Plan what you want (ten buyers who will order, one distributor, a press story), take cards or a way to write a lead down on the spot, write each lead's name and what they asked for that evening, and follow up in the week after, since most leads die in the following month. Check the fair's buyer list, last year's numbers, and the cancellation terms. Kept apart from Renting land or a place to trade (a market pitch you run to sell to the public); Paying to be shown (an advert or a sponsorship); and Paying a retailer to list your product (a shelf in a chain's store). It usually starts when a fair is announced in your trade, a distributor tells you to show up, or a launch needs buyers in one room.

examples.card: Take a stand and plan the leads.
examples.filled: A fair in Paris has a 9-square-metre stand for €4,200. Take it, aiming for ten buyers who leave an address?

examples.card: Check the permit for samples.
examples.filled: The fair is in Dubai and your jam has no Arabic label. Ask the organiser what a sample needs?

examples.card: Follow up the leads.
examples.filled: You came home with 34 cards from the fair. Write each one's name and what they asked for, and send the first note by Friday?

examples.card: Share a stand with others.
examples.filled: A regional board offers a shared stand with five other makers for a third of the fee. Take a corner?

you do this when: You rent a stand for a few days to show your food to buyers, and the leads are what you are paying for.

name: Selling your data as a panel

sides.from: Selling your data as a panel

card: A research firm will pay £6 a month for your weekly shopping record and a short survey, with your name removed. Join its panel?
note: You let a research firm or a company read your record, or answer its questions, again and again for a fee, so it can learn what people like you eat and buy. Your data is not property, since a fact about you can be known by others without leaving your hands, so what you sell is your signed word that they may read it and your promise about it, and what they promise in return is the part to read: what exactly they see (which fields, which months), whether your name goes, who else sees it, how long they keep it, what they may do with it, and how you stop. Nothing leaves your node without your yes, and the read-back shows who will see each block. A price that is high for little data, or a promise to anonymise that cannot be kept (a few rare facts name you), is a warning. You can leave at any time and what they already read stays with them as their copy, so choose what you share with that in mind. Kept apart from Sharing a record (someone reads it for a time, not as a panel); Selling what you know before it is read (a finding you made and sell once); and Telling others a price (a price shared for free with no names). It usually starts when a firm invites you to a panel, a survey arrives with a fee, or you learn that your shopping record has value to someone.

examples.card: Choose what a panel sees.
examples.filled: A panel wants your shopping record for £6 a month. Share the grocery lines and keep the rest of your record out?

examples.card: Ask how long they keep it.
examples.filled: The panel's terms say they may keep your answers for ever. Ask for them to be dropped after two years or leave?

examples.card: Leave a panel.
examples.filled: You have been on a panel for 14 months and the survey takes an hour a week. Leave and say what they may keep?

examples.card: Check who else sees it.
examples.filled: A research firm says it shares results with partners and does not name them. Ask who the partners are before you join?

you do this when: You are paid, again and again, for letting a research panel read part of your record; it is your word, never a handed-over thing.

name: Paying for market research
card: You will launch a hot sauce in three cities and do not know who will buy it. Pay a researcher £2,800 to ask 300 shoppers?
note: You pay someone to find out what a market wants before you decide: a survey of shoppers, a taste test, interviews with buyers, a count of what competitors sell and at what price, or a report on a market's size. Decide the question you want answered first and what you will do differently for each answer; if no answer changes what you do, do not buy it. Ask who will be asked (how many, from where, how chosen), how it is done, what you will receive (the raw answers as well as the report), when, and whether the researcher may sell it to others. A small honest sample of the right people is worth more than a large one of the wrong; a survey of friends only tells you what friends say. What they find is their word and the data they collected; it is not a guarantee of sales, and the decision stays yours. Kept apart from Advising someone on their work (someone who knows your trade tells you what to do); Selling what you know before it is read (the seller of findings, not you who commission them); and Checking market prices (you look up what things are going for yourself). It usually starts when you plan a new product or a new place, a price change worries you, or an investor or a bank asks for numbers.

examples.card: Ask a question worth buying.
examples.filled: You are weighing a vegan version of your pie. Pay a researcher £900 to ask 150 of your customers whether they would buy it?

examples.card: Ask for the raw answers.
examples.filled: The report says 62% would try your sauce but gives no table. Ask for the answers and the list of who was asked?

examples.card: Run a taste test.
examples.filled: Three new flavours of granola could go to market. Pay a lab to test them with 40 shoppers, blind?

examples.card: Buy a market-size report.
examples.filled: A trade body sells a report on the size of the cold-pressed juice market in your country for ₹35,000. Buy it before you borrow?

you do this when: You commission a study of a market and the answers are findings that you decide from; it is not advice on what to do.
